current_roster.description: Purpose: The objective of this study is to assess right ventricular (RV) function in dogs at various stages of myxomatous mitral valve degeneration (MMVD). Background: Myxomatous mitral valve degeneration (MMVD) is the most common cardiovascular disorder of dogs and a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Current methods of prognostication in this disease are inadequate owing to functional and phenotypical heterogeneity of MMVD, breed-specific disease progression, and various trigger events that can precipitate decompensation. Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, assessed by 2-dimentional and 3-dimensional echocardiography, is a strong and independent predictor of outcome in people affected by MMVD. While RV function assessment methods have been described in normal dogs, RV function has yet to be investigated in dogs with MMVD. Inclusion: Dogs eligible to participate in this study must meet the following criteria: Have been diagnosed with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) Weigh less than 20 kilograms 5 years of age or older Not receiving any medications for treatment of their heart disease Have a normal arterial blood pressure, and Must be able to lay on his/her side for echocardiographic assessment. Exclusion: Dogs at risk for MMVD without structural heart disease (stage A) and dogs in refractory heart failure (stage D) will be excluded from the study. Dogs on cardiac medications are also excluded. Study Design: Dogs will be classified into 3 groups depending on their level of disease stage following the scale established by the ACVIM for MMVD in dogs (B1, B2 and C from the least to the most severe, respectively). All dogs will be evaluated using 2D and 3D echocardiography as well as thoracic radiography as a standard of care in dogs affected by MMVD. Client Compensation: The financial incentives provided will depend on the stage of the dogs heart disease. Classification of heart disease and the associated financial incentives are as follows: Stages B1 and B2 MMVD (e.g., dogs that are not in heart failure) the costs associated with medical chart generation, physical examination, echocardiographic assessment, Doppler blood pressure, and thoracic radiographs will be completely covered by the study ($450.25). Stage C MMVD (e.g., dogs that are in heart failure) the costs associated with the Cardiology Service consultation, echocardiographic assessment, Doppler blood pressure, and thoracic radiographs will be completely covered by the study ($485.25). Hospitalization, medications, and nursing care to treat heart failure are the responsibility of the client and not paid for by the study.Adverse events associated with the diagnostic testing are not likely to occur. However, if complications develop associated with the testing or sedation, the study will cover standard medical care to address such complications up to $1000.
current_roster.name: Dogs with heart valve disease

current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To determine if administering prednisone prior to surgery affects the factors used to define the grade of mast cell tumors, and thus potentially affects prognosis and treatment recommendations. Background Mast cell tumors are the most common malignant skin tumor in dogs. The prognosis is highly-dependent upon the tumor grade, which can only be determined by histopathology (biopsy). For low-grade tumors, complete surgical removal is curative. However, nearly 100% of dogs with high-grade tumors will succumb to their disease within 6 months to a year of diagnosis. Treatment with prednisone is an effective treatment as sole therapy. It is also used prior to surgery to shrink the tumor or as part of a chemotherapy protocol used in dogs with high-grade tumors. However, it is unknown how the use of prednisone prior to surgery affects the factors used to define the tumor grade, which has potential to impact the prognosis and recommended further treatment options. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED
current_roster.name: Effect of tumor-reducing prednisone on the staging of mast cell tumors in dogs

current_roster.description: Description: This study is to compare genetic and behavior information (by online survey) between human directed aggressive dogs and non-aggressive (to both humans and animals) dogs in 3 different breeds to see if potential genetic and/or biomarkers may be identified. Eligibility: Pure bred Labrador Retrievers, Beagles or Standard Poodles that are either affected dogs (human aggressive dogs) or control dogs (no aggression toward humans or animals) are eligible. Financial Incentive: no cost for collection of samples (blood). Blood collection can be also performed at the primary veterinarian office and shipped to us (cost for blood collection and shipping will be covered).
current_roster.name: Canine Aggression Study in Labrador Retriever, Beagle, and Standard Poodle

current_roster.description: Purpose: To evaluate canine stomach serosa microcirculation in patients undergoing anesthesia for routine spay andstomach tacking, and determine correlation between stomach serosal and cheek mucosal microcirculatory parameters. Background: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the microcirculation of the stomach and cheek in the apparently healthy dog. Many disease processes involve loss of the stomachs blood flow that can make the disease worse and contribute to death. Evaluation of the blood flow in these diseases may improve the treatment. However, to fully understand these diseases and the changes on blood flow, the normal blood flow must be determined. This study will involve evaluation of the blood flow of the cheek and stomach in the normal dog.There has been no research that has evaluated the microcirculation of the stomach. Although previous research has evaluated the normal microcirculation of the cheek, this study also aims to determine if the cheek microcirculation can act as surrogate for the stomach microcirculation. It will also measure blood flow with blood levels of lactate, a product that increases in the blood when there is decreased blood flow.While anesthetized for a routine spay and stomach tacking, the microcirculation of the cheek and the stomach will be evaluated with a machine that does not damage any tissue. This machine will identify red blood cells within the smallest blood vessels of the organs. Inclusion Criteria: Dogs must be undergoing routine spayandstomach tacking. Study Design: Dogs undergoing routine spayandstomach tacking will be treated based on standard of care, with the addition of microcirculatory imaging of the buccal mucosa and gastric serosa using sidestream dark field microscopy during surgery Client Compensation: The study covers the cost of laboratory tests associated with the study and thirty minutes of general anesthesia. Client Cost: The client will be responsible for all costs associated with the surgical procedure, postoperative care and any complications that could arise.
current_roster.name: Stomach and cheek microcirculation in Dogs

current_roster.description: Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disorder in the world estimated to affect approximately 27 million adults and over 14 million dogs in the US. Despite this high frequency in people and animals, the ideal treatment of OA is still unclear. While many treatment options are available, there is a lack of treatment options that offer pain relief and improve quality of life without the risk of adverse effects. Even when available pain medications are provided, more than half of the adults with knee OA in one study showed inadequate pain relief with such treatment. Hence, there is a clear need for safe, non-invasive, and effective treatments for OA. Acupuncture has been shown to have beneficial effects for the treatment of pain associated with OA in people and dogs. However, the benefits are generally small and short-term with a large amount potentially being attributable to placebo effects. While a caregiver placebo effect exists in dogs, objective gait analysis provides unbiased outcome measures in canines with OA. The only study using objective outcome measures after acupuncture in dogs did not show significant improvement of objective outcome parameters, however, only 9 dogs were used in this study. Further evaluation of acupuncture in dogs is imperative to evaluate whether this treatment is beneficial in dogs, to provide baseline data for future research and allow for evaluation of the indications and potential modifications of acupuncture techniques. We hypothesize that acupuncture will result in improvement of objective gait analysis, physical activity monitoring and validated client questionnaires.
current_roster.name: Does acupuncture help to treat pain associated with arthritis in dogs?

current_roster.description: Purpose: To evaluate the gastric serosal microcirculation in canine patients with naturally occurring GDV and to determine if buccal mucosa microcirculation or systemic parameters may serve as a surrogate, and compare gastric microcirculatory assessment to intra-operative determination of tissue viability. Background: Many disease processes involve loss of the stomachs blood flow which can make the disease worse and contribute to death. Evaluation of the blood flow in these diseases may improve the treatment. One such disease process is gastric dilatation volvulus. This disease occurs when the stomach fills with air and twists on its axis, trapping gas and causing great stretching of the stomach wall. This stretching leads to loss of blood flow and possible death of the tissues. This study will involve evaluation of the blood flow of the cheek and stomach in dogs with gastric dilatation volvulus. There has been no research that has evaluated the microcirculation of the stomach or cheek in this disease state. It will also measure blood flow with blood levels of lactate, a product that increases in the blood when there is decreased blood flow, and amount of tissue oxygen. While anesthetized for surgical correction of this disease process, the microcirculation of the cheek and the stomach will be evaluated with a machine that does not damage any tissue.This machine will identify red blood cells within the smallest blood vessels of the organs. Inclusion Criteria: Canine patients with naturally occurring gastric dilation volvulus (GDV) Study Design: The patients will have a Microscan performed on the stomach. This involves a handheld device that will be positioned gently on the surface of the stomach using a sterile probe cover. Prior to surgery, three-twenty second videos of the cheek microcirculation will be obtained. Once in the abdominal cavity and before the stomach is rotated, three-twenty second videos of the stomach microcirculation will be obtained. This will be repeated for the cheek at the level of the carnassial tooth. After the stomach is rotated, three-twenty second videos of the stomach microcirculation will be obtained. It will measure blood flow with blood levels of lactate, a product that increases in the blood when there is decreased blood flow, and amount of tissue oxygen. The machine will identify red blood cells within the smallest blood vessels of the organs Client Compensation: Laboratory tests necessary for study data- $111 covered by the study One hour of general anesthesia- $40 covered by the study Client Cost: Any charges associated with the surgical procedures, postoperative care and any complications from the anesthesia or surgical procedures
current_roster.name: Dogs with Stomach Torsion (Gastric Dilatation-Volvulus)

current_roster.description: Brief Explanation of Study: Diabetic cats usually require insulin injection to survive although after a period of treatment with insulin they sometimes recover enough and are able to survive without it (i.e. they experience clinical remission). However, the disease process that causes diabetes is still present and most cats that go into remission eventually relapse and become dependent again on insulin injections. Exenatide extended-release (Bydureon) is the first drug to be FDA approved as a once-weekly injection for the treatment of diabetes in people. Exenatide mimics the action of GLP-1, a hormone that augments secretion of insulin from the pancreas in response to elevations in blood sugar levels. Exenatide also enhances the ability of cells that produce insulin to withstand damage caused by disease and increases their chances of survival. It also simulates their growth and proliferation. As such, exenatide has the potential to treat the underlying disease process that leads to diabetes and maintain the cat in a state of clinical remission. We recently tested the effects of Bydureon in healthy cats, finding that Bydureon improves the control of blood sugar for more than 4 weeks after a single injection with no apparent side effects. Here we will compare the effect of Bydureon and placebo in diabetic cats in remission. All cats will receive an injection (of Bydureon or placebo) once every month for 12 months or less if their diabetes recurs. At each monthly recheck, a thorough history will be obtained, a physical exam performed, and blood glucose concentrations measured. Serum fructosamine concentrations will be measured if the blood glucose is high (>180 mg/dl), if clinical signs of diabetes are noted by the owners, or if significant weight loss is recorded. If serum fructosamine is high the cat will be considered out of remission. All cats will be fed a high protein, low carbohydrate diet throughout the study diet (dry or canned; meal fed or ad lib). Concurrent diseases will be treated as needed with standard protocols. Patients will be withdrawn from study if owners do not comply with the study protocol, if excessive weight loss occurs (>2% per week), if the cats body condition score is below ideal, if the cats appetite is persistently decreased or if any other adverse events that may be associated with drug administration are noted. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the benefit of Bydureon for maintaining diabetic cats in remission (in an insulin-independent state). What qualifies my cat for enrollment in this in this trial? To be eligible for participation in this study: 1. Your cat must be a diagnosed diabetic with a recent onset of remission according to the following criteria: Previous diagnosis of diabetes mellitus based on clinical signs and a high serum fructosamine Treated with insulin (any type) for at least 2 weeks. Has not required insulin treatment for at least 4 weeks but no more than 12 weeks Has no current evidence of diabetes relapse (normal serum fructosamine and no clinical signs such as increased drinking, urination or appetite) 2. Your cat must be routinely fed a diabetic diet (a high protein, low carbohydrate diet such as Hills m/d, Purina DM etc.). 3. Your cat must be in good body condition (cannot be under-weight). 4. Cats that have the following are NOT eligible to participate: Recent administration (previous 2 months) of oral hypoglycemic agents Significant concurrent disease (any disease that may require exogenous steroid administration, reduce life-expectancy to <12 months or require intensive management, e.g. gastrointestinal, pulmonary, cardiac, hepatic, neoplastic, or renal disorders "CKD IRIS Stage 3 or higher") Overt evidence of peripheral neuropathy (plantigrade stance, inability to jump). Overt evidence of acromegaly Untreated for hyperthyroidism. Cats will not be excluded if have controlled hyperthyroidism or are receiving methimazole and/or ACE-inhibitors. 5. You must agree to return with your cat for rechecks after the initial visit once a month (every 27-32 days). These rechecks will include:An injection of either placebo (sterile saline) or BydureonA complete physical exam and history taking What does enrolling my cat in this clinical trial involve? The study duration is 1 year (12 month). Before entering the study we will draw blood and urine from your cat to screen for concurrent diseases. Your cat will then be allocated randomly into one of the two treatment group: Bydureon or placebo. Because this is a blinded study (i.e. you are should not be aware to which group your cat is allocated) and because the syringes used to inject the two treatments are visibly different, your cat will receive all injections while you are not present. After receiving the injection we will schedule your next recheck for the next month (in 27-32 days).In each subsequent recheck, a blood sample will be drawn from your cat and blood glucose will be measured. If high, a serum fructosamine will be measured as well. If the serum fructosamine is high or if your cat has been showing signs consistent with diabetes since the last recheck (increased drinking, urination, appetite, etc.) your cat will be considered out of remission and will not continue in the trial. Resuming insulin therapy at that time will be considered and discussed with you and with your referring veterinarian.Throughout the duration of the study, decisions regarding your cats health will be made in consultation with your regular veterinarian as usual. Those decisions shall not and will not be affected by participation in the study. Client Compensation They study will pay for one third of the cost of the first office visit as well the full cost of screening tests (including urinalysis and blood tests CBC, Chem, T4, fPLI and IGF-1). All drug expenses (12 months worth of Exenatide-ER injections, roughly equivalent to $1500) and all follow-up rechecks (including office visits, blood glucose measurements and fructosamine concentrations) will be covered by the study.
current_roster.name: Keeping diabetic cats in remission (Off insulin)

current_roster.description: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to better understand the role of genes in the development of immune-mediated diseases. Additionally, we hope to find similarities among different immune-mediated diseases that may point to common causes. Background: Immune-mediated diseases in dogs and cats are common, and may contribute to significant medical problems and premature death. We are recruiting dogs with primary IMHA, ITP, Addison s disease, and IMPA from a number of different veterinary teaching institutions. We will use these DNA samples (along with the associated phenotypic information) to conduct a genome-wide association study (GWAS) for each disease. Samples will be sent as batches to North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine for targeted re-sequencing of genomic regions with single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNPs) that strongly discriminate between affected and unaffected animals. We believe that our analysis may uncover certain SNPs or haplotypes that can predict patient outcomes and response to therapy. It is our hope that by obtaining a better understanding of the pathways that cause immune-mediated diseases in dogs, more targeted therapies can be employed that lead to better outcomes in our patients. Inclusion Criteria: To qualify for enrollment in this study, dogs must have: IMHA ITP Addisons Disease IMPA Study Design: We will need to take a small blood sample from your dog or cat to evaluate his or her genetic makeup. During this same blood draw, we may also collect two additional vials of blood to aid in the diagnosis of your pets condition. Client Compensation: All costs associated with the blood are covered by the study. Client Cost: The client is responsible for all costs associated with the dog's care at OSU that are not part of this study.
current_roster.name: Genetic basis of two immune-mediated diseases in dogs

current_roster.description: Overall survival in dogs with osteosarcoma is dismal. Developing an osteosarcoma cancer vaccine holds promise as an adjunct treatment to surgery and chemotherapy. In previous studies ofnormal dogs and dogs withmelanoma we showed thatthe vaccine causesa measureable immune response in is associated with increase insurvival. We propose to vaccinate 20 dogs with osteosarcoma. The dogs will be vaccinated monthly for 4 treatments and then monitored every 3-6months for life or until lost to follow up. The outcome of this study will help us understand the immune process associated with cancer vaccines for osteosarcoma and hopefully improve survival. This study covers the cost of the vaccines only. Staging, surgery, and chemotherapy costs are the responsibility of the owner.
current_roster.name: Vaccine for Dogs with Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine outcomes associated with partial forelimb amputation and prosthetics in canine patients. Dogs with pathology of the lower forelimb (to the level of the wrist) that require a limb amputation may be eligible for enrollment in this study. Participation in this study requires several weekly rechecks followed by monthly recheck visits for the first six months, a single recheck at nine months, and a single recheck at 12 months. Your dog will be required to wear an activity-monitoring collar and we will ask you to fill out several questionnaires. The study requires you to pay the cost of a regular amputation ($2,000), however, all additional and subsequent costs related to the study will be covered by the research fund. Additional costs covered by the study include the extra cost of the partial amputation surgery, the prosthetic device, and all rechecks and aftercare associated with the prosthetic device for the duration of the study. We hypothesize that prosthetic limb use can be documented via daily activity counts on a prosthesis-mounted Actical monitor and owner-based wearing-log and prosthesis use will improve continuously over a 12 month period of time. We also hypothesize that gait will normalize over time in the partial limb amputation group based on objective gait analysis.
current_roster.name: Are prosthetics a feasible option for dogs?

current_roster.description: Description: A study to compare behavioral and physiological responses to identify the dogs at risk of social anxiety (both home and an exam room environment). Eligibility: Clinically healthy dogs that must be neutered/spayed and between the age of 1-13 years old can participate the study. Owner's compliance to complete online survey, to video tape at least 20 minutes of the dog during their absence and to collect saliva samples at home. Financial Incentive: no cost for collection of samples. Primary Investigator: Dr. Niwako Ogata
current_roster.name: Behavioral and Physiological Responses in Dogs Under Social Anxiety

current_roster.description: Calcium oxalate (CaOx) urinary stones are a common and painful health problem for dogs. Medical treatment is ineffective, and stone removal is required for cure. Recurrence rates are high, and the efficacy of current preventative interventions is low. There is an inherited component to CaOx stone risk with strong breed predispositions. We performed genetic studies in two highly predisposed breeds, the Miniature Schnauzer and the Bichon Frise, and identified chromosomal regions and mutations significantly associated with stone risk. We are now working to critically validate the association of the regions and specific mutations with CaOx stone risk in independent and larger study populations, including other breeds than those initially studied.
current_roster.name: Genetic mutations imparting risk for calcium oxalate urinary stones in dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to determine how amino acid status and markers of inflammation are affected in dogs with PLN. We will evaluate plasma amino acid concentrations and markers of inflammation "C-reactive protein (CRP); tumor-necrosis factor- (TNF- ); interleukin-6 (IL-6)" in order to then develop novel medical and dietary therapeutic strategies for dogs with PLN. Background: Protein-losing nephropathy (PLN) is a common disease in dogs and can be difficult to treat. Although nutritional therapy is one of the main components of managing this disease, optimizing nutrition is extremely challenging. Dietary protein restriction is recommended to reduce proteinuria. However, at the same time, these dogs have accelerated loss of lean body mass and also may have alterations in amino acids. Additionally, inflammation has been shown to be inversely correlated with amino acid status in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD). All of these factors can contribute to loss of lean body mass and subsequent harmful effects on strength, immune function, morbidity and mortality. An optimal nutritional approach would reduce dietary protein enough to decrease proteinuria without contributing to lean body mass loss. Our hypothesis is that dog with PLN will have altered amino acid profiles and that this will be correlated with increased inflammation as compared to healthy control dogs.The ultimate goal of this study is to determine if we can better optimize nutritional management of PLN in dogs. In people with PLN, feeding low protein diets with concurrent supplementation of keto acids or essential amino acids can improve whole body protein status but minimize nitrogen load. It can also improve hypoalbuminemia and reduce proteinuria. Amino acid supplementation may have some anti-inflammatory properties that may benefit dogs with PLN. If we can identify consistent amino acid imbalances in dogs with PLN, we may be able to tailor nutritional management to improve overall survival and outcome. Inclusion Criteria: To qualify for enrollment in this study, dogs must have: Dog must have a clinical diagnosis and clinical parameters consistent with PLN +/- mild chronic kidney disease (CKD) creatinine < 2.0 mg/dl. Dog must be at least one year of age. Dog must not be diagnosed with any other disease known to affect urinary protein loss (eg, urinary tract infection, hyperadrenocorticism) or amino acid status (eg, protein-losing enteropathy). Study Design: Your dog will have blood and urine collected to evaluate a complete amino acid profile and a few markers of inflammation. Your dog will only need to have blood and urine collected at one time and the total amount of blood collected is considered very safe for dogs. Client Compensation: The study will cover the costs of a, CBC, chemistry profile, urinalysis, urine culture, urine protein:creatinine (UPC) ratio and blood pressure. Blood will be collected for future evaluation of amino acids and inflammatory markers. Client Cost: Owners are responsible for all other costs.
current_roster.name: Dogs with Protein-Losing Nephropathy (Kidney disease)

current_roster.description: Corneal endothelial dystrophy (CED) is a devastating disease in dogs that can result in blindness and severe ocular pain from secondary complications. The endothelial cells comprise the most inner aspect of the cornea and are responsible for maintaining a proper fluid balance. This function is critical to ensuring that the cornea remains transparent for vision. In many animals, including dogs, corneal endothelial cells have a very limited capacity to regenerate following injury. In canine patients with CED, the endothelial cells degenerate until the cells still remaining can no longer function properly. This results in swelling of the cornea (edema) which results in decreased vision as well as formation of small fluid-filled blisters (bullae) on the cornea which can rupture and cause ocular discomfort. There are palliative treatments such as hypertonic saline to decrease corneal bullae formation but the only definitive treatment for this condition is a corneal transplant (penetrating keratoplasty). Unfortunately, corneal transplants are rarely performed in canine patients with CED due to the expense of the surgery and follow-up care, relatively high risk of complications, and lack of appropriate donor tissue.Several dog breeds, including Boston Terriers, German Shorthaired Pointers and German Wirehaired Pointers, are seen more commonly for CED in comparison to other breeds. This observation suggests that this disease may have a genetic component. A similar condition called Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) exists in humans and several genes associated with FECD have been identified. We propose to identify the region of the dog genome associated with CED in Boston Terriers, German Shorthaired Pointers and German Wirehaired Pointers. In order to do this, we will perform thorough eye examinations and use non-invasive advanced imaging techniques to examine Boston Terriers, German Shorthaired Pointers and German Wirehaired Pointers with CED and age-matched control dogs. We will collect blood from these dogs to obtain DNA. The entire canine genome will be evaluated for an association with CED. This work will be used to identify the gene(s) responsible for this condition in Boston Terriers, German Shorthaired Pointers and German Wirehaired Pointers. The ultimate goal will be to develop a genetic test for CED in Boston Terriers, German Shorthaired Pointers and German Wirehaired Pointers and possibly other breeds, such as Chihuahuas and Dachshunds, with an increased risk of CED.
current_roster.name: Understanding Corneal Endothelial Dystrophy in Boston Terriers, German Shorthaired Pointers and German Wirehaired Pointers

current_roster.description: What is osteoarthritis? Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive degenerative disease of the joints. The body parts making up the joint become worn out and can be swollen, stiff, and painful. Osteoarthritis is a common condition in dogs. Signs of osteoarthritis often develop slowly. Dogs may develop increased stiffness, especially after rest, or during cold weather. Dogs with osteoarthritis pain may become less active during play, during walks, when going up or down stairs, or jumping. These can be signs of osteoarthritis, and can reduce the quality of your pet's life. Objective of the clinical trial: The objective of this study is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of two investigational drugs in dogs diagnosed with pain due to osteoarthritis of joint(s) of the legs (shoulder, elbow, hip, and knee). What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial, your dog must have: Diagnosis of pain due to osteoarthritis of joint(s) in hind and/or forelimb(s). At least one joint must be affected. Dogs at least two years of age and weighting between 33-110 pounds (15-50kg) at visit 1. Generally healthy dogs with no evidence of other serious chronic disease. Owner must be able and willing to comply with the visit schedule, dosing instructions and other responsibilities during the study. Must have been on the same diet for at least one month before visit 1, and remain on same diet throughout study. Other specific inclusion and exclusion criteria will be used to determine eligibility for enrollment. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? If your dog qualifies for the study, and you agree to participate, your dog will be randomly assigned to one of four treatment groups.You will be required to administer study medication twice daily for approximately 14 days, as capsules that are given to the dog by mouth. Each dog will receive, either an investigational drug, carprofen (a traditional non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or a placebo.Treatment groups will be is randomly assigned. Neither you, nor the veterinarian, will know your dog's treatment group. Client Compensation: All study proceduresare provided free of charge, including: Thorough orthopedic examination Required radiographs (and associated sedatives if needed) Office visits Electrocardiogram Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, chemistry profile, heartworm test, urinalysis and fecal parasite evaluation . In return for your dogs enrollment and your participation in the study, you will be eligible to receive a $150 Visa gift card provided your dog is not withdrawn due to non-compliance and you complete the study. If your dog is withdrawn due to other factors, you would be compensated for the portion for the study you did complete.
current_roster.name: Dogs with osteoarthritis

current_roster.description: Hypothesis and aims: In this exploratory study, we aim to investigate the preliminary safety of intravenous mesenchymal stem cell administration in Boxer dogs with ARVC. We also aim to generate pilot data on the potential effects of MSC administration on arrhythmia frequency, echocardiographic measures, and selected biomarkers of inflammation and cardiac remodeling that may be used to obtain funding for a larger scale clinical trial. We hypothesize that IV MSC administration will be safe and may lead to improvements in cardiac function. Study design: Client-owned Boxers with ARVC of any sex and >1 year of age will be recruited for this study. At the first screening visit a physical examination, 6-lead ECG, echocardiogram, and 24-hour Holter monitor will be performed. Eight ml of blood will be collected via jugular venipuncture for measurement of baseline CBC and serum chemistry profile and genetic testing for the striatin mutation. Dogs will be fasted for at least 8 hours prior to venipuncture. Twelve dogs that meet the inclusion criteria will be randomized into 3 groups (placebo, low dose MSC, and high dose MSC, respectively) via computer randomization. The attending cardiologist and pet owners will be blinded to the type of injection given. Administration of antiarrhythmics or other cardiac medications deemed necessary by each dogs clinical condition will continue throughout the study; however all dogs will have been on a stable medication regimen for at least 2 weeks prior to the first MSC injection. A total of 2 injections will be administered to each dog, separated by a 2 week interval. Each dog will return within 1 month following the screening visit for the first IV injection of MSC or placebo. Dogs in the low-dose MSC arm will receive a dose of 2106 cells/kg with each injection while dogs in the high dose arm will receive 5106 cells/kg each time. Dogs in the placebo arm will receive vehicle (1% autologous serum) injections at the same interval. Prior to the first injection, the patient will be fitted with an in-house continuous ECG (telemetry) unit to allow for real-time safety monitoring of the cardiac rhythm during and after the injection. An IV catheter will be placed and 10 ml of blood will be collected for baseline measurement of selected biomarkers of inflammation and cardiac remodeling. Dogs will remain in the hospital for continuous ECG and clinical monitoring for at least 4 hours after receiving each injection. Heart rate and rhythm and respiratory rate will be monitored hourly during this period. Blood pressure, body temperature, and cardiac troponin-I (cTnI) will be repeated before and after 4 hours of each MSC injection. Two weeks later, the dogs will return for an additional IV injection of same-dose MSC or placebo. Sixteen ml of blood will be collected during this visit for a CBC, serum chemistry profile and measurement of inflammatory biomarkers. The dogs will be monitored for any adverse effects for 4-6 hours in the same manner following this injection, and a 24-hour Holter monitor will be placed at the time of hospital discharge. Three months following the first injection the dogs will again return for a recheck Holter monitor, CBC and chemistry profile. An exam, echocardiogram, ECG, Holter monitor, CBC, chemistry profile and biomarker measurement will be repeated at 6 months and any changes in antiarrhythmic therapy will be documented. The final recheck exam will take place 12 months from initial presentation; another echocardiogram, ECG and Holter monitor will be performed at this time. These patients will continue to be monitored by the Tufts cardiology service longitudinally for continued management of their cardiac disease whenever possible following termination of the study. Endpoints: The primary objective of the study is safety and feasibility of MSC administration. The primary study end-points are Holter arrhythmia frequency, clinical signs, survival, and serial assessment of CBC and chemistry profile. The secondary endpoints to measure efficacy of the treatment are changes in certain echocardiographic measurements of cardiac function and biomarker levels. Holter arrhythmia frequency will also be assesses in this regard for any improvements in arrhythmia frequency or complexity.
current_roster.name: Heart Disease in Boxers

visible_sc_items.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Traumatic Radius-Ulna fractures require surgical treatment in order to restore normal function and limit the occurrence of complications such as non-union and mal-union. Classically, these fractures have been repaired with bone plates applied through open surgical approach that allows direct visualization of the fragments. This conventional osteosynthesis (Open reduction and internal fixation ORIF) approach has proven to be efficient in many cases and is currently the standard of care in the treatment of radius-ulna fractures in small animals. However, CO has been associated with complications that include infection, delayed union (slow healing rate) and implant failure. A newer approach, known as minimally invasive osteosynthesis (MIO), has been devised in an attempt to reduce complications and improve healing rates but only limited information is available at this point on the benefits and limitation of MIO techniques. Objective of the trial: The purpose of our study is to compare both surgical techniques prospectively to determine if one technique should be recommended over the other. The surgery will be performed by a board certified orthopedic surgeon. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To qualify for enrollment in this study, dogs must have: Dog must be suffering from a traumatic Radius-Ulna fracture What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will be assigned to one of the two study groups. The assignment will be randomized since there is no evidence of superiority from either technique in the treatment of radius-ulna fractures. The surgery will be performed by a board certified orthopedic surgeon.After surgery, you will be required to come back to OSU for follow-up examinations. The first recheck will be scheduled at three weeks post operatively. At that time and for each subsequent recheck, we will perform a lameness evaluation followed by a radiographic assessment of healing. The radiographs will be taken under sedation to minimize your dog discomfort during the examination and guarantee images quality. Further rechecks will be scheduled every three weeks until complete healing is observed which typically takes 6-9 weeks. Costs associated with recheck examinations will be covered by the study fund. A final recheck, also covered by the study, will be scheduled at 6 months postoperatively. This recheck is necessary to ensure that no complication occurs long term, that all implants remain in place, and that the bone remodels appropriately. Client Compensation: A $300 incentive payment will be applied to your overall bill if all rechecks were performed on time. Costs associated with recheck examinations will be covered by the study fund.
current_roster.name: Large dogs with forelimb fractures

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Canine brachycephalic airway syndrome (BAS) is a disease of dogs with a compressed nose and face such as that seen with English bulldogs. Currently, clinical evaluation of the dog with BAS involves direct visualization of the external nose and back of the throat with surgical intervention aiming to resect obstructive tissue. Little attention is given to the effect of excessive tissue within the nasal cavity itself, even though airway obstruction is most severe within the nasal cavity. The overall prognosis for surgery is good; however, some dogs respond well to surgery and others have little clinical improvement.There is no non-invasive method available in veterinary medicine to objectively assess if a reduction in airflow resistance is accomplished by current surgical techniques. Objective of the trial: The aim of this pilot study is to evaluate a novel computed tomography (CT)-based quantitative index of airflow resistance in brachycephalic dogs before and after surgical intervention. English bulldogs over the age of 8 months of age with BAS severe enough to warrant surgery will be considered for this clinical trial.
current_roster.name: Airflow resistance in English Bulldogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: Conventional chemotherapy protocols typically include one or sometimes multiple chemotherapeutic agents, that are directly toxic to the cancer cells, administered at maximally tolerated doses and intervals. Newer metronomic (low-dose continuous) chemotherapy protocols exert their anti-cancer activity differently, impacting the tumor microenvironment, angiogenesis and immune system. Furthermore, the mechanisms of acquired resistance to chemotherapy seem different when comparing high-dose conventional chemotherapeutic agents and metronomic agents. This is all strong evidence to support a combined treatment regimen.Toceranib phosphate ( Palladia ) was the first veterinary anti-cancer agent to obtain FDA approval based on demonstrable safety and efficacy in the treatment of canine mast cell tumors. Toceranib has subsequently demonstrated benefit in the treatment of numerous canine malignancies. Toceranib has direct anti-cancer, as well as anti-angiogenic activity, and recent research suggests a role in immune system modulation. Previous studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison have clearly demonstrated that toceranib can be safely administered in combination with piroxicam, resulting in antitumor responses in canine carcinomas and sarcomas, in combination with CCNU, and doxorubicin, and vinblastine resulting in additive and synergistic effects in canine mast cell disease. Objective: The primary purpose of this study is to establish the safety and maximum tolerated dose of carboplatin when administered in combination with toceranib ( Palladia ) in dogs with malignant tumors. The secondary objective of this study is to demonstrate the efficacy/clinical benefit of this chemotherapeutic combination protocol in treating dogs with malignant tumors. What does enrollment into this trial involve? All dogs enrolled in this study will receive toceranib administered by mouth every other day for the duration of the study, and carboplatin administered intravenously every 21 days for a total of four treatments. Blood and urine samples will be collected at baseline, immediately prior to each subsequent dose of carboplatin, and 7, 14, and 21 days post-each dose of carboplatin. Imaging studies will be required for those patients with internal tumors only measurable with x-ray or ultrasound at least twice, but up to four times, during the study.After study day 84 (or sooner if your dog is removed from this study for any reason), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional and / or ongoing treatment options with you as the dogs owner and primary care giver. Client Compensation: The cost of the toceranib phosphate ( Palladia ) and carboplatin will be paid for by the study. Also covered will be the required recheck appointments, monitoring blood tests, urine tests, blood pressure evaluations and any imaging studies deemed necessary by the clinician. Treatment required for unanticipated side-effects will also be covered by the study up to $100. The owner is responsible for the costs of the initial appointment and the diagnostic work-up required prior to approval and enrollment in the study to ensure your dog is an appropriate study candidate, including the blood tests, urinalysis, blood pressure measurement and any imaging studies.
current_roster.name: Palladia®  and carboplatin combination chemotherapy in dogs with naturally-occurring cancer

current_roster.description: Hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer that commonly occurs in the spleen, liver, and the right side of the heart. The current standard of care for splenic hemangiosarcoma is surgical removal of the spleen followed by chemotherapy. Despite surgery and chemotherapy, the disease usually spreads and most dogs succumb to their disease within 6-12 months of diagnosis. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is a growth factor that may contribute to the spread and growth of hemangiosarcoma. In this clinical trial, we will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of an antibody therapy designed to inhibit VEGF and delay or prevent spread of the disease after surgery.
current_roster.name: Safety and efficacy of antibody therapy for dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description: Hypothesis: Four intra-lesional injections of 20 x 106WJ-MSC to dogs with canine perianal fistulas is safe and reduces lesion dimensions, clinical severity and the dose of cyclosporine necessary to maintain the disease under remission. Type and cha racteristics of the study: This is a randomized controlled double b lind study, whereby the owners and interventionist and Pl (Lluis Ferrer) and Dermatology Service associates (faculty, staff, students) are unaware of group assignment; the co Investigator (A Hoffman) and laboratory personnel that manufacture the WJ-MSC (Dawn Meola) will be aware of treatment status and responsible for randomization and recording these data. Protocol: A full physical examination, complete blood count, and serum biochemistry will be evaluated and eligibility for the trial determined. Dogs will remain on the same cyclosporine dose for at least 30 days after starting treatment with WJ-MSC. On day 0, the perianal lesions will be recorded (measured and photographed) , the dogs will undergo sedation and Colonic biopsies will be taken by a board-certified internist (Dr. Sarah Crain) during the same sedation protocol used for debriding and treating peri-anal fistulas. Biopsies will be taken during (and prior to) the first stem cell treatment. In total six endoscopic pinch biopsies will be extracted: Three from the macroscopically most inflamed mucosa, and three from the adjacent non- inflamed mucosa. If there are no discrete areas of inflammation, representative samples will be taken from throughout the section of colon visualized. Samples will be obtained from the sigmoid colon. Two biopsies from the inflamed mucosa and two biopsies from the non-inflamed mucosa will be destined to RNA extraction and the other 2 for histopathology analysis and then and receive WJ-MSC "2 million WJ-MSC/mL, total volume 10 ml; total dose 20 million cells per dog distributed over all lesions" will be injected subcutaneously around the opening of fistulas , into fistula lumens, and into the walls of the fistula (where feasible)" . After the injection of the WJ-MSC, the fistula openings will be sealed with fibrin (EviCell, Ethicon,-4ml" and the patients' sedation will be reversed with atipamezole (0.2 mg/kg, J M). This procedure will be repeated at 2, 4, and 8 weeks after the initial injection. The patients will be examined prior to each injection, and at 3 and 6 months after day 0. At baseline (day 0) and at 1, 3, and 6 months after day O a CBC and serum chemistry will be repeated. The number, extension and depth of the perianal fistulas will be measured and photographed at each time point shown (in table). After first month (T2) the cyclosporine dose will be adjusted to reach the lowest dose that maintains the disease under remission (at T2, T3, T4 and Ts). The daily cyclosporine dose (mg/kg) of the last month of the study will be compared with the daily dose at the beginning of the study for each patient. Also, the mean cyclosporine dose at the end of the study of both groups will be statistically compared.
current_roster.name: Stem Cell treatment of Canine anal fistulas

current_roster.description: Maropitant is a well established anti-emetic in dogs that has also been shown to have analgesic (i.e. pain relieving) effects in anesthetized dogs. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of this medication as a post-operative add-on analgesic following a hemilaminectomy surgery, to be used in combination with traditional opioids, as part of a multimodal pain management approach. This study will compare the analgesic efficacy of maropitant in comparison to the traditionally administered medication gabapentin, to determine whether the former reduces the need for opioid analgesics and the number of days of hospitalization.
current_roster.name: Determining if a new add-on medication to standard therapy improves pain levels in dogs post-hemilaminectomy surgery

current_roster.description: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a common progressive disease condition in elderly cats with no known cause and no definitive cure other than kidney transplantation. Therefore, novel and effective therapeutic options are highly desired for treating this disease in cats. Administration of mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) has been shown to improve kidney function in rodent models of CKD, in part by reducing inflammation and scarring in the kidney. CKD in cats is characterized by inflammation and scarring within the kidney, and thus treatment with MSC might improve kidney function. Previous studies in cats have demonstrated that systemic intravenous administration (in a leg vein) of cultured MSC harvested from donor cats and administered to cats with CKD is safe and results in variable improvement in kidney function. However results have not been as striking as those seen in rodent models. When MSC are administered intravenously the entire dose likely does not reach the kidney and therefore alternative methods of more effective administration should be assessed. Delivery via the artery going into the kidney using minimally-invasive image guided interventional radiologic techniques is particularly advantageous because it bypasses the initial uptake of the stem cells by the lungs and other organs and delivers a larger number of cells directly to the diseased kidney. The aim of the proposed study is to assess the safety and efficacy of MSC harvested from the fat of donor cats and administered directly into the kidney artery using minimally-invasive image guided interventional radiologic techniques
current_roster.name: Assessment of Renal Intra-arterial Administration of Allogeneic Mesenchymal Stem Cells for the Treatment of Feline Chronic Kidney

current_roster.description: This protocol is to study the use of rabacfosadine (Tanovea) in the treatment of dogs with lymphoma (LSA), lymphoid leukemia (LL), or multiple myeloma (MM). This study will evaluate the safety and efficacy of Tanovea when used in dogs with these cancers. Prior treatment for these cancers is acceptable but not required.This will be a single-arm, open-label, clinical trial. Doses are based on preclinical toxicology/pharmacology and prior clinical information. Dogs will receive rabacfosadine every 21 days for up to 5 cycles. This is considered a compassionate use trial, and soVetDC is providing rabacfosadine at no cost to owners. Partial funding is provided to cover some of the costs associated with recheck exam fees and some diagnostic testing.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs with Lymphoma, Multiple Myeloma and Lymphoid Leukemia

current_roster.description: This study is intended to provide an early proof-of-principal evaluation of the new stem cell vaccine technology in dogs with melanoma and its ability to induce anti-tumor immunity. Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a series of 8 immunizations over a 3-month period (4 weekly immunizations, followed by 4 bi-monthly immunizations). The vaccines will be administered under the skin over the flank (2 sites). For dogs that experience an objective tumor response, the vaccine will be made available for 3 additional monthly administrations (total of 6 months of treatment). Animals that develop aprogressive disease (increase in tumor volume by more than 50%), develop tumor-related adverse events, or develop any serious medical illnesses, will be removed from the study.Partial funding is available to help cover costs associated with study screening and examinations. Study patients will receive the study vaccine at no cost.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs with measurable oral melanoma

current_roster.description: The usual treatment of solid equine skin tumors is complete surgical removal. If complete surgical removal is not possible, the usual treatment is surgical debulking and treatment of any remaining tumor with cryotherapy, laser therapy, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy. The purpose of this study is to investigate the treatment effects of an anti-CD47 antibody treatment on the destruction of tumor cells. Equine skin tumor cells have been shown to overexpress the CD47 protein, which may be key in preventing the destruction of the tumor cells. Blocking the protective effect of CD47 using the anti-CD47 antibody will ideally encourage phagocytosis of the tumor by macrophages. We have shown thus far that the antibody treatment is safe. No serious adverse effects have occurred in the cases enrolled and treated - one case developed a transient anemia. Some cases have been treated with control treatments; enrolling more cases will give us better information - as we can include greater numbers of treated cases. We have also seen that some of the treated cases had at least a transient decrease in tumor size.
current_roster.name: Use of anti-CD47 antibodies as a treatment for equid skin tumors.

current_roster.description: Canine degenerative myelopathy (DM) is an inherited adult-onset neurodegenerative disease of dogs caused by a mutation in the superoxide dismutase 1 gene(SOD1) and thus is similar to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The purpose of this study is to evaluate a promising new drug as a treatment for DM with hopes to slow disease progression. There are no effective therapies for ALS. The discovery of SOD1 mutations as causative for a proportion of the inherited forms of ALS led to the generation of rodent SOD1 mutation models in the hope that these animal models would provide new therapeutics. Although the rodent ALS models have provided many advantages for the study ALS and therapeutics, such animal models have failed to accurately predict therapeutic responses in ALS patients. However, clinical similarities between the inherited SOD1-related ALS and the more prevalent ALS with no SOD1 mutation, and recent findings of SOD1 aggregates in tissues of sporadic ALS patients, suggest that further study of SOD1 still is relevant to all ALS. Canine degenerative myelopathy (DM) is an inherited, progressive adult-onset neurodegenerative disease that has many similarities to human ALS and potentially serves as an important novel model for therapy development. Recently, we found that an E40K missense mutation in SOD1 underlies most cases of canine DM. Similarities between the canine and human nervous systems and homogeneity of the DM phenotype will facilitate translation of therapies into ALS patients. Furthermore, dogs with DM offer a ready clinical population in which therapies can be evaluated in an environment closely mimicking human clinical trials. A promising therapeutic strategy using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that target SOD1 mRNA to suppress SOD1 protein was recently demonstrated in a rodent ALS model. The SOD1 ASO decreased amounts of SOD1 in neurons and slowed disease progression. Studies of canine DM, with its spontaneous SOD1 mutation, may yield data more relevant to human ALS and help advance SOD1 ASO clinical trials in ALS patients. Guided by supportive preliminary data, studies will be conducted to achieve the following Specific Aim 1)Evaluate the safety and preliminary therapeutic effects of intrathecally administered SOD1 ASO in DM-affected dogs. If canine DM is to serve as an effective disease model by which to evaluate ALS therapies, we must demonstrate therapeutic efficacy through a comparative approach using objective measures of disease progression that are shared across species.Electrodiagnostic testing, fluid evaluations andMRI studies are expected to serve as an ideal biomarkers for therapeutic translation in DM-affected dogs because the techniques are also performed in ALS patients. The proposed research is innovative because it focuses on a promising therapeutic approach in a naturally-occurring canine disease that is analogous to human ALS. It is anticipated that we will be able to develop an optimized protocol, with minimal side effects, for intrathecal administration of ASOs in dogs. The effects of this therapeutic intervention will be evaluated long-term in DM-affected dogs. We expect the infusion of SOD1 ASO in dogs with DM will slow disease progression. If successful, this model can be used to efficiently optimize future human clinical studies of ASO administration and other potential treatments. Dogs will be administered a canine specific SOD1 ASOthat will repress the production of the SOD1. The ASO has been tested in a preclinical setting for safety in dogs. The drug will be injected into the spinal fluid at the low lumbar region of the spinal cord. The study will be randomized and double blinded; meaning the investigator and the pet owner will not know whether the dog receives the drug. We will monitor clinical disease progression and evaluate cerebrospinal fluid and muscle and nerve function. These techniques have been used extensively on ALS patients in order to monitor and predict disease progression. We would like to use these same techniques on DM-affected dogs for monitoring disease progression and to evaluate for efficacy of the therapeutic.
current_roster.name: Development of a Therapy for Treatment of Canine Degenerative Myelopathy

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Recent studies indicate that a certain immune cells such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes play an important role in tumor metastasis in diseases such as osteosarcoma. Certain anti-tumor drugs, such as toceranib, have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib (PalladiaTM) is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib as well. In addition, we have discovered that the angiotensin receptor blocking (ARB) drug losartan also functions to block monocyte activity. In recent studies, we have also determined that treatment with the combination of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as toceranib, together with losartan exerts significantly greater antitumor activity than either drug alone.
current_roster.name: Reversal of Myeloid Cell Immune Suppression with a CCR2 Inhibitor Combined with a Myeloid Cell Depleting Agent for Treatment of Os

current_roster.description: To determine the pain relief from stereotactic radiation and the immune response to the therapy. Dogs are evaluated for inclusion in the study by undergoing a physical exam, laboratory tests and a CT scan under anesthesia. If accepted into the study, patients receive three TomoTherapy (radiation) treatments in one week. Patients return for recheck exams at 1, 2 & 4 weeks and 2 & 3 months after treatment. This includes an orthopedic exam and force-plate testing. The force plate test measures the amount of weight (force) a dog will put on each leg while walking across a plate in the floor. Blood samples are collected at each visit. Clients pay for the initial work-up to determine if their pet qualifies for the study. Radiation treatment and recheck exams are provided at no cost through a generous grant from the Puppy Up Foundation.This radiation protocol involves fewer visits to the hospital for radiation treatment and fewer episodes of anesthesia as compared to conventional radiation protocols. The new treatment may be more effective at providing pain relief and fighting the cancer. There is no cost for the radiation therapy or related follow-up exams.
current_roster.name: Stereotactic radiation and chemotherapy for pain relief and immune modulation

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of a cell-based therapy injected directly into the stifle (knee joint) of dogs with osteoarthritis. This study will assess whether pain is relieved and joint function is improved by the substance. Dogs will be randomly assigned to receive the study medication or a placebo, or be in a sham group. This study involves five visits to Penn Vet over the course of 2 months.
current_roster.name: A randomized placebo controlled blinded pilot study to assess a cell based therapy in canines with osteoarthritis

current_roster.description: This study is a pilot dose confirmation study to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of an intra-articular (into the joint) injection of a novel therapeutic for the control of pain associated with osteoarthritis. This study will involve six clinic visits over the course of six months as well as several telephone visits. Dogs will be randomly assigned to receive an injection of a novel therapeutic into the most affected elbow joint; or a sham treatment (no injection). This novel therapeutic targets and deactivates the nerves responsible for pain in the elbow joint. Eligibility: Dogs at least 1 year of age weighing at least 10kg (22lbs) Pain primarily in one elbow joint present for at least 3 months Not currently on pain medications, or able to washout from such medications for the duration of the study Additional eligibility criteria determined based on questionnaires and radiographs Costs of radiographs (x-rays) and routine blood work are covered by study. Compensation is provided for time and travel.
current_roster.name: A Study Evaluating an Injection for Dogs with Elbow Arthritis

current_roster.description: The primary objective of this study is to identify and characterize iris vasculature (arrangement of blood vessels in the eye) abnormalities present in diabetic canines, as compared to normal canines, using a camera adaptor via anterior segment angiography. Angiographic techniques are well established within physician based medicine; however its use is limited in veterinary medicine. It involves the injection of a fluorescent dye (sodium fluorescein;SF or indocyanine green;IG) into a vein. Following this injection, images of the ocular vasculature (arrangement of blood vessels in the eye) may be obtained using this camera adaptor highlighting the presence and distribution of the dye. A second objective of this study is to compare and contrast the diagnostic utility of SF and IG for detecting iris vasculature abnormalities in diabetic canines. Finally, we will correlate the prevalence, severity, and progression, of iridal (of the iris) abnormalities with glycemic control (fluctuation of the amount glucose in the blood) and duration of disease. We hypothesize that the iris vasculature of canines with diabetes mellitus will exhibit structural (i.e. leakage) and blood flow abnormalities (i.e. delayed perfusion) which have not been previously identified. Furthermore, we hypothesize iridal abnormalities will be more prevalent and severe in canines with a history of poor regulation and/or those with a greater duration of disease. Vascular abnormalities will be documented via anterior segment angiography (ASA) using an inexpensive camera adaptor system. Both SF and IG will be employed.
current_roster.name: Changes in the eye of the diabetic dog

current_roster.description: The VCIC is now enrolling dogs with a torn cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) for a clinical trial assessing the clinical outcome of dogs with this condition. Dogs will undergo a TPLO surgical procedure to repair the torn ligament and then will be followed for one year to assess arthritis development in that joint following surgery. Dogs enrolled will make seven (7) visits in one year to the University of Pennsylvania Veterinary Hospital.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of long term arthritis in dogs with CCL rupture

current_roster.description: Background: Currently, there is no well-defined study regarding the survival and quality of life for dogs with lymphoma treated with prednisone, an orally administered, inexpensive steroid, despite the drug's inclusion in almost every treatment protocol for lymphoma. Why prednisone? Chemotherapy for canine lymphoma is costly, time-consuming, and has a risk of serious complications. Prednisone is thought to improve quality of life and reduce lymph node size. But the benefit of this inexpensive, orally administered drug has not been formally studied. Purpose of Study: The Canine LYmPhoma Steriod Only (CALYPSO) is a multi-center study involving 100 dogs with high grade lymphoma from approximately 15 contributing veterinary schools and specialty practices.We are interested in determining the response to therapy, how long does it last, if certain types of lymphoma respond better than others to prednisone, and most importantly, how quality of life is improved. Does my dog qualify for the study? Participant dogs need a confirmed diagnosis of intermediate to high-grade lymphoma. Your veterinarian can send aspirates or tissue samples for analysis to the laboratory of her/his choice or we can do this for you at the hospital. Dogs with lymphoma in peripheral lymph nodes qualify for the study. Dogs with skin or gastrointestinal lymphoma are not eligible for the study.Dogs with lymphoma in the spleen and liver only without peripheral lymph node involvement are not eligible.Dogs receiving any chemotherapy or prednisone before they visit our hospital are not eligible. What happens during the study? On the first day, your dogs quality of life at home will be assessed by having you answer questions about how he/she is feeling. This questionnaire will be repeated on Day 7, Day 14, and then monthly thereafter.Someone will contact you at home and review the questions with you if you do not revisit the hospital. Because the response to prednisone may differ between dogs based on the type of lymphoma (T-cell or B-cell), a fine needle aspiration of a lymph node will be obtained at the beginning of the study so it can be sent to a lab for special staining. After routine lab tests and a thorough physical exam including lymph node measurements are completed, your dog will start taking prednisone daily by mouth at home.All dogs get the same dosage.
current_roster.name: Canine lymphoma treated with prednisone (steroid) only
