current_roster.description: Management of acute seizures is a common problem in dogs. Diazepam and midazolam are two benzodiazepines commonly used as first line medication in both hospital and home to treat acute seizure activity. Rectal diazepam in the dog is being used for many years for the treatment of emergency seizures within a hospital or mainly at home. In humans, many trials have been performed using intranasal midazolam for controlling acute seizures. The results have shown that intranasal midazolam appeared to have faster action compared to rectal diazepam in the treatment of seizure exacerbations and proved easier to administer with an overall satisfaction. However, effectiveness of intranasal midazolam for controlling status epilepticus has not yet been officially evaluated in dogs under clinical field conditions. Therefore, there is no published clinical evidence whether or not it is an effective method for controlling the acute seizures in dogs with acute seizures. This protocol may prove if an alternative method (i.e. intranasal midazolam) for controlling acute seizures is effective and convenient for the management of canine status epilepticus and if it can replace rectal diazepam for the at-home management of seizures by the owners. If so, intranasal administration could be then established as a routine method by the owners to control emergency seizures at-home (replacing the rectal diazepam) and maybe by the veterinarians at hospital in various situations (e.g. when no iv line is accessible, initial quick control of the seizures before administration of further drugs).
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the effectiveness of intranasal midazolam administered via a mucosal atomization device and rectal diazepam as first

current_roster.description: Penn Vet is currently enrolling dogs with clinical signs of Canine Chronic Enteropathy (CCE) in a clinical trial aiming to determine the composition of the microbiome (the naturally occurring bacteria) of the gastrointestinal tract before, during and after treatment. CCE is a common syndrome in dogs, resulting in clinical signs such as diarrhea, vomiting and weight loss. The duration and severity of these symptoms vary, as does response to treatment, suggesting that there are multiple forms and causes of this disease. Common causes include food sensitivity and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The microbiome--an ecosystem of bacteria living in the intestine--has been shown to be important in human inflammatory bowel disease. Understanding how these bacteria change in dogs being treated for CCE may lead to better diagnostics and treatments for inflammatory diseases in pets. Dogs enrolled in this study will receive the standard of care treatment for CCE for up to 8 weeks. During that time, stool samples will be collected in order to analyze the microbiome of the GI tract. The study requires a minimum of four visits to Penn Vet and the collection of stool samples at home.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs with chronic gastrointestinal upset

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study Osteosarcoma is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Even after surgical tumor removal and chemotherapy, the cancer often spreads (metastasizes) and dogs usually die of metastatic disease within an average of 12 months after diagnosis, despite aggressive therapy. However, interestingly, survival times have been shown to sometimes double in osteosarcoma patients who develop infections associated with surgical removal of the primary tumor. These infections may be capable of activating white blood cells such as monocytes to promote anti-tumor activity. The role of monocytes needs to be better understood in general in order to exploit their anti-tumor capabilities. Study Objective The purpose of this study is to characterize differences of monocytes between normal dogs, and osteosarcoma dogs. This will help us define changes that occur in monocytes of an osteosarcoma dog and enhance our understanding of the monocytes ability for tumor suppression. Our long-term goal is to harness the anti-tumor potential of monocytes to develop new therapies using these cells to increase survival in osteosarcoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? We are recruiting dogs in five different categories: 1.Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and have underwent limb amputation and full course of standard chemotherapy (no clinical trial dogs), one or more months after final chemo, no maximum amount of time. These dogs must be free of pulmonary metastasis. 2. Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and have underwent a limb-sparing surgery and have been diagnosed with a limb-spare associated infection. Samples that qualify for this category can be collected off-site and shipped to NCSU. This study will cover the cost of overnight shipping. 3. Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and not yet undergone treatment. These dogs can be enrolled at any time after diagnosis, just prior to treatment to include amputation. These dogs must be free of pulmonary metastasis. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign an informed consent for venipuncture. Blood will be drawn from each patient, either at time of diagnosis prior to commencement of any therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation) orafter definitive treatment (amputation/stereotactic radiation + chemotherapy) has been completed. This study requires only a one-time participation blood will be drawn during a single hospital visit. No other obligations will be required. Client Compensation Following determination of your dog's eligibility, costs associated with this study will be provided, to includea complete blood count. Client Contact Please contact Lyndy Harden,lbharden@ncsu.edu or Joanne_tuohy@ncsu.edu for more information about this study.
current_roster.name: Phenotypic characterization of peripheral blood monocytes in canine osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The goal of the TAHITI diabetes study is to determine whether an injected, plasmid-based therapy administered weekly for 12 weeks leads to reduced anti-insulin immune responses and improved clinical performance in dogs with Type-1 Diabetes (T1D) treated with human neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin as the standard of care. The concept behind this therapy is similar to allergy shots, aka allergic hyposensitization therapy, given for common allergens. In this case, we arehypo-sensitizingthe body to insulin such that the body tolerates insulin therapy better. This approach has been shown to be safe and to improve the clinical status of laboratory animals and human patients with type-1 diabetes. Results of this study will provide information to develop a therapy for both dogs and humans with this incurable, chronic autoimmune disease. Dogs are screened with an exam, 10-12 hr glucose curve, blood work and urine tests. Once enrolled, dogs are treated weekly for 12 weeks at the Veterinary Medical Center by the Clinical Investigation Center (CIC) staff with the investigational product. Owners keep a daily log at home. Dogs will receive two additional glucose curves (minimum) at week 12 and week 20. Costs of the study: The study will cover up to $250 of the costs for the initial screening visit, as well as the full cost of the experimental treatment and the recheck visits. To enroll or learn more about the study, please contact Andrea Eckert or Dr. Modiano (above).
current_roster.name: The TAHITI study: Tolerizing against human insulin in dogs with type-1 diabetes

current_roster.description: Although it is a relatively rare disease, pemphigus foliaceus (PF) is the most common form of pemphigus and probably the most common cutaneous autoimmune disease in the dog. PF usually presents in one of two forms, a mucocutaneous and encrusted pustular disease, with the latter form associated with systemic signs such as fever or lethargy. Most commonly affected areas include the dorsal muzzle, nasal planum, pinnae, periorbital skin, and the paw pads, and a generalized and encrusted (often pruritic) dermatitis. Nasal planum and haired dorsal muzzle will typically be affected concurrently. BTKi drugs act by inhibiting the BTK kinase in non-T cell white blood cells, reducing downstream signaling from the B cell receptor, as well as the effects of FC?R (surface IgG receptor) on B and other non-T cell cell types. The effects of a BTKi on canine pemphigus foliaceus may not only add another medication that can be used to treat this disease, but also could be generalizable to human pemphigus foliaceous and pemphigus vulgaris due to the common mechanisms shared by these diseases.The goal of this study is to assess the efficacy and safety of a drug that is a Brutons Tyrosine Kinase inhibitor (BTKi) as a therapy for canine pemphigus foliaceus. Procedures: Procedures include a biopsy and several blood and urine collections over 20 weeks. There is evidence that a) this type of drug works in similar diseases in humans and b) it is a safe medication in dogs. This medication is given orally. Owner Responsibilities: We expect that participation in this clinical trial will last for 20 weeks. You will need to bring your dog in to scheduled appointments every week for the first month (except Week 3) and then every month after that for the next four (4) months. Additionally, you will need to give your dog the prescribed drug as instructed by the Dermatology Service at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital.
current_roster.name: Finding a New Treatment for Pemphigus Foliaceus

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study The purpose of this research is to compare two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for horses (flunixin and firocoxib). Flunixin is currently used in the management of colic patients, but a new medication that may have a higher safety profile (firocoxib, Equioxx) has become available on the equine veterinary market. Although firocoxib is presently labeled for use in horses for treating arthritis, we believe it may be useful for treating colic. What qualifies my horse for enrollment in this trial? To be considered ELIGIBLE for enrollment in the study, your horse must be admitted to the NCSU- Veterinary Health Center andundergo surgery for treatment of colic. In each case, the decision to administera non-steroidal anti-inflammatorydrug (NSAID) and duration of hospitalization will be dictated by the attending clinician based on the horses condition, the surgical procedure and the patients systemic status. What does enrolling my horse in this clinical trial involve? Your horse will undergo a comprehensive assessment to determine its eligibility for enrollment in this clinical trial, including a disclosure of its complete history, a physical examination, and initial blood work evaluation. If you agree to participate in this study and your horse is found eligible, the surgical procedures, drugs administered (other than the choice of NSAID), and postoperative care will be routine, and subject to the admitting clinicians discretion. Your horse will have blood collected at admission, 6-8-hours after NSAID administration, and at 24 and 48 hours. It is routine to perform these tests, except for the 48-hour collection, which will be paid for by the study. Your horse will receive one of the two NSAIDs as part of its recommended treatment while here at NCSU. The NSAID will be randomly chosen for each individual horse. The specific NSAID administered to your horse will not be known until the study is completed. ALL horses enrolled in this study will receive pain medication. Client Compensation If your horse is entered into the study, you will receive a discount of $400 off the cost of the initial colic examination ($650). Additional clinical trial blood tests will also be performed free of charge to you. All other medical costs will NOT be covered by this study Client Contact For more information regarding this study, please contact the NCSU Clinical Studies Core, Janet Bogan at 919-515-2633 orjrbogan@ncsu.edu.
current_roster.name: Flunixin or Firocoxib in Postoperative Colic Patients

current_roster.description: Description: The purpose of this study is to investigate whether an innovative tissue imaging technology, known as biodynamic imaging (BDI), can be used to predict the responsiveness of canine diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) to chemotherapy. We will also investigate whether BDI can select, from an array of available chemotherapy drugs, a single drug with best predicted efficacy against each dog's lymphoma at the time of relapse. Half of the dogs in the study will be randomly assigned to BDI-selected therapy, and half will be assigned to empiric therapy with lomustine. Dogs will be assessed by a clinician blinded as to the treatment group during the randomized part of the trial. Eligibility: Biopsy- confirmed DLBCL diagnosis of lymphoma No prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy, including prednisone Expected survival of at least four weeks Absence of other serious illness Adequate bone marrow function in order to receive chemotherapy Financial Incentive: Cost of biopsies and initial staging tests are paid for by the study. Owners' financial responsibility for chemotherapy treatments is capped at $50 per visit to Purdue. Pet owners are financially responsible for costs arising from medical management of treatment-related side effects, as well as other medical conditions not related to lymphoma. Primary Investigator: Dr. Michael Childress For more information on Oncology Clinical Investigations please visit their website at:http://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/
current_roster.name: Novel live tissue imaging technology to personalize therapy for dogs with lymphoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Michael Childress, DVM, MS, DACVIM, Professor, Comparative Oncology

current_roster.description: Obstruction of the rabbit GI tract is a devastating disease of pet rabbits and currently there is limited data to guide veterinarians towards the best treatment option for each case. The goal of this study is to build and strengthen our database on naturally occurring cases of gastrointestinal obstruction in pet rabbits in order to improve survival rates. By accumulating a larger amount of data on these cases we aim to better define the disease in our patients and determine if certain patients are better served with surgery, medical management, or a combination of the two.
current_roster.name: Determining the Best Treatment for Naturally Occurring Gastric Outflow Obstruction in Rabbits

current_roster.description: Purpose of the study: To evaluate a new medication for its effectiveness to alleviate pain following surgery Primary Eligibility Criteria: Systemically healthy dog presenting for surgery. No invasive procedures for 14 days. No procedures that would interfere with accurate pain assessment. No concurrent conditions that could interfere with pain assessment. No therapy with long acting glucocorticoids (2 weeks), sustained release opioids (7 days), topical anti-inflammatories (24 hours), other pain modulating drugs (24 hours). Must have a temperament that will allow repeated exams and assessments Study Protocol: Once the dog has been deemed eligible to participate, surgery is performed. During surgery pain medications will be administered, at surgical closure the study drug will be administered for post-surgical pain control. The dog is kept in the hospital for 72 hours following surgery to carry out pain assessments, and collect blood samples. If the dog is found to be uncomfortable with the new medication alone, other types of pain medications will be used to control pain. A clinical trials team member will contact the owner 4-7 days following discharge from the hospital to follow up. Owner Responsibilities: Costs associated with the surgery, care related to surgery, and other tests recommended by your pets clinician. Costs of treatment following discharge from the hospital after surgery. Financial Incentives: Study covers costs associated with the study drug, as well as hospitalization for 72 hours following surgery. $500.00 credit to VTH account, to be put towards the cost of surgery.

current_roster.description: Background - Recognition and alleviation of pain in oncology patients is essential for maintaining quality of life. Pain in these patients may be due to the cancer itself, a treatment modality being used (e.g., radiation or surgery), or a concurrent disease (e.g., osteoarthritis). To adequately control pain, a combination of more than one pain medication (NSAIDs, opioids, and adjuvant drugs such as gabapentin) is routinely required. Practitioners have at their disposal comprehensive sources of information on pain management. Most notably, the recently updated AAHA/AAFP Pain Management Guidelines for Dogs and Cats provide current recommendations for a multimodal approach to preempting and controlling pain. However, too much is often as deleterious (if not more) than not enough, in pain management! Aim - To put in adequacy pain management with pain mechanisms in cancerous canine patients, while establishing a pain mechanisms-based approach for analgesia in canine oncology. Design - Prospective, longitudinally open, baseline-controlled clinical trial. Methodology - Client-owned dogs affected by cancer (exclusion: lymphoma, mastocytoma, visceral hemangiosarcoma, and multiple myeloma) will be refereed to CVRS Oncology service for entering in an original study establishing pain mechanisms in cancerous dogs requiring palliative care. In addition to physical examination, clinical pathology tests, and global (visual analogue scale - VAS) pain assessment by the oncologist, global assessment by the owner (VAS, and canine health-related quality of life index - CHQLI), cinematic assessment (static stance weight-bearing and accelerometry), quantitative sensory tests (QST) will characterize the pain profile of the cancerous dog: * Primary punctate mechanical threshold, primary dynamic tactile threshold, secondary mechanical threshold, and conditioned pain modulation would respectively establish the presence of peripheral and/or central sensitization, as well as the value of diffuse nociceptive inhibitory control. * Analgesia would follow a step-wise approach, including NSAID (cimicoxib), anticonvulsant (gabapentin), and tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline). Cimicoxib is expected to target inflammatory peripheral / central sensitization. Gabapentin, as calcium channel blocker, would counteract spinal windup. Amitriptyline, as serotonine / noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, would re-enforce descending inhibitory controls. The whole duration of follow-up would be less than one month, including 5 consultations for assuring animal welfare assessment, detection of potential drug side effects. and potential requirement to rescue analgesia. Potential benefits - To improve the quality of care provided to patients affected with cancer.
current_roster.name: Cancer pain in dogs

current_roster.description: Objective: The primary purpose of this study is to demonstrate the safety and efficacy of a combination therapeutic protocol, incorporating chemotherapy and immunotherapy (ECI-LYM-1) which utilizes an autologous tumor vaccine and also infusion of autologous tumor specific T-cells, in dogs with naturally-occurring B cell lymphoma. What does enrollment into this trial involve? All dogs will undergo lymph node removal with blood sample collection (for confirmation of diagnosis and vaccine development) and three doses of doxorubicin chemotherapy for treatment of their lymphoma. Two weeks following the final doxorubicin treatment, a course of three vaccinations will be administered at weekly intervals. At the time of the last vaccination, a skin test will be performed to assess the immune response to the vaccine which will require 2 nights of hospitalization. Apheresis will be performed to extract tumor-specific T lymphocytes from the blood one week after the final vaccination. Your dog will remain hospitalized for two nights following this procedure and receive an additional skin test to assess their immune response to the vaccine. Low-dose, oral chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide) will be administered over 2-4 days at home in the week following apheresis. The T cells extracted during apheresis will be expanded at ELIAS Animal Health and will be re-infused 1 week after apheresis. Low-dose IL-2 will be administered starting 24 hours after the T cell infusion and will continue for 5 total injections under the skin on an every other day basis. A post treatment follow up visit will occur on day 93. Client Compensation: Once informed consent is obtained and preliminary diagnosis and staging is performed, this trial provides full funding for all treatment-related costs including surgery and all subsequent re-evaluations while on trial, all necessary diagnostics (bloodwork, radiographs), treatment, vaccine administration, apheresis, T cell infusion, and management of adverse events that are possibly attributed to therapy. The owner is responsible for the costs associated with the initial oncology consultation, lymph node aspirate, and diagnostic cytometry to confirm diagnosis.
current_roster.name: Trial for dogs with newly diagnosed B cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study Feline gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoblastic lymphoma (FGLL) is a debilitating disease of older cats. Chemotherapy for treatment of FGLL has been used with limited success and long-term survival is uncommon. Radiation therapy (RT) is used to treat localized lymphoma in humans and in two small studies of cats with lymphoma confined to the intestinal tract treated with RT, clinical signs improved in most cats. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the addition of abdominal cavity RT to oral chemotherapy (lomustine), daily oral prednisone, and weekly parenteral cobalamin will improve response to therapy, survival times, and quality of life of affected cats. If the addition of RT improves outcome, this therapy may be adopted as the standard of care for cats with FGLL and may be used to further study the use of RT for lymphocytic lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease. What qualifies my cat for enrollment in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your cat must: - Have been diagnosed with FGLL via needle aspirates of affected organs and/or histopathology of resected abdominal masses - Have ALT and total bilirubin  14 days prior to enrollment into the study - An expected survival of > 3 weeks regardless of therapy What does enrolling my cat in this trial involve? Once enrolled in the study, cats will receive 2 doses of RT and 4 doses of chemotherapy as part of the study. Cats will be expected to return to NC State at weeks 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 12 (a total of 6 visits after initial consultation and staging). You will be responsible for administering daily oral medications (prednisolone) and weekly vitamin B12 injections (under the skin) as part of the treatment for your cat's cancer. You will also be required to complete a written quality-of-life (QOL) survey at each visit. If your cat passes away at any time during or after the study, you must bring your cats remains to NCSU for an autopsy. Client Compensation The cost of the initial appointment, including baseline diagnostics, study medications (lomustine, cobalamin, prednisolone), physical exams, blood work, day time hospitalization, radiology, radiation and chemotherapy will be paid by the study, approximately $2000. Client Contact NCSU Clinical Studies Core at 919-515-2633 or ccmtr_csc@ncsu.edu
current_roster.name: Treatment of feline gastrointestinal lymphoblastic lymphoma (“FGLL”) with cobalamin (vitamin B12), prednisone, lomustine, and 8 Gy

current_roster.description: Objective of the trial: The primary objectives of this pilot study are to evaluate the blood levels of an investigational drug (RV2001), and to assess its overall effect on the severity of clinical signs associated with atopic dermatitis in dogs. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: - Have a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis - Be at least 12 months of age and weigh more than 5 pounds (2.2kg). - Be a generally healthy dog with no evidence of other serious chronic disease. (Such as heart disease, kidney disease and liver disease). We have 17 very specific inclusion criteria as well as 10 exclusion criteria that will be used to determine eligibility for enrollment. Eligibility for this clinical trial is also based on bloodwork, urinalysis, positive intradermal skin test or serum allergy test. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? A schedule of study events will be provided if your dog in enrolled. He/she will always receive a complete physical examination and dermatologic assessment upon arrival. If no obvious abnormalities are detected with on the physical examination your dog will have a small blood sample taken and then receive the first dose of RV2001 (day 0, Visit1) and have small amounts of blood taken at 2, 4, 6 and 8 hours after the drug administration. This will allow us to establish blood levels of the drug. A total of 7 visits will be needed. A recheck examination will occur after 7 days (Visit 2) and then once weekly for the next 3 weeks, with the final two visits (visits 6&7) occurring 14 days apart. You will be giving the drug daily to your dog. Small biopsies of the skin will be performed at the time of enrollment (Prescreening) then at day 56 (Visit 7, final visit) to evaluate the drug effect on skin TSLP expression. A small amount of blood (1-2 teaspoons) will be drawn at each study visit to evaluate changes in blood markers that may indicate activity of RV2001. A small amount of blood (1 teaspoon) will be used to evaluate if the antibodies produced to allergens that are making your pet itch have decreased with treatment. A mild sedative will be given and an intradermal skin test with allergens that include molds, grasses, trees, weeds and various house dust and storage mites will be performed at the pre-screening visit to ensure that skin reactivity to allergens are present. The sedative will be reversed. On the day (pre-screening visit) that your dog receives an intradermal test and skin biopsies, he/she will be provided a medical pet shirt that will be worn for protection of these areas for the next 24 hours. Client Compensation There are no costs associated with your dogs participation in this clinical trial. All costs associated with this clinical trial and treatment of any side effects will be covered by the study sponsor. We consider your dogs participation invaluable to not only the scientific community but also for humans and other dogs with environmental allergies. Therefore, upon completion of the clinical trial (final visit 7 at day 56), a $500 credit will be available for additional therapy or medical appointments at the VMC. This credit will be valid for one year, starting from the completion of the study. Client Contact Dr. Lorch, DVM, PhD, Diplomate ACVD lorch.2@osu.edu

current_roster.description: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is composed of a high concentration of platelets and growth factors that have been shown to promote cartilage health and counteract the cartilage breakdown that is associated with osteoarthritis.This study is to evaluate the efficacy of PRP for the treatment of elbow osteoarthritis in the canine. This will include twenty client-owned canines with an arthroscopic diagnosis of mild, moderate, or severe elbow osteoarthritis, as determined by arthroscopic evaluation using a Modified Outerbridge Scoring System, and that meet eligibility criteria.Platelet-rich plasma is made by processing a patients own blood sample.Ten patients will receive an intra-articular injection of PRP in the affected elbow(s). Ten patients will receive a sham treatment consisting of clipping and aseptically preparing the medial aspect of the affected elbow(s). Rescue injections will be performed at day 90 for the ten patients that received the sham treatment. Reassessment will be performed at day 14, 30, 60 and 90 and will include a physical examination, orthopedic evaluation, humeral musculature measurement, goniometric measurement of elbow extension and flexion, assignment of subjective lameness score, temporospatial gait analysis, and Canine Brief Pain Inventory form completed by the client.

current_roster.description: We greatly appreciate your interest in our clinical study to bank tissues from canine brain tumors, for shared use by investigators nationally, to better understand tumor behavior and develop new treatments. Your pets clinician will explain the disease characteristics of your pets brain tumor as well as available treatment options. If you choose to participate in this clinical study, this handout will provide you with some insight into the purpose of this study and will explain your responsibilities and patient procedures. What are clinical trials? Clinical trials are research studies. They are used in all specialties of medicine to evaluate new types of treatment. Clinical trials may be designed to determine the anti-cancer effects and side effects of new drugs, new surgical procedures, new radiation therapy procedures, or novel approaches to treatment (such as gene therapy or immunotherapy). In this case the clinical trial is to collect brain tumor and other tissues that will be used in numerous other future studies evaluating these topics. Your pets clinician and the Clinical Trials team will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Lack of access to good quality canine brain tumor tissues and tumor cell cultures is the biggest barrier in advancing the field of brain tumor investigation and therapeutic development. Very few veterinary institutions in this country have an actively-funded tumor biorepository, and fewer actively acquire and bank brain tumor tissues. Where canine biobanks exist, brain tumors remain strikingly underrepresented. Thus, there is a great importance to collecting and banking canine brain tumor tissues for shared use among comparative brain cancer researchers. Comprehensive information about tumor genetics, biology, and the molecular landscape of brain tumors, will allow specific determination of which pathways or tumor types/subtypes provide the best model for comparative and translational studies to advance human therapies. The availability of comprehensive data from the canine model will help promote identification and development of novel therapeutics that are targeted to molecular pathways or triggers for cancer development that co-occur in humans and dogs, and identify appropriate use of canine clinical trials that may promote more rapid approval of novel therapeutics through regulatory mechanisms. Tissues from the CSU Tissue Repository are made available to other institutions that wish to collaborate brain tumor studies, so the collection and banking of brain tumor tissues here at CSU will have far-reaching benefits to other institutions as well. The NIH National Cancer Institutes Comparative Brain Tumor Consortium (of which CSU is a member and active participant) already has in place collaborations among several key players in the area of brain tumor research, many of whom are in need of brain tumor specimens for their studies in tumor genetics, molecular biology, and therapeutic development. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? Dogs must have a diagnosis of a brain tumor that is deemed surgically resectable/accessible based on MRI characteristics. They cannot have had any prior radiation therapy or chemotherapy for their tumor. They must have good function of the liver and kidneys, have acceptable blood counts, and be free of severe underlying disease that might affect safe administration of anesthesia. Dogs must undergo some diagnostic testing prior to starting the study to ensure that they are eligible, including blood work (complete blood count, chemistry profile), urinalysis, and brain MRI. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? After eligibility is confirmed, your dog will go under anesthesia for brain tumor resection. During surgery, the tumor tissue will be removed and evaluated by histopathology to obtain a diagnosis, as normally occurs with any clinical case. A portion of the tumor tissues collected will be processed and stored in the tissue biobank, for future use in various investigations of brain tumor biology or development of novel treatments. In addition to tumor tissue, blood, a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid, and a small sample of skin from the edge of the incision, will also be collected and banked. What side effects or risks may my pet experience while participating in this clinical trial? The act of tissue banking has no inherent risk, and this tumor tissue would normally be removed surgically; however, your pet may experience side effects associated with brain tumor surgery. The surgical technique has been used in veterinary brain tumor resection routinely. Nevertheless, surgery of any kind, and in particular surgery within the brain, does have risks associated with it, which could be mild or severe (including death). Your pets clinician will discuss possible side effects with you and help you manage them if they occur. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your clinician or Clinical Trials team. How long will my pet be in the clinical trial? After surgery is complete, your pets participation in the clinical trial is finished. Your pets clinician will discuss options for continued treatment and diagnostic testing once the trial has ended. Can my pet withdraw from the clinical trial? You may decide to withdraw your pet from the clinical trial at any time. Tell your pets clinician and/or the Clinical Trials team if you are considering withdrawing your pet. It is important to discuss withdrawal in order to determine a plan for continued treatment of your pets brain tumor. The clinician may stop your pet from continued participation in the clinical trial at any time if he/she believes it is in your pets best interest or if the trial is discontinued or if the trial protocol is not followed. What financial incentives will CSU provide for my pets participation? The study will apply a credit of up to $8000 to your VTH account to be put towards the costs of brain surgery. These credits can only be applied after your dog has been deemed eligible and you have chosen to enter the trial, and will be credited to your account after surgery is completed. What are my responsibilities during the clinical trial? You are responsible for any and all other costs relating to your dogs care not covered by the study, including the cost of the initial examination and pre-anesthesia testing required prior to entering the study or after the study ends, any costs of diagnostic testing or treatment beyond those covered by the credit, as well as any optional adjunctive cancer therapies you might elect. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Questions? Please do not hesitate to obtain additional information from your pets clinician or the Clinical Trials team if you do not understand something about the study or your pets care and treatment. current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To determine the prevalence of bacteria in the urine of patients with Cranial Cruciate Ligament (CCL) injury and to discover whether patients with asymptomatic bacteriuria have a higher risk of developing a surgical site infection in dogs that have undergone surgery. Background Bacteriuria is the presence of bacteria in the urine. Many times, bacteria in the urine indicates an underlying urinary tract infection (UTI). Patients with bacteriuria may experience symptoms such as increased urinary frequency, blood in the urine, or painful urination. A small population of dogs with bacteria in the urine display no symptoms of infection. These dogs are termed asymptomatic bacteriuric.Research in human patients who undergo elective orthopedic procedures suggests that asymptomatic bacteriuric patients do not require post-operative antibiotics, nor are they are at increased risk of surgical site infections. Our goal is to identify asymptomatic bacteriuric patients in dogs presenting with CCL injury and whether these patients are at risk for surgical site infections after surgery to repair a CCL injury. The results of this study could be used to guide veterinarians on timing of surgery and the discriminate use of antibiotics. Judicious use of antibiotics may decrease antibiotic resistance, unnecessary treatment and unwanted side effects. Study Design A small amount of urine will be analyzed for the presence of bacteria in all dogs with CCL injury. A questionnaire detailing any signs of lower urinary tract disease will be recorded. The first 70 positive urine culture patients and 70 negative urine culture patients will be included for follow up after surgery for CCL injury. Dogs that have undergone surgical repair of CCL injury are not routinely sent home on antibiotics. As part of the study, patients will not be treated with antibiotics post-operatively. Follow-up evaluations with repeat urinalysis and urine culture will be done at 8 weeks post-operatively. An owner questionnaire on limb use, incision healing and any signs of lower urinary tract disease will be recorded at 8 weeks and during phone follow-up at 6 and 12 months post operatively. Compensation Clients are responsible for the cost of CCL surgery, including the examination fee, hospitalization, surgery, anesthesia, analgesia, overnight care, e-collar, sling and diagnostic pre- and immediate post-operative radiographs, CBC/chemistry and urinalysis.The cost of initial urine culture submission will be provided by the study in all enrolled dogs. Costs of the 8-week recheck will be at no cost for qualifying dogs (the first to be enrolled: 70 urine culture positive dogs and 70 urine culture negative dogs). It will include urinalysis and urine culture, post-operative radiographs, and sedation for enrolled dogs. On average, this represents a $325 value. Complications attributable to the surgical procedure are not covered by the study. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Contact Barbara Kafka, Surgery Case Coordinator Office Phone: 540-231-3821 | Email:bkafka@vt.edu Dr. Cheslymar Garcia, Surgery Office Phone: 540-231-4621 | Email:cheslyg@vt.edu

current_roster.description: Currently, there is no standardized approach in veterinary medicine to assess for metastasis in oral malignant melanoma in dogs. Previous research has found that feelinglymph nodes on examination can be an inaccurate assessment for cancer spread as they can be normal in size and still contain tumor cells. Needle aspirates of lymph nodes can be obtained to evaluate for evidence of spread at the cellular level, but there are several lymph nodes in the head and neck region which can be involved, and some are difficult to access on examination. Some of these lymph nodes are not generally found on physical examination, require advanced imaging to be detected, and can be challenging to acquire aspirates. Advanced imaging most commonly includes a neck ultrasound or a computed tomography (CT) scan of the region. This is part of the reason for the CT scan in your dog. This scan allows for better determination of the extent of the primary tumor, but also the lymph node appearance. As such, CTs are commonly used for surgical and/or radiation planning.As a diagnostic regularly utilized in current practice, we seek to determine whether CT is a sensitive and specific indicator for lymph node metastasis in dogs with oral malignant melanoma. In human medicine, staging for similar head and neck tumors also regularly includes the functional imaging positron emission tomography (PET) combined with CT, which assesses for regions of increased metabolic activity and has been found to correspond with cancer in the body. Currently, the accuracy for prediction of metastasis as well as for the local extent of disease is unknown for PET/CT in canine melanoma. In this study, palpation, CT, and PET appearance of lymph nodes of your dog will be compared to histopathologic (biopsy)results. We hypothesize that CT and PET will provide an increased sensitivity and specificity over palpation alone and will be accurate enough to eliminate unnecessary sampling or resection of lymph nodes in the future.
current_roster.name: CT for detection of metastasis in canine oral malignant melanoma

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include various types of chemotherapy; however, there are no approved drugs for these cancers in dogs, very few dogs are cured and most will relapse. New drugs remain necessary to treat these drug-resistant relapses. Rabacfosadine is an intravenous chemotherapy agent that has been used both in normal dogs and in more than 350 dogs with cancer. It has been shown to induce remission in 60 to 100% of dogs with lymphoma. The goal of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of rabacfosadine, given once every 21 days, when combined with another commonly used chemotherapy drug, asparaginase.
current_roster.name: Protocol for the Combined Use of TANOVEA™-CA1 (Rabacfosadine for Injection) and Asparaginase in Dogs with Relapsed Lymphoma: VC-01

current_roster.description: Cachexia is defined as weight loss and muscle atrophy that cannot be reversed by consuming more calories. This can occur in humans and animals with chronic illnesses, such as cancer, heart disease, and kidney disease. It has also been associated with a worse prognosis in these diseases. The melanocortin pathway in the central nervous system is believed to be a major player in the control of food intake and metabolism. Activation of melanocortin receptors in the brain leads to decreased food intake and increased metabolism. By blocking these receptors with a novel drug, the hope is that pets will have increased food intake and decreased metabolism, resulting in weight gain. Preclinical studies suggest that this new MC4R antagonist will improve appetite, energy level, and weight gain, providing an overall improvement in quality of life. The goal of this study is to determine the side effects and effectiveness of a new melanocortin 4 receptor antagonist in the treatment of canine cachexia.
current_roster.name: Melanocortin 4 Receptor Antagonist in the Treatment of Canine Cachexia

current_roster.description: While surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy can be effective for a variety of cancers, there remain a number of cancers for which standard forms of therapy either do not work, or are effective for a period of time but are eventually associated with relapse. New forms of treatment are necessary for these tumors. svL4 is a small protein that has been shown to stimulate certain cells of the immune system in mice, and in canine immune cells in the laboratory. This may result in production of compounds by the immune system that can help to control cancer. The goal of this study is to evaluate the safety and immune effects of svL4 when given to dogs with cancer once every other day.
current_roster.name: Pilot, Open-Label, phase-1 Study of svL4 in Tumor-Bearing Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose: This study aims to determine whether cystocentesis helps to increase the ease of passing a urinary catheter, and thereby trauma to the urethra. Background: Urethral obstruction is a common emergency situation for domestic male cats. Performing a cystocentesis (using a needle to directly remove urine from the urinary bladder) can aid in initial stabilization and may improve likelihood of successful catheterization. As such, cystocentesis currently part of the standard of care for the treatment of urethral obstruction at the Ohio State University. However, the benefits of cystocentesis have not been definitively proven and may carry some risk of damage to the bladder and leakage of urine or bleeding. A recent study has shown that this risk appears to be extremely low (0 cases in 46 enrolled). The results of this study will help veterinarians determine the safest, most effective treatment protocol for feline urethral obstruction, particularly whether decompressive cystocentesis should be performed prior to urethral catheterization. Inclusion Criteria: Feline with urethral obstruction Study Design: Your cat will be randomly assigned once enrolled to either have a cystocentesis performed or not, and then grading the difficulty of passing the urinary catheter. In addition, an abdominal ultrasound will be performed at the time of presentation and 15 minutes after cystocentesis is performed, and again 4 hours later determine if any urine leakage from the bladder occurs. If fluid is found, a sample will be obtained by inserting a needle into the abdomen (abdominocentesis) under ultrasound guidance and analyzed to determine the type of fluid present (blood or urine). Client Cost: Owners are responsible for all costs associated with the treatment of the urethral obstruction including the emergency fee, hospitalization, treatment, medications, blood work and radiographs. Client Compensation: The ultrasound will be at no cost to the owner.
current_roster.name: Cats with urinary blockage

current_roster.description: Heart disease in the Boxer is most commonly a disease of the heart muscle that leads to electrical disturbances. The disease is inherited but some dogs are more severely affected than others. It is possible that changes in thyroid level may impact if a dog will have a mild or severe form of the disease. Understanding the role of thyroid in the severity of disease will greatly improve the ability to manage this common and sometimes fatal heart disease.
current_roster.name: Boxer Cardiomyopathy and a Link to Thyroid Hormone

current_roster.description: Feline gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoblastic lymphoma (FGLL) is a debilitating disease of older cats. Chemotherapy for treatment of FGLL has been used with limited success and long-term survival is uncommon. Radiation therapy (RT) is used to treat localized lymphoma in humans and in two small studies of cats with lymphoma confined to the intestinal tract treated with RT, clinical signs improved in most cats. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the addition of abdominal cavity RT to oral chemotherapy (lomustine), daily oral prednisone, and weekly parenteral cobalamin will improve response to therapy, survival times, and quality of life of affected cats. If the addition of RT improves outcome, this therapy may be adopted as the standard of care for cats with FGLL and may be used to further study the use of RT for lymphocytic lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease.
current_roster.name: Combination of Prednisone, Cobalamin, Lomustine, and Radiation Therapy for Treatment of Feline Gastrointestinal Lymphoblastic Lymp

current_roster.description: Glaucoma is a painful, blinding disease in dogs which currently does not have a cure. Very little is known regarding the cause of glaucoma and the factors that lead to progression of the disease. To evaluate the role that inflammatory mediators may play in the development of canine glaucoma, cytokine levels present in aqueous humor of dogs that will develop glaucoma will be compared to those of dogs that will not develop glaucoma
current_roster.name: Aqueous Humor Cytokines in Canine Glaucoma

current_roster.description: 20 dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma will be enrolled in this study. All dogs will receive surgical removal of their tumor followed by standard of care chemotherapy. Once standard of care chemotherapy is completed, 10 of the dogs will receive an additional investigational chemotherapy agent.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial in Dogs with Newly Diagnosed Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if a new drug is able to safely and effectively treat Tritrichomonas foetus infection and diarrhea in cats that have previously failed treatment with ronidazole. Currently there are no alternatives to ronidazole for treatment of cats with T. foetus infection. Tritrichomonas foetus was first described 20 years ago. The infection causes a foul diarrhea that is debilitating in kittens and can persist unrelentingly for up to 2 years. The infection is enduring and results in relapsing bouts of diarrhea throughout life. Cats in every corner of the world are afflicted by T. foetus infection and untold numbers of these cats can never be cured. Despite many attempts to identify an effective treatment for T. foetus, only ronidazole has been identified as capable of eradicating the infection. Unfortunately, ronidazole can cause neurotoxicity in cats and 36% of treated cats fail to clinically benefit from the drug. In the near future, new FDA guidelines will likely prevent veterinary pharmacies from further compounding of unapproved bulk-chemical drugs such as ronidazole. Therefore there is a critical need to identify safer, more effective, and FDA-approved drugs to eradicate T. foetus infection in cats. Without such a drug, T. foetus will continue its worldwide spread and plague cats and their owners with chronic incurable diarrhea.
current_roster.name: Efficacy of a New Drug for Treatment of Cats with Ronidazole Resistant T. Foetus Infection

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Chronic kidney disease is common in cats. Blood levels of phosphate increase when the kidneys are not working well, and medications are frequently needed to decrease the blood phosphate levels back towards normal. One of the main medications used contains aluminum. Aluminum has been linked to a number of side effects in people, but we do not know about its effects in cats. We do not know what normal blood aluminum levels are in cats and whether they are similar to levels in people. New technology has made testing blood for aluminum possible with small blood samples. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this study is to determine whether there is a significant difference in Aluminum levels between healthy cats and those with various stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD). We will also evaluate aluminum levels in cats receiving medication containing aluminum as part of therapy for their CKD, as well as cats eating a primarily canned versus primarily dry diet. Identifying elevated aluminum levels may help us to determine whether these subsets of patients are at risk for developing aluminum toxicity, and may assist us in clarifying risk factors. What qualifies my cat for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trialyour cat must: - Have been diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (Chemistry or renal panel simultaneously or within 1 week). What does enrolling my cat in this clinical trial involve? All cats will receive a CBC on the day of enrollment, which the study will pay for, unless that test has been performed at the Ohio State Diagnostic Lab within the week and does not need to be repeated. Additionally, a chemistry panel within one week is required for enrollment; the study will NOT pay for that test. A blood sample will be drawn and placed in a special tube, and at the end of the study, the sample will be tested for aluminum levels. Client Compensation Testing of serum aluminum is at no cost to the client. Owners that participate will receive an incentive in the form of a free complete blood count.
current_roster.name: Aluminum Concentrations in Cats with Kidney Disease

current_roster.description: This is an ongoing study, that collects data from all horses admitted for colic. The data is then used to answer questions such as "What are the risk factors for a certain type of colic?" or "Which postoperative treatments improve the survival rate and reduce complication rates?" The data is also used to generate average survival and complication rates for common types of colic and common surgical procedures, for client and veterinary education purposes and for comparison with other large referral hospitals.
current_roster.name: NC State Equine Colic Database

current_roster.description: Background: There are many cases of malignant tumors in dogs that are not amenable to conventional therapeutic approaches, such as surgery, because of their location on the body or their advanced stage of disease. For such patients, therapeutic options are limited, because intravenous systemic chemotherapy may not be tolerable for these patients in their debilitated state, or perhaps it does not seem practical to put such patients through a prolonged radiation protocol away from their owners and home. The primary purpose of this study, therefore, is to demonstrate the feasibility and safety of a therapeutic protocol that may prove clinically beneficial in that subset of patients with externally-measurable malignant tumors, that are not amenable to surgery for whatever reason. This therapeutic protocol incorporates the localized intratumoral (subcutaneous) administration of a nanoparticle formulation of hyaluronan conjugated cisplatin (HA-Pt) in combination with palliative radiation therapy. Clinical Protocol: All enrolled dogs will receive HA-Pt subcutaneously to the primary tumor on study days 0, 7, 14, and 21, at incrementally increasing doses. Within 4 hours of HA-Pt administration, enrolled dogs will also concurrently receive one fraction of radiation therapy to the tumor site (for a total of 4 factions). Blood samples will be collected immediately prior to each dose of HA-Pt and also weekly for three weeks following the final dose. After study day 42 (or sooner if your dog is removed from the study), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional treatment options with you.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of hyaluronan conjugated cisplatin localized nanoparticle therapy combined with palliative radiation therapy in dogs wi

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Mast cell tumors are the most common skin tumor in dogs, comprising between 16 and 21% of all canine malignant skin cancers. The currently accepted approach to therapy for high grade mast cell tumors is surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, or other adjuvant therapy. You, the owner of a dog with a suspected mast cell tumor (MCT) have already elected surgical excision of your dogs tumor. This study is specifically focused on the generation and characterization of a panel of cell lines established from canine mast cell tumor tissues. Your participation in this study is only to donate your dogs tumor tissue to a panel of other MCTs for further research. This panel of canine mast cell tumor cell lines will then be utilized by researchers for future investigations into mast cell-mediated disorders, specifically for the development of enhanced diagnostic, monitoring and treatment approaches for canine mast cell tumors. These canine mast cell tumor-derived cell lines will also be crucial to translational research by helping to further elucidate human mast cell neoplasia, and other human and canine diseases characterized by mast cell-mediated immune dysregulation. Clinical Protocol: This study involves only the staging of the mast cell tumor disease and the use of the resected tumor tissue in in vitro research. Owners of dogs diagnosed with a suspected mast cell tumor that have already elected to have the tumor surgically removed, will be agreeing to donate their dogs tumor tissue to this study.
current_roster.name: Characterization of canine mast cell tumors and generation of primary cell lines.

current_roster.description: Antiplatelet drugs (aspirin and clopidogrel) are used to decrease death from blood clots in dogs with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), but it is unknown whether dosages developed using healthy research dogs achieve optimal effects in dogs with IMHA. Furthermore, both antiplatelet drugs and steroids, the mainstay of treatment for IMHA, cause gastrointestinal bleeding in people. In pilot investigation, we identified inadequate platelet inhibition in dogs treated with steroids and either aspirin (3/3) or clopidogrel (2/3) for 28 days. Further, gastrointestinal bleeding developed in dogs receiving steroids with either antiplatelet drug (aspirin 3/3, clopidogrel 2/3). Based on these results, we believe sustained administration of antiplatelet therapy at currently recommended doses will inhibit platelet function in dogs with IMHA, but inhibition will be inadequate and clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding will each occur in 60% of cases. We will compare non-invasive lab tests and capsule endoscopy results for dogs with newly diagnosed IMHA before and after 28 days of treatment with immunosuppressive (prednisone and cyclosporine) and antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel). Results will clarify the effects of IMHA treatment on platelet function and gastrointestinal health in dogs. If antiplatelet responsiveness or gastrointestinal bleeding differs between dogs that receive clopidogrel versus aspirin as part of their management, this will drastically affect antiplatelet and gastroprotection strategies for dogs with IMHA. If both drugs result in inconsistent antiplatelet effects or gastrointestinal bleeding, investigation into alternative drugs or dosages should be pursued. Results of this study will, thus, immediately and profoundly impact clinical management of dogs with IMHA. Note: We are currently collecting cases for use as pilot data. These data will be used to secure grant funding for a multi-center, fully funded study.
current_roster.name: Gastrointestinal and platelet changes in dogs with Immune-Mediated Hemolytic Anemia (IMHA)

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to evaluate the clinical and immunologic activity of Immunolight Therapy (IT) in dogs with spontaneously-occurring solid tumors. The effect of IT on locally treated solid tumors will be measured via tumor size reduction (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; RECIST). The effect of IT on pulmonary metastatic lesion will be assessed via serial thoracic radiography. Changes in local, regional, and systemic immune activity will be measured via flow cytometry of tumor, regional lymph node and distant lymph node samples, for lymphoid and myeloid markers, as well as PD-1 expression. The effect of localized IT treatment of 2 lymphomatous lymph nodes on systemic disease burden will be measured through a combination of lymph node size reduction (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; RECIST), radiographic assessment of thoracic lesions, and cytologic assessment of previously affected nodes.Safety will also be assessed; all clinical and biochemical toxicities will be graded according to the Veterinary Comparative Oncology Group Common Terminology criteria for Adverse Events (VCOG-CTCAE) v1.1 (Veterinary Comparative Oncology, 2011).
current_roster.name: Clinical Trials of Immunolight Therapy for Pet Dogs with Cancer

current_roster.description: The objective of this pilot study will be to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a specific dose of CNTX-4975 (purified transcapsaicin) administered by intra-articular injection to control pain associated with osteoarthritis (OA) in dogs. Various variables and criteria for treatment success will also be evaluated.The results of this pilot study will be considered in the design of a pivotal study. The results of the pivotal study will be submitted to FDAs Center for Veterinary Medicine as substantial evidence to complete the requirements of the New Animal Drug Application(NADA) effectiveness technical section.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial Studying Safety of Intra-articular Injection for Dogs with Osteoarthritis

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a devastating disease for both dogs and humans, which is extremely difficult to treat effectively. Sildenafil (Viagra) is currently the drug of choice for treating dogs with pulmonary arterial hypertension, but the disease often becomes refractory to this therapy over time and no other effective agents are currently available. Toceranib phosphate (Palladia) has been recently proposed as an alternative or complementary agent for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension in dogs, given the efficacy of a related drug, imatinib, in humans, as well as anecdotal case reports in dogs. The primary purpose of this study, therefore, is to preliminarily evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and tolerability of toceranib phosphate (Palladia) in dogs with spontaneously-arising pulmonary arterial hypertension.
current_roster.name: Efficacy of toceranib phosphate (Palladia®) in dogs with spontaneously-arising pulmonary arterial hypertension: a proof-of-concept

current_roster.description: This project aims at testing a new construct that blocks dog IgE in dogs with atopic dermatitis. Enrolled dogs will be those currently controlled with standard-of-care anti-allergic therapy. Dogs will be treated one month apart with the "IgE blocker", and, two weeks after their first injection, the anti-allergic drugs will be discontinued. The time to flare will be calculated from the date of the end of anti-allergic drug therapy (circa Day 14) till the time of pruritus flare. It is expected that the IgE blocker will delay such flare to a minimum of two months.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial studying "IgE blocker" on atopic dermatitis in dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and brief explanation of Study: This study is evaluating the potential for drug resistant Ancylostoma caninum in Blood Donor greyhounds and dogs seen through Community Practice for routine health care. Feces voluntarily passed by the dog will be collected and analyzed for parasite ova. Identified dogs with a positive patent hookworm infection will be followed. Owners of these dogs will be asked if they would like a free follow-up fecal test after administering dewormer. This study has no impact on the selection of the commercially available dewormer. The decision for the prescribed and recommended dewormer is made by the attending veterinarian based on the dogs needs and clients decision. The follow-up fecal examination is to be delivered to the VMC Small Animal Clinic by the client within 12 hours of the dog passing the feces, and the feces should not be refrigerated. The samples will be packaged according to directions (non-leak bag) in a secondary container. The result of this follow-up fecal evaluation is provided to your attending clinician.
current_roster.name: CLINICAL TRIAL FOR DOGS WITH PATENT HOOKWORM INFECTIONS

current_roster.description: Spinal cord lesions caused by canine degenerative myelopathy (DM) are undetectable on standard clinical MRI, limiting our ability to diagnose and monitor the disease. Studies in people with a similar condition, Lou Gehrigs disease, have shown that an advanced MRI technique called diffusion tensor imaging is able to detect the microscopic changes in the spinal cord caused by this condition. This project aims to determine if this technique is able to identify the spinal cord lesions caused by degenerative myelopathy by comparing imaging results from a group of dogs with the condition with a normal group. Diffusion tensor imaging has the potential to become a reliable imaging method for the diagnosis and monitoring of degenerative myelopathy. Eligibility for the study: This study will recruit two groups: 1) Dogs with a positive SOD1 test for degenerative myelopathy that are showing clinical signs consistent with degenerative myelopathy. 2) Dogs with a normal neurological examination that are over the age of 8 years. Procedure: Enrolled dogs will be admitted to the Cornell hospital for animals and undergo have a pre-anesthetic blood screen and anesthesia for an MRI examination. Dogs can go home the same day.
current_roster.name: Using Advanced MRI Techniques to Diagnose Canine Degenerative Myelopathy

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Despite surgery and chemotherapy treatment, most dogs develop metastatic disease (spread) to the lungs, which is ultimately their cause of death. Zoledronate is a drug used to treat osteoporosis, as well as bony metastases in humans. It has also been used in dogs with bone tumors to relieve pain. It may also have anti-tumor effects, and there are some reports of stable or improved disease in people with lung metastases. This trial is investigating the use of zoledronate in dogs with pulmonary metastatic disease.
current_roster.name: Drug treatment for dogs with lung involvement of bone cancer

current_roster.description: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma is a rare form of lymphoma where cancerous lymphocytes localize to the skin or mucocutaneous sites (i.e. gums). Dogs typically present with multiple lesions spread over the body, inhibiting the use of local therapies such as surgery or radiation therapy. This disease tends to be responsive to chemotherapy; however, the duration of response to our standard protocols is typically short. Lomustine is an oral chemotherapeutic drug commonly used for cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL). While the majority of dogs treated for CTCL with lomustine will improve, only around 30% of dogs will achieve a complete remission from this drug alone. Combination chemotherapy protocols are the gold standard of treatment for other forms of canine lymphoma. These protocols have been shown to not only have the highest remission rates, but also the longest remission durations. The goal of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of combining lomustine with another chemotherapeutic agent, asparaginase, specifically for dogs with CTCL.
current_roster.name: Combined Lomustine and Asaparaginase for Treatment of Canine Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Regulatory T-cells (Tregs)are immune cells that have been found to be increased in humans and dogs with cancer. The immune system of cancer-bearing cats has not been evaluated. This study aims to assess the numbers of Tregs in three populations of cats: those with lymphoma, those with carcinomas, and those with sarcomas.
current_roster.name: Assessment of immune cells in cats with cancer

current_roster.description: Purpose To determine if dogs with chronic liver disease have decreased platelet function and if post-liver biopsy bleeding is associated with platelet function. Background Chronic liver disease is common among adult dogs. Liver biopsy is usually required to identify the underlying cause and to institute optimal treatment. Since dogs with liver disease often have abnormal coagulation, bleeding is a risk of biopsy. Routine screening for clotting abnormalities in dogs with liver disease does not necessarily predict excessive biopsy-induced bleeding, which makes preventing hemorrhage during liver biopsy difficult. This study will investigate whether decreased platelet function in dogs with liver disease contributes to bleeding. The specific aims of the study are to determine if dogs with chronic liver disease have decreased platelet function and if there is a correlation between platelet function and bleeding after biopsy. Eligibility Dogs 1 year or older Dogs with ALT >2.5 times the reference interval for more than one month or with biochemical evidence of hepatic dysfunction for more than one month Clinical indications that a liver biopsy is warranted Exclusion Criteria Sight hound breed Heart murmur Concurrent illness (moderate to severe) von Willebrands disease Portosystemic shunt Received the following drugs within the last 7 days: Calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, fish oil supplementation, or corticosteroids Received a beta-lactam antibiotic within the last 2 days Platelet count < 120,000 Packed cell volume or hematocrit < 35% Study Design Platelet function will be measured in dogs with chronic liver disease using the platelet function analyzer (PFA-100) and buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT). Von Willebrand factor will be measured in these patients as well. These tests require a single blood sample. Dogs will undergo routine ultrasound guided percutaneous liver biopsy under sedation. As part of routine liver biopsy, the dogs will be kept overnight in our ICU for monitoring after the procedure. An abdominal ultrasound and packed cell volume will be performed before and after liver biopsy to assess for hemorrhage. Compensation The study will cover the costs of the initial examination, complete blood count, plasma chemistries, plasma von Willebrand factor, buccal mucosal bleeding time, abdominal ultrasound, heartworm test, ultrasound guided liver biopsy, and clotting tests. The cost savings to the owner is over $500. Clients will be responsible for other costs, including other laboratory tests recommended and any treatment that is indicated if complications may arise. Contact Dr. David Panciera, Internal Medicine Phone: 540-231-4628 | Email:Panciera@vt.edu Ashley Wilkinson, Internal Medicine Email:AshleyRW@vt.edu If your query is urgent, please call the Small Animal Hospital on 540-231-4621.
current_roster.name: Platelet function in dogs with chronic liver disease undergoing liver biopsy

current_roster.description: The VCIC is conducting a clinical trial for dogs who have had a cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) rupture and meniscaltear that has been surgically repaired with atibialplateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO). The purpose of this study is to evaluatethe safety and efficacy of a novel therapeuticon the development and progression of osteoarthritis in dogs. Dogs will be randomly assigned study medication or placebo to be given daily, and will be followed for one year. Eligibility: Dogs 2 years of age or older weighing between 30-110 lbs. Dogs who have been diagnosed with unilateral (one knee) CCL rupture within the last 9 months and TPLO surgery has been performed no more than 4 months prior to enrollment. Dogs not currently on any pain medications. Benefits: All study visits are covered by the study. Compensation is provided for time and travel.
current_roster.name: (CI85) Assessing a novel therapeutic on the development and progression of osteoarthritis in dogs following CCL rupture and TPLO s

current_roster.description: This clinical trial seeks dogs with osteosarcoma to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a new vaccine following standard of care therapy. Bone cancer or osteosarcoma (OSA) is a common, highly aggressive cancer that frequently affects the long bones of large breed dogs. Current standard of care therapy consists of surgical limb amputation plus 4 doses of chemotherapy, given in a vein, every 3 weeks. The immune system plays an important role in identifying and targeting cancer cells in the body. In this study, we aim to use a new approach to stimulate the bodys own immune system to attack remaining tumor cells in dogs that have undergone limb amputation and chemotherapy for the treatment of OSA. We will use a study vaccine, which has been modified to express a tumor protein (HER-2/neu) that is found in many cancer cells, including canine bone cancer cells and cancer stem cells. The hope is that when injected into the bloodstream, the vaccine stimulates the immune system to attack cells expressing the HER-2/neu tumor protein. This approach aims to delay and/or prevent the spread of cancer (metastases) following removal of the primary bone cancer tumor (limb amputation) and chemotherapy. Interactions with other drugs are unknown, so it is necessary to disclose any medications (and supplements) your dog is currently taking to the oncologist. It is strongly encouraged to eliminate all unnecessary medications. **Please note that all staging diagnostics (including but not limited to radiographs, ultrasound, and blood work) must be performed at Cornell University prior to surgery and chemotherapy. Full amputation surgery must also be performed at Cornell within 10 days of the initial staging diagnostics. Following surgery all chemotherapy and vaccine administration appointments must also be performed at Cornell. Please contact the clinical trials coordinator for more information.
current_roster.name: Evaluating a Vaccine for the Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Mast cell tumors are the most common malignant skin tumors in dogs and surgery is the treatment of choice for addressing these tumors. These tumors can spread (metastasize) to other areas and drain into the surrounding lymph nodes. If a tumor has spread into the lymph node it may also spread to the spleen, liver, and bone marrow and additional diagnostic tests may need to be performed. Identification and surgical removal of a draining lymph node (the sentinel lymph node) is used for determining local metastasis and can impact prognosis and treatment recommendation. As every dog and tumor is different, it has been shown that the node closest to the tumor is not necessarily the sentinel node. The goal of this study is to utilize computed tomography (CT) to identify the sentinel lymph node prior to surgical removal. For this study, enrolled dogs will be sedated and will have a contrast media injected under the skin around the primary tumor in order to identify the draining lymph node with a CT scan. The draining lymph node will then be removed at the same time as the mast cell tumor removal.
current_roster.name: Using CT Imaging to Identify the Draining Lymph Node in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: A new combination of drugs (ibrutinib + mivibresib) will be tested in a phase II clinical study in untreated dogs that have been newly diagnosed with B-cell lymphoma at both Cornell University Hospital for Animals and Cornell University Veterinary Specialists. After owner consent, a peripheral lymph node excision will be performed prior to treatment, and for all dogs, a fine needle aspiration will be performed in an involved node, both before and at 2 and 4 weeks after study initiation, if palpable tumor remains. Serum and blood for germline DNA will be collected prior to treatment and at remission or at 4 weeks, whichever is later. Dogs will be followed every week for the first four-week cycle and every four weeks after that. Treatment will continue until progression or for six cycles, whichever comes first. Doses in the only reported study with ibrutinib in canine B-cell lymphoma ranged from 2 to 20 mg/kg, responses were seen at all concentrations, and the receptor occupancy was 100% for 24 hours at all dose levels. For this study, we chose a dose of 5mg/kg as a tolerable dose in the lower end of this range that was similar to the ~8mg/kg used in human studies. Mivibresib dose was recommended based on PK studies done by Abbvie (0.1 mg/kg/day). To ensure safety in the clinical trial, the starting dose of ibrutinib will be held constant at 5mg/kg and the dose of Mivibresib will be reduced by 50% in the first four dogs treated with each combination to ensure that dogs with lymphoma respond similarly to healthy research beagles. If no dose limiting toxicities are encountered after one cycle of treatment, the dose of Mivibresib will be increased to 100%, and subsequent dogs will be treated at 5mg/kg ibrutinib + full dose of Mivibresib. If toxicity occurs at any cycle of treatment, dose adjustments will be made first to Mivibresib (reduce dose by 25-50% at the discretion of the treating oncologist), and then to ibrutinib (reduce dose to 2.5mg/kg) if side effects still persist at a 50% dose reduction of the partner agent. If side effects persist after these dose reductions, the patient will be removed from the study.
current_roster.name: Evaluating a New Drug Combination to Treat Lymphoma

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are tumors that arise from various skin and connective tissues under the skin, such as fat, muscle, cartilage, nerves, or small blood vessels. These tumors can occur from any site on the body and commonly regrow after tumor removal. While surgical removal and other therapies are available to treat these tumors, little is known as to why the occur in the first place. Dr. Andrew Miller and his lab are collecting samples of canine soft tissue sarcomas in order to determine their RNA molecules, otherwise known as transcriptome. This information will one day lead to new treatments and preventives for these tumors.
current_roster.name: Determining the Transcriptome of Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Protein in the urine (proteinuria) is common in dogs and causes further damage to the kidneys. This study aims to determine whether the standard drugs used to treat proteinuria can completely suppress one of the hormones involved in kidney regulation, and whether lack of complete suppression affects the amount of proteinuria.If this study finds that standard drugs (i.e., ACE inhibitors like enalapril or benazepril or angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARB) like telmisartan) do not completely suppress aldosterone production, it opens an avenue for further research into additional drugs that could be used. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - Proteinuria from primary kidney disease - A urine protein:creatinine ratio of > 1 on two occasions What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? At the initial visit, each dog will have a physical examination, blood pressure measurement, blood tests (chemistry panel and CBC), and urine tests (urinalysis, urine protein:creatinine ratio, urine culture, and urine aldosterone test). Treatment for proteinuria with an ACE inhibitor or ARB will start within one week of that visit, if the dog was not already receiving one of those drugs. Follow-up: Follow-up visits will be needed at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months after enrollment. At each visit, each dog will have a physical examination, blood pressure measurement, blood and urine tests (chemistry panel, CBC, urinalysis, urine protein:creatinine ratio, urine aldosterone). For each of these visits, you will need to bring two urine samples from your dog, and an additional urine sample will be obtained while during the visit, either by voiding naturally or by cystocentesis (standard method of urine collection that involves inserting a needle into the bladder to obtain a sample). Client Compensation Following entry into the study, cost for the urine culture at the start of the study, and for the CBC and urinalysis tests on Month 1, 2, 4, and 6 visits, will be covered by the study.
