Osteosarcoma is a common primary bone tumor particularly in medium to giant breed dogs affecting appendicular bones such as the distal radius, proximal humerus, distal femur and proximal tibia. The osteolytic/osteoproductive behavior of this tumor results in significant discomfort. Amputation +/- adjuvant chemotherapy represents the standard treatment approach though amputation may not be ideal due to co-morbidities such as osteoarthritis in other limbs. When amputation is not pursued, hypofractionated radiation therapy +/-bisphosphonate therapy may be used to help manage pain. The Sponsor has generated a therapeutic cocktail which includes bestatin, amethylparatyrosine, dihydrotestosterone and melanotan diluted with 0.9% NaCL delivered as 3 times weekly subcutaneous (SQ) administration. The combination of these agents is proposed to alter tumor cell metabolism and thereby improve pain in dogs with appendicular OSA. This combination of compounds is currently under evaluation in human oncology.
current_roster.name: A FUNDED CLINICAL STUDY FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PAIN IN DOGS WITH OSTEOSARCOMA

current_roster.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. current_roster.tagline: Ethos-PUSH: Hemangiosarcoma
current_roster.name: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)

current_roster.description: Mast cell tumor (MCT) is the most common malignant skin tumor in the dog. While surgery is the main treatment for most MCT, a subset have a high potential for eventual recurrence and spread, and require medical treatment in addition to surgery in an attempt to delay or prevent eventual recurrence. Furthermore, many dogs may present with disease that cannot be removed owing to size, location, or tumors that have already spread. Medical therapy for these patients needs improvement. Both low dose continuous (metronomic) chlorambucil (MC) and toceranib (TOC) have been used safely in dogs with MCT, and the combination is sometimes used in patients. However, the combination has not been scientifically tested for effectiveness. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this combination given to dogs with measurable MCT. Dogs will receive MC orally once daily, and will receive TOC orally every other day. They will be rechecked 2, 4, 6 and 8 weeks after starting then every 6 weeks thereafter. Visits will generally take about 1 hour. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and the dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease stabilization or meaningful tumor shrinkage). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound, CT). Standard bloodwork, urinalysis and blood pressure measurement will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the effect of MC and TOC on immune function. Dogs must come to CSU for all visits related to the study.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Combined Chlorambucil and Toceranib for Treatment of Canine Mast Cell Tumors

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to compare the effectiveness and side effects of two standard-of-care chemotherapy protocols (CHOP vs. LOPP) to see if one is more beneficial for the treatment of T-cell Lymphoma in dogs. Dogs that are enrolled will be randomly assigned to receive either CHOP or LOPP. Participating dogs will have an initial screening visit to assess overall health and confirm eligibility, including a free in-house flow cytometry screen to differentiate between T-cell and B-cell lymphoma. Once eligible for enrollment, the cost of some additional testing is covered and there are gift card incentives at milestone timepoints during the trial. The cost of chemotherapy is not covered and is the responsibility of the pet owner.
current_roster.name: Comparison of the efficacy & impact on suppressor cells of CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy in canine T-cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: All procedures will be carried out at the owner's primary veterinarian's hospital or their subsequent referral hospital, less the collection of feces if this can be done from their private residence. The owner's primary veterinarian or referring veterinarian will collect the blood, urine, biopsy samples. Veterinarians at Texas A&M University are also encouraged to enroll patients following the same steps as veterinarians working on private premises (collecting blood, urine, and biopsy samples). The owner will likely collect the fecal samples. Enrollees from around the nation are encouraged to participate and are not limited to those only in the state of Texas. With the exception of biopsies, additional blood, urine (at the discretion of the veterinarian), and feces will be asked to be collected for the purposes of this study. We will screen enrollment to only patients which have been selected to undergo gastrointestinal biopsies as part of their normal diagnostic work-up as per their veterinarian's discretion. In this case, biopsies will not be collected for the sole purpose of our study, rather we will enroll and provide free histopathology interpretation services to those patients that were already selected to undergo the procedure and collect subsequent biofluids at our request. Owners of participating dogs will be asked to collect one fecal sample of about 3-5g of feces (approximately the size of a golf ball) immediately after a naturally passed bowel movement per day on three consecutive days (three samples total). Fecal samples are collected into ziplock bags. These samples need to be frozen immediately after collection and will need to be kept frozen until analysis. Owners of dogs enrolled in the study will be asked to fill out a study questionnaire providing general information about their dogs. The dog's primary care veterinarian will be asked to complete a clinical disease activity scoring sheet to provide specific information about the dog's general and gastrointestinal health status. The dog's primary care veterinarian will draw a blood sample of about 5-10 mL by venipuncture of a peripheral vein. Dogs will be manually restrained for these procedures. A single naturally voided urine sample will be obtained from each dog enrolled in the study. Alternatively, at the discretion of the clinician, a 10 mL (approximately the volume of two teaspoons) urine sample will be collected by cystocentesis (i.e., aspiration of the urinary bladder contents using a syringe with a needle) or catheterization (i.e., placing a flexible tube through the urethra into the bladder to drain the urine). Dogs will be manually restrained for these procedures. All specimens and required forms will be shipped overnight to the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at Texas A&M University. The collection of serum, urine, and fecal samples will be performed at least once upon initial presentation of the patient, and may be repeatedduring follow-up visits to the veterinarian, with at least a three-week interval between sample collections. The veterinarian will decide the best time to perform the follow-up sampling; the maximum number of follow-up tests will be three. If the collection of gastrointestinal biopsies (i.e., endoscopic or surgical full thickness biopsies of the fundus and/or antrum of the stomach, the duodenum, the jejunum, ileum, and/or the colon, and/or adjacent lymph nodes) is planned as part of the medical work-up of the patient by the primary care veterinarian or at a referring institution and performed as considered good veterinary practice (i.e., standard of care), these tissue biopsies will be submitted as tissue share to be utilized in this study and read through the Histopathology Service of the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at Texas A&M University.
current_roster.name: Canine Chronic Enteropathy - IBD Study

current_roster.description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. Using minimally invasive surgery, specifically video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), we predict patients will be recovered from the procedure within 2 days and will be able to begin to return to normal life. The goal of our study is to assess the feasibility and tolerability of VATS for lung metastasis and eventually deliver this care as an outpatient procedure. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.tagline: Video Assisted Lung Tumor Removal
current_roster.name: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial

current_roster.description: The intestinal microbiota (bacteria, fungi) are a group of organisms in the intestines that are highly functional, producing substances that may have effects on multiple organs in the body. Intestinal dysbiosis is a term used when there is an imbalance in the normal bacteria found in the intestines. Intestinal dysbiosis in people has been found to be an important contributing factor in many diseases. The currently available tests for intestinal dysbiosis are typically fecal tests that rely on identification of the bacteria and other micro-organisms that are present. This study is the first step in identifying the function of the intestinal microbiome in health and in the diseased state. In this study blood, urine, and stool samples will be collected to evaluate the intestinal microbiome. With this information we can begin to understand the microbiomes effects on the entire body. We will eventually be able to use this information to help uncover if and how intestinal dysbiosis is contributing to diseases of the intestine and other organs.
current_roster.name: Metabolomics Trial to Evaluate for Systemic Consequences of Dysbiosis

current_roster.description: Previous studies have demonstrated durable responses to inhaled IL-15 in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma without any recognized toxicity. Unfortunately, IL-15 did not work for the majority of dogs and this may be due to the fact that resident NK cells may not be present or may be exhausted. We are therefore investigating whether the addition of autologous activated NK cells might improve response rates in canine patients receiving inhaled IL-15. The primary endpoints of this study are to determine the safety and preliminary evidence of efficacy for this combination treatment.
current_roster.name: Inhaled IL-15 and Autologous NK Immunotherapy for Treatment of Lung Metastases
current_roster.top_investigator: Robert Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine the safety, ideal dose, and effectiveness of a new therapy for oral squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in cats. Oral SCC is an aggressive cancer that invades locally into bone and soft tissues of the mouth. In cats, the tumors are usually too large to be safely removed with surgery and other treatments are not very effective. STAT3 is a signaling molecule known to function abnormally in many SCC tumors in cats and people and we believe that the STAT3 decoy we are studying may be able to shut off STAT3 function and slow or stop this cancer in cats and people.
current_roster.name: STAT3 Decoy for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: We are actively recruiting senior cats aged 17 years or older (super seniors) to partake in our longevity research study. As part of study participation, every qualifying cat should have an up-to-date clinical record. An oral swab collection kit will be used to obtain a DNA sample. Each feline DNA sample will undergo whole genome sequencing (WGS). We will use WGS data from a randomly selected cohort from the general domestic cat population as a control group and perform Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to identify any potential genetic variants and clinical characteristics associated with a longer lifespan and healthspan in domestic cats. Results from this study could help inform the development of therapies targeting age-related chronic diseases and improving the quality of life of senior cats.
current_roster.name: Unraveling the genetics behind feline longevity

current_roster.description: Feline CKD is often diagnosed at the late stages of disease, when significant damage has already occurred and treatment options are limited. The goal of our study is two-fold. First, we are looking to understand whether particular genotypes might contribute to a higher likelihood of developing CKD. In addition to this, we want to investigate whether there is a correlation between the state of the oral microbiome and the presence of CKD, a connection that has been previously indicated in studies on human CKD patients. This project could lead to the development of an early detection feline CKD test and also inform therapeutics development in this disease area. An oral swab collection kit will be used to obtain a DNA sample, we are actively recruiting cats diagnosed with any stage of CKD from across the age spectrum. However, we are particularly interested in cats diagnosed with CKD before their fifth birthday. For our control group, we are recruiting cats of all ages that have not been diagnosed with any known dental or systemic diseases.
current_roster.name: Feline Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) Study

current_roster.description: STUDY CLOSED Purpose To evaluate the incidence of tonsillar metastasis based on histopathology in dogs with various types of malignant oral tumors. Background Squamous cell carcinomas and melanomas are common types of oral tumors in dogs. While canine oral squamous cell carcinomas and oral melanomas both are known to metastasize to the tonsil, the incidence of tonsillar metastasis has not been reported in veterinary medicine yet. We do know that primary tonsillar tumors such as tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma can (SCC) behave very aggressively and are also a highly metastatic disease. The prognosis for canine tonsillar SCC is poor, and tonsil tumors, whether primary or metastatic from an oral tumor, generally behave very aggressively. Therefore, an assessment of tonsillar metastasis in dogs with oral tumors will be an important factor for determining the overall prognosis. Study Design Dogs undergoing complete staging of a malignant primary oral tumor at theAnimal Cancer Care and Research Center in Roanoke, VAwill be evaluated for this study. Staging examination: The minimum diagnostics of complete blood count, serum biochemical analysis, fine needle aspiration of bilateral mandibular lymph node, three-view thoracic radiographs, and computed tomography (CT) of the head /neck, thorax and abdomen are required to be included in this study. These are the standard staging procedures for dogs with oral cancer, and are not part of the research study. Bilateral tonsillar and primary oral tumor biopsy: Under general anesthesia, we will perform a thorough oropharyngeal examination, tonsillar assessment, and right and left tonsillar and primary oral tumor biopsies. The biopsy tissues will be submitted to board-certified pathologists. This biopsy will be done specifically for this study. The results of this biopsy will be shared with you, and they may help to guide treatment planning for your dog. Compensation Participants will receive a CT scan, primary tumor and bilateral tonsillar biopsy procedures, histopathology, anesthesia, and oral pain medications at no cost. Owners will be responsible for all other medical fees related to the diagnosis and treatment of their dogs cancer.
current_roster.name: Assessment of Tonsillar Metastasis as Standard Staging Examination in Dogs with Primary Oral Tumors

current_roster.description: The University of Wyoming is requesting blood or necropsy tissues from hedgehogs with a clinical diagnosis of Wobbly Hedgehog Syndrome. All procedures will be carried out at the owners primary veterinarians hospital or their subsequent referral hospital, or in the case of necropsy, the Wyoming State Veterinary Laboratory. The owners primary veterinarian or referring veterinarian will collect the blood and if applicable, necropsy tissues. Enrollees from around the nation are encouraged to participate and are not limited to any specific state residence. We will screen enrollment to only hedgehog patients which have been selected to undergo blood draws or necropsy as part of their normal diagnostic work-up as per their veterinarians discretion. In this case, blood or necropsy tissues will not be collected for the sole purpose of our study, rather we will enroll and provide free shipping of samples and histopathology interpretation services to those patients that were already selected to undergo the procedure and collect subsequent biofluids at our request. Veterinarians of participating hedgehogs will be asked to collect serum during normal diagnostic work-up. At the discretion of the veterinarian, samples are collected into red-topped blood collection tubes, let sit on the countertop to separate, and transferred to a new tube, and refrigerated (4C) or frozen (-20C) until shipping. Also at the discretion of the veterinarian, tissues collected during necropsy or whole hedgehog carcasses can be shipped in addition to serum samples. If requested by the owner, whole carcass shipments to the University of Wyoming will include free cremation and free shipping of cremated remains back to the owner. Veterinarian staff will contact Rae Van Sandt (rvansand@uwyo.edu) at the University of Wyoming to obtain a free shipping label and a hedgehog health history questionnaire. Other shipping supplies (shipping container, ice packs, etc.) can be sent if contact to Rae Van Sandt is made in advance of the clinical procedures.
current_roster.name: Investigating the Cause of Wobbly Hedgehog Syndrome

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to develop a new diagnostic procedure to measure how much oxygen is present in tumors, and how much it is reduced by giving different doses of an oxygen carrying drug (OMX). One of the reasons that tumor cells can be resistant to radiation therapy is that the center of tumors often do not have a lot of oxygen present. This imaging trial is to find the best way of detecting hypoxia with imaging studies, and testing how much we can improve oxygen in the tumor with OMX. We will use this information in future studies to improve response to radiation therapy. There will be about 24 pets taking part in this study.
current_roster.name: Non-invasive measurement of improving oxygen in dog tumors with PET imaging and an oxygen carrying molecule

current_roster.description: GSTs (glutathione-S-transferases)are enzymes which help the body eliminate (detoxify) environmental chemicals and certaindrugs. People that have low activity genetic variants in GSTs have a higher risk of certain cancers, such as lymphoma and bladder cancer, especially if they are exposed to certain chemicals in the environment.We want to determine whether the same is true for dogs. Human patients with low activity GST variants also havea higher risk of toxicities from certain drugsused to treat cancer and immune-mediated diseases. We also want todetermine if this is true in dogs. We are focusing on four canine GST genes, GSTT1, GSTT5 (unique to dogs), GSTM1 and GSTP1. We have found variants that are likely to affect enzyme function in each of these genes in dogs.Our overall goal is to see whether these variants are a risk factor for environmental cancers such as lymphoma, bladder cancer, and other tumorsin dogs, and whether risk for these tumors is a combination of GST variants andexposure to environmental chemicals (as measured in the urine or blood).
current_roster.name: Urinary biomarkers of environmental exposures in dogs with bladder cancer

current_roster.description: Our study willevaluate the effects of probiotic administrationon seizure frequency and the microbiome in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy (IE) receiving anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs). 1.The primary objective of the study is to compare the frequency of seizures per month in dogs during periods of not receiving probiotics and while receiving probiotics. Study participants will continue to receive their prescribed AEDs throughout the entire duration of the study. 2.The secondary objectives include evaluating the microbiome of dogs with IEprior to receiving probiotics and their microbiome while receiving probiotics, as well as the long-term effects of being on a probiotic on the canine microbiome once the probiotic is no longer being administered.
current_roster.name: Effect of Probiotics on Seizure Frequency and Microbiome in Dogs

current_roster.description: We are seeking a candidate gene for primary closed angle glaucoma in dogs, a disease in which the optic nerve and retina are damaged resulting in vision loss, often due to alterations in the pressure inside the eye. Affected dogs are blinded, often in both eyes, and pain due to pressure elevation may necessitate removal of one or both eyes. In this study, we will collect data about various parameters of eyes of different breeds of dogs with and without glaucoma that may be correlated with the development of glaucoma, and will collect cheek swabs and blood from animals to compare genetic changes with the ocular findings. With the clinical findings and genetic testing, we may be able to identify a gene associated with glaucoma that will allow us to test dogs prior to breeding to decrease the incidence of this blinding disease. Dogs will be recruited by various breed clubs, at dog shows, and in the clinic. The owners will sign a consent form. Each dog will undergo the same procedures routinely done to evaluate clinical patients who have glaucoma or are suspected to be predisposed to glaucoma. Initially each dog will be gently restrained and undergo a complete ophthalmic examination, including slit lamp biomicroscopy, indirect ophthalmoscopy and tonometry (intraocular pressure measurement). Topical anesthetic will then be applied, and gonioscopy (drainage angle evaluation) will be performed. The eyes will be dilated for indirect ophthalmoscopy, then ultrasound of the eye will be performed to obtain measurements of different parts of the eye. A cheek swab or a venous blood sample will be obtained from each dog.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of risk factors and identification of candidate genes for primary closed angle glaucoma in dogs

current_roster.description: Ante-mortem (neurologic exam and blood pressure should be performed prior to sedation): 1 - Owners will fill out a questionnaire about their cat's behavior at home. 2 -Cats will have a complete neurologic exam performed. 3 - Cats will have a blood pressure performed by oscillometry. 4-Cats will have indirect ophthalmoscopy & slit lamp biomicroscopy. 5 - Cats will have basic blood work (complete blood count,biochemistry, and T4) performed,using sedation (if needed). 6.-Cats will be euthanized. Post-mortem:All tissue collection will bepost-mortem for this study. In addition to tissue, urine samples will be collected post-mortem. The study population are client-owned cats that are over 12 years old and have been euthanized at UWVC for any reason.
current_roster.tagline: Feline cognitive dysfunction
current_roster.name: Feline Cognitive Dysfunction

current_roster.description: Radiation therapy uses high-energy radiation to shrink tumors and kill cancer cells. The radiation is intended to damage the DNA of the cancer cells beyond repair so that they stop dividing or die. Radioembolization with Y90 is an advanced form of radiation therapy that delivers high-dose radiation with precision, enabling precise targeting of a tumor with minimal damage to nearby healthy tissue.Y90 has been used to successfully treat liver tumors in over 100,000 human patients. Studies have revealed that Y90 is well-tolerated by the patient, results in minimal complications or side effects, maintains or improves the quality of life, and results in equivalent survival times when compared to surgery for patients with operable tumors.Eye90 microspheres are currently being studied in humans with liver tumors.
current_roster.name: FIDO TREATS

current_roster.description: The primary purpose of this study will be to assess the safety and effects of Lattice SBRT in the treatment of dogs and cats with very large tumors. This study also seeks to better understand the underlying changes to the tumor itself, as well as the immune system.
current_roster.name: Lattice SBRT for palliation of large tumors

current_roster.description: During surgery, the natural defense mechanisms to maintain body temperature are diminished. As a result, temperature regulation can be disrupted resulting in hypothermia (low body temperature) under anesthesia. Addressing hypothermia is critical because multiple scientific studies in people have shown complications linking hypothermia to postoperative outcomes. Surgical drapes are routinely used during surgery to maintain sterility while also contributing to passive warming. The 3M Ioban 2 Antimicrobial Incise Surgical Drape (commonly referred to as Ioban) is an example of an adhesive surgical drape that is readily available, fairly inexpensive, and has multiple benefits in regards to reducing contamination. Due to the adhesive properties of these surgical drapes, they may also decrease wetness and decrease the risk of hypothermia. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of Ioban in dogs undergoing abdominal surgery to determine if 1. Ioban can help maintain normal body temperature alongside the use of routine active warming devices and if 2. Ioban reduces surgical site complications. Because Ioban usage is already implemented by surgeons the addition or absence of this device will not provide a substantial change to the surgical procedure. There are no known adverse effects of using barrier drapes such as Ioban. This research is important to address anesthesia-induced hypothermia to provide better patient care and reduce postoperative complications.Your dog will undergo abdominal surgery as discussed by your dogs doctor. Patients will be randomized to determine which patients receive Ioban application. Each dog will be routinely prepped for surgery using the same technique. During surgery,the use of Ioban as an additional surgical drape will be the only difference between treatment and control groups. Using an aerobic and aerobic culture swab, the subcutaneous tissue will be sampled to look for the presence of bacterial growth. With the goal of monitoring temperature, temperature will be measured at the start of surgery, multiple times throughout the procedure, at the end of surgery, and up to 1 hour after surgery. Standard warming techniques will be used during surgery for all patients in the study. All patients will be housed post-surgery in temperature-controlled wards. Patient incisions will be assessed at 2 weeks for normal healing.
current_roster.name: Investigation of Ioban Use During Canine Celiotomy

current_roster.description: Liver cancer can occur in dogs, and pre-operative planning and staging is important in these patients to understand the full extent of their disease and look for spread of cancer elsewhere. In veterinary medicine, this is typically accomplished with imaging techniques such as computed tomography (CT), or standard abdominal ultrasonography. However, these imaging studies often miss additional tumors or underestimate the severity of disease, and more extensive disease may be found at the time of open abdominal surgery, changing the treatment plan. This places emotional and financial burden on the owner, and puts the patient through a possibly unnecessary invasive, painful surgical procedure.In people, laparoscopic ultrasound (LUS) has been used successfully for staging of liver cancer and is now considered the gold-standard. Laparoscopic ultrasound is a minimally-invasive imaging technique that involves placing an ultrasound probe through a small incision into the abdomen, and directly placing the probe on the liver to acquire images. This is advantageous due to the ability to better visualize the liver without other organs in the way and by directly seeing the liver with the laparoscope (camera) at the same time. Additionally, LUS can be used to guide minimally-invasive surgery of the liver.The purpose of this study is to describe the use and feasibility of laparoscopic ultrasonography of the liver in healthy dogs. Our ultimate goal is to eventually apply this technique to dogs with liver cancer to advance the clinical management of these cases. Each dog will undergo a complete physical exam and have screening bloodwork performed to ensure they are healthy prior to undergoing anesthesia and surgery. Dogs will be placed under general anesthesia, and a small (2 cm) incision will be made into the abdomen, through which all procedures will be performed. One to two additional small incisions (0.5-1cm) may also be needed to provide adequate access to perform the spay and/or gastropexy. A laparoscope (camera) and special ultrasound probe intended for laparoscopic use will be inserted through the incision to perform thorough imaging and evaluation of the entire liver. No surgical procedure will be performed on the liver. Following the acquisition of both laparoscopic images and ultrasound images, each dog will have their intended elective procedure (spay, gastropexy, or both) performed.
current_roster.tagline: laparoscopic ultrasonography of the liver
current_roster.name: Description of Laparoscopic Ultrasound of the Liver in Healthy Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Evidence exists to suggest that aging of the kidney may contribute to the onset and progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Rapamycin is a drug that is a known modulator of the aging process and additionally may decrease the formation of fibrosis (scarring) in the kidney. A feline formulation of the drug is available and the purpose of this study is to assess the potential benefit of the drug in cats with CKD. What qualifies my pet for enrollment in this in this trial? Cats with stable IRIS stage 2 CKD (serum creatinine 2.0 - 2.8 mg/dL) Amenable to pill administration Body weight > 2.7 kg (6 lbs) Other concurrent therapies such as dietary management, potassium supplementation, anti-hypertensive medications and subcutaneous fluids are acceptable if they were initiated at least 28 days prior to enrollment and are given consistently throughout the study period. Exclusion criteria include congenital CKD (dysplasia or polycystic kidney disease), diabetes mellitus, other uncontrolled systemic illnesses, complications of CKD such as kidney infection or ureteral obstruction, moderate to severe anemia (PCV < 25%), decompensated CKD requiring hospitalization and intravenous fluid therapy. Prohibited concurrent therapies include cyclosporine, cisapride, beta-blocking agents, antifungal agents, diltiazem and other medications that could affect rapamycin concentrations. What does enrolling my pet in this clinical trial involve? At the time of screening, your cat will receive a physical examination and comprehensive laboratory screening to confirm stage of CKD and exclude other newly diagnosed conditions (eg. hyperthyroidism, hypertension). At one of the screening visits an abdominal ultrasound and radiographs will also be performed (these procedures typically require light sedation).After confirmation of enrollment, your cat will be randomized to receive Rapamycin or placebo which will be administered orally as a whole tablet (followed with water or food to ensure swallowing) once weekly for 12 weeks. Some cats may require two tablets per dose. You will fill out a quality of life assessment at the beginning of the study and then twice more during the study as well as an owner diary. You will be asked to bring your cat back for three recheck visits (day 14, 42 and 84) for a physical exam, blood and urine collection and blood pressure measurement. Client Compensation Your cat will receive complimentary assessment and management of disease by a board-certified specialist in feline CKD as well as standard of care laboratory monitoring regardless of study group. Cats randomized to the study drug group will possibility benefit from this therapy. There is no cost to you for enrolling your cat in this study. You will receive complimentary physical examination for your cat and diagnostic testing. You will also receive $25 per visit incentive.
current_roster.name: Rapamycin in cats with chronic kidney disease
current_roster.top_investigator: Jessica Quimby, Professor; Vice Chair of Research

current_roster.description: Many sarcomas in both people and dogs can be resistant to the available treatment options. A new way of fighting these sarcomas is with immunotherapy, which helps the bodys own immune system fight the cancer. There is a type of immune cell in the body, called a macrophage, that normally helps fight bacteria and viruses, as well as helps heal wounds. However, it is also known that macrophages can help sarcomas grow and spread. There is a new drug, a small molecule called NCGC00413972 (NIH 972), which can re-program these macrophages to instead fight against the tumor. This has been shown to be successful in cells and in mice. There is also information that this drug is safe to give to healthy dogs. The primary goal of this trial is to evaluate the safety and biologic effects of NIH 972 in dogs with cancer. A secondary goal of this trial is to evaluate any anti-tumor effects it may have in dogs with sarcomas. If the exams, tests, and procedures show that your dog can take part in the study, and you choose to enroll them, then the following will happen as part of the study: On the first day your dog receives the new drug, they will have blood drawn at multiple time points and will be in hospital for close monitoring for at least 8 hours after their first dose. They will either need to stay overnight with us or come back for an additional blood draw 24 hours from their first dose. They will receive a tablet daily and be rechecked 1, 2, 4, and 6 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening, and the drug is well tolerated. On these follow-up visits, we will collect additional blood, both to assess how they are handling the drug and to store for research purposes. If needed to monitor their cancer, they will also have imaging performed at certain visits. Two weeks after starting the drug, they will have another biopsy of their tumor in addition to additional blood draws. Sedation will be required for the biopsies and imaging (if applicable to your dog). In the unfortunate event of your dog passing away or being humanely euthanized while in this trial, a necropsy will be performed to help understand the cause of death.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment for Dogs with Sarcomas
current_roster.name: Phase I Clinical Trial of NCGC00413972 (NIH 972) in Dogs with Spontaneously Occurring Sarcomas

current_roster.description: Randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial to assess a potential new treatment for oral melanoma in dogs. Investigational product or placebo will be administered once every 2 weeks for approximately 6 months (15 scheduled visits). All trial visits must occur at one of the designated clinical trial sites. Period lab work and thoracic radiographs will be performed to asses each dog's overall health. Owners are required to sign a consent form before their dog is enrolled, complete owner diaries at home, and complete a single Quality of Life assessment question at each visit.
current_roster.tagline: Dogs with Oral Melanoma
current_roster.name: Oral Melanoma Study in Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate cats with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) for abnormal blood clotting activity Background Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common form of acquired heart disease in cats. Cats with HCM are at a higher risk for abnormal blood clot formation, but the way that this happens isnt well understood. This study hopes to determine if cats with HCM have evidence of hypercoagulability, which is the tendency for blood to clot excessively.
current_roster.tagline: A new way to test blood clotting in cats with HCM
current_roster.name: Evaluating cats with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) for abnormal blood clotting activity

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate the activity of a type of communication signal released from cells in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas after they are treated with non-invasive histotripsy ablation Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of skin cancer in dogs. They tend to develop slowly and dont usually metastasize when they are low grade. A biopsy is needed to determine the tumor grade. Surgery is the treatment of choice, but if a minimal surgery (removal of only the tumor that can be seen or felt) is performed, the tumor is likely to grow back. Removal of the tumor and several centimeters of normal-appearing tissue is required for complete removal. However, this can be impossible without amputation or the addition of radiation therapy, particularly when the tumors are large or affect certain areas of the body like the limbs or face. Alternative treatments to surgery or radiation are needed. We have previously evaluated a non-surgical, non-radiation, non-thermal focused ultrasound treatment (histotripsy) to kill soft tissue sarcomas affecting pet dogs. This technology has also been used in humans with liver tumors. Histotripsy focuses microsecond-long soundwaves through the skin onto a precise target area of the tumor. This causes air bubbles in the tumor tissue to expand and collapse, mechanically disintegrating the surrounding tumor tissue. Research in rodents, pet dogs, and humans have shown that the liquified tissue stimulates the immune system to recognize cancer in other parts of the body. The purpose of this study is to evaluate one type of communication signal released from cells, termed extracellular vesicles (EVs). EVs carry protein and genetic messages that cause immediate changes in the receiving cell. EVs and their cargo can be used as a non-invasive way to diagnose a tumor or look for signals to predict response to treatment or prognosis. We will extract and measure EVs and their immune signal cargo from the liquified tumor tissue, the lymph nodes, and the blood after histotripsy treatment of soft tissue sarcomas. We hope to find that histotripsy increases the number and type of EVs in the blood, which would be the first step in developing a liquid biopsy for diagnosis; we also hope to find that histotripsy treatment changes the communication with the immune system, serving as a mechanism to explain the changes seen in the immune response after histotripsy. To determine how histotripsy may affect EVs, we are recruiting dogs with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo histotripsy treatment of the tumor. An existing tumor must be present for treatment. The application of this experimental therapy has the potential to directly enhance the quality of life of dogs diagnosed with soft tissue sarcomas and defray the cost of treatment. At the same time, the results of our study may lead to improved liquid biopsy and treatment options for human cancer patients.
current_roster.tagline: Ultrasound ablation of soft tissue sarcomas
current_roster.name: Treating soft tissue sarcomas in dogs with non-surgical ultrasound ablation

current_roster.description: Client-owned dogs that are presented to the cardiology service at the University of Florida Veterinary Hospital for medical treatment and monitoring of CHF secondary to severe degenerative valve disease will be screened for inclusion in this study. Only dogs with documented hypochloremia and congestive heart failure(CHF) secondary to degenerative valve disease will be enrolled. Dogs will be randomly assigned in a 1:1ratio to either placebo or acetazolamide (5-15 mg/kg q12 hr) treatment and both owner and investigator will be blinded to treatment. Other inclusion criteria are: weight >2kg, currently receiving medications that are standard of care for CHF (loop diuretic of either furosemide or torsemide, ACE-inhibitor of either enalapril or benazepril, pimobendan, and spironolactone) and willingness to feed a diet optimally formulated for dogs with CHF. Dogs not meeting inclusion criteria for diet or medications will be started on the appropriate ones and enrolled at a subsequent visit 2 weeks later. Below is a timeline and description of each visit over a 10 week period. Bloodwork and urine will be monitored at each visit to determine if blood chloride levels increase with treatment and to monitor for side effects of dehydration, increased kidney values, and electrolyte derangements. Thoracic radiographs and echocardiography will be done at the initial visit to characterize disease and ensure inclusion criteria are met. Thoracic radiographs will be assessed at the end of the study to assess CHF control. 1. Visit 1: Screening: Dogs will be screened for enrollment at this visit to establish a baseline and ensure inclusion criteria are met. Examination, blood pressure, serum comprehensive renal panel, urine comprehensive renal panel, thoracic radiographs, and echocardiogram will be performed. Dogs will be screened by phone or email prior to this study visit to determine eligibility based on historical bloodwork showing hypochloremia and thoracic radiographs documenting CHF, but this visit will verify that dogs meet enrollment criteria. Dogs that are not on standard of care treatments (furosemide or torsemide, pimobendan, enalapril or benazepril, and spironolactone) will be started on medications at this visit. Diet history will be reviewed and dogs will be transitioned to a diet that is optimally formulated for congestive heart failure(Royal Canin Early Cardiac Support) if not already eating this diet. Dietary uniformity is necessary to control oral electrolyte intake to ensure that the amount of chloride in the diet is not a confounding variable. 2. Visit 2: Enrollment: Dogs will be sequentially enrolled as they are presented to the University of Florida Veterinary Hospital and randomized to placebo or acetazolamide in a 1:1 ratio at this visit. The examination with blood pressure, diet history, and comprehensive renal panel on serum and on urine will be performed during this visit. Inclusion criteria (especially presence of hypochloremia) will again be verified and this visit will serve as a 2 baseline (no treatment)visit to help determine the variability in biochemical measurements. Owners will be asked to bring their study medications to future visits so administration can be verified by capsule count. 3. Visit 3: Short-term recheck: Dogs will return 2 weeks after starting on study treatment. This visit will involve history with confirmation of diet recommendations and counting of remaining capsules to ensure administration of treatments. Examination, blood pressure, and serum and urine comprehensive renal panels will be performed. 4. Visit 4: Medium-term recheck: Dogs will return 2 months after starting on study treatment. This visit will involve history with confirmation of diet recommendations and counting of remaining capsules to ensure administration of medications. Examination, blood pressure, thoracic radiographs, and serum and urine comprehensive renal panels will be performed. A prior power analysis based on previous work we have done characterizing blood chloride levels in CHF dogs indicates that we will need 62 dogs to show a difference in chloride concentrations between treated and non-treated groups (31 in each group which accounts for an anticipated 20% attrition). We anticipate that enrollment will be completed within an 18 month period based on the current caseload.
current_roster.name: Tolerability and clinical efficacy of acetazolamide for treatment of hypochloremia in canine congestive heart failure

current_roster.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo amputation or radiation followed immediately by vaccination every 3 weeks for 6 vaccines. If no metastases are found at the last staging visit (1 month after the last vaccine), dogs will then receive 6 monthly boosters for life or until progression. Alternatively, if early metastases (single or multiple small lung nodules " 700 dogs with melanoma or OSA) will be treated and monitored for an hour, with resolutions of symptoms the dog will be returned to the owner. In future vaccinations, these dogs will receive an antihistamine medication 20 min prior to vaccination. In the unlikely event that the vaccine sites/dog show severe changes such as pain, inflammation, necrosis with ulceration, dermatitis, or severe swelling the dog will be treated.
current_roster.name: Vaccine study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Sepsis is a condition caused by the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream and the resulting reaction that the body has when trying to fight off the infection. The most common cause of sepsis in dogs is a condition called a septic abdomen. In this condition, there is an infection within the abdominal cavity, which was the origin for the bacteria that entered the bloodstream. The most common reason for an infection within the abdomen is the rupture of an intestine with leakage of the intestinal contents into the abdomen. Septic abdomen is a critical condition that requires emergency surgery to resolve the infection followed by intensive postoperative care to keep the patient stable and treat any remaining infection.Because of the critical nature of septic abdomens, the prognosis associated with the condition is guarded. This highlights the need for improved diagnostic tests and treatments for dogs diagnosed with septic abdomens. The ORBITS study seeks to collect blood samples from dogs diagnosed with septic abdomens as well as healthy dogs to look for blood-based markers that could be used to develop novel diagnostic tests for septic peritonitis. Additionally, these blood samples will undergo various forms of genomic analysis (DNA, RNA, and proteins) to identify alterations that occur during sepsis that may be used to develop new treatments that could improve the survival rate. current_roster.description: Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a disorder characterized by severely low platelets due to attack by white blood cells. This is often associated with bruising and occasionally severe bleeding episodes. The first-line treatment of ITP usually includes steroids, chemotherapies, and various other immunosuppressive agents.Treatments are targeted at rapid increases in circulating platelets, to decrease life-threatening bleeding.Embolization, a minimally invasive, catheter-based procedure, has been used on the spleen to treat hypersplenism and splenic trauma in humans.A unique observation in these patients was the development of a consistent and prolonged thrombocytosis and erythrocytosis (high platelet count, high red blood cell count).Partial splenic embolization, where particles are dispensed to the blood vessels that feed the spleen, was subsequently used as a direct treatment for low platelets. The effectiveness of partial splenic artery embolization (PSAE) for ITP has been reported in humans, with curative responses occurring in >80% of patients, despite being refractory to traditional steroid therapy.Preclinical studies in dogs have demonstrated the safety of partial splenic artery embolization (PSAE) in healthy dogs. The primary aim of this study is to describe the procedure of PSAE in dogs diagnosed with ITP. A secondary aim will be to define feasibility by the extent and length of effect through serial platelet count monitoring. current_roster.description: Dogs are affected by a range of eye diseases involving melanocytes, the pigment-containing cells within and around the eye. Many of these diseases such as ocular melanosis affect certain breeds more heavily than others, indicating a likely genetic contribution to which dogs are affected. Many of these melanocytic diseases can have vision-impairing and/or painful consequences for dog eyes, including glaucoma (high eye pressure), uveitis (eye inflammation),and cataract formation (opacity of the eye's lens); and many of them affect both eyes simultaneously (at the same time). In some scenarios, painful and blind eyes from affected dogs must be surgically removed as the only means of providing comfort to the affected dog. The objectives of this protocol are (1)to collect genetic and clinical data todetermine how affected dogs inherit these diseases (i.e. how are they passed along to offspring from two parents), (2) investigate and identify genetic mutations or other genetic factors that may contribute to those diseases, and (3) to determine which mutations may be possible targets for eventual prevention and/or treatment of those diseases. For example, if a genetic mutation can be identified as a risk factor or cause for a melanocytic eye disease, a genetic test can be developed to screen dogs prior to breeding in order to decrease a disease's incidence moving forward.
current_roster.name: Ocular melanosis in Cairn Terriers

current_roster.description: Cutaneous epitheliotropic lymphoma is a rare neoplastic condition in dogs. Current treatment options are limited and duration of response is often short. Laverdia-CA1 (verdinexor) is a conditionally approved oral tablet for treatment of lymphoma in dogs. Laverdia has been evaluated for the treatment of multicentric nodal lymphoma but has not yet been evaluated for the treatment of cutaneous epitheliotropic lymphoma.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Laverdia-CA1 (verdinexor) for Treatment of Naïve Canine Cutaneous Epitheliotropic Lymphoma

current_roster.description: This is anopen-labelclinical for dogs with non-seasonal, moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (AD). Theclinical trial will evaluate the efficacy and safety of OKV-1001 (a new formulation of mycophenolate).Prednisolone will be regularly used at the beginning of the study (1mg/kg q24 hours for 1 week and everyother day for another week) and as needed throughout the study as rescue medication.
current_roster.name: A Field Efficacy and Safety Pilot Study of OKV-1001 for theTreatment of Chronic, Non-Seasonal Moderate-to-Severe AtopicDermatitis

current_roster.description: Xylitol is an artificial sweetener commonly found in sugar-free gum. Although safe for humans, xylitol is highly toxic to dogs. In dogs, xylitol causes severe drops in blood sugar, damage to the liver, and can be fatal if left untreated. The mainstay of therapy includes treatment with IV fluids, sugar supplementation, and the administration of liver protectant products to blunt/reduce the severity of the liver damage that is induced. This study will compare the liver protective capacity of two veterinary liver protectant products in dogs suffering from xylitol toxicity.
current_roster.name: Comparison of resolution of ALT elevations using two liver nutraceutical products for canine acute hepatic toxicity secondary to x

current_roster.description: The goal of the Valley Fever WOOF study is to prospectively study the outcomes of dogs recently diagnosed with coccidioidomycosis. We will evaluate length of time to response to treatment, how frequently dogs fail initial antifungal therapy, and whether regional differences in treatment protocols exist.
current_roster.name: The Valley Fever WOOF (Web-based Observations, Outcomes, and Findings) Study

current_roster.description: Verdinexor is a chemotherapy drug that has been conditionally approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine lymphoma. Verdinexor is a selective inhibitor of nuclear export (SINE) compound, and this family of drug has demonstrated encouraging results in preclinical studies when combined with other chemotherapeutic drugs. These studies offer encouragement that these types of combinations and clinical results could be achieved in dogs. This study seeks to establish the tolerability of verdinexor in combination with doxorubicin in dogs with cancer. The results of this study could be used to advance the study of this combination of drugs in future clinical trials that focus on a specific cancer types. The study duration is 120 days and consists of a total of 10 hospital visits. The trial is fully funded with no costs to the owner. current_roster.description: A large number of different canine and human cancers appear to rely on signaling through 2 important cellular pathways; the MAPK pathway and the PI3K/mTOR pathway. The drugs trametinib and sapanisertib, which target signaling through these 2 pathways, appear to have significant antitumor effects both in tissue culture and in mouse models. When these 2 drugs were given to laboratory dogs at the doses we plan to test, they were well tolerated and the amount of drug appearing in the blood was predicted to be enough to inhibit tumor growth. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety, biologic effects, and antitumor activity of combined trametinib and sapanisertib given to dogs with measurable malignant tumors. Your dog will receive trametinib orally once daily and sapanisertib orally every other day. They will be rechecked 6 days, and 2, 4, and 8 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening and the drugs are well tolerated. Visits will generally take about 1 hour, except for the first visit and the Day 6 and Week 4 visits, which may take several hours or all day. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease is stable or smaller). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound). Standard bloodwork and urinalysis measurement will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the amount of trametinib and sapanisertib appearing in the blood and for changes in other blood markers. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 5 teaspoons. Before starting treatment and after 6 days and 4 weeks, your dog will have a small sample of tumor tissue removed through a biopsy to look for changes in signaling in the tumor cells, if your dog’s tumor is in a location where it can be biopsied. This helps us know if the drugs are finding their targets in the cancer cells. This biopsy will require short acting sedation, and your dog may receive several days of oral pain medication after the procedure.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Therapy for Dogs with Cancer
current_roster.name: Combination Trametinib and Sapanisertib Clinical Trial Pilot Study for Canine Malignant Neoplasia

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN)) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine / piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer also known as urothelial carcinoma. We will evaluate tumor response, clinical side effects, and quality of life as part of this study. Additionally, we will evaluate immune response and characterize the stool and urine microbiome and metabolome to understand the potential effects of the probiotic. Our broader goal is to improve cancer care and outcomes in dogs with bladder cancer.
current_roster.name: TCC Probiotic

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, safety, efficacy and anti-cancer immune stimulation of a novel method of delivering radiation therapy, lattice radiation therapy, in cats with measurable oral squamous cell carcinoma. Lattice radiation therapy is special type of stereotactic radiation therapy utilizing a state-of-the-art linear accelerator that has on board advanced imaging capabilities and sophisticated software to deliver precisely-targeted radiation at much higher doses, in only a few treatments, as compared to traditional radiation therapy. This permits maximum dose delivery within the target while minimizing dose to the surrounding healthy tissue to minimize side effects. SBRT is used routinely to treat brain tumors in veterinary medicine and has been used to treat various cancers in cats.
current_roster.name: FOSCC Lattice

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.
current_roster.tagline: feline metastatic mammary carcinoma
current_roster.name: EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF A NOVEL ANTI-CANCER THERAPEUTIC FOR THE TREATMENT OF METASTATIC MAMMARY CARCINOMA IN CATS

visible_sc_items.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

current_roster.description: Feline atopic skin syndrome (FASS) is a prevalent skin condition in cats characterized by chronic inflammation, itching (pruritus), and discomfort. It often results from hypersensitivity to environmental allergens such as pollen, dust mites, or certain foods. Felines affected by FASS may exhibit incessant scratching, licking, and chewing, leading to secondary skin infections and hair loss. Typical management strategies currently combine allergen avoidance, anti-inflammatory medications, and, in severe cases, immunosuppressive therapy. Topical treatments, such as medicated shampoos or spot-on products, can provide relief for localized symptoms. However, these strategies have limited efficacy or can have significant side-effects. We are now opening a clinical trial for a novel monoclonal antibody (MAB) that targets FASS. It is double-blinded, placebo controlled study. The clinical trial aims to evaluate both efficacy and safety of the MAB in affected felines.
current_roster.tagline: Clinical Trial for a New Drug Aimed at Providing Relief for Feline Atopic Skin Syndrome
current_roster.name: Novel Monoclonal Antibody for Feline Atopic Skin Syndrome (FASS)

current_roster.description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of a Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL) when given to dogs with cancer. This clinical trial conducted in pet dogs with cancer is designed to test whether the immune responses generated through routine vaccination against common viruses can be re-directed toward cancer cells. The approach appears to work in mouse models of cancer, and we are interested in evaluating it in pet dogs that have naturally occurring cancers that are very similar to humans. If successful, this research would help develop safe, effective, and low-cost ways of treating cancer that would benefit a wide variety of patients, especially those that live in communities with minimal access to cutting-edge cancer care (such as developing and low-resource countries). Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. As part of this study, your dog will be randomized to receive one of two vaccine protocols: either combination treatment with Shingrix/Garadasil vaccines or a rabies vaccine. Your dog will come to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for the primer phase, which includes 1-3 weekly injections of the vaccines. Two weeks later, they will return to start weekly visits for injection of the VPL directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. Dogs will be treated with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) prior to the injection and then will be monitored for 4-6 hours post-injection. One final visit will be required one week after the last injection (total length of study 12-14 weeks). Physical exam and blood collections for study purposes will be performed at each visit. A complete blood count will be performed every week during the treatment phase; blood and urine for serum chemistry profile and urinalysis will also be collected on Weeks 1, 5, and 9. Chest x-rays +/- abdominal ultrasound will be checked prior to the primer vaccine and at Week 9. Lymph node aspirates for study purposes will be obtained at Weeks 1, 5, and 9 of the treatment phase. Biopsies of your dogs tumor will also be collected prior to the first dose of the drug (pre-treatment), on Week 5, Week 5 at 24hrs, and Week 9 depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general.
current_roster.tagline: Using Immunity from Vaccines to Treat Cancer
current_roster.name: COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers: Validation in Canine Patients

current_roster.description: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common oral tumor in cats and this cancer shares many similarities with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck of people. This tumor is very aggressive in both cats and people and new treatments are greatly needed. This study is investigating a novel oral drug, called a lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD-1) inhibitor, that has been shown to slow the growth and metastasis of oral squamous cell carcinoma in people and mice in laboratory models. This medication has not been previously used in the treatment of oral squamous cell carcinoma in cats and the goals of this study are to establish the dosing, safety and anti-cancer properties when given to cats that have been diagnosed with oral squamous cell carcinoma. Cats participating in this study will have a low dose of the study medication administered in the hospital followed by collection of small amounts of blood throughout the day. These blood samples will be submitted to a lab to determine what dose of medication your cat will receive as part of this study. Once your cats dose of the study drug has been determined (approximately one week after the 1st study visit), your cat will return for tumor biopsies under either heavy sedation or general anesthesia. Some cats will also have a PET/CT scan performed at this visit. You will be dispensed the study medication to give at home once daily for the next three weeks. You cat will have weekly study visits for the next three weeks for examinations and blood collection to make sure they are tolerating the study medication. At the final study visit, your cat will be sedated or anesthetized for additional tumor biopsies +/- a PET/CT scan, if one was performed at the beginning of the clinical trial.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
current_roster.name: Novel Therapy with LSD1 inhibitor for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: Epilepsy is the most common nervous system disorder of dogs, affecting up to 0.75% of the canine population. Approximately one-third of dogs with epilepsy fail to achieve adequate seizure control with anti-seizure medication, and are considered to have drug resistant epilepsy. The mechanisms that lead to drug resistance are poorly understood. Alterations in the population of intestinal bacteria in the Lactobacillus group are believed to play a role in the development and progression of several human diseases of the nervous system, including anxiety/depression, autism, multiple sclerosis and Alzheimers disease. An association between epilepsy and both celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease has been identified in humans, which suggests that changes in intestinal bacterial might play a role in the progression of epilepsy as well. We hypothesize that dogs with epilepsy have alterations in the population of Lactobacillus species in the gastrointestinal tract compared to normal dogs that can influence the course of disease. The objectives of this pilot study are to determine differences in bacterial populations and quantify the Lactobacillus component of the feces of untreated epileptic and control dogs, and to determine the effect of antiepileptic medication on Lactobacillus growth rates. This study will provide preliminary information on the role of gastrointestinal tract bacteria in canine epilepsy. This information has the potential to further our understanding of epilepsy and drug resistance in dogs, and ultimately lead to more successful management of the disorder.
current_roster.name: The microbiota-gut-brain axis in canine epilepsy: determining the role of Lactobacilli

current_roster.description:
Background and Justification To evaluate the effectiveness of verdinexor for the treatment of lymphoma in dogs, it is necessary to understand the natural course of the disease without treatment. The use of a negative (i.e.,untreated) control group will allow for study conduct under masked conditions and to determinethe time to disease progression for dogs receiving placebo tablets. Once enrolled in the study, dogs will be closely monitored for progression and may be removed from the study so that standard therapy may be initiated at the discretion of the veterinarian and owner.

If you elect to enroll your dog in the study, the study sponsor will provide the investigational treatment to be used during the study and pay for the cost of the examinations and tests. If your dog has any adverse events that are study related and require treatment, the sponsor will cover the costs of reasonable treatment.

current_roster.description:
Canine histiocytic sarcoma (HS) is a highly aggressive and often fatal type of cancer that occurs more frequently in certain breeds, including Bernese mountain dog (BMD) (>25%), flat-coated retriever (36%), golden retriever, Rottweiler, and miniature schnauzer. Dogs with HS invariably carry a poor prognosis due to a rapid disease progression and limited effective clinical arsenal.

First line conventional chemotherapy, Lomustine, provides a response rate of 29% for only a median of 96 days

In this proposed trial, we will investigate a novel drug, Trametinib, to determine the antitumor activity (shrinkage of tumor) of the drug in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma using progression-free survival (PFS).

PFS is defined as the percentage of dogs that are progression-free at 6-months post treatment initiation.

Clinical Protocol: - Prior to treatment, a tumor biopsy, and a blood sample (less than one ounce) will be collected. - Upon enrollment, every patient will undergo a complete history, physical examination, laboratory analysis, blood pressure measurement, and diagnostic imaging. - Trametinib will be administered orally, once daily, indefinitely as long as progressive disease is not observed (i.e., stable, partial, or complete response). - The dog will need to return for evaluation of tumor response and/or monitoring of side effects at week 2, then every 4 weeks until week 14, and then every 8 weeks thereafter, until there is evidence of disease progression. - The dog will return for evaluation (physical examination, clinical laboratory assessment of blood, and tumor measurements) on week 2. - Starting on week 4, and every other 4 weeks until week 14, blood and urine sample will be taken, and x-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be repeated to monitor your dog’s response to treatment. - Cardiology consultations (Paid by owner)during Pre-treatment, week 6, week 14 and every 8 weeks till progressive disease. - Starting on week 14, the rechecks will be spaced out to every 8 weeks.

Adverse Events (AEs) will also be evaluated at any unscheduled visit. Owners will be asked to fill out Quality of Life questionnaires prior to study.

current_roster.name: Phase II - Multicenter Clinical Trial of Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma

current_roster.description:
Melanoma is the most dangerous form of skin cancer and kills over 9,300 people a year in the US. Melanoma is also the most common oral cancer in companion dogs and like human melanoma, it is an aggressive cancer that spreads to lymph nodes, lungs, liver, brain, and kidney.

Unfortunately, once melanoma spreads to distant sites, it is usually incurable. Despite advances in standard-of-care therapies (e.g., surgery, radiation therapy (RT) , and chemotherapy), the average survival in dogs with melanoma of advanced stage is less than one year after diagnosis, and less than 6 months if the melanoma has already spread. Therefore, as in human melanoma, new treatments for canine melanoma are needed to improve survival. Treatments that activate the patient's own immune system (immunotherapy) to fight the melanoma have worked very well in some human and dog patients.

We are evaluating a combination of 3 types of therapy all of which have shown immune activation and anti-melanoma activity as single therapies in patients with melanoma. The three therapies include: administration of an immune stimulant directly into the tumor, radiation therapy targeted at the primary tumor, and intravenous administration of an antibody that potentially enhances the body's immune response to the melanoma. We hypothesize that by combining these therapies, we will be able to further extend the life of patients with melanoma.

There are 3 parts to this study: Part 1 has been completed, and we have determined the dose of the immune stimulant to be administered directly into the tumor; In Part 2, the immune stimulant was combined with radiation therapy targeted at the same tumor, and; in Part 3 (Aim 1), the immune stimulant was administered to all sites of palpable disease in addition to the treatments in Part 2. Both Part 2 and Part 3 (Aim 1) are completed.

In Part 3 the immune stimulant is administered directly into the tumor combined with intravenous (IV) Anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor , [ICI]) and radiation therapy directed at the primary oral tumor. The information from this study will guide further clinical trials in both dogs and humans.

Owner Responsibility The owner is expected to make and keep all appointments according to the study protocol. The pet will receive the first ICI therapy and then will receive the RT treatment 2 weeks later along with the second ICI treatment. Six days after the RT treatment, your dog’s tumor will be injected with the IT-IC treatment for 3 consecutive days. ICI treatments will be given 3 more times at 3-week intervals. Chest X-rays will be performed prior to treatment and every 6 weeks thereafter. A biopsy of the tumor and blood/urine sample collection will be performed prior to treatment, on the day they receive RT, on the day they receive the first IT-IC, and again 2 and 5 weeks later.

current_roster.name: The safety of the combination of local radiation, systemic monoclonal antibody and intratumoral cytokine in dogs with melanoma

current_roster.description:
DNA methylation (transformation of normal cells to cancer cells at DNA level) is a critically important modification in cancer cells, which use this mechanism to activate cancer genes and silence of tumor-suppressor genes. Targeting DNA methylation in cancer using DNA hypomethylating drugs reprograms tumor cells to a more normal-like state by affecting multiple pathways, and also sensitizes these cells to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of two DNA hypomethlating drugs TdCyd and Aza-TdC when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. - A biopsy will be collected prior to the first dose of drug (pre-treatment), on Day 8, Day 12 and possibly on Day 22 depending on how the dog has responded to therapy. - The dog will return to UW Veterinary Care on Days 8, 12, 15 and 22. - Serial blood collections (5 time points) will occur on Day 1 of the study. Subsequent, single time point collections will occur on Days 8, 12, 15 and 22. - You will be required to administer doses of TdCyd or Aza-TdC at home on Days 2, 3, 4 and 5 and on Days 9, 10, 11. Your clinician will provide instructions on when and how to provide this medication to your dog.

If the dog’s cancer responds well to the treatment they have been assigned, you will have the option to continue to give the same treatment to your dog for an additional 22 days. During that time, owner will need to continue to regularly visit UW Veterinary Care for blood collection, as well as a biopsy of the dog’s tumor.

current_roster.description:
Osteoarthritis (OA) is estimated to affect as many as 60% of the nearly 90 million adult dogs in the United States. The quality of life in affected dogs is adversely affected by pain, stiffness, various degrees of lameness, and an overall decrease in normal activity.

Osteoarthritis is initiated by articular cartilage damage resulting from a wide range of causes such as trauma, infection, and mechanical or developmental disorders. Management of affected dogs is generally multifaceted and may include weight reduction, surgery, exercise and activity modification, physical rehabilitation, disease-modifying osteoarthritic agents, the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and injections of medications or biologic therapies.

Management of OA with injectable agents is especially attractive because of the perceived efficacy and relative lack of adverse events. As patients with elbow OA age, susceptibility to adverse drug events (ADEs) in dogs treated with drugs such as NSAIDs seems to increase, and many dogs with pre-existing concurrent medical conditions are at higher risk for ADEs. Furthermore, some owners are reluctant to use NSAIDs due to concerns raised about NSAID used in animals as well as in people. Therefore, there is a need to effectively improve the quality-of-life of patients with OA. While injectable agents such as corticosteroids may be effective, there are also a number of adverse events, some of which may result in more rapid deterioration of cartilage.

Biologic therapies, while effective, are costly. A cost-effective, safe, and easy to administer intra-articular treatment for elbow osteoarthritis is attractive. Arthramid Vet is a novel device composed of 2.5% cross-linked polyacrylamide hydrogel, which is non-absorbable and remains in the joint for a prolonged period of time. It is biocompatible, non-toxic, neuro-innocuous, and integrates into the joint tissues, providing shock absorption properties within the joint.

current_roster.description:
Purpose
To evaluate the use of urine samples as a liquid biopsy tool to monitor disease progression in canine osteosarcoma

Background
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs, and it often spreads aggressively. In dogs, metastasis develops in more than 80% of cases. Even with treatment, more than 90% of affected dogs do not survive for more than two years following diagnosis.

Our team has developed a technique (Raman molecular analysis) that can detect changes in the urine that are associated with tumor growth. In this study, we are testing this tool to see how different types of treatment given to dogs with osteosarcoma affect what we’re able to detect in the urine. We’ll use these results to further refine the Raman molecular analysis technique so that it can be more useful in helping us understand and predict the behavior of osteosarcoma.

This study is funded by Virginia Tech’s Focused Ultrasound Innovation Fund.
