current_roster.description:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a frustrating disease to manage for both veterinarians and pet owners. This condition can significantly impact the quality of a pet’s life, requiring frequent visits to the veterinarian and many diagnostic tests. The cause in dogs is unknown but is believed to have a genetic component. Using organoid models, it has been found that stem cells from humans with IBD fail to express certain genes. This is important because these genes are involved in the function of the normal intestinal wall. The same could be true in dogs. This study will look at the genetic differences in dogs with IBD compared to normal dogs using organoid models. Organoids are tiny collections of cells that imitate the organ they were sampled from, in this case, the intestine. By comparing the organoids of healthy dogs to those of dogs with IBD, researchers will gain insights into the cause of IBD, which could lead to more effective treatments for IBD in the future.


Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a free gastrointestinal endoscopy including anesthesia and histopathology of two intestinal sites (duodenum and colon). This is a direct benefit to you and your pet, as this procedure is required to diagnose IBD.
current_roster.tagline: Assessment of the intestinal epithelial barrier of dogs with inflammatory bowel disease using an organoid model
current_roster.name: Assessment of the intestinal epithelial barrier of dogs with inflammatory bowel disease using an organoid model
current_roster.top_investigator: Matthew Wun, DVM, MS, DACVIM (SAIM), Research Affiliate

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin or carboplatin and temozolomide with propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin or carboplatin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.
current_roster.tagline: Combination therapy for dogs with Hemangiosarcoma
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a combination of three drugs in dogs with hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description: Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA, also referred to as autoimmune hemolytic anemia or AIHA) is a life-threatening blood disorder that occurs when the body attacks its own red blood cells. The disease has a high risk of complications and death, and is challenging for owners and veterinarians alike. The goal of this study is to investigate the genetic and immunologic underpinnings of the disease in two dog breeds: Cocker Spaniels (American or English) and English Springer Spaniels.
current_roster.tagline: Understanding the genetic and immunologic basis of IMHA in dogs
current_roster.name: Immune-Mediated Hemolytic Anemia (IMHA) in Dogs

current_roster.description:
Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common form of bladder tumors in dogs. Fractionated radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment options for this form of tumor, and is typically combined with chemotherapy and an NSAID medication. Lapatinib is a newer therapy that has been used as a single agent for the treatment of dogs with this form of bladder tumor. The goal of this trial is to see if the combination of radiation therapy and lapatinib will be safe and well tolerated in dogs with TCC.


If your dog participates in this study, they will receive oral lapatinib through the course of the approximately 4-month study, as well as oral NSAIDs. 5-7 days after starting these medications, they will also complete 15 daily (M-F) fractions of radiation therapy, which requires daily general anesthesia. Patients will get a urinary ultrasound at the beginning and end of the study, which may require sedation for some patients. They will also receive routine bloodwork throughout the course of the study, as well as blood collection at the beginning of radiation, end of radiation, and the conclusion of the study for study purposes.
current_roster.tagline: New combination treatment for dogs with bladder tumors
current_roster.name: Radiation + Targeted Therapy for Bladder Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description:
The goal of the study is to assess the microscopic extension of soft tissue sarcomas. The enrollment will be limited to dogs cytologically or histologically diagnosed soft tissue sarcomas that are undergoing a wide excision. Wide surgical excision, defined as three-centimeter lateral margins and of layer of fascia (dense tissue) deep to the mass, will be performed as the standard of care. While under general anesthesia and immediately prior to routine surgery, sterile tattoo ink will be used to mark specific margins around the tumor. All tattoo ink will be within the tumor sample and planned margin with no tattoo ink applied outside the tissue to be removed.


There are no additional costs associated with the study beyond those acquired through routine care for the underlying condition. The study provides only costs toward the surgical procedure (mass removal) itself and the histopathology (biopsy) charges. This combination of charges would typically be $441-$1074 depending on tumor size. All other costs are the responsibility of the owner.
current_roster.tagline: Soft tissue sarcoma undergoing wide excision
current_roster.name: Characterization of Soft Tissue Sarcoma Microscopic Extension
current_roster.top_investigator: Hunter Piegols, DVM, DACS-SA, ACVS Fellow-Surgical Oncology

current_roster.description: Anal sac cancers in dogs often spread to other areas of the body. This is called metastasis. Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. Removing lymph nodes with cancer improves outcome. However, assessment of the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor can be challenging. A safe and common test is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. This is where we test the first lymph node(s) that drain fluid from a tumor for cancer cells. It has been used in dogs with anal sac cancer. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis. So far SLN mapping on dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. We have successfully done SLN mapping for anal sac cancer with MIS techniques in dog cadavers. We want to evaluate these SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors. We also want to see how this compares to a previously studied method called CT-lymphography that is done before surgery. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.
current_roster.tagline: Finding Draining Lymph Nodes in Anal Sac Tumors in Dogs
current_roster.name: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery

current_roster.description:
Obesity is one of the most common and impactful chronic health conditions in companion cats, affecting an estimated 40–60% of pet cats in the United States. Feline obesity is associated with decreased quality of life, reduced life expectancy, and increased risk of metabolic disease, including diabetes mellitus, osteoarthritis, hepatic lipidosis, and chronic kidney disease. Effective and practical medical treatments for weight management in cats remain limited.


OKV-119 is an investigational, first-in-class, ultra-long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist implant designed specifically for veterinary use. The implant leverages the NanoPortal™ drug-delivery platform to provide continuous, smooth release of exenatide over multiple months. In laboratory studies with healthy cats, OKV-119 demonstrated sustained pharmacologic activity and was generally well tolerated, supporting evaluation in client-owned obese cats.


This study is designed as the first randomized, placebo-controlled clinical evaluation of OKV-119 in clinically obese cats (Body Condition Score [BCS] ≥7/9). The aim is to characterize the implant’s efficacy in inducing and maintaining weight loss, to evaluate metabolic changes (including HbA1c), and to assess safety and tolerability under real-world conditions in primary care and specialty veterinary clinics.
current_roster.tagline: Testing a new “Pawzempic” treatment to help overweight cats lose weight safely and effectively
current_roster.name: MEOW-1 (ManagEment of OverWeight cats with OKV-119)

current_roster.description:
Purpose

To evaluate the effects of histotripsy, a high-precision ultrasound-based treatment that can non-invasively destroy tumor tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with oral tumors. 


Background

Histotripsy is an emerging technology that uses focused ultrasound waves to mechanically destroy tumor tissue. Histotripsy has the ability to precisely destroy tumors non-invasively and without using heat or radiation. Histotripsy also has the potential to stimulate the immune system into fighting off remaining or microscopic tumor. Our team’s previous research has evaluated the safety and efficacy of histotripsy for bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumors in dogs. Additionally, histotripsy was FDA-approved for the treatment of liver tumors in humans in 2023, with promising clinical results. We are now interested in how histotripsy affects oral tumors in dogs. 


Study Design

Dogs will undergo CT and/or MRI scans (if not obtained previously during diagnostics) to visualize the oral tumor and plan the histotripsy treatment. The histotripsy treatment approach will be patient-specific to accommodate for unique tumor sizes and locations.  

On the day of treatment, hair will be removed from the area overlying the tumor to allow for maximum transmission of the ultrasound waves. Histotripsy treatment will be delivered non-invasively through the skin to mechanically disintegrate the underlying tumor. Dogs will be maintained and monitored under anesthesia. After the treatment, images (CT and/or MRI) will be taken to assess the immediate effects of the ultrasound treatment. Most patients recover uneventfully and go home the same day.

One day after the completion of histotripsy treatment, dogs will undergo standard-of-care surgical resection. This allows us to assess the effects of the ultrasound treatment. At this point, participation in the study is complete.
current_roster.tagline: Histotripsy to treat oral tumors in dogs
current_roster.name: Non-invasive treatment of oral tumors in dogs

current_roster.description:
Background

Equine sarcoids are the most common skin tumors in horses, associated with bovine papillomavirus (BPV). These locally invasive tumors lead to lesions that cause discomfort, pain, and functional limitations, significantly impacting a horse’s quality of life. Sarcoids are persistent and prone to recurrence, making their removal essential for preventing complications like infections or interference with tack. Current treatments, including surgery and cryotherapy, can be invasive, inconsistent, and have high recurrence rates, emphasizing the need for novel, effective solutions.

Histotripsy is a non-invasive ultrasound therapy that uses focused ultrasound waves to create microbubbles that mechanically disrupt targeted tissue. Unlike thermal methods, histotripsy’s non-thermal mechanism ensures precise ablation with minimal damage to surrounding tissues. Developed for human medicine, histotripsy shows promise in veterinary applications due to its precision, real-time imaging, and adaptability.

Non-invasive therapeutics like histotripsy are vital for improving animal welfare, minimizing recovery time, and reducing risks associated with invasive procedures. For equine sarcoids, histotripsy could offer a safe, precise, and effective alternative that could transform treatment outcomes and set a new standard of care for equine cutaneous neoplasia.
current_roster.tagline: A Non-Invasive Approach to treating Equine Sarcoids
current_roster.name: Histotripsy ultrasound therapy effectiveness on equine sarcoids

current_roster.description:
Narrative: This is a single-dose per site, prospective, randomized, controlled comparative parallel design study with post-treatment clinical and analytical evaluations of several factors related to safety and effectiveness such as performance outcomes. A minimum of 40 equicentCTM candidate horses and 30 control plan candidate horses/site will be enrolled within a maximum 6-month time-period, and complete the study with 14-, 30- and 90-day follow-up by the identified veterinarians and client surveys. At 180 +/- 14 days, the practice veterinarian or Principal Investigator will contact the owner/PR requesting follow-up information related to the safety and performance outcomes.

Study title (recommended):

Clinical Safety and Effectiveness of an Equine Umbilical‑Derived Connective Tissue Matrix Allograft (equicentCTM) for Joint, Ligament, and Tendon Administration in Horses.

Sponsor / organization:

Equine Performance Labs, LLC (Austin, TX, USA).

Principal Investigator:

Alicia L. Bertone, DVM, PhD, Biali Consulting

Clinical Sites: Austin Equine Hospital; Palm Beach Equine Clinic, Equine Athletic Performances Services KY, Tryon Equine Clinic, Ocala Equine Hospital, Peterson Smith Equine Hospital, Equine Performance Center.


Species:

Horse (Equus caballus).

Ethics / IACUC:

East Tennessee Clinical Research IACUC protocol ETCR‑24‑0329, approved 17 Oct 2024 prior to the start of the clinical study.

Study dates / status:

  1. First enrollment / first injection: 10/30/2024 (study start).
  2. Recruitment Status: Active but enrollment is closed; not recruiting for now through March 2026.
  3. Anticipated final completion as 03/31/2026

Intervention:

equicentaCTM, single 1.5 mL dose per site, intra-articular or intralesional; cryopreserved product (~‑80°C) thawed prior to injection; formulation includes 0.9% NaCl and 5% DMSO with microparticulate equine umbilical cord tissue suspension.

Comparator / control:

Contemporaneous control management plan (standard-of-care, non-steroid), documented on Day 0, with protocol constraints.

Design / allocation:

Prospective controlled field study using modified alternating block design (initial random assignment by coin toss at each site, then alternating assignments with limited exceptions).

Outcomes (high level):

  1. Safety: adverse events; lameness/pain/swelling parameters post injection.
  2. Effectiveness: lameness improvement and performance outcomes through Day 180 (as collected).
current_roster.tagline: Umbilical tissue allograft prospective controlled clinical trial for joints, tendons, ligaments in horses
current_roster.name: Clinical Safety and Effectiveness of an Equine Umbilical‑Derived Connective Tissue Matrix Allograft (equicentCTM) for Joint, Ligament, and Tendon Administration in Horses.

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description:
Although limb sparing for bone tumors has been performed for over 30 years in dogs, the complication rate for this surgery remains high. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat.


3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely anorganic (deproteinized) bone mineral (ABM). Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the ABM, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing would be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. The goal of this study is to evaluate a novel personalized implant system for limb sparing in dogs with primary bone tumors and identify complications associated with this surgical approach.


Dogs will undergo imaging with a PET-CT scan, which is a special form of imaging that involves giving a small dose of a radioactive substance to help identify any areas of cancer spread. The data from this imaging will also be used to create the patient-specific implant and tools for surgery, which is anticipated to take 5 days or less. Once the supplies are ready, the limb sparing surgical procedure will be performed. Dogs will return two weeks after surgery for suture removal and to start carboplatin chemotherapy as long as the surgical site is well-healed. Carboplatin will be given every 3 weeks for 6 treatments, and dogs will be followed for up to 20 months after surgery. X-rays of the chest and limb will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study, and force plate gait analysis will be done every 6 months. Some of these follow-up visits can be done with your regular veterinarian if you choose; however, the study will not be able to cover the costs of these visits.
current_roster.tagline: 3-D Printed Implant to Save Leg in Dogs with Bone Cancer
current_roster.name: 3D-Printed Implant that Replaces Bone for Limb Sparing in Giant Breed Dogs with a Primary Bone Tumor

current_roster.description:
Cannabidiol (CBD) is a non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid from the Cannabis sativa plant. It has a wide range of reported physiological and biochemical interactions. In addition, it has been investigated for its use in treating pain, anxiety, and epilepsy in canine patients, with varying results. Most of these veterinary studies use different formulations of CBD ranging from specific isolates to full spectrum products, with most pharmacokinetic (PK) studies with these formulations being performed on in-bred laboratory animals. Accordingly, product-specific clinical field studies are needed to understand the optimal dose/regimen and schedule of any CBD-based therapeutic. In addition, the variable manufacturing approaches for most CBD formulations available over-the-counter have created significant uncertainty for veterinarians and pet owners seeking to understand how to best deliver the potential benefits of CBD to patients. Indeed, the labeled amount of CBD in some products has been shown to significantly vary from what is actually labelled on the bottle, with some having heavy metal contamination.


The primary objective of this study is to define the tolerability of a novel CBD/CBDV/CBC drug formulation through a dose escalation design in healthy dogs. Following completion of the dose escalation cohorts, the dose that is deemed to be acceptably tolerated and is considered to be biologically relevant will be used to enroll a new cohort of dogs to evaluate the steady state PK of the drug.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluation of a novel CBD supplement in healthy dogs.
current_roster.name: Dose Finding Study for a Novel CBD Supplement in Healthy Dogs

current_roster.description:
In collaboration with the UW Carbone Cancer Center, we are developing an innovative treatment for canine Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma (PTCL). This study aims to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and optimal dosage of ⁹⁰Y-NM600 targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) in dogs with PTCL. Our research indicates that targeted RPT can effectively reach tumors, regardless of tumor location.


Please note that this is not a double-masked trial; ALL enrolled patients will receive the targeted RPT.


This funded study (after initial screening) covers the following expenses:

  1. All required examination visits EXCEPT for the initial screening visit.
  2. All laboratory work (CBC, blood chemistry, urinalysis), EXCLUDING the initial lab work needed for initial screening.
  3. Tumor Biopsy
  4. PET-CT scans.
  5. Hospitalization.
  6. All costs related to RPT.
  7. Additionally, up to $1,000 is available to help manage any treatment-related side effects, should they occur.
  8. Please be aware that there is no financial incentive for enrolling your pet in this trial. 


Dogs showing a positive response or stable disease at the day 21 assessment may be eligible for an additional 90Y-NM600 dose.


Dogs with progressive disease will be withdrawn from the study and offered either standard of care chemotherapy (at the clients expense) or treatment discontinuation, based on the client's preference.


Please note that the standard of care chemotherapy is NOT part of the trial.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a new targeted radiation therapy for dogs with Peripheral  T-cell lymphoma
current_roster.name: Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (RPT) in Companion Dogs with Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma (PTCL)
current_roster.top_investigator: David Michael Vail, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description:
An absence seizure disorder has recently been identified in the Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCS) breed, similar to absence seizure disorders seen in people. A wide range of presenting signs have been reported, including myoclonus (“head nodding”), episodes of decreased awareness, sleep disturbances, unexplained behaviour changes, and potentially fly-catching. It is currently unclear how this disorder is best managed. The goal of our study is to identify the most effective medication.


What will happen during this study?

Prior to enrolment, the dog's recent medical records will be screened to assess their eligibility for inclusion. Caregivers will then have a 10-20-minute telephone call with a researcher to help prepare them and their dog for the first visit. At the first visit, enrolled CKCS will undergo a full examination and potentially some blood testing. A 4-5 hour electroencephalogram (EEG) will then be performed by a researcher. If an absence seizure disorder is confirmed by EEG, the dog will be randomly assigned to one of two treatments. Treatments are in the form of an oral capsule, which will be administered twice daily at home for 3 weeks, before a second assessment that includes a repeat EEG. This is a blinded study, meaning caregivers will not know which treatment group their dog was assigned to until the end of their enrolment. Caregivers will additionally be asked to complete a 20-60 minute online questionnaire, both before and after the treatment period.


EEG is considered to be safe and generally well-tolerated. Some dogs may require sedation to facilitate placement of the electrodes. This sedation is then reversed after the electrodes are placed.
current_roster.tagline: Understanding treatment efficacy for absence seizures in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCS)
current_roster.name: Understanding treatment efficacy for absence seizures in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCS)

current_roster.description: Feline chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS) is a painful and often debilitating condition, marked by oral inflammation that can last for months or even years. While the exact cause of FCGS remains unclear, it is widely believed to result from an inappropriate immune response. Low-dose radiation therapy is an effective treatment for a variety of painful inflammatory conditions, including arthritis. Similarly, we believe that radiation therapy may be an effective alternative to extensive surgery or life-long oral medications in FCGS. Therefore, this clinical trial is designed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of radiation therapy in cats with FCGS.
current_roster.tagline: Radiation Therapy for Feline Chronic Gingivostomatitis (FCGS)
current_roster.name: Radiation Therapy for Feline Chronic Gingivostomatitis (FCGS)

current_roster.description:
The primary objective of this trial is to evaluate the real‑world clinical impact of adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) in dogs with drug‑resistant epilepsy, with a focus on seizure frequency, seizure severity, quality of life, and caregiver burden. We hypothesize that VNS, when added to standard medical management, will be associated with clinically meaningful improvements in seizure control and quality‑of‑life outcomes.


This trial is designed as a multicenter, single-arm, before and after, interventional trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of Milo VNS in dogs with drug-resistant epilepsy. Each subject serves as its own pre-implantation control. Two enrollment cohorts are analyzed separately:

  1. Cohort A (retrospective enrollment): dogs implanted with Milo prior to the date of protocol v1.0 sign-off, enrolled into the trial via owner re-consent and site PI confirmation that the dog meets the inclusion criteria. Cohort A contributes to safety, long-term durability, real-world adherence, and secondary analyses. Cohort A is not included in the primary efficacy endpoint analysis.
  2. Cohort B (prospective enrollment): dogs implanted on or after the protocol v1.0 sign-off date with standard prospective informed consent at the time of implantation. Cohort B contributes to the primary efficacy endpoint and all secondary endpoints.

Pre-specified analysis timepoints are on a 3-monthly basis beginning 3 months pre-implantation and ending 36 months post-implantation. Follow-up is for the lifetime of each subject.
current_roster.tagline: Efficacy of VNS seizure control for epileptic dogs
current_roster.name: Milo VNS Trial
current_roster.top_investigator: Dane W. Grasse, Chief Technology Officer

current_roster.description:
The primary goal of this study is to identify genes or genomic areas that may be associated with cervical spondylomyelopathy (CSM). The second goal is to identify breed-specific genetic variations and potential mutations that may contribute to CSM.

Dogs that present to the Ohio State University Veterinary Medical Center (OSU-VMC) will undergo a neurological examination, blood collection, and oral swab. Dogs that enroll virtually may have a 1-2 minute video of their gait submitted for evaluation, along with medical records documenting the diagnosis of CSM, and a cheek swab sample collected and mailed back to be submitted for DNA analysis.

Costs of mailing saliva samples will be covered by the study. For dogs enrolled during a visit to OSU, the full cost of the neurologic examination and blood collection (if applicable) will be covered by the study.
current_roster.tagline: Sample collections from dogs with CSM identifying genes/genomic areas associated with CSM.
current_roster.name: Unraveling the Genetic Basis of Canine Cervical Spondylomyelopathy (wobbler syndrome)
current_roster.top_investigator: Ronald da Costa, DMV, MSc, PhD, DACVIM

current_roster.description: Pain-relieving drugs like opioids are often used to prepare dogs for surgery, but they can cause unwanted side effects such as nausea and vomiting. Vomiting is unpleasant for the animal and can also be dangerous, as it increases the risk of complications like aspiration during anesthesia. The goal of this study is to test whether giving these medications at a special point between the ears (called GV20), instead of by the usual muscle injection, can lower the chance of vomiting while still providing the same level of calming and sedation. If successful, this approach could make the pre-anesthesia time safer and more comfortable for dogs by reducing the risk of vomiting and nausea. Safer, smoother anesthesia means less worry for pet owners and fewer complications for veterinary staff to manage. This study will add new knowledge about using “pharmacopuncture” (giving medications at acupuncture points) which may open the door to improved anesthetic techniques for veterinary medicine, and possibly inform approaches in other species as well.
current_roster.tagline: GV20 Pharmacopuncture for Reducing Opioid-Induced Vomiting in Dogs
current_roster.name: GV20 Pharmacopuncture for Reducing Opioid-Induced Vomiting in Dogs

current_roster.description:
Dogs can develop a serious blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This disease often gets worse quickly, and there is no standard treatment that reliably helps dogs live longer.

This study is testing a drug called trametinib to see if it may help dogs with AML. Trametinib is a medication used in people to treat some cancers. It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow. This drug is experimental for use in dogs with AML, and its safety and effectiveness for this condition are not yet known. In this study, all dogs will receive trametinib along with prednisone, which is commonly used to help dogs with leukemia feel better. About 13 dogs are expected to take part in this study.


Treatment is done with your local oncologist. As part of this study, pets will have the following things done:

• A physical exam by a veterinarian

• Blood tests to check blood counts and organ health

• Urine tests

• A cheek (buccal) swab to collect DNA for future research studies related to leukemia and treatment response

• Regular follow-up visits approximately 1 week and 2 weeks after starting treatment, approximately every 2 weeks through Week 12, and approximately every 4 weeks thereafter while dogs remains on study

• Dogs will take trametinib by mouth once daily at home

• Dogs will also take prednisone as directed by your veterinarian
current_roster.tagline: Trametinib clinical trial in dogs with AML
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial of Trametinib in Dogs with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

current_roster.description:
Canine appendicular osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. Standard treatment is amputation and chemotherapy with median survival around 13 months. Some patients are not candidates for amputation due to obesity, orthopedic conditions or other mitigating circumstances. Limb sparing is another option but limited in availability and is considered invasive.


Targeted bone electrochemotherapy (ECT-B) is an emerging focused cancer treatment therapy predominantly utilized in people with metastatic cancer to bone as a component of reducing bone pain and retarding tumor growth. It involves the insertion of a single pole electrode into the tumor and drawing chemotherapy directly to the tumor. In addition, once treatment is rendered, the remaining bone defect will be filled via sterile orthopedic bone cement, the patient recovered and discharged the same day.
current_roster.tagline: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Electrochemotherapy of Bone with Cementoplasty
current_roster.name: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Bone Electrochemotherapy with Cementoplasty; Alternative to Amputation

current_roster.description:
The objective of this study is to evaluate the utility of pupillometry (objective changes in pupil size) in dogs with a traumatic brain injury. We hypothesize that decreased pupil

reactivity as measured by pupillometry will be an early predictor of neurologic deterioration and be a poor prognostic indicator. A pupilometer measures aspects of pupil constriction, including speed and reaction time non-invasively. The eyelids might need to be opened slightly by the person helping with the exam if the dog doesn't hold them open on its own. The measurements will be taken at the time of hospital admission, 6 hours, 12 hours and then every 24 hours during hospitalization. This test will be compared to standardized scoring system that will also be performed in your dog.
current_roster.tagline: Use of Quantitative Pupillary Light Reflex Assessment in Traumatic Brain Injury Patients
current_roster.name: Use of Quantitative Pupillary Light Reflex Assessment in Traumatic Brain Injury Patients
current_roster.top_investigator: Jacob Wolf, Doctor of Veterinary Medicine

current_roster.description:
In the past, osteoarthritis (OA) was thought to be a disease where the smooth cartilage in a joint slowly breaks down. Today, scientists know that OA affects the whole joint, not just the cartilage. This includes the bones, ligaments, meniscus, and the lining of the joint.

Even though doctors can see joint damage, there is a big problem: the amount of damage does not always match how much pain someone feels. Pain can be confusing

and different for each person or animal. For example, two patients—whether they are horses, dogs, or people—can have joints that look the same on X-rays, but one may

feel a lot of pain while the other feels very little. This means that x-ray severity of joint injury does not correlate to the level of pain experienced.

In people, scientists have many ways to measure pain, but in horses this is much harder. We can study how a horse walks and measure lameness using special tools,

but we do not have good, reliable ways to measure how much pain a horse feels. The goal of this study is therefore to use validated pain-testing methods from people and

adapt them for horses, especially for horses with osteoarthritis in the fetlock joint.

Pain has been studied in horses before by looking at things like how they move, how active they are, and their heart rate. However, these behaviors are usually studied one

at a time, and researchers have not always checked how accurate or consistent these

tests are.

This research will study non-invasive tests used in people and see how well they work in horses. The study will focus on three areas: how horses sense pain (Aim 1), how they move (Aim 2), and their activity and natural behaviors (Aim 3).

By doing this, researchers hope to better understand pain in horses and improve how

pain is measured, bringing horse pain research closer to the level used for people.


Procedures

1) Online enrollment survey

2) First Visit – Veterinary physical and lameness evaluation, including jogging, lunging, x-rays, blood sample and IV sedation if needed

3) Second Visit – blood sample, hair and fecal collection, heart rate monitoring and ECG collection with equipment, lameness evaluation using videography, continuous activity monitors with GPS sensors, quantitative sensory testing using noninvasive methods, using tactile, vibration, thermal and pressure tests which are routinely used in humans. At this visit, they will also have overnight behavioral observation using an IMU device and video observation.

** at the conclusion of the second visit, some phenylbutazone tablets will be given to the owner to administer before the third visit*

4) Third Visit – a repetition of the exercises performed at the 2nd visit, now with phenylbutazone on board for the horse to evaluate how this drug modulates the

sensation of pain level in the horse. At this visit, they will also have overnight behavioral observation using an IMU device and video observation.

5) Fourth Visit – will occur one year after the conclusion of the initial testing and will form a similar visit schedule as during the initial year 1 testing outlined above.
current_roster.tagline: GALLOP
current_roster.name: Gait, Activity, and Locomotion Links to Osteoarthritic Pain (GALLOP)

current_roster.description:
Full-thickness skin grafts are often required for dogs with large or complex wounds. Although these procedures are commonly performed, some grafts fail to fully attach or heal, leading to delayed recovery, additional surgeries, or discomfort for the patients. 


The study investigates whether a placental matrix – a biologic material rich in natural healing factors derived from bovine placental tissue – can improve graft success and reduce complications when applied at the time of skin grafting. Placental matrices contain growth factors and structural molecules that may enhance graft adherence, improve blood vessel formation and reduce inflammation within the graft bed. 


Treatment: As part of the standard grafting procedure, your dog will receive general anesthesia. During surgery, a full-thickness meshed skin graft will be harvested from a donor site on your dog and placed over the wound bed. As the research component of this procedure, a single application of placental matrix will be applied topically to the graft surface at the time of surgery. This application is non-invasive, painless, and performed while your dog is already under anesthesia. A non-adherent dressing and bandage will then be applied in a routine fashion. 

Following surgery, your dog will be monitored in hospital for 12-24 hours before discharge. The first recheck visit will occur approximately 5 days after the procedure, with subsequent visits every 3-7 days as determined by the attending veterinarian based on the graft site and any complications. Grafts are anticipated to be healed within 21-30 days on average. At each visit, a brief wound assessment and standardized photographs will be obtained to measure graft healing progress.
current_roster.tagline: Using Placental Matrix with Canine Full-thickness Meshed Autogenous Skin Grafts
current_roster.name: Clinical Evaluation of using Placental Matrix with Canine Full-Thickness Meshed Autogenous Skin Grafts

current_roster.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). 

For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.
current_roster.tagline: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
current_roster.name: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. Geoffrey Wood, DVM, PhD, DVSc Geoffrey Wood

current_roster.description:
Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.


Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.
current_roster.tagline: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
current_roster.name: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery

current_roster.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.


What happens in this study

  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imaging


  1. Advanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesia


  1. Minimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatment


  1. Intravenous administration of an investigational drug (BAQ-13) twice weekly for 4 weeks


  1. Concurrent radiation therapy (standard of care)


  1. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collection at specified time points


  1. Overnight hospitalization following biopsy procedures


  1. Follow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-ins


  1. Completion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effects


  1. End of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog’s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.



IACUC: 24515

Study number: VCCT-26-001
current_roster.tagline: A research study evaluating a novel drug alongside radiation therapy for dogs with brain tumors.
current_roster.name: CARE Trial: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation therapy to improve Efficacy in Canine Glioma

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study: We are trying to develop better ways to treat advanced cancer. Specifically we are developing ways to activate the immune system to attack cancer. We are hoping to benefit dogs with advanced cancer and hoping this information may also help inform future human clinical trials. Contact: The Oncology Clinical Trial Coordinators via email (oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu) or phone (530-752-0125 or 530-752-9759) Participation Requirements: Dogs (> 1 year old and > 5kg) diagnosed with at least one measureable metastatic sarcoma or melanoma lesion outside of the field of radiation. Initial Evaluation for Participation: confirmed diagnosis of Oral melanoma or Soft Tissue Sarcoma with one measureable metastatic lesion. Procedures: If you agree to let your dog participate in this study, the following will happen: We will do a CT scan to measure the tumor and to use for planning for radiotherapy, take small biopsies of your dog's tumor and local lymph node (if possible) and collect blood. Every week for four weeks, we will irradiate your dog's tumor (radiotherapy), inject the tumor with the experimental drug, take a tumor sample, and collect blood all while your dog is anesthetized. One week, one month and three months after finishing radiotherapy, you will need to bring your dog back in for a recheck, another CT scan, blood draw, and biopsy of the tumor and possibly lymph node if there is disease present. If your dog dies during the study, we respectfully ask that you allow us to perform a necropsy. Benefits: If you agree to take part in this research study, we will pay for the immunotherapy, blood work, biopsies, CT imaging and follow up CT imaging as well as subtract $ 2,000 from the cost of the radiation. We cannot promise any benefits to your dog or other animals from your taking part in this clinical trial; however, possible benefits include response of your dog's cancer. Owner Responsibilities: You will need to pay for the radiation therapy required for the study. If you allow your dog to participate in this study, you will be responsible for bringing your dog to all of their appointments.
current_roster.name: Radioimmunotherapy for metastatic sarcomas and melanomas

current_roster.description: Rational: The goal of this trial is to evaluate the ability of 18F-FDG-PET to assist surgeons with tumor resection and pathologists identify active tumor populations. Active tumor sections identified by the scan will be compared to standard slices of the tumor by the pathologist and determined if the scan guidance improves the ability to identify aggressive tumors. 1.Purpose: The goal of this project is to determine the biologic behavior of soft tissue sarcomas on PET and correlate it with a more traditional histological grading system. This will be accomplished by using a well-established methodology which utilizes 18F-FDG-PET. Although limited studies have been performed in this regard with some encouraging results, there is a need for further clarification of this technology in assessing patients with sarcomas beyond the initial diagnosis. While structural imaging such as CT and MRI reveal the presence of sarcoma, they fail to characterize the current and future biologic behavior of the tumor. Although the latter technologies have become very import in the surgical management of patients, they have played a limited role in characterizing the biologic nature of the variable and complex cancer. Based on prior date, information gained form molecular characterization of cancers by 18F-FDG-PET has aided in the management of cancer patients. A need exists for prospective studies designed to answer critical question that will define the role of this powerful modality in the management of patients with sarcoma. Our aim is to demonstrate that 18F-FDG-PET imaging provides accurate information about this malignancy by correlating SUV-(standard uptake valve) 18F-FDG-PET with the pathologic grading system of patient with sarcoma as well as determine if SUV changes within a tumor correlate to differences amongst the aggressiveness of tumor cells, thereby enabling a biopsy directed towards the most viable and aggressive tumor cells. A correlation between SUV and prognosis, disease free progression and overall survival will also be evaluated. 2. Exclusions: Recurrent sarcoma, prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy to tumor site, tumor < 10 mm. 3. Expected Duration: Approximately one week. 4. Description of Procedures: All patients enrolled will undergo staging procedures which will include a physical examination, Complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, urinalysis, and thoracic radiographs. Prior to surgery patient will be anesthetized for CT scanning, followed by an 18F-FDG-PET scan with two biopsies of the tumor. Patients will be placed in the University of Missouri-Columbia Veterinary Health Center (UMC-VHC) radiation isolation ward for 24 hours, at which time they will be released without further restriction. Patient will be available for planned clinical surgery here at the UMC-VHC following release from radiation isolation.Histopathologic evaluation will be performed on biopsies and tumor following excision. No other interventions will be part of this clinical trial for the participating dogs.
current_roster.name: Use of CT/PET for imaging and the histologic evaluation of soft tissue sarcomas

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of surgery combined with an injection of ALVAC IL-2 (feline interleukin-2) as a treatment for feline fibrosarcoma (FSA). FSA is one of the most common cancers in cats. These tumors develop in the subcutaneous tissues and can invade extensively into the adjacent skin and muscle. Because of this, complete surgical removal can be difficult and recurrence of the tumor is common. Current standard of care treatments include various combinations of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. ALVAC IL-2 is a type of immunotherapy. It is an injection designed to help a cat's immune system to kill any cancer cells that remain following surgery. Surgical removal of the fibrosarcoma tumor is required. Each cat will be randomly assigned (like flipping a coin) to one of three treatment groups: low dose ALVAC IL-2, high dose ALVAC IL-2, or no ALVAC IL-2. Each cat will be in the treatment portion of the study for 2 months and in the follow-up portion of the study for up to two years. Eligibility: Cats with confirmed diagnosis of feline fibrosarcoma that is able to be surgically removed (not on the head, tail, or lower limbs) Cats without evidence of metastasis Cats not currently undergoing chemotherapy Benefits: Costs of all treatments with the study medication and study-related follow-up visits are covered by the study. The costs of the eligibility staging and tumor removal are not covered. If you are interested in participating in this clinical trial or would like to learn more about it, please contact the VCIC at 215-573-0302 or email vcic@vet.upenn.edu
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a new treatment in cats with feline fibrosarcoma

current_roster.description: The Veterinary Clinical Investigations Center at the University of Pennsylvania is now enrolling fifteen (15) dogs with measurable malignant melanoma for a clinical trial assessing the benefits of apheresis in the treatment of malignant melanoma. Unlike traditional cancer therapy, apheresis does not affect healthy cells. Using a blood circulating machine, it removes, filters, and returns blood back to the patient to increase the immune system's ability to fight the cancer cells. Inclusion Criteria: Dogs at least six (6) months of age, weighing 5 kgs (11 pounds) or more Confirmed diagnosis of malignant melanoma (with tumor still intact) No other significant health concerns Not currently being treated with anticancer or immune-suppressive therapies Benefits: Financial coverage for tumor analyses/imaging (x-rays and CT scans), blood work, urinalyses, and apheresis treatments Follow up care including: oncology examinations, blood work, urinalyses, and tumor analysis/imaging (x-rays and CT scan) for up to one year If interested in enrolling your dog in this study, or would like to learn more, contact the VCIC at 215-573-0302 or vcic@vet.upenn.edu for more information.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the Safety and Effectiveness of the Immunicom Apheresis Immunoabsoption Affinity Column in Combination with the Teru

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study: Surgical removal is generally recommended as the first step in treatment of mast cell tumors; however, sometimes surgery is not possible due to the size or location of the tumor or due to financial limitations. In that situation, treatment with steroids, chemotherapy or targeted therapies such as Masitinib may be beneficial in controlling the disease. Preliminary studies of Masitinib in dogs showed that it caused tumor shrinkage in 50% of dogs with mast cell tumors and increased 1- and 2-year survival rates in dogs with nonresectable mast cell tumors compared to placebo. Based on this data, Masitinib has conditional approval by the FDA for treatment of non-resectable grade 2 or 3 mast cell tumors in dogs. The objective of the study is to evaluate the anti-cancer effects of Masitinib in comparison to a placebo in dogs with grade 2 or 3 mast cell tumors that have not been previously removed or treated with chemotherapy or radiation. If this study confirms these results, the drug will become fully approved. Contact: The Oncology Clinical Trial Coordinators via email (oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu) or phone (530-752-0125 or 530-752-9759) Participation Requirements:Please Contact us for specific requirements Initial Evaluation for Participation: Please contact Oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu Procedures: If your dog is enrolled, a small biopsy will be taken from the mast cell tumor to confirm grade and for additional testing. Your dog will then be randomly assigned to receive treatment with either Masitinib or a placebo with two-thirds of the dogs receiving Masitinib and one-third receiving placebo. You will not know whether you are giving the study drug or the placebo (even after you dog has completed the study). Your pet will come in every other week for examination, tumor measurement, blood work and imaging tests (x-rays and/or ultrasound) to check for cancer progression and/or side effects from the drug. No more than 1 tablespoon of blood will be drawn per visit. More invasive testing (fine needle aspiration) will only occur if your veterinarian is concerned about spread of the cancer or to monitor spread to a lymph node that has already occurred. Your dog cannot receive steroids or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs during the study period, but can receive medications to treat nausea, diarrhea, infection, itchiness, and pain if needed. Benefits: You are responsible for the initial consult visit fee at UCDavis. If you and your dog meet the inclusion/exclusion criteria, staging will be covered by study (Blood work, Biopsy, Bone Marrow Aspirates, Radiographs, Ultrasound) regardless if your dog qualifies. Although not all tumors will respond to Masitinib, it is possible that the drug may help control your dogs mast cell tumor. The information gathered from this study may help other dogs with mast cell tumors in the future by determining whether Masitinib is an effective treatment for non-resectable grade 2 or 3 mast cell tumors. Owner Responsibilities: If you elect to participate in this study, you will be responsible for scheduling and keeping appointments every two weeks. If you have to miss an appointment, please try to reschedule as soon as possible by calling 530-752-1393 (press 3,3 to reach the Oncology Schedule Coordinator). You will also be responsible for giving your dog the study medication as directed every day and for reporting any side effects of the drug to your doctor in a timely manner.
current_roster.name: Assessing a Potential Treatment for Mast Cell Tumors

current_roster.description: Cancer cachexia is a syndrome that is described in both veterinary and human medicine. Patients with this syndrome lose body weight and muscle mass, have a decreased appetite, and fell unwell overall. These patients also have a poor response to cancer treatments and a decreased survival compared to patients that do not have the syndrome. The purpose of this study is to document and compare the body weight, body condition, and blood levels of inflammatory proteins in normal weight cats with cancer, underweight cats with cancer, and normal weight healthy cats. Cats presenting to the Penn Vet oncology service with a newly diagnosed cancer will be eligible. Approximately 10 mL of blood will be taken from each cat. Each cat will be weighed and given a body condition score.
current_roster.name: Clinical and Molecular Markers of Cancer Cachexia in Cats

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study: The purpose of this study is to prospectively evaluate the response of nasal cancer to a combination of therapies (chemotherapy and radiation therapy) in dogs. Contact: Contact Dr. Culp for details at wculp@ucdavis.edu or (530) 752-1393. Participation Requirements: Dogs diagnosed with nasal tumors Initial Evaluation for Participation: Contact Dr. Culp for details at wculp@ucdavis.edu or (530) 752-1393. Procedures: Dogs that are scheduled to receive radiation therapy for the treatment of nasal cancer can be enrolled in the study. Dogs will be placed into a group receiving radiation therapy alone or with chemotherapy. Response to these treatments will be assessed with CT scans (done before and after treatment). Benefits: The CT scans, chemotherapy administration, and part of the radiation therapy will be paid for by the study. Owner Responsibilities: The owner will be responsible for providing follow-up information to the treating clinicians and returning the dog 4 weeks after initiation of radiation therapy for a second CT evaluation (the first is performed prior to treatment).

current_roster.description: Rational: This single armed Phase I/IIa clinical trial is designed to obtain a preliminary determination of whether ECI-OSA-1, a combination vaccine and T cell therapy, significantly improves clinical outcomes when used to treat newly diagnosed surgically resected osteosarcoma compared to historical control data of surgery alone or surgery plus chemotherapy. 1. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to evaluate a new immunotherapy approach to treat osteosarcoma in dogs following limb amputation. We will determine whether ECI-OSA-1, an immunotherapy procedure that combines autologous cancer cell vaccination and adoptive transfer of cancer antigen-specific effector T cells, will improve clinical outcomes in dogs with newly diagnosed osteosarcoma following limb amputation. The results will be compared to historical control data obtained using amputation alone and amputation plus chemotherapy. 2. Expected Duration: The initial phase of the study is expected to last 7-9 weeks. Follow-up procedures will be performed every 3 months after completion of the initial phase. Most visits are time sensitive and must be performed at the University of Missouri-Columbia Veterinary Health Center (UMC-VHC) 3. Description of Procedures: Initial staging is to include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry panel, urinalysis, cytologic or histologic diagnosis of osteosarcoma, thoracic radiographs and a bone scan (nuclear scintigraphy) prior to limb amputation. Tumor tissue obtained during amputation will be utilized for vaccine preparation. The first vaccination will be administered in four sites one, two and threeweeks following amputation.Two weeks after the final vaccination the dog will undergo general anesthesia and blood for T cell extraction will be collected by apheresis.Six to eight days following apheresis, the treated T cells will be transfused back into the patient. Starting on the day following T cell infusion, the dog will receive injections of interleukin-2 (IL-2) on alternate days, for a total of five injections. One week after the last IL-2 injection the dog will be evaluated with blood work, and thoracic radiographs. Thoracic radiographs will be repeated every 3 months after this visit. Bone scans and/or CT scans may be performed at these times to confirm suspected metastatic disease. When a bone scan is performed, the dog must be hospitalized in the UMC-VHC radiation isolation ward for approximately 24 hours following the procedure.
current_roster.name: Amputation and ECI-OSA-1 for the treatment of Appendicular Osteosarcoma in Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: PAK4 is a protein present in cells that is involved in helping to control the rate of cell growth. In normal cells, PAK 4 is tightly regulated so that growth occurs in a normal ordered manner. It is now known that abnormalities occur in PAK4 in cancer cells that contribute to driving uncontrolled tumor growth. In some cells there are mutations in PAK4 that cause it to be turned on all the time, and in others its expression is very high causing the tumor cells to divide uncontrollably. Based on the role of PAK4 in cancer there has been great interest in developing inhibitors of this protein that can be used to treat tumors and possibly halt their growth. Karyopharm Therapeutics has developed a drug called KPT-9274 that is given orally and binds to PAK4, thereby blocking its ability to drive cell growth. KPT-9274 has shown good activity against tumor cell lines in the laboratory and also inhibits tumor growth in mouse models of cancer. KPT-9274 has been tested in normal dogs and is well tolerated with no side effects when given at doses between1.5-6 mg/kg orally given on a Monday/Thursday or Monday/Wednesday/Friday schedule. KPT-9274 has also been tested in dogs with cancer, and doses ranging from 2-4 mg per given on a Monday/Wednesday/Friday schedule for 28 days were not associated with any side effects. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the activity of KPT-9274 when given in combination with doxorubicin chemotherapy for the treatment of canine lymphoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - A diagnosis of lymphoma (T or B cell, newly diagnosed). - Dogs must be free of other diseases (heart, liver, and kidney) and be feeling good (playing, good appetite). - Your dog will be screened for eligibility based on bloodwork (complete blood count, biochemistry profile, urinalysis, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound) What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? If enrolled dogs will receive KPT-9274 for 4 doses (Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Monday followed by the administration of doxorubicin 24 hours after the last dose of KPT-9274. Recheck exams will be performed weekly (days 14, 21, and 28) for 1 month, then monthly thereafter. Routine bloodwork and urinalysis will be performed at these visits. Client Compensation All costs for the first 4 weeks of the clinical trial are covered, and a credit of $500 will be available for standard of care chemotherapy if/when your dog should fail treatment with the drug combination. If your dog does well (i.e., achieves a complete remission for over 28 days) with the treatment combination, then you will be offered an opportunity to re-treat with the drug combination. For retreatment, KPT-9274 will be offered at no cost, although you will be responsible for the administration of the doxorubicin.
current_roster.name: Phase I study of KPT-9274 in dogs with lymphoma

current_roster.description: Feline gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoblastic lymphoma (FGLL) is a debilitating disease of older cats. Chemotherapy for treatment of FGLL has been used with limited success and long-term survival is uncommon. Radiation therapy (RT) is used to treat localized lymphoma in humans and in two small studies of cats with lymphoma confined to the intestinal tract treated with RT, clinical signs improved in most cats. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the addition of abdominal cavity RT to oral chemotherapy (lomustine), daily oral prednisone, and weekly parenteral cobalamin will improve response to therapy, survival times, and quality of life of affected cats. If the addition of RT improves outcome, this therapy may be adopted as the standard of care for cats with FGLL and may be used to further study the use of RT for lymphocytic lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease. Eligibility: - Cats with a cytologic or histologic diagnosis of FGLL (to include stomach, small intestine, large intestine, pancreas, mesenteric lymph nodes, and/or liver) - An expected survival of > 3 weeks regardless of therapy - Baseline ALT and total bilirubin < 2 x baseline Exclusion Criteria: - Cats with obstructing intestinal masses that are amenable to surgery - Patients that have received prednisone or other chemotherapy drugs < 14 days prior to enrollment in the study
current_roster.name: Treatment of Feline Gastrointestinal Lymphoblastic Lymphoma (FGLL) with Cobalamin (Vitamin B12), Prednisone, Lomustine, and 8 Gy A

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to identify aberrant epigenetic (DNA methylation) changes in lymphoma cells to develop biomarkers of each class of lymphoma, and in turn, identify new therapy targets for affected Golden Retrievers. More significantly, because DNA methylation changes occur so early in the process of cancer formation, these investigators hypothesize that they could serve as biomarkers of risk, allowing medicine or diet to prevent lymphoma in Golden Retrievers before it develops. Finally, they propose to fully phenotype cancer stem cells in lymphoma by surface markers and DNA methylation changes for the purpose of targeting those cells which feed cancer metastasis. Individually each project advances a current frontier of research. By performing them in parallel, the discoveries made in each project can be combined, correlated, and translated into biomarkers of risk, diagnosis, and prognosis to advance the prevention and management of lymphoma in Golden Retrievers. The goal is the establishment of genetic risk alleles, defining the gene expression profile and the role of cellular activation in lymphoma and hemangiosarcoma. Title: Evaluation of biomarkers as risk factors for lymphoma in Golden Retrievers. Contact Person: Heather Wilson, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology) Clinic Phone: 979-845-2351 Email: oncology@cvm.tamu.edu Species: Canines Inclusion Criteria and General Background Information: Any golden retriever with lymphoma may qualify for this trial. Exclusion Criteria: Dogs without lymphoma or with other tumors may not qualify for this trial. Owner Commitments: Dogs will participate with a cheek swab on a one time bases. Participation in this trial is expected to add no more than 30 minutes to the total visit time. Financial Incentives: There is no cost for participation in this trial. There are no financial benefits for participation in this trial.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of biomarkers as risk factors for lymphoma in Golden Retrievers.
