current_roster.description: Purpose of the Study: Photodynamic therapy combines a drug, known as a photosensitizing agent, with a specific type of light, commonly laser, to kill cells. The goal of this study is to determine if photodynamic therapy would be useful in treating dog and potentially human lung tumors. The steps of photodynamic therapy include injection of a photosensitizing agent into the blood. The drug is absorbed all over the body, but stays in cancer cells slightly longer than in normal cells. Two days after drug absorption, the tumor is exposed to a light source. Photosensitizer agents in the cells absorb the light and produce an active form of oxygen which destroys nearby cells. Patient Entry Criteria: Eligible patients include dogs having a single lung tumor greater than 2 centimeters in diameter. The patient will need to have a needle aspirate taken of the tumor which confirms a diagnosis of carcinoma prior to enrollment. Also recent chest radiographs, a complete blood count, a serum biochemistry panel, and a urinalysis are necessary prior to enrollment. The study is limited to dogs not having evidence of metastatic disease and who are in otherwise good health. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? Each dog will receive an intravenous injection of a photosensitizing agent on Day 0. Two days later on Day 2, each dog will be anesthetized for a chest CT scan and additional outpatient procedures. Following the CT scan while still anesthetized, a bronchoscopy (a flexible camera placed inside the trachea and lung airway branches) will be combined with fluoroscopy (a version of real-time chest xray imaging) to deliver a lighted wire through the bronchoscope for temporary placement into the lung tumor of each dog. Just prior to the lighted wire placement, a second photosensitizing agent acid will be given either orally or intravenously. Once the lighted wire has been activated to stimulate photosensitizing drugs within the lung tumor to cause cell death, the wire and scope will be removed. Two days later on Day 4, each dog will be readmitted to the hospital for routine surgical removal of the lung tumor via traditional thoracic surgery. Reevaluation with the Clinical Trials team at Colorado State University will be expected at two weeks, four weeks, and six weeks after the traditional thoracic surgery. Your pet will experience side effects. Specifically, dogs will experience light sensitivity, or photosensitivity, following administration of the photosensitizing drugs. The light sensitivity is expected to last from two to six weeks, the estimated amount of time for the drugs to be eliminated from the body. It is anticipated the ears may be the most sensitive to side effect, and will be a barometer for overall photosensitivity, but any exposed or lightly haired area of the body is susceptible including the belly, mouth, and eye tissues. Any strong light, including indoor as well as sunlight, could affect photosensitivity. Thus dogs will need to be kept mostly indoors during the time period of about one month, until the drugs are metabolized. Use of sunscreen products will not be of benefit. Dogs will need to be protected against unrestricted outdoor sunlight exposure in the first month following treatment by being supervised on a leash long enough to allow for urinations and defecations. If the ears become red or show signs suggestive of a 'sun burn' while a dog is being quarantined indoors, then less use of bright indoor lights will be recommended to reduce exposure effects. Importantly, controlled light exposure is the key for metabolism of the photosensitizing agents. Combined use of two photosensitizing agents in this study is anticipated to reduce the light sensitivity side effects in dogs. Owner Responsibilities: You are responsible for an initial examination, complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, and needle-aspiration diagnosis of your dogs tumor. You are also responsible for the costs associated with your dogs traditional thoracic surgery (minus the $1000 credit), for recheck fees at the fourth- and sixth-week visits following traditional thoracic surgery, and any other tests recommended by your pets oncologist. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Financial Incentives: Enrollment in this clinical trial provides a $1000 credit to be used towards your pets traditional thoracic surgery for removal of the lung tumor. Enrollment in the trial also includes a free CT scan, bronchoscopy, and fluoroscopy, studies valued at over $2000.
current_roster.name: Photodynamic Therapy for Canine Lung Tumors

current_roster.description: The Morris Animal Foundation and the National Cancer Institute are sponsoring a clinical trial in dogs with newly diagnosed Osteosarcoma. This trial is being conducted by the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium. 180 dogs will be enrolled in this study. All dogs will receive surgical removal of their tumor and receive standard of care chemotherapy. Dogs will be randomized at time of enrollment to either receive standard of care alone or standard of care with orally administered rapamycin. Eligibility: Confirmed osteosarcoma diagnosis. Has not received any prior treatment for osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most common bone tumor in dogs. Amputation and chemotherapy significantly improves median survival times for dogs with this tumor type, from around 4-6 months to around 10-12 months. However, most dogs are not cured, and die due to the spread of their disease (metastasis) within 1-2 years. Better treatment options to treat cancer spread are needed to improve survival time for these patients. Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a drug that works through the blockade of mTOR, a cellular pathway that is associated with tumor spread. Preliminary studies have been performed in cell lines, in mice, and in dogs that demonstrate anti-tumor activity. Previous studies have also established a safe dose in healthy dogs and dogs with cancer. The addition of this drug to standard amputation followed by carboplatin chemotherapy is hoped to delay or prevent tumor spread, thus improving patient survival. All dogs receive the current recommended therapy for osteosarcoma (standard of care: SOC), consisting of amputation followed by 4 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy, given 3 weeks apart, initiated within 10-14 days of surgery. Your dog will then be randomly assigned to enter the study group that receives SOC alone, or the group that has the addition of the drug rapamycin (Rapa). All dogs in both groups will return every two months for monitoring for disease progression, including chest radiographs. Rapamycin is an oral drug, given at home, daily on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of each week, with no drug administered on Fridays, Saturdays, or Sundays for a total of four months. Additional visits for the Rapa group of dogs includes 5 overnight stays (two the first month, then 3 additional monthly visits) for the purposes of a 24 hour blood collection to determine the levels of the drug in your dog's body. In order to minimize the number of times your dog's vein must be punctured for blood collection, a central venous catheter will be placed, under minor sedation.
current_roster.name: Treatment of bone cancer in dogs

current_roster.description: Previous studies have shown that the drug Palladia (toceranib) can reverse resistance to doxorubicin (a commonly used anticancer drug). We have recently completed a study evaluating toceranib in combination with doxorubicin as treatment for cancer in dogs. The combination was well tolerated and the maximum tolerated dose of doxorubicin when combined with Palladia was determined. The goal of this study is to evaluate the safety and maximum tolerated dose of combination toceranib and doxorubicin in cats with naturally occurring cancer. Cats that have a confirmed diagnosis of new or recurrent cancer will be eligible for this study. Cats will receive Palladia every other day (given orally by the owner). Doxorubicin will be administered intravenously every 3 weeks for a total of 4 treatments. Cats will be evaluated prior to each doxorubicin treatment and one week after each treatment for assessment of side effects and efficacy of this combined treatment. The owner is responsible for the cost of initial staging (including pretreatment labwork and pretreatment blood pressure measurement) and recheck examination fees throughout the study period. The study will cover all other study-related costs.
current_roster.name: Safety Evaluation of Palladia (Toceranib Phosphate) in Combination with Doxorubicin

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and sponsored by the Morris Animal Foundation seeks to evaluate in dogs with osteosarcoma the safety and effectiveness of adjuvant oral rapamycin following Standard of Care therapy. Standard of Care is defined as definitive surgery, being amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on an every 21 day schedule. Carboplatin has been shown to safely and effectively improve survival in dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma for over 20 years. ALL dogs enrolled onto study will receive Standard of Care (SOC) therapy; however, through a randomization process, some dogs entered into study will also receive additional therapy with oral rapamycin. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved to induce immunosuppression in human patients receiving organ and bone marrow transplants. Early work with rapamycin suggests that this agent might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting (reducing the effects of) an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. Preclinical studies of rapamycin in mice, as well as recent data using analogous drugs (rapalogs) in human patients, suggest that mTOR blockade might be effective in the treatment of several cancers. Study Objective This study will evaluate if orally administered rapamycin following SOC therapy improves long-term disease control in dogs with osteosarcoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - Confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma - Primary appendicular osteosarcoma that is amenable to surgical removal via amputation (No evidence that the tumor has spread to the lung (metastasis) based upon physical exam, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound). - ONLY newly diagnosed dogs are eligible with no prior therapy (conventional or metronomic chemotherapy, ionizing radiation, bisphosphonates) for osteosarcoma. - Dogs receiving analgesics including NSAIDs, gabapentin, tramadol, or other will be eligible for study inclusion. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign informed consent allowing the surgical amputation of your dog's affected limb. Following amputation, your dog will return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 3 weeks for 15 weeks for evaluation. On weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 your dog will receive a dose of carboplatin. Precautions should be taken against contact with your dog's urine or feces for 48 hours after carboplatin treatment. Blood work will be done on your dog prior to carboplatin administration. After completion of SOC therapy, and depending upon initial study randomization, you might be required to administer oral rapamycin (PO) at home for 4 months. The schedule for rapamycin administration will be daily on Monday-Thursday (4 days on), with a drug holiday on Friday, Saturday and Sunday (no dosing, 3 days off). This will allow us to determine if oral rapamycin can be safely administered chronically and will require serial collections of blood on scheduled reevaluations to allow for measurements of rapamycin within your dog's blood. Your dog will have a total of five 24-hour serial blood draws completed over the course of 4 months. At the end of the each study cycle (Day 25), your dog must return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital for reassessment and further blood collections. If your dog has been randomized to receive oral rapamycin, these visits are required for inclusion in the study. If your dog is in the Standard of Care arm only, you will be required to return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 8 weeks for evaluation. Client Compensation Following determination of your dog's eligibility and limb amputation, costs associated with this study will be provided, including a $1000 hospital credit towards your dog's limb amputation. Client Contact NCSU Clinical Studies Core: cvmclinicalstudies@ncsu.edu for more information about this study.

current_roster.description: Transitional cell carcinoma is a devastating disease. This study will test whether a adenovirus based vaccine followed by a DNA plasmid administered via electrogenetransfer can elicit anti-tumor immunity and increase survival times. The vaccine will be an additional therapy to standard of care treatment. In people, Her2/neu has been expressed in this cancer and is associated with a poor prognosis. In unpublished canine testing, HER2/neu has been expressed and opens a therapeutic target against this cancer. Int Urol Nephrol. 2014 Nov 11. "Epub ahead of print" Prognostic role of HER2 expression in bladder cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Zhao J1, Xu W, Zhang Z, Song R, Zeng S, Sun Y, Xu C. The vaccine targets this Her2/neu pathway of tumorigenesis allowing the body's immune system to battle the cancer in addition to standard therapies. PROCEDURE: Currently, the vaccine is a series of 5 treatments (2 adenovirus/Her2/neu) followed by 3 DNA/plasmid administered via electrogenetherapy (EGT). Each is administered every 2 weeks and there is an option for continued monthly boosters for those patients maintaining remission. The first two (2) adenovirus vaccines (prime) are administered via simple intra-muscular injection. The last three (3) of the series (boosters) are administered under a short anesthesia via EGT. No placebos are involved and the study is unfunded and follows USDA regulations. This immunotherapy is an extension of the center's telomerase cancer vaccine that has shown success against canine lymphoma in Europe. There is no guarantee and some patients may not benefit. Our group recently published on this: Overexpression of HER-2 via immunohistochemistry in canine urinary bladder transitional cell carcinoma - A marker of malignancy and possible therapeutic target.Millanta F,ImpellizeriJ, McSherry L, Rocchigiani G, Aurisicchio L, Lubas G.Vet Comp Oncol. 2017 Sep 4. doi: 10.1111/vco.12345. If you are interested in this clinical trial, please go to our website http://www.petcancerinformation.com and have your veterinarian fill out our referral form. Please fax or email this along with pertinent lab results. Most patients are candidates, however a formal phone consult will determine options. Thank you for your interest.

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study: Standard therapy for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma has long been amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy to prevent the spread of cancer. With this form of treatment, survival times of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma is on average about 10 to 12 months with little improvement in survival occurring over the past two decades. Rapamycin is a drug that potentially can inhibit an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. The purpose of this study is to determine if adding the oral drug Rapamycin into the treatment protocol for dogs with osteosarcoma will be safe and improve efficacy of current standard therapies for osteosarcoma in dogs. There will be about 160 dogs taking part in this study that is enrolling dogs nationwide. Initial Evaluation for Participation: If you allow your dog to participate in this study, you will be responsible for the cost of the initial examination with the UC Davis Oncology Service as well as the cost of the screening diagnostic tests, which include a complete blood count (CBC), biochemical profile, urinalysis, chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound. Participation Requirements: Most of the exams, tests, and procedures you will have are part of the usual approach for your dogs treatment for osteosarcoma including amputation of the affected limb and carboplatin chemotherapy given once every three weeks for 4 doses followed by monitoring of chest x-rays once every two months. Week 1 evaluation - amputation Weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 evaluation-blood work and carboplatin treatment (and chest x-rays at week 9) Week 15 evaluation-chest x-rays Every 8 weeks recheck chest x-rays-Some extra sample (tumor and blood) collections for dogs enrolled in both study groups will need to be taken if you take part in this study. Additionally, dogs enrolled in the Rapamycin Group will have extra visits required of them during the 4 months that they are receiving oral rapamycin and owners are expected to administer the oral rapamycin once daily Monday through Thursday. Benefits: Benefits of standard therapy include removal of the painful cancerous tumor in your dogs bone and delay of spread of cancer by providing chemotherapy with carboplatin. Once enrolled, the study will provide a $1000 hospital credit toward the cost of your dogs amputation and will provide the total cost of carboplatin chemotherapy and follow-up examination and diagnostics. For dogs enrolled in the Rapamycin Group, we cannot promise any benefits to your pet or other animals from your taking part in this clinical trial. Owner Responsibilities: Once enrolled in the clinical trial, you are responsible for scheduling and keeping all appointments needed for study participation and reporting any side effects of the treatment to your doctor in a timely manner. You will be responsible for the cost of amputation above and beyond the $1000 hospital credit provided by the study. You will also be responsible for any costs associated with management of side effects from the standard therapy portion of this study (amputation and carboplatin chemotherapy). All other study costs associated with study participation will be covered by the study. Multiple Institutions are participating For a complete list, go to: https://ccrod.cancer.gov/confluence/display/CCRCOPWeb/Current+Open+Trials Contact: The Oncology Clinical Trial Coordinators via email (oncologyclinicaltrials@ucdavis.edu) or phone (530-752-0125 or 530-752-9759)

current_roster.description: This collaborative study involving researchers from Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Colorado is investigating the effectiveness of minibeam radiation treatments for treating malignant brain tumors in dogs. Clients who choose to include their dogs in the study will pay only a fraction of the regular treatment cost and will have their animals randomly selected to receive stereotactic radiation therapy or the minibeam radiation treatments, in which the radiation is delivered in 1 mm parallel beams. Study Population: Client-owned dogs with spontaneously occurring brain tumors will be recruited. To increase patient accrual, costs associated with the planning imaging and treatment in excess of $900.00 (CN dollars) will be covered by the study. Inclusion Criteria: Diagnosis of a primary brain tumor based on cross-sectional imaging, informed client consent for follow-up imaging and post-mortem examination of brain tissue. Exclusion Criteria: Concurrent illness expected to limit life expectancy to less than 1 year. Staging: Dogs will undergo a complete blood cell count, serum biochemistry, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain prior to acceptance into the study. Treatment: Dogs will be randomized to receive stereotactic radiation therapy or minibeam radiation therapy. Radiation treatment will be administered daily for 1-3 days. Follow-up: After the treatment neurological examinations will be performed at the Veterinary Medical Centre for local clients and at the referring veterinary clinic for distant clients once every 3 months. Quality of life surveys will be administered by an email survey system or telephone from the Veterinary Medical Centre every 2 months for life. Post-treatment magnetic resonance imaging will be performed every 6 months for life, or at the time of suspected disease progression.
current_roster.name: Mini Beam Radiation Treatment for Canine Brain Tumors

current_roster.description: Purpose This study will evaluate the safety and feasibility of MRI-guided High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (HFIRE) for the treatment of brain cancers and aim to optimize the technology to achieve tumor destruction of multiple brain tumor types. Background HFIRE is a newer generation technology, similar to the NanoKnife system which is in clincial trial in humans for the destruction soft tissues (i.e. tumors or cancers) via irreversible electroporation (IRE). We have previously demonstrated the safety of IRE for the treatment of canine brain tumors and have safely performed HFIRE on soft-tissue tumors, including brian tumors, in client-owned dogs, cats, and horses. By placing thin electrodes within tissue, IRE uses electrical pulses to destroy tissues by disrupting cellular membranes. The IRE method is less invasive and disruptive than traditional methods of surgical tumor resection. HFIRE offers additional advantages over traditional IRE in that the high-frequency pulses do not result in electrically induced muscular contractions, eliminating the need for more anesthesic agents, and offering the potential to selectively kill cancer cells and spare normal, healthy cells based on the physical characteristics of the cells. Therefore, HFIRE is ideally suited to the treatment of cancers in anatomically sensitive areas, such as the brain. Our newest generation of HFIRE technology allows the neurosurgeon to perform the HFIRE treatment while the patient is in the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner, which should improve the safety and efficacy of the procedure. Eligibility MRI evidence of a solitary mass lesion (consistent with glioma or meningioma) in the cerebrum that is at least 10 mm in diameter. Dogs with tumors previously treated with surgery are also eligible if there is MRI documented evidence of tumor progression. Clinical signs of mild to moderate neurologic dysfunction referable to the brain (Karnofsky Performance Score >70). No clinical or other diagnostic evidence of other significant systemic disease. Exclusion Criteria Dogs that are pregnant Uncontrolled seizures or other severe neurological signs Bone marrow suppression, or significant kidney or liver dysfunction evident on blood tests Concurrent infections or malignancy Prior treatment of the tumor with radiation therapy of any kind Study Design The HFIRE electrodes will be inserted into the brain tumor with MRI guidance and HFIRE pulses delivered using a treatment plan customized for each patient. Dogs will be cared for post-operatively using standard-of-care procedures for brain tumor patients, and monitored daily in the ICU for adverse events until discharge from the hospital. Following discharge, clinical follow-up examinations will be recommended and continued to be performed off-study according to standards of care for each patients specific type of tumor. Compensation The fees associated with the HFIRE treatment and the associated pre- and post-operative hospitalization costs will be covered by the study sponsor. An additional follow-up clinical visit and brain MRI examination 6-8 weeks after the surgery to evaluate the treatment will also be covered by the study.
current_roster.name: MRI-guided treatment for gliomas in dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose of the study: To evaluate the safety and immune system effects of a vaccine using TBI-4000 in dogs with melanoma. TBI-4000 is a novel immune stimulant that has shown significant effectiveness in mouse models of cancer, including melanoma, when used as part of a vaccine. Primary Eligibility Criteria: Dogs with a confirmed diagnosis of melanoma whose tumors have been controlled with surgery or radiation therapy. 3 week washout from chemotherapy; no prior or current immunotherapy. Study Protocol: Tests to determine eligibility: physical exam, blood work, urinalysis, chest x-rays, aspirate of lymph node. TBI-4000 vaccine given as an injection under the skin every 2 weeks for 4 treatments and then every 2 months as long as the tumor does not progress. Recheck visits required on days 0, 14, 28, & 42 and then every 2 months. Blood samples collected at every visit; chest x-rays and lymph node aspirates done prior to starting treatment, on day 42, and then every 2 months. Owner Responsibilities: Cost of treatment (surgery or radiation therapy) to provide local disease control. Follow appointment schedule required by study protocol. Financial Incentives:Study pays for all costs associated with trial except recheck exam fee at each visit ($40). 750 credit to VTH account which can be used for future treatment after completion of the trial. Can be applied to costs of initial staging to determine study eligibility if enrolled or treatment while on the study

current_roster.description: This clinical trial, led by the National Cancer Institute and Vyriad, Inc., assesses the safety and effectiveness of a cancer-killing virus (VSV-IFN-NIS) when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in mice, normal dogs, and in a small study of pet dogs with cancer have shown the virus to be safe at certain doses. This virus is currently being evaluated in human patients with liver cancer in an FDA-approved trial. Results of this study will be used to help design future clinical trials evaluating VSV-IFN-NIS in dogs with relapsed or refractory cancer. Principal Investigator at the University of Minnesota: Mike Henson, DVM, PhD, DACVIM. Eligible dogs must: - have a malignant tumor that is accessible and large enough (>1 inch in most cases) to allow samples to be collected from it for analysis (biopsies) - tumors can be either newly diagnosed or recurrent and of almost any type except mast cell tumors or hemangiosarcoma - weigh 20 kg or more (44 lbs) be feeling well with no significant health concerns, other than the malignancy, identified on routine diagnostic testing (blood and urine tests, x-rays, ultrasound) - be up to date on vaccines, flea/tick prevention and internal parasite control - not be in contact with livestock - have stopped any drug therapies for the cancer at least two weeks prior to enrollment - have stopped any radiation therapy for the tumor at least six weeks prior to enrollment Other restrictions may apply, call for details. Other restrictions may apply, call for details. Study summary: A screening visit to determine eligibility to include physical exam, history, bloodwork, chest x-rays, possible abdominal ultrasound. First day of the study (Mondays): pre-treatment physical exam, tumor measurements, blood samples, lymph node aspirates, tumor biopsies. Second day (Tuesday): Virus administration intravenously, monitoring, blood, urine, fecal and saliva sampling. Depending on the group to which a dog is assigned, a 2nd intravenous dose of virus may be given on the second day. Dogs must remain in the VMC until Friday for monitoring and sampling. Follow-up visits are necessary the VMC on Day 8, Day 15, Day 22, and Day 29 to measure tumor response and collect samples (e.g. blood, urine, saliva, feces). Dogs will be anesthetized for collection of biopsy samples prior to treatment and on Day 3, Day 8 and Day 29. Please contact Andrea Eckert, CVT for more information or to inquire about enrolling in this study.

current_roster.description: Progress has been slow to improve therapies and outcomes for dogs diagnosed with a very common tumor - lymphoma. To accelerate our understanding of this cancer in dogs and identify novel treatments to improve survival, we are collecting a sample of lymph node tissue from dogs diagnosed with lymphoma that have not yet begun therapy for their cancer. The tissue collected will be used to identify ways to improve disease detection, prognosis, and treatment options for dogs with multicentric lymphoma. The project is part of theCornell Lymphoma Programand involves researchers across the Cornell Ithaca campus and at Weill Cornell in New York City. Your only commitment is to bring your dog forhis/her initial evaluation, diagnostic tests, and lymph node removal. We would also like to contact you and/or your veterinarian in the future to obtain follow-up information about your dog. Total expectation for hospitalization for diagnostic tests and surgery is two days.

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to determine a safe dosage of a re-purposed antibiotic to use in dogs with lymphoma. This antibiotic may affect cancer cells through a variety of mechanisms and the most appropriate dosage to use in dogs with cancer is unknown. Certain high dosages used to treat infections are associated with a high incidence of liver toxicity in dogs with lymphoma. This study evaluates the safety and tolerability of a lower dosage. The initial appointment will include the physical examination to determine eligibility and diagnostics that include blood work, x-rays of the chest, ultrasound of the abdomen, and dispensing of the medications. Owners must be willing to give their dog the medication orally twice daily at home and return to the hospital for recheck visits (5-6 visits over 1 month).
current_roster.name: Study for Dogs with Lymphoma Using a Re-Purposed Antibiotic

current_roster.description: Purpose: The goal of this study is to use the newest generation of cardiac CT scanners to investigate the coronary circulation of English bulldogs. Background: The English bulldog is the most commonly afflicted breed with pulmonary valve stenosis (PS), a congenital narrowing of one of the valves in the heart. The therapy for PS is to dilate the thick and narrowed valve with a balloon catheter. However, bulldogs are also known to have abnormal coronary arteries, the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle, which can wrap around the pulmonary valve. If the coronary artery wraps around the pulmonary valve, then a balloon procedure cannot be performed due to the risk of tearing or damaging the coronary artery.Historically, the only way to confirm that a dog suffers from an abnormal coronary artery is to catheterize the dogs heart, which is both costly and requires general anesthesia. New computed tomographic (CT) scanners are very fast and are able to visualize the heart in excellent detail. Such scanners have proven useful in humans to define and clarify the coronary arteries without requiring cardiac catheterization. Our goal is to show that this is a viable method for evaluating the dogs coronary circulation at less cost and without the need for general anesthesia. Inclusion Criteria: Clinically healthy English bulldogs and English bulldogs with PS are eligible for this study.The healthy bulldogs must not have any known underlying medical condition and must pass a careful physical examination.Bulldogs with PS must not be in heart failure or have clinically significant heart rhythm disturbances at the time of examination. Study Design: Your dogs health condition will be evaluated, including a brief review of your dogs medical history and a thorough physical examination. Blood will be drawn to measure your dogs red blood cell levels and to store a blood sample for DNA collection. If your dog qualifies, they will receive a sedative and have an intravenous catheter placed. The CT scan will be performed with the dog resting comfortably on their chest and intravenous contrast will be given to highlight the arterial circulation. The contrast agent is given routinely to dogs undergoing CT and is proven safe in animals. Once the CT images are acquired, your dog will recover from the sedation and either return home with you if fully awake, or be monitored at the Veterinary Medical Center overnight if the imaging is performed in the evening. Because the imaging occurs at a human medical facility, it will require having your dog come to the Veterinary Medical Center in the early evening or on a weekend. This will conclude the study and no further recheck or follow up is required. Client Compensation: The study will pay for all charges associated with the CT procedure (e.g., exam fee, blood work, sedation, scanner time, recovery overnight if necessary). The results of the CT scan will provide you with an overall assessment of your dogs heart and benefit our understanding of the English bulldog.If your dog has PS, the study will help to confirm whether your dog has an abnormal coronary circulation and whether they can undergo a balloon procedure.The study does not cover the screening cost for the initial diagnosis of PS, only for the CT evaluation his/her coronary arterial circulation once such a diagnosis has been made by your veterinarian. Client Cost: The client is not responsible for any cost other than adverse events exceeding $2,000.

current_roster.description: Purpose: The purpose of this clinical trial is to assess the effectiveness of thromboelastography, which is amethod of testing the efficiency of blood coagulation,in dogs receiving blood transfusions. Background: Thromboelastography (TEG) variables are strongly influenced by hematocrit. This may be due to direct effects of red blood cells on clot formation, ormay be due to the effects of red blood cell content on whole blood viscosity. We believe the TEG is altered by changes in red cell mass independent of whole bloodviscosity. TEG is becoming an increasingly popular methodology for assessment of whole blood coagulation in veterinary species as well as humans. As its use is increasing, limitations or biases of the instrument need to be understood so that the information gathered can be correctly interpreted in the clinical setting. In this study we would like to study canine anemia of any cause requiring non-urgent, non-intraoperative packed red blood cell transfusion in the ICU. Inclusion criteria: Anemic dogs hospitalized at the Ohio State Veterinary Medical Center for red blood cell transfusion (packed or whole blood) Study Design: Anemic dogs hospitalized for red blood cell transfusion (packed or whole blood) will have one 4.5mL citrated blood tube drawn prior to transfusion and one identical sample drawn after transfusion. The blood will be run on the TEG 30 minutes after phlebotomy. Samples will have viscosity measured shortly after TEG is run. The method of phlebotomy will be standardized, but the site of phlebotomy will be at the discretion of the attending clinician (jugular will be preferred if no clinical objection).These blood draws will be coordinated with phlebotomy for other samples (blood typing, PCV/TS to minimize needle sticks beyond what would be normally clinically indicated. Client Compensation: Cost associated with the blood collection will be covered. There is no financial incentive for this trial.Clients are responsible for all cost related to hospitalization and treatment/supportive care.

current_roster.description: Objectives: To compare the sort and medium-term outcome of the Knotless Anchor (KA) versus traditional Fabello-Tibial Suture (FTS) in dogs with unilateral CCL rupture. To report the major and minor complication rates of KA versus FTS and determine if these rates differ between the two procedures. Hypothesis: Based on ex-vivo work and substantial clinical experience, the authors hypothesize that stabilization of the CCL deficient stifle with KA fixation will result in superior outcomes and reduced complication rates when compared to a traditional FTS technique..

current_roster.description: Brachycephalic obstructor syndrome (BOS) is a commonly encountered disease process in veterinary medicine. Physiologically, dogs with relative upper airway obstruction exhibit increased inspiratory effort which can result in an increase in negative intrapleural and intraesophageal pressure. This, in turn, can lead to cranial motion of the stomach into the thoracic cavity during inspiration with subsequent gastresophageal reflux (GER) and hiatal herniation (HH). The effect of increases in inspiratory effort on GER and HH have been evaluated in people with asthma and it has been shown that asthmatics with some degree of airway obstruction had significantly lower esophageal sphincter pressures, greater esophageal acid exposure and more frequent reflux episodes than controls. In veterinary patients, in which chronic upper airway obstructions are a much more common clinical entity, an association between respiratory and gastroesophageal disease has long been hypothesized, especially in brachycephalic breeds. However, a direct causal relationship has never been established and objective documentation of the response to amelioration of the upper respiratory obstruction on the severity of GER and/or HH has never been thoroughly investigated. Despite the frequent concurrence of respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms in brachycephalic dog breeds the area has been the subject of very little investigation in the veterinary literature. This may, in part, be due to the difficulty in diagnosis of these pathologies in the past. In recent years better diagnostic tests for the diagnosis of the associated pathologies have become available. Contrast-enhanced videofluoroscopy has become the gold standard for diagnosis of a host of gastroesophageal disorders and has been established as the primary diagnostic assessment of GER and HH in the authors institution for several years. Lower esophageal pH evaluation using 24hr ambulatory monitoring is now available and has been shown in people to correlate well with GER disease. When the pH drops below a certain threshold (usually set at a pH of 4) an episode of gastric acid reflux has occurred. Twenty-four hour pH monitoring is used extensively in people for investigation of reflux-related symptoms that are refractory to proton-pump inhibitor therapy and can help to guide therapy in these patients. Impedance planimetry using the Endoflip device (Crospon Inc. Galway, Ireland) is a modality that provides real-time information on the dimensions and distensibility of the lower esophageal area in dogs. A balloon tipped catheter is passed down the esophagus and positioned across the lower esophageal area. Monitoring high-resolution manometry (HRM) allows accurate assessment of neuromuscular activity within the esophagus and esophageal sphincters using a probe incorporating 36 pressure sensors. The device allows the creation of spatiotemporal plots of esophageal pressure activity along the entire length of the esophagus and helps to elucidate the functional anatomy of the structures involved in HH. HRM has been evaluated for diagnosis of HH in humans and traditional water-based manometry has been evaluated for diagnosis of the condition in a canine model. These new diagnostic modalities will be used in addition to standardized client questionnaires filled out pre and post-operatively to evaluate the effect of palliation of the upper airway obstruction on the severity of HH. Procedures:Brachycephalic (short-nosed breeds) dogs suffer from relative upper airway obstruction which causes a decrease in pressure in the chest during inspiration which can lead to their upper stomach area being pulled into the chest (hiatal herniation). We would like to evaluate the effect of surgical palliation of this upper airway obstruction on the severity of hiatal herniation using several new objective diagnostic tools that are at our disposal (videofluoroscopy, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, impedance planimetry (Endoflip), 24 hour pH-metry and high-resolution manometry as well as a standardized client outcomes tool) Owner Responsibilities: If you allow your dog to participate in this study, you will be responsible for bringing the dog to the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital (VMTH) for the study-related visits for the duration of the time stipulated and for providing the clinical information stipulated.
current_roster.name: Assessing airway surgery for treatment for hiatal hernias in dogs
