Samples to test the chemotherapy concentrations will be taken during the study. Eligibility: Dogs that have been tentatively diagnosed with a glioma brain tumor by MRI. Dr. Bentley must confirm the suspicion of glioma by reviewing the MRI before enrollment. Chest radiographs and bloodwork must also have been performed (within the last month). Financial Incentives: The brain tumor surgery, the chemotherapy, the bloodwork to monitor the chemotherapy and therepeat MRI will all be provided at no charge.
current_roster.name: Surgery and Metronomic Chemotherapy for Brain Tumors (Glioma) in Dogs

current_roster.description: Background Urethral obstruction is a common emergency situation for domestic male cats. Performing a cystocentesis (using a needle to directly remove urine from the urinary bladder) can aid in initial stabilization and may improve likelihood of successful catheterization. As such, cystocentesis currently part of the standard of care for the treatment of urethral obstruction at the Ohio State University. However, the benefits of cystocentesis have not been definitively proven and may carry some risk of damage to the bladder and leakage of urine or bleeding. A recent study has shown that this risk appears to be extremely low (0 cases in 46 enrolled). The results of this study will help veterinarians determine the safest, most effective treatment protocol for feline urethral obstruction, particularly whether decompressive cystocentesis should be performed prior to urethral catheterization. Inclusion Criteria Feline with urethral obstruction StudyDesign Your cat will be randomly assigned once enrolled to either have a cystocentesis performed or not, and then grading the difficulty of passing the urinary catheter. In addition, an abdominal ultrasound will be performed at the time of presentation and 15 minutes after cystocentesis is performed, and again 4 hours later determine if any urine leakage from the bladder occurs. If fluid is found, a sample will be obtained by inserting a needle into the abdomen (abdominocentesis) under ultrasound guidance and analyzed to determine the type of fluid present (blood or urine). Client Cost Owners are responsible for all costs associated with the treatment of the urethral obstruction including the emergency fee, hospitalization, treatment, medications, blood work and radiographs. Client Compensation The ultrasound will be at no cost to the owner.
current_roster.name: Cats with urinary blockage

current_roster.description: Purpose The objective of this study is to assess the efficacy of tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) for thrombolysis in feline acute aortic thromboembolism (FATE) Background The clinical syndrome of aortic thromboembolism (ATE) in cats is initiated by sudden migration of a left atrial thrombus into the systemic arterial system. Treatment options are limited with up to 90% of affected cats euthanatized due to the poor prognosis associated with standard therapies. Indeed, the survival rate for cats hospitalized and treated medically is only 30-40%. Although thrombolytic therapy is the standard of care for acute thrombotic disorders in humans, treatment of feline ATE (FATE) has focused on supportive care. Despite case reports of thrombolytic therapy in cats with FATE, no controlled clinical trials of therapy have been conducted. The study described herein prospectively evaluates the use of TPA in acute FATE. Inclusion Cats eligible for inclusion in this trial will meet these criteria: A diagnosis of ATE affecting at least 2 limbs An observed onset of ATE Rapid clinical assessment that permits initiation of TPA infusion within 6 hours of the thromboembolic event. Exclusion Study exclusion criteria will include: Cats moribund at presentation ATE affecting all four limbs Unstable congestive heart failure or cardiogenic shock A patient whose pain cannot be effectively controlled with opiates An owner unwilling to cover the initial assessment, or unwilling to hospitalize the cat for at least 48 hours Previous use of TPA. Study Design Cats will be randomized to Control (placebo) or Treatment (TPA) group, this means that half of the cats will receive the study drug (TPA) and the other half will not receive the study drug. The doctor making clinical decisions, as well as the owner, will be unaware of the treatment the cat is receiving. The primary treatment outcomes are functional limb score (using a previously-published method) and the proportion of cats discharged at 48 hours for each treatment group. Secondary outcomes are survival to discharge, length of hospitalization, and rate of euthanasia. Client Compensation The study will cover the admission and initial assessment costs, the study drug and treatment, monitoring and hospitalization up to 48 hours for up to $1700. The study will not be responsible for hospitalization beyond 48 hours, as well as long term complications such as surgery, bandage change, or disposal costs.
current_roster.name: Cats with blood clots

current_roster.description: Horses with severe colic require surgery to correct intestinal obstruction, and it is this population of horses that requires the most intensive care to save their lives. Survival rates have continued to increase as equine anesthesia and surgery has progressively improved. This has shifted the emphasis of colic treatment to intensive medical care that is required before and particularly after surgery. There are a number of treatments that have become the standard of care for horses with severe colic, including intravenous fluids and anti-inflammatory medications, such as flunixin meglumine (Banamine). However, just as there have been advances in anesthesia and surgery, there have also been advances in medical therapy. One such advance has been the development of drugs called COX-2 inhibitors, which have an action similar to flunixin, but target inflammation much more specifically. Recent scientific discoveries have shown that the COX enzymes are responsible for beneficial functions, such as digestive and kidney health via COX-1, and detrimental functions, such as pain and inflammation via COX-2. Flunixin inhibits both COX enzymes, so it has benefits to horses with colic (pain relief and reduced inflammation) as well as side effects (stomach ulcers, kidney damage). We have recently discovered a new side effect of flunixin it slows down repair of the gut because it inhibits COX-1. However, since 2010, an intravenous COX-2 inhibitor has been released on the market specifically for horses called firocoxib (Equioxx). We have shown in research trials comparing flunixin and firocoxib that while both provided excellent levels of pain relief, flunixin reduced the rate at which the bowel could recover from colic-induced injury, whereas firocoxib allowed the bowel to recover more rapidly. We believe this may be a very important consideration when treating horses with surgical colic. To properly test this, we are proposing a multi-institutional clinical trial in which owners of colic patients going to surgery at NC State University, Michigan State University, or the University of Pennsylvania will have the option of enrolling their horse in a clinical trial in which flunixin or firocoxib will be given. The drug being used will be hidden from the veterinarians (they will know one of two anti-inflammatory drugs are being given). We will also give the drugs to horses in random order. This is all part of running a high level clinical trial, to make sure the results are as meaningful as possible. Clients will be given a small financial incentive to enroll their horses in this trial, and all other aspects of medical and surgical treatment will be kept the same. We will determine if one drug is advantageous over the other by measuring a comprehensive series of clinical measures (e.g., level of shock) as well as blood levels of bacterial toxins and markers of septic shock. The outcome will be a far greater understanding of the effects of both flunixin and firocoxib in horses with surgical colic, which we believe will help clinicians enhance their level of medical care in these critically ill horses.
current_roster.name: The study of optimal non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for horses with severe colic

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Canine atopic dermatitis (AD) is the second most common allergic skin disease in dogs. The term atopy is associated with an inflammatory skin condition that causes dogs to be itchy and predisposes them to developing secondary bacterial and fungal infections. A diagnosis of canine AD is made by the exclusion of other allergic diseases (flea allergy, contact allergy and/or cutaneous adverse food reaction). An intradermal test (IDT) and serum allergy test (SAT) are used in canine AD to identify common allergens causing allergic dermatitis in the dog.Once offending allergens are identified in an individual animal they are used to formulate allergen-specific immunotherapy. The needed dilution of allergen extract used in an IDT is defined by determining threshold concentrations (TCs) in normal non-allergic dogs. An allergen extract used at too dilute of a concentration may predispose to false negative skin test reactions, whereas an allergen extract used in too high of a concentration may cause false positive skin test reactions. Initial evaluation of TCs for finding the exact concentration of allergens that should be used in an IDT are determined by comparing skin test reactivity with serial dilutions of allergen extract in non-hypersensitive patients. Currently, there are no allergenic extracts that have been standardized for use in veterinary medicine. As reference standards are not established there is great variation in potency and reactivity both among lots of allergen extracts and between suppliers. This trial will establish threshold concentrations of allergens from a new veterinary allergen supplier. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this study is to establish threshold concentrations of allergens by a new veterinary allergen company. Which dogs are eligible to participate in this study? Dogs with no prior history of allergy or any other dermatological skin or ear disease are eligible for this study. You will be given a questionnaire to answer prior to patient enrollment. The question content regards your dogs itch level, medication use, medical history and behaviors performed at home. Your dog must also be feeling good (normal activity level, good appetite) and be free of other diseases (such as heart disease, kidney disease and liver disease). We have 13 very specific inclusion criteria as well as 9 exclusion criteria that will be used to determine eligibility for enrollment. A physical exam, hemogram and biochemical will be performed and the patient must be deemed overall healthy. What does enrolling my dog in this study involve? Initially your dog will be on a food trial for a period of 8 weeks prior to and then during the testing period. The diet that you will be required to feed your dog is Blue Buffalo Freedom grain-free Chicken dry kibble for adult dogs. The study will take place over a period of 4 hours in one day. The evening prior to the study we ask that you not feed you dog past 10 p.m. the offering of water is fine until presentation. The following day 1-2 teaspoons of blood will be collected from your dog for a serum allergy test. The left side of your dogs chest will be shaved. A mild sedative will be given and an intradermal skin test with allergens that include molds, grasses, trees, weeds and various house dust and storage mites will be performed. After 15 minutes the reactions will be read by the investigator. On completion an ice pack will be applied at the site of the test for 10 minutes followed by application of a 1% hydrocortisone lotion. The sedation will be reversed and your dog will be able to go home at the end of the day. This test is no different than the routine intradermal test used for regular patients of the veterinary medical center. What are my financial responsibilities if my dog participates in this study? There are no costs associated with your dogs participation in this study. The diet will be provided free of charge.All costsassociated with this study and treatment of any side effects will be covered by the study sponsor. We consider your dogs participation invaluable to not only the scientific community but also for dogs with environmental allergies. Therefore, upon completion of the clinical trial, a $200 credit will be available for additional therapy or medical appointments at the VMC and must be used within 1 year. If you decide to withdraw your dog from the study prior to study completion, this credit will not be applied to your account. However, if your dog is removed from the study by one of the study investigators due to medical concerns as it is believed to be in the best interest of your dog, then you will still receive the credit.
current_roster.name: Allergy test in Non-Allergic Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose: The objective of this study is to see if low-level laser therapy is an effective adjunctive treatment for acral lick dermatitis (ALD) Background: Canine acral lick dermatitis (ALD) is a frustrating disease that manifests as excessive, compulsive licking at a focal area on a distal limb that results in a proliferative and ulcerative lesion. These lesions usually have secondary deep infection. ALD can have multiple primary causes including allergic disease, hypothyroidism, orthopedic abnormalities, neurologic, pain and psychogenic. Eventually the licking behavior can become a primary factor. Conventional therapy for ALD generally consists of oral antibiotics for deep infection and systemic behavioral-modifying medications. Oftentimes conventional therapy does not fully resolve the licking behavior. Low-level laser therapy is an alternative therapy used to treat conditions associated with pain, pruritus (itching) and inflammation. We hypothesize that low-level laser therapy may be helpful in decreasing licking behavior in dogs with ALD. Inclusion: Dogs with a lesion consistent with ALDLesion must be present for at least 3 weeksTopical or oral flea prevention for at least 2 months or longerPatients are allowed to be on certain medications if used long-term such as: - Allergen specific immunotherapy (allergy vaccine) if used for greater than 1 year -Oral glucocorticoids, Apoquel (oclacitinib) and Atopica (cyclosporine) if used for greater than 4 months -Antihistamines if used for greater than 1 monthTopical therapies (shampoo, sprays, mousse, lotions) are permitted if used for greater than 1 month and not used directly on the lesion Study Design: Dogs will have a full physical and dermatologic exam, basic dermatology diagnostics (skin cytology, deep skin scrape). Dogs will be sedated for radiographs, bacterial and fungal culture and biopsy to confirm the diagnosis of ALD and receive treatment with an oral antibiotic and anti-anxiety medication for 4 weeks. Treatment group receives laser therapy, control group receives sham laser (laser is off). Laser therapy will be performed 3 days/week for 2 weeks, then 2 days/week for 2 weeks for a total of 10 treatments. Client Compensation: Owners are responsible for the initial consultation fee of $125. All other diagnostic and treatment costs are covered by the study. Free 6 month flea/tick prevention on completion of the study
current_roster.name: Dogs with lick dermatitis

current_roster.description: Purpose: To obtain BAER data from normal hearing CKCS dogs between the ages of 1 to 2 years old with no history of hearing loss. This is a 2-day study. Procedures performed include hearing testing (BAER test), a Computed Tomography (CT) scan and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI); study pays for all testing. Background: Hearing disorders are a common condition recognized in many breeds of dogs. In the dog breed Cavalier King Charles Spaniel (CKCS), hearing disorders may be due to conductive hearing loss, which may occur with primary secretory otitis media (PSOM), or do to sensorineural hearing loss, which may occur when there is damage or an abnormality of the sensory cells in the cochlea or the auditory nerve. Evaluation of a dogs hearing ability is done using the brain-stem auditory evoked response (BAER) test. However, in order to identify an abnormality on the BAER test, the results from an individual dog must be compared to normal BAER values. Inclusion criteria: To qualify for enrollment in this study, dogs must: Be a CAVALIER KING CHARLES SPANIEL DOG A pedigree is required Has no hearing problems
current_roster.name: Hearing test in cavalier king charles spaniel dogs

current_roster.description: Phase 1: The proposed study will develop and evaluate a series of protocols based on basic clinical information and simple diagnostics to aid the general practitioner in diagnosing and managing chronic diarrhea in dogs. Dogs with chronic diarrhea seen either by local veterinary practices (Mississippi, Alabama and Tennessee) that deal regularly with the Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine (MSU-CVM), or by the MSU-CVM Community Veterinary Services practice, will be enrolled in the study, with the agreement and consent of the pet owners. Individualized diagnostic and therapeutic plans will be devised by Drs. Bryan, Cade, Sullivant and Mackin of MSU-CVM, in consultation with the patients primary veterinarian. Plans will be based on history, physical examination and results of simple diagnostic tests. In most cases, diagnosis and treatment will be performed at the local veterinary practice, by the dogs primary veterinarian, in consultation with MSU-CVM, without the need for the dog or pet owner travel to MSU-CVM. Each veterinarian will be provided funding support (up to $300) from MSU-CVM to fund reasonable diagnostic and therapeutic plans for management of chronic diarrhea for each individual dog enrolled. Diagnostic and therapeutic plans will be individualized based on the circumstances of each patient, but can be reasonably be expected to include: Diagnostic tests including fecal flotation, fecal cytology, fecal culture, rectal scrapings and fecal assays for infectious organisms. Therapeutic trials including food trials, parasiticides, antibiotic trials with drugs such as tylosin and metronidazole, and pre- and pro-biotics. Long-term advice and follow-up (minimum of 3 months) will be provided by Drs. Bryan, Cade, Sullivant and Mackin, in collaboration with the primary veterinarian. Prior to, and then monthly over the 3 month follow-up period, outcome surveys will be conducted, both with owners and with primary care veterinarians. For those dogs that fail to respond to reasonable diagnostic and therapeutic plans for the management of chronic diarrhea, subsidized referral to MSU-CVM for specialist-level investigation will be offered. Phase 2: The proposed study will entail specialist-level investigation of dogs with chronic diarrhea that have failed to respond to standard therapy. In dogs that still have chronic diarrhea despite appropriate therapy at their primary veterinarian or through the Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine (MSU-CVM) Community Veterinary Services practice will be referred to the MSU-CVM Small Animal Medicine service, under the supervision of Drs. Sullivant and Mackin, for a full investigation. At the time of admission, Dr. Sullivant will develop (but not implement) a theoretical best guess aggressive treatment plan that would typically be instituted if owners declined referral work-up despite failure to respond to standard therapy. Individualized specialized-level diagnostic and therapeutic plans will then be devised by Dr. Sullivant. Each enrolled case will be funded for the amount needed for a full referral investigation and appropriate therapy (typically, $1,500 to $3,500). Diagnostic and therapeutic plans at MSU-CVM will be individualized based on the circumstances of each patient, but can be reasonably be expected to include: Diagnostic tests including blood tests (complete blood count and serum biochemistry), abdominal radiography and ultrasonography, and non-invasive gastrointestinal biopsy via endoscopy or, uncommonly, laparoscopy or, rarely, more invasive biopsies by exploratory surgery. Targeted therapy based on the final diagnosis, including aggressive immunosuppression for inflammatory bowel disease, antifungal drugs for fungal diseases such as histoplasmosis, and chemotherapy for cancers such as lymphosarcoma. Long-term advice and follow-up (minimum of 3 months) will be provided by Drs. Sullivant and Mackin, in collaboration with the primary veterinarian. Prior to, and then monthly over the 3 month follow-up period, outcome surveys will be conducted, both with owners and with primary care veterinarians. Additionally, one of the other specialist internists within the MSU-CVM Medicine service will then be asked to analyze the entire case. Based on the comprehensive set of diagnostic results available, the internist will develop a complete treatment plan based on the final diagnosis. The internist will then be provided with Dr. Sullivants theoretical best guess protocol, and will then assess the likelihood of success of the theoretical protocol compared to the therapeutic plan based on the final diagnosis.
current_roster.name: Practical & Cost-Effective Approach to Chronic Diarrhea in Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: An issue of debate is whether topical ophthalmic steroids interfere with blood sugar control in diabetic dogs. Currently, no studies have evaluated possible systemic effects of topical ophthalmic steroids in diabetic dogs. Topical steroid and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory ophthalmic drops are used to treat inflammation inside the eye caused by cataracts as well as to control inflammation in the eye after cataract surgery. Cataract formation is very common in dogs with diabetes mellitus; therefore, diabetic dogs constitute approximately 50% of all dogs presented to a veterinary ophthalmologist for cataract surgery. Human diabetics undergoing cataract surgery that were treated with a topical ophthalmic steroid (dexamethasone) experienced significantly increased blood glucose levels. Treatment with ocular steroids may produce similar effects in diabetic dogs. The results of this study are expected to alter medication selection in diabetic patients, especially in poorly controlled diabetic dogs. Objective: To evaluate and compare the effects of a topically applied ophthalmic steroid (prednisolone acetate) to a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (diclofenac) on blood glucose concentrations, serum fructosamine concentrations, and clinical scores in diabetic dogs with cataracts. Enrollment Criteria: Dogs with cataracts and insulin-treated diabetes mellitus determined to be controlled per history and physical examination findings will be enrolled in the study following client consent.
current_roster.name: The Effects of Ophthalmic Prednisolone and Diclofenac on Diabetes Mellitus Regulation in Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: If enrolled into this study, your dogs own tumor will be used to generate a very specific anti-cancer vaccine. Cancer vaccines represent a form of active immunotherapy, whereby they exert an antitumor effect by engaging the host immune response. Additional advantages of cancer vaccines are exquisite specificity, low toxicity, and the potential for a durable therapeutic effect / benefit as a result of the induction of immunologic memory. Autologous cancer vaccines, such as the K9-ACV (MediVet Biologics) utilized in this proposed project, are polyvalent therapeutic vaccines derived from whole tumor cells. Such vaccines are formulated on an individual case basis using tumor tissue biopsy samples from the actual patient. The vaccine system being employed in this project was developed by researchers at the University Of Kentucky College Of Medicine, in conjunction with MediVet Biologics, and was modeled on a vaccine system previously developed by the same research group at the University of Kentucky and investigated in human lung cancer patients. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of a newly formulated anti-cancer vaccine (K9-ACV, MediVet Biologics) in dogs diagnosed with a spectrum of naturally-occurring cancers. We will be measuring the patients' systemic immunologic anti-tumor response to the vaccine. It is hypothesized that this vaccine will elicit an antitumor immunologic response resulting in improved disease-free intervals and median survival times in dogs with various tumor types without compromising quality of life. What does enrollment into this trial involve? After your dog is enrolled into this study, surgery will occur atVHC to remove ordebulk the primarytumor. Part of the tumor tissue will be submitted for histopathologic diagnosis, grading and surgical margin assessment, and the remainder (minimum 5g) for vaccine formulation by the team at the University of Kentucky/MediVet Biologics. While the vaccination series cannot start until 7-14 days after the initial surgery, as this is how long the vaccine formulation takes, approval of enrollment, accompanied by owner informed consent, is required prior to surgery. In all cases of enrolled dogs, the surgical procedure to be performed would be considered standard of care treatment of that particular tumor type. Following surgery, enrolled dogs will be placed into one of two treatment groups at the owners request; the first receiving simply the vaccination series, and the second receiving the vaccination series in combination with the appropriate standard of care chemotherapy.If post-operative chemotherapy is elected by the owners, it will be performed by VHC Oncology Service. Recheck exams and blood work are required for monitoring of the patients immune response to the vaccine, as well as periodic monitoring chest x-rays and ultrasound. All study activities must occur at the VHC. Client Compensation: This study covers the cost of vaccine formulation and administration, as well as recheck exams and blood work for enrolled dogs. Periodic monitoring chest x-rays and ultrasound are also covered by the study for up to one year. Owner is responsible for the cost associated with pre-enrollment work-up and staging, which includes chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, blood work and urinalysis. In addition, the owner is responsible for the cost of surgery to remove or debulk the tumor.
current_roster.name: Anti-cancer vaccine (MediVet Biologics K9-ACV) for dogs with any malignant tumor

current_roster.description: Systemic fungal infections such as aspergillosis are rare in animals with a competent immune system. Certain dog breeds (namely the German shepherd, Rhodesian ridgeback and Hungarian vizsla) are reported to have a higher risk of this disease. A genetic etiology is suspected to cause this over-representation. We propose to use a technique called genome-wide association analysis to evaluate the differences in the genetic material of affected dogs (dogs infected with Aspergillus spp.) and healthy, unaffected dogs.
current_roster.name: Genetic analysis of the susceptibility to systemic Aspergillus infections in dogs

current_roster.description: Description: A study to develop biomarkers to assess anxiety disorders in dogs. Eligibility: Clinically healthy dogs that must be neutered/spayed and between the age of 1.5-7 years old. All participants (either separation anxiety dogs or non-anxious dogs) will be pre-screened foreligibilitythrough a questionnaire and a 20-minute video clip at home. Financial Incentive: no cost for collection of samples (blood). Primary Investigator: Dr. Niwako Ogata
current_roster.name: Separation Anxiety disorder and Non-Separation anxiety disorder dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine whether repeat vaccinations with a vaccine made from dogs' own immune cells (B cells) can prevent relapse of lymphoma when given following a standard 19-week course of chemotherapy. Eligible dogs: - Newly diagnosed with lymphoma - Have not yet received treatment (with either chemotherapy or steroids) - Planning to undergo treatment with 19-week course of chemotherapy - No evidence of leukemia - Otherwise systemically healthy Dogs who are in remission following induction chemotherapy will receive three vaccinations, each given three weeks apart. After this, dogs will be vaccinated every two months to try to prevent lymphoma relapse. There is no fee to participate in the study. The costs for the clinic visits, vaccines and follow-up monitoring will be covered by the study.
current_roster.name: RNA-transfected CD40-B cell vaccines for dogs with newly diagnosed lymphoma

current_roster.description: Hypothesis: The central hypothesis is that a novel ventral cervical fusion technique requiring minimal cervical disk removal and utilizing a combination of PEEK (poly-ether-ether-ketone) intervertebral spacers along with stabilizing pedicle screws and connecting rods will be a safe and effective way to fuse a cervical interdisk space in a horse within 6 - 12 months post-surgery. We predict that these implants utilized for cervical fusion will maintain complete stabilization and improve clinical signs of ataxia throughout the study period. Specific Aims- 1) To determine if a novel cervical fusion technique requiring minimal cervical disk removal and utilizing a combination of PEEK (poly-ether-ether-ketone) interbody spacers along with stabilizing pedicle screws and connecting rods will be a safe and effective way to achieve complete and successful cervical fusion within 12 months of surgery. Background and Significance: Neurological gait deficits resulting from cervical vertebral disease in horses is not uncommon. These deficits lead to decreased athletic abilities at a minimum, with recumbency and even death in severe cases. Cervical vertebral compressive myelopathy (CVCM) results in intermittent or continuous extradural compression of the spinal cord. Clinical signs include symmetrical ataxia along with paresis and spasticity that is often worse in the hindlimbs. CVCM is the leading cause of non-infectious spinal cord ataxia in the horse. It is estimated that it effects approximately 2% of Thoroughbred horses resulting in significant economic losses and welfare concerns. Most recently, a multicenter case-control study reported that 173 of 263 (66%) of CVCM cases were euthanized before discharge from the hospital. Many of the horses affected are young, with early clinical signs noted between 1 and 2 years of age. However, older horses are also affected as a result of osteoarthritis of the caudal cervical articular process joints. CVCM leads to Wallerian degeneration, malacia and fibrosis at locations of cord compression and demyelination of white matter. Unfortunately, these neurologic lesions often result in a horse that is not suitable for its intended purpose, leading to euthanasia in many scenarios. While the cause of CVCM has not been completely identified, multiple factors are believed to contribute, including rapid growth, trauma, nutrition, and abnormal biomechanical forces. There is currently no evidence confirming that CVCM is heritable. Both medical and surgical treatments are performed for the treatment of CVCM. Conservative treatments consist of nutritional restrictions of carbohydrates and proteins, systemic anti-inflammatory drugs, along with local therapeutics to the cervical vertebral articulations. A recent retrospective study evaluating racing records following conservative management of cervical vertebral malformations showed a prognosis for racing of 30%. Surgical treatment consists either of cervical fusion resulting in improved stability or dorsal laminectomy resulting in reduced spinal cord compression. Neurologic function was improved in 56 of 73 horses (77%) that underwent surgery. However, only 23% of surgically treated horses went on to either train of return to racing. The most commonly performed surgical procedure is cervical fusion with a Bagby Basket or Kerf-Cut Cylinder through a ventral approach. Overall, the success rate for surgeons utilizing this technique is approximately 60%. This technique relies solely on compression for stabilization, resulting in micromotion, a large amount of unwanted bone formation, and slow fusion rates (approximately 1 year). This technique also leaves very little room for error and can result in numerous catastrophic complications including ventral migration of the implant and vertebral fractures. The current procedure carries a reported fatality rate of 9%. More recently, a few studies have evaluated the use of a ventral locking plate to provide stabilization for cervical fusion. This technique has not been thoroughly evaluated clinically, but implant failure has been reported in animals as young as 3-months, making the technique questionable on the basis of biomechanical strength. In the dog, cervical stabilization is typically performed with a Steinman pin and bone cement technique with positive post-operative outcomes in about 80-90% of patients. In people, anterior discectomy and fusion is the mainstay for treatment of patients with cervical spondolytic myelopathy and some cases of discogenic radiculopathy. Spinal fusions in people are very common with over 300,000 procedures performed annually. A variety of techniques have been evaluated for fusion, including the use of plates and pedicle screws and rods in conjunction with bone allograft and autograft, intervertebral cement, or interbody cages. Recently, much research has been performed to develop an ideal interbody cage that will allow rapid growth of bone across the disc space in order to rapidly achieve full fusion. Poly-ether-ether-ketone (PEEK) cage is an interbody fusion device that has replaced allografts and metal implants such as the Bagby Basket and Kerf-Cut cylinder in human spinal fusion. PEEK is biomechanically similar to native bone, highly impervious to degredation or damage, biocompatible and radiolucent. The combination of a PEEK interbody fusion device and pedicle screws with connecting rods is currently the gold standard technique for lumbar fusion in people. The horse, in comparison to the human and the dog, offers a unique set of challenges due to their size and limitations in our ability to completely control post-operative motion, necessitating an extremely stable construct for cervical fusion. The Surgical Research Laboratory at Colorado State University has extensive expertise in the area of spinal fusion, performing over 3,500 cervical or lumbar fusions in sheep to evaluate novel implants, devices and biomaterials. From our extensive preclinical experience with spinal fusion, we feel that that stabilizing techniques and implants utilized in humans can successfully be translated to the horse for cervical fusion. The advantages of the PEEK device with pedicle screws and connecting rods are numerous. These implants are easy to use and readily available. Unlike the current equine techniques, error is less likely to result in serious complications. Less disk space removal is required and immediate stability is provided in compression and tension. The combination of both factors is likely to result in improved fusion rates as early as 4-6 months based on our previous experience in spinal fusion in sheep. To date the technique has been successfully employed in at least 10 horses. Research Design and Methods: This protocol has been approved by the Colorado State University Animal Care and Use Committee. Horses undergo an extensive neurologic evaluation including objective gait analysis prior to enrollment. Also horses undergo imaging including cervical radiographs, myelography, and CT to achieve a diagnosis of CVCM. Horses will undergo ventral cervical stabilization for cervical fusion utilizing a PEEK interbody fusion device with pedicle screws and connecting rods. The horse will be placed under general anesthesia in dorsal recumbency with the neck extended in full flexion. Fluoroscopy will be utilized throughout the procedure to ensure that the compressied site(s) is/are identified and that implants are accurately placed in the correct location. A ventral midline approach to the cervical spine is used similar to the published Kerf-Cut cylinder technique. The ventral aspect is exposed and the disk space is identified. A small section of keel will be removed and used as a bone graft. Using a Midas-Rex neurologic drill, a bone window is created through the keel and into the disk space to a depth of approximately 35mm. The bone window will accommodate a 30mm length x 24 mm depth x 14mm height PEEK intervertebral fusion device. The bone removed from the keel will be broken into small pieces and placed into the openings of the PEEK device to act a bone graft. The device will be impacted into the space and in close contact to the endplate. Once the PEEK device is in place, a 3.2mm unicortical hole will be drilled into the left and right side close to the disk space and approximately 5cm apart. A 4.5mm x 30mm polyaxial pedicle screw will be screwed into each hole to an appropriate depth under fluoroscopic guidance. Once the pedicle screws are in place, a 5.0mm connecting rod cut to the appropriate size will span the disk space and placed into the head of the polyaxial pedicle screws. Torque-limited set-screws will be placed on top of the connecting rod and screwed into place, but not locked. A compression tool will be placed on either side of the pedicle screws to compress the disk space against the PEEK device, while the set-screws are locked in placed with a torque limiting wrench. A final fluoroscopic image will be taken and the tissues are closed routinely in 4 layers. A stent bandage will be placed over the incision to provide pressure to the wound during the initial healing stages. The horse will be taken to a padded recovery and allowed to recover from anesthesia in a routine fashion. All horses will receive perioperative antibiotics (cefazolin 11mg/kg IV q 8hr) and anti-inflammatory medications (phenylbutazone, 2.2mg/kg IV q 12hr).Horses will be confined to a stall for the first 30 days, followed by controlled exercise for another 60 days after which a rehabilitation program will be discussed. Full neurological examinations will be performed at 24 hrs, 48 hrs, and 1 week, followed by monthly examinations. A complete series of cervical radiographs focused on the fused sites will be performed at 3, 6 and 12 months throughout the study period.
current_roster.name: Novel surgery for horses with Wobblers Syndrome (CVSM, CVM, cervical vertebral malformation, cervical vertebral myelopathy)

current_roster.description: A prospective placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, multi-site study to evaluate the efficacy and safety ofainvestigational drug(IVP) compared to placebo (ICP) for the treatment of RAO and SPAOPD in client owned and university owned horses. The study is divided into two phases. Phase 1 is designed to assess clinical efficacy and safety of IVP and ICP in horses under field conditions. Phase 2 is designed to further assess clinical safety of IVP for up to 90(4) additional days as well as to better define the need for and timing of repeated treatment intervals. Treatment is administeredby inhalation for 10 consecutive days to horses diagnosed with RAO and/or SPAOPD under field conditions (Phase 1). In addition, safety will be evaluated for an additional 90 (4) days in approximately 100 horses with RAO and/or SPAOPD during which time horses may be retreatedwith the active investigational drugfor recurrence of symptoms (Phase 2). The extended use phase of the study will support the repeated use of this treatment during recurrence of clinical signs.
current_roster.name: Efficacy& Safety Field Study for Horses with Recurrent Airway Obstruction (RAO) and/or Summer Pasture Associated Obstructive Pulmo

current_roster.description: Rationale: Neuropathic pain affects 90% of people living with spinal cord injury (SCI), yet it is an under-appreciated morbidity in canine patients with the same disease. This is likely because assessment of neuropathic pain in people relies heavily on self-reporting, something our veterinary patients are not able to do. Objective methods to quantify neuropathic pain have been used in rodent models of SCI and in the human clinical setting. Our laboratory has recently adapted one such technique for use in dogs. The time frame for development of neuropathic pain in dogs with SCI is currently unknown, as is the frequency of its occurrence. Hypothesis/objectives: Our hypothesis is that neuropathic pain is a common morbidity in dogs with SCI and that its presence and response to therapy can be monitored reliably in the clinical setting using quantitative sensory testing (QST). Study design: Will use a non-invasive method for testing mechanical sensory threshold to document the time course for development of and frequency of occurrence of neuropathic pain in dogs with SCI caused by intervertebral disc extrusion (IVDE).
current_roster.name: Neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury

current_roster.description: Approximately one-third of the estimated 0.62% -0.75% dogs with epilepsy have seizures that are refractory to treatment, and suffer an increased morbidity and fatality associated with poor seizure control. Although death can be a consequence of seizures and associated complications, more dogs are euthanized due to the negative impact of uncontrolled seizures on the dogs quality of life and the financial and emotional burden placed on the caregiver. There is a critical need to address the challenges faced by caregivers in the medical management of these refractory epileptic dogs, in order to improve quality of life for both the dog and its caregiver and lead to more successful outcomes. One consistent source of worry for caregivers is the risk of seizures occurring while a dog is left unattended. This concern is shared by caregivers of humans with epilepsy, and has led to the recent emergence of wrist-worn accelerometers that detect seizure activity as an important tool in the management of humans with epilepsy. We propose to evaluate the use of accelerometry to detect seizure activity in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy, and hypothesize that a commercially available, collar mounted accelerometer can be utilized to reliably detect generalized seizure activity in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy. Specific objectives are: 1) To determine the sensitivity and specificity of the Whistle Activity Monitor to detect generalized seizures in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy, based on a predefined algorithm; 2) To determine if sensitivity and specificity can be improved by refining the algorithm based on an individual dogs seizure and activity patterns; and 3) To document any beneficial or adverse effects associated with use of the Whistle Activity Monitor in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy. Forty idiopathic epileptic dogs that experience 3 or more generalized seizures per month will have a Whistle Activity Monitor mounted on their collar for 6 months. The recorded seizure activity, based on caregiver observation and video monitoring, will be compared to the number of seizure events detected by the device, and specificity and sensitivity calculated. During the initial 3-month period, a predefined algorithm will be used for seizure detection. For the next 3 months, an individualized algorithm will be utilized based on data obtained in the first period. Quality of life assessed through a caregiver questionnaire will be compared between study initiation and completion. The availability of a noninvasive, inexpensive device to reliably detect seizures in dogs would significantly improve the management of idiopathic epilepsy in dogs. The risk of injury or death from unobserved seizures would likely decrease, as would the accompanying caregivers worry. Overall outcome would be expected to improve, with fewer epileptic dogs being euthanized. In addition, the device would advance research into canine epilepsy treatment, by providing an unbiased, objective tool for recording seizure activity during therapeutic trials
current_roster.name: Use of accelerometry to detect seizure activity in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy

current_roster.description: Canine Brain Tumor Vaccine Clinical Trial We greatly appreciate your interest in our clinical study evaluating the use of a vaccine in dogs with brain tumors, specifically glioma. Your pets clinician will explain the disease characteristics of glioma as well as available treatment options. If you choose to participate in this clinical study, this handout will provide you with some insight into the purpose of this study and will explain your responsibilities and patient procedures. What are clinical trials? Clinical trials are research studies. They are used in all specialties of medicine to evaluate new types of treatment. Clinical trials may be designed to determine the anti-cancer effects and side effects of new drugs, new surgical procedures, new radiation therapy procedures, or novel approaches to treatment (such as gene therapy or immunotherapy). Your pets clinician will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Gliomas in dogs are known to be a very aggressive cancer with relatively short survival times despite our best efforts at treatment. Because of this, we are always looking for new ways to treat this disease. Many new cancer treatments are aimed at activating the patients own immune system (called immunotherapy) to potentially make it more effective at fighting off the cancer. One form of immunotherapy is tumor vaccines. This vaccine was developed in the Dow Laboratory, and targets the cancer stem cells, which are the precursor cells that then migrate and mature into active tumor cells with appropriate biochemical signals. These cancer stem cells are thought to be responsible for the inevitable recurrence of gliomas. These cells are present in the subventricular zone of the brain, and as such are not accessible for resection with the primary tumor. As these precursor cells are not in active division and thus are resistant to chemotherapy and radiation therapy, immunotherapies are likely the key to achieving improved outcomes for gliomas. A successful vaccine that targets these cancer stem cells would be invaluable. The goal of this study is to evaluate preliminary tumor response to vaccination as well as vaccine tolerability. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? To be eligible for this study, dogs must have a brain tumor that is presumed to be in the glioma family based on MRI characteristics. They must also have sufficiently stable clinical signs to allow likely survival of at least one month. The patients neurological status must be such that he/she is strongly ambulatory without assistance, and that seizures (if occurring) are controlled with anti-convulsant medication. Dogs must not be receiving prednisone, or must be on a dose <0.5 mg/kg/day for at least 72 hours prior to starting the vaccine series, and maintain below that threshold for at least 7 days post-final vaccine. Past radiation therapy patients and chemotherapy patients are not eligible. Dogs with preexisting allergic airway disease or low heart rate may not receive propranolol, which is one of two medications given in addition to the vaccine to enhance the vaccine effect, and may be excluded at the investigator's discretion. Dogs must undergo some diagnostic testing at CSU prior to starting the vaccines to ensure that they are eligible, including complete blood count, chemistry profile, urinalysis, and needle biopsy (not debulking) of the tumor (costs will be covered by the study). What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? If enrolled, dogs will first have a needle biopsy of their tumor, and if confirmed glioma, then they will receive a vaccine under the skin once every other week for a total 6 vaccines, followed by once monthly vaccine boosters. Serial neurological exams will be performed at each visit during the study period, and recheck MRI scans of the brain will be done every 3 months after the first vaccine. Additional blood samples will be collected for study purposes prior to the first vaccine and then serially throughout the study to assess antitumor immune response. In addition to the vaccine, two additional medications (losartan and propranolol) will be given orally (by mouth) to enhance the effect of the vaccine. Once your pet has died or been euthanized, a post-mortem exam will be required for additional characterization of tumor type, growth, and cellular markers. What side effects or risks may my pet experience while participating in this clinical trial? Your pet may experience side effects. Possible side effects associated with the vaccine treatment include: Local vaccine site reactions (swelling, pain, redness, itching) Fever, mild loss of appetite, and/or lethargy for first 24 hours after vaccine injection Risk of anaphylaxis (rare) Cerebral edema and worsening of neurological signs (unlikely) due to peritumoral inflammation from exuberant response of tumor to vaccine Losartan may cause low blood pressure or lethargy; if this occurs the dosage will be decreased Propanolol may cause slow heart rate, low blood pressure, or lethargy; if this occurs the dosage will be adjusted Needle biopsy side effects may include: transient neurological decline, hemorrhage, infection, or less commonly permanent neurological decline or death The study is able to cover up to $500 in treatment costs for vaccine-associated adverse events if they occur. Adverse events are not anticipated, and most likely would involve simple local reactions that would require only oral medications to treat. Your pets clinician will discuss possible side effects with you and help you manage them if they occur. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your clinician. How long will my pet be in the clinical trial? The study period is 1 year. However, the length of your pets participation will depend on his/her response to the treatment. If your pets clinical signs are worsening or there is concern for tumor progression, your pet may be withdrawn from the study before it is completed. Your pets clinician will discuss continued treatment and diagnostic testing once the trial has ended. Can my pet withdraw from the clinical trial? You may decide to withdraw your pet from the clinical trial at any time. Tell your pets clinician if you are considering withdrawing your pet. It is important to discuss withdrawal in order to determine a plan for continued treatment of your pets cancer. Your clinician may stop your pet from continued participation in the clinical trial at any time if he/she believes it is in your pets best interest or if the trial is discontinued or if the trial protocol is not followed. What financial incentives will CSU provide for my pets participation? All required study activities once enrolled (not including the diagnostic tests to determine eligibility), will be performed at no cost. (Costs for medications or treatments that are not included as part of the study, are not covered by the study). There is no charge for the postmortem examination. In addition, up to $500 will be available for treatment of vaccine-related adverse events. What are my responsibilities during the clinical trial? You are responsible for the costs of any elective services, medications, or additional hospitalization fees not required by the study. In addition, any costs for treatment of adverse events beyond the $500 covered by the study will be your financial responsibility, as well as the cost and any other tests recommended by your pets neurologist that are not a required component of the study. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Questions? Please do not hesitate to obtain additional information from your pets neurology clinician if you do not understand something about the study or your pets care and treatment. CSU Principal Investigator: Dr. Rebecca Packer, (970) 297-4543, email: Rebecca.Packer@colostate.edu Emergency Assistance: CSU VTH, (970) 297-5000. 2008, Animal Cancer Center, Colorado State University
current_roster.name: Canine brain tumor vaccine clinical trial

current_roster.description: Which dogs can participate in this study? In this study, dogs that have been diagnosed with a surgically resectable brain tumor, based on MRI, are eligible for the study. Study Activities In this study, surgery would proceed according to normal standard of care; however, during surgery a novel imaging device will be used to record the chemical signal of the tissues visible during surgery. This imaging device is completely noninvasive, and will allow us to learn the differences in chemical signal of normal brain tissue compared to tumor tissue. This is important because visually some brain tumors look identical to tumor tissue, so improved methods of recognizing abnormal cells during surgery are vital to improving surgical accuracy. The readings obtained during surgery will be compared to the biopsy samples obtained as a normal component of tumor resection. This study only requires noninvasive acquisition of biochemical recordings during surgery. The surgery itself is performed in the same manner as any standard surgical resection of your pet's brain tumor. Financial Incentives This study does not include administration of novel therapies; however, it does offer a $5000 subsidy towards the cost of surgical resection. Please note that specific estimates for the remaining out-of-pocket surgical expenses can be provided upon request based on your pet's tumor location, neurological status, and specific surgical approach required.
current_roster.name: Validation of a novel imaging device to detect cancerous vs normal cells during brain tumor resection

current_roster.description: Most mast cell tumors (MCTs) are associated with long-term survival after surgical excision, however, when surgery is not feasible due to location, size, or owner preference, there is no true standard of care. Therefore, an effective treatment that can induce regression on these tumors with minimal side effects is needed. In a recent pilot study in dogs treated with intra-tumoral injections of human IL-2, there was a promising anti-MCT effect.The purpose of this trial is to determine the efficacy and safety of the ALVAC IL-2 immunomodulator for the treatment of cutaneous MCTs in dogs. All upon entry into the trial, patients will receive weekly intra-tumoral injections and then close monitoring thereafter.This study is partial funded and will covermostof the cost for staging (blood work, cytology, consultation) and subsequent weekly study treatments (exam and blood work). Upon completion of the study, owners are also provided some financial incentive to help defray the cost of either surgery or additional therapies.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for measurable canine mast cell tumors

current_roster.description: Hypothesis: We hypothesize horses presenting for suspected small intestinal strangulating lesions that have a positive bacterial culture of peritoneal fluid obtained on admission will have larger amounts and more compromised small intestine as compared to horses that have no bacterial growth. In addition, positive bacterial culture would predispose horses to increased post-operative complications (ileus, laminitis, incisional infections, adhesions and post-operative colic). Animal Groups: All horses involved in this study are client-owned animals presenting to the Tufts Hospital Large Animals for evaluation of colic. Further examination by admitting clinicians (large animal medicine and surgery residents) will determine if the horses have a suspected strangulating lesion of the small intestine Materials and Methods: Horses included in this study will be client-owned animals presenting to TCSVM with colic signs attributable to small intestine strangulation. Historical parameters obtained will include: duration of colic, medications administered prior to admission, and examination findings obtained by the referring veterinarian (physical examination, rectal examination, nasogastric reflux volume). Horses receiving antibiotics prior to admission will be excluded. At admission, horses will undergo physical examination, rectal examination, nasogastric intubation, and abdominal ultrasound. In addition preliminary blood work (packed cell volume, total solids, and lactate) and abdominal fluid analysis will be performed. Horses will be determined to have a suspected small intestinal strangulating lesion with the following inclusion criteria: palpable dilated or thickened small intestine on rectal examination; non-motile, dilated small intestine on ultrasound examination (diameter > 4 cm); net nasogastric reflux > 4 liters; elevation of peripheral blood lactate (>2 mmol/L); serosanguinous abdominal fluid with elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L); tachycardia (> 48 b/min); and persistent abdominal pain. When a small intestine strangulating lesion is suspected by the admitting clinician, venous blood samples will be collected and submitted for a venous blood gas (NOVA) and complete blood count. In addition, abdominal fluid samples will be collected using routine sterile technique and submitted for cytology, blood gas analysis (NOVA), as well as aerobic and anaerobic bacterial culture. Abdominal fluid will be submitted to IDEXX Laboratories in culturettes with transport media and in blood culture vials. Horses with strangulating lesions necessitate surgical evaluation and treatment via a ventral midline celiotomy, thus strangulating lesions will be confirmed at the time of surgery (prior to submission of samples). Please note that venipuncture and abdominocentesis are performed in all horses presenting with a suspected small intestinal strangulating lesion and no additional procedures are performed in horses with inclusion in this study.
current_roster.name: Horses with strangulating small intestinal lesions

current_roster.description: Dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca =KCS) is a serious condition in dogs, affecting up to 20% or more of some breeds. The basis for dry eye is unknown, although the gland (lacrimal gland) that keeps the eye lubricated is badly damaged by cells of the body that maintain our defenses (immune cells). Thus it is called an auto-immune disease. A human disease called Sjogrens Disease has a similar appearance, thus dry eye might be a model for human Sjogrens Disease. The specific objective of this study is to improve our understanding of the cause of dry eye, by analyzing blood and saliva which contain clues (i.e., biomarkers, specifically in the form of microRNA) to the origin of the disease. The hypothesis is that these biomarker miRNA in saliva and blood will shed light on the underlying cause because miRNA control the function of our genes (DNA). The explicit goal is to find which miRNA differentiate dogs with dry eye from normals. Dogs with a diagnosis of dry eye/KCS presenting to the ophthalmology service at TCSVM prior to initiation of therapy (e.g. cyclosporine A or Tacrolimus) will be enrolled using voluntary/informed consent for collection of blood and saliva. Following sample collection, study involvement of each canine will be completed.
current_roster.name: Canine KCS

current_roster.description: Feline chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS) is a poorly defined disease characterized by inflammatory lesion, mostly ulcerative or proliferative in nature, affecting the gums and the back of the mouth. None of the treatments that are currently available are ideal, predictable and without possible complications. In our previous studies in over 20 cats, systemic (intravenous) administration autologous feline stem cells were shown to not only be safe, but, in most cases (about 70%), substantially improved or completely resolved the stomatitis. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to treat cats for which all current treatment modalities have failed and have a poor quality of life. Multiple tracks of the study are currently available and are decided based on predefined criteria.
current_roster.name: Stem cells treatment of gingivostomatitis

current_roster.description: Vitamin D not only plays an important role in regulating calcium in the body, but it also promotes a healthy immune system. We currently do not know if dogs with autoimmune disease have low levels of vitamin D, and if so what role that may play in promoting autoimmunity. Low vitamin D levels have been associated with autoimmune disease in rodent models and people. This study seeks to determine blood levels of vitamin D in dogs with immune mediated disease compared to healthy dogs. Markers of immune function will also be assessed. Vitamin D levels will then be compared to patient outcomes to determine if dogs with lower vitamin D levels have poorer prognoses.
current_roster.name: Determining if Dogs with Autoimmune Disease have Low Vitamin D Levels

current_roster.description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and sponsored by the Morris Animal Foundation seeks to evaluate in dogs with osteosarcoma the safety and effectiveness of Standard of Care therapy, with or without adjuvant rapamycin administration. Standard of Care is defined as definitive surgery, being amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on a q21 day schedule. Carboplatin has been safely and effectively used to treat appendicular osteosarcoma in dogs for > 20 years, but the potential for unforeseen potentially life-threatening side effects from surgery, chemotherapy, and/or progressive cancer does exist. ALL dogs enrolled onto study will receive Standard of Care therapy; however, through a randomization process, some dogs entered into study will also receive additional therapy with oral rapamycin. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved for immunosuppression during preparatory and maintenance regimens for organ and bone marrow transplant in human patients. Early work with rapamycin suggests that this agent might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting (reducing the effects of) an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. Preclinical studies of rapamycin in mice, as well as recent data using analogous drugs in human patients (rapalogs), suggest that mTOR blockade might be effective in the treatment of several cancers. Studies in mice have shown rapamycin to be safe when used to treat experimental cancers. In a recently completed study of rapamycin in dogs with cancer, a dose and schedule for rapamycin administration have been defined which appears to be safe and tolerable by most dogs. These 2 studies (COTC021 and COTC022) will evaluate if orally administered rapamycin following Standard of Care improves long-term disease control.
current_roster.name: COTC021: Evaluation of Orally Administered mTOR Inhibitor Rapamycin in Dogs in the Adjuvant Setting with Osteosarcoma; COTC022: A

current_roster.description: ENROLLMENT FOR THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To assess the accuracy of using heart sonograms (echocardiography) in determining blood pressure in the pulmonary vessels in dogs with heart valve disease (CVD). Background This study is intended to assess the accuracy of echocardiography in determining pulmonary artery pressure in dogs with CVD. The results of the study will improve the diagnostic evaluation of pulmonary hypertension (PH) in dogs and our understanding of dogs with pre-clinical CVD, providing for the first time important data on cardiac function. Because early phases of PH in dogs with CVD may be reversible, it is important to recognize the condition as soon as possible as this may affect therapeutic decisions and therefore, outcome of affected dogs. Eligibility Dogs with mitral valve disease (also known as endocardiosis) that have: o an enlarged heart on chest X-ray o mitral valve disease confirmed by cardiac ultrasound (echocardiography) o tricuspid regurgitation (backflow through the tricuspid valve) identified by cardiac ultrasound (echocardiography) My dog is being treated for heart disease, can he be enrolled in the study? Yes, your dog can be enrolled while being treated for heart disease if he or she has had no change in symptoms or medications in the last month. Exclusion Criteria Dogs with mitral valve disease that do not have an enlarged heart Dogs that have other significant diseases such as kidney disease Dogs weighting less than 5 kg (11 pounds) Study Design Dogs will undergo standard echocardiographic examination to establish baseline measurements. Dogs will then be sedated and a catheter will be inserted into the jugular vein so that pressures in the right side of their heart and pulmonary blood vessels can be measured. These measurements will be compared with the echocardiographic findings. A recheck including an echocardiographic exam and chest X-rays will be performed after 3 months. Compensation Enrolled dogs will receive, at no cost, a physical examination/office visit, renal function profile, thoracic radiographs (chest x-rays), right-sided cardiac catheterization, and complete echocardiographic examination. One follow-up visit after 3 months is also included. The value of these services is estimated at over $500. The costs of an initial screening exam may be covered for patients who are likely to be eligible. Contact Mindy Quigley, Clinical Trials CoordinatorOffice Phone: 540-231-1363 | Email:vettrials@vt.edu Dr. Michele Borgarelli , Principal InvestigatorEmail:micheb1@vt.edu ENROLLMENT FOR THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED
current_roster.name: Accuracy of Non-Invasively Determined Pulmonary Artery Pressure in Dogs with Chronic Valve Disease (CVD)

current_roster.description: Prior to enrollment into this study, your dog has been determined to have severe problems with his (her) hind legs due to disk herniation with degenerative material slipping into the spinal canal confirmed by advanced imaging. Due to the loss of "pain perception" in the hind legs and tail, the prognosis is guarded for recovery, with many dogs not improving after surgery. We are evaluating the use of umbilical cord tissue stem cells called Whartons Jelly Mesenchymal Stem Cell" treatment combined with decompressive surgery, to determine if this treatment will help patients improve more quickly and more completely. However, since this a randomized study, there is a 50% chance that your dog will not receive a stem cell treatment.
current_roster.name: Stem cell therapy for paralyzed dogs

current_roster.description: Atopic dermatitis (AD) affects approximately 10% of the canine population globally and is likely the most prevalent skin disease in the dog requiring medical intervention. Affected individuals are genetically predisposed to developing inflammatory skin disease with characteristic clinical features associated with lgE antibodies directed against environmental allergens, such as house dust mites, pollens, and molds. Current treatment options for canines include antihistamines , corticosteroids , cyclosporine A, oclacitinib , and allergen specific immunotherapy (ASIT) administered subcutaneously or sublingually, as well as adjunctive treatments such as topical and systemic antimicrobial therapy . Avoidance of implicated allergens is impractical or impossible in most cases. These approaches to treatment are not entirely reliable, have potential for adverse reactions, or they come with significant financ ial burden. There is a great need for finding a novel, safe, and effective treatment for the management of canine AD Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been extensively evaluated in human medicine for their clinical applications in the repair of damaged tissues and in the treatment of chronic, degenerative inflammatory diseases because of their diverse wound healing and anti inflammatory properties"1" . Recently it was shown that MSC reduce mast cell degranulation to control AD in mouse models of AD"2" . Our primary goal is to investigate the safety and biological activity of canine placental (fetal) derived MSCs (Wharton's Jelly MSC = WJ-MSC) in alleviating the clinical signs associated with canine AD. Our secondary goal is to investigate the feasibility of this protocol for future applications in larger scale randomized controlled double-blinded clinical trials. Dogs enrolled in the study will continue to receive any immunosuppressive therapy they have been on as we are effectively looking for dogs that are only partially or completely refractory to standard of care treatment.
current_roster.name: Stem cell therapy for atopic dermatitis

visible_sc_items.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

current_roster.description: Platelets are small blood cells that contain protective growth factors in the blood. Current studies in human medicine are showing that by injecting these concentrated platelets (via platelet rich plasma, or PRP) into joint capsules, they may help to provide pain relief and maintain healthy cartilage. This study is determining if the same effects are seen in canine patients and to understand how autologous PRP might be utilized to alleviate pain of osteoarthritis in dogs with one affected knee. Dogs will receive a full examination with the Sports Medicine and Rehabilitation service and gait analysis will be performed utilizing force mat systems to record gait proficiency. Dogs will be sedated and blood will be drawn to be processed into PRP. The prepared PRP will be injected into the affected knee and the dog will returned to owners once awake. Dogs will return to Cornell monthly for recheck visits and repeat gait analysis for up to 3 months. Owners will fill out pain scoring questionnaires both before the injection and at each recheck visit. If no effect is seen at any time throughout the study, owners may remove their dogs from the study and additional treatments or therapy may be performed if requested.
current_roster.name: Using Platelet Rich Plasma (PRP) Injections for Treating Arthritis in the Knees of Dogs

current_roster.description: To determine if Telmisartan, a medication used to reduce protein loss through the kidneys, is broken down and processed differently in dogs with kidney disease compared to healthy dogs. To compare the ability of Telmisartan to control protein loss through the kidneys in dogs with protein-losing kidney disease (protein-losing nephropathy, or PLN) with benazepril, one of the medications in the class of medications (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) that is currently standard therapy for this disease. We hypothesize that the processing of Telmisartan in dogs with PLN will be altered compared to the patterns previously established in healthy dogs, and that Telmisartan will be equally or more effective than benazepril at treating PLN.
current_roster.name: Use of Telmisartan vs benazepril in dogs with kidney disease

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma (OSA), the most common bone tumor found in the dog, has already spread by the time we diagnose 90% of the cases. Survival times are limited, from 3-4 months with surgery alone, and 9-14 months with the addition of chemotherapy. In order to improve survival in dogs, newer therapies are needed. We are studying genetically modified Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV-IFN-NIS) which has been shown to be effective against cancer in the laboratory and in a pilot study of eight dogs. The study will treat dogs with VSV intravenously, followed by amputation of the affected limb 10 days later, then followed by chemotherapy with carboplatin. February 2018: expanded trial to placebo-controlled. Dogs will be screened for acceptability, including a CT scan under anesthesia. Once enrolled, dogs typically spend the week at the Veterinary Medical Center (VMC). We will perform a tumor biopsy under anesthesia and take baseline samples of blood, cheek, urine and stool on Monday. On Tuesday dogs receive the treatment with VSV-IFN-NIS or saline placebo and will be housed in isolation, closely monitored by our team, for a period of time (6-24 hrs). We will sample blood, cheek, urine and stool periodically to detect virus shedding and immune responses. On Wed - Fri, we will monitor the dog and take additional samples. Dogs go home on Friday. Recheck visits are weekly for 1st month. Day 10 is the amputation surgery. Chemotherapy begins about Day 21, and will continue for six treatments (standard protocol through the Oncology Service). Study rechecks are at months 3, 6, and one year. We will repeat a CT scan typically at the 3 month visit.
current_roster.name: VIGOR Trial

current_roster.description: Purpose of study: The primary purpose of this study is to test two investigational medications to determine if either one, or both, work to potentially decrease signs of pain of osteoarthritis in dogs. As a result of this study, the veterinary medical researchers and scientists hope to learn more about osteoarthritis, and how these medicines might work to help osteoarthritis. The medicines being tested could be further developed for either animals or humans. Description of study: - Four randomly assigned groups: one with each investigational drug, one with Rimadyl and onewith placebo - Visits: Visits 1 and 2 for screening diagnostic tests (exam, lameness evaluation, X-rays, ECG, blood and urine sampling), Visit 2 becomes dosing visit if dog qualifies, Visit 3 at two weeks following, Visit 4 two weeks after Visit 3 - All study drugs given orally in clinic on visit days, and at home by owner (twice daily dosing) The study covers costs of study visits, screening diagnostics, study medications and study-related tests. Owners who complete the study are eligible for a Visa gift card up to $150. For questions and to schedule an appointment, please contact Sara Pracht (see above).
current_roster.name: TCMR0002 (investigational drugs for dogs with osteoarthritis)

current_roster.description: Vagal nerve stimulation has been used in people for treatment of various diseases including epilepsy. Recently, a noninvasive method of vagal nerve stimulation has become possible with a handheld device which has been used in people for treatment of primary headaches and acute asthma. It is possible that, much like implanted vagal nerve stimulators, these new devices could have a widespread effect on the electrical and neurochemical environment resulting in seizure control, and will therefore allow a practical, cost-effective and accepted treatment for canine patients with poor seizure control. As part of a pilot study, we have treated 8 dogs with seizure disorders using this device and can confirm that there have been no side effects noted or safety concerns raised by the owners. Prior to enrollment, each dog will need to have a 2 month seizure diary documenting previous seizure frequency. Dogs will be randomized to one of two treatment groups: a treatment group in which the device will be used on dogs for the initial eight week period and a group in which the device will not be used for the initial 8 week period. Approximately 5 ml of blood will be collected at the week 0 and the final rechecks for labwork (CBC, chemistry profile, bile acid and Phenobarbital testing), in addition to urine for urinalysis. Dosage of preexisting anticonvulsant treatment will not be altered throughout the study. All owners will be asked to keep a daily diary regarding the use of the vagal nerve stimulator and any side effects that might be related to its use, as well as a diary that outlines seizure events. Treatment with the vagal nerve stimulator consists of applying the device to the left side of the dogs neck 3 times per day (i.e., in the morning, afternoon, and evening, with 8 hours separating treatments) for 90 seconds duration for each treatment. At the end of the initial 8 week period, dogs will return for a recheck and will be then be treated with the device for an additional eight week period, regardless of his/her previous treatment assignment. A final recheck after the second 8 weeks will complete enrollment. Upon acceptance into the study, all recheck evaluations, and initial and follow up lab-work will be paid by the sponsor. The vagal nerve stimulators will be provided by the sponsor for use during study enrollment. The client is responsible for the cost of the initial examination and any diagnostics performed outside of study specifications. Duration of study: This study is currently OPEN. Study participation is at least 16 weeks duration following enrollment. Potential benefits to veterinary medicine: If effective, this study may provide a novel, noninvasive treatment for refractory idiopathic epilepsy with minimal side effects, which may ultimately provide a valuable option to veterinary practitioners for treatment of complicated epilepsy cases.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a Hand Held Nerve Stimulator (GammaCore VET™) for the treatment of refractory seizure activity associated with a dia

current_roster.description: This clinical trial sponsored by AB Science, assesses the safety and effectiveness of masitinib compared to placebo when given to dogs with mast cell tumors (grade 2 or 3) that cannot be surgically removed. Study summary: Screening visit for physical exam, tumor biopsy, blood and urine sampling Baseline visit for physical exam, tumor measurements, aspirate of lymph node(s), ultrasound, chest X-ray, blood and urine sampling Oral medication either placebo or masitinib, given daily at home. Dogs have a 2 out of 3 chance to receive masitinib.
