Each canine will be given a minimum of one dose of cefepime as primary or adjunctive therapy for this condition. Pharmacokinetics (PK) will be measured at specified time points. Results of this study will be used as preliminary data to enable proper design of a larger funded study.
current_roster.name: Clinical Study for Dogs with Bacterial Pneumonia

current_roster.description: VCA West Los Angeles Animal Hospital is pleased to announce a new clinical study to evaluate the effects of a topical medication (lanosterol) for the treatment of cataracts in dogs. Dogs will be considered candidates for the study following an initial or recent diagnosis of cataract by the primary care practitioner, veterinary internist or veterinary ophthalmologist. Cataracts are one of the most significant ophthalmologic diseases in veterinary medicine. The prevalence of cataract is also influenced by age and affects 17% of the 7-15+-year old dog population.
current_roster.name: Effect of Topical Lanosterol on Canine Cataracts

current_roster.description: Vinblastine has been used in feline cancer patients mostly as a component of multi-drug treatment protocols for lymphoma. Response rates, progression-free survival and lymphoma-specific survival are similar between cats receiving vinblastine or vincristine as part of a multi-drug protocol for lymphoma. However, cats receiving vinblastine may have a lower incidence of gastrointestinal toxicity, and this can be a deciding factor in choosing vinblastine over vincristine for treatment of lymphoma in cats. The incidence of neutropenia in cats following administered vinblastine versus vincristine does not appear to differ and dose reductions due to neutropenia are sometimes required during vinblastine therapy. No pharmacokinetic data exist for vinblastine in the cat. In other species, vinblastine demonstrates either a bi- or tri-exponential decline in plasma concentrations with abundant distribution to tissues that occurs rapidly after dosing. Vinblastine readily accumulates within the cellular component of blood, as it binds to tubulin within platelets and blood cells; up to 50% of drug may distribute to the cellular compartment of blood within 20 minutes of administration. Consistent with the findings of abundant tissue distribution, vinblastine has a large volume of distribution for and plasma protein binding values ranging from 43-99% depending on the species studied. Extensive hepatic metabolism of vinblastine leads to formation of one major metabolite, 4-desacetylvinblastine, suggested to have equal or greater antitumor activity to the parent molecule in dogs and humans. It is unknown if metabolism in cats also produces this active compound. Of note, pharmacokinetic studies in all other species have identified substantial inter- and intra-individual variability in pharmacokinetics which is noted clinically by the equally large variability in neutropenia following equivalent doses.It is important to understand the pharmacokinetics of vinblastine in the population of patients that are receiving this drug; older, cancer-bearing cats that may have other co-morbid diseases that can affect pharmacokinetic profiles, i.e. hepatic or renal disease. Variability in pharmacokinetics is likely to be larger in this population when compared to younger, healthy cats. This study is designed to obtain the information required to describe the pharmacokinetics of vinblastine in cats and associate the variability in pharmacokinetic parameters with patient variables.
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetic analysis of vinblastine in tumor bearing cats and analysis of population covariates

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Standard therapy for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma has long been amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy to delay the spread of cancer. With this form of treatment, survival times of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma is on average about 10 to 12 months with little improvement in survival occurring over the past two decades. ADXS31-164c is a vaccine that is designed to cause the immune system to inhibit an important receptor that may aid in cancer progression known as HER2/neu. The purpose of this study is to determine if adding the vaccine ADXS31-164c into the treatment protocol for dogs with osteosarcoma will be safe and improve efficacy of current standard therapies for osteosarcoma in dogs.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a recombinant, attenuated Listeria monocytogenes expressing a chimeric human HER2/neu protein in dogs in the adjuvan

current_roster.description: Dozens of veterinary patients are treated with radiation for tumors of the chest each year at Colorado State University VTH. How much these tumor move during the breathing cycle in dogs is critical for radiation treatment planning and safe delivery of radiation. Further, it is important for our radiation oncology practice to determine when we need to manage breathing under anesthesia, such as with breath holds. To date, no information exists which describes the degree or direction of motion that chest tumors in dogs undergo during the breathing cycle. Performing breath holds (holding the patients breath for them under anesthesia for a short period of time, usually 30-45 seconds) lengthens treatment time and requires experienced staff; however, we believe this procedure is warranted for select cases. The goal of this study is to determine how much tumors in or on the chest of dogs move during the breathing cycle.
current_roster.name: Excursion of canine thoracic masses with inspiratory and expiratory breath holds

current_roster.description:
Nasal cancer in dogs and cats are uncommon with carcinomas being most common in dogs. Treatment has been limited to external beam radiation therapy at significant expense and often multiple days of anesthesia needed. Median survival is about 1 year and side effects are common. Electrochemotherapy is the use of electrical impulses to open cell membranes driving chemotherapy locally, i.e. a targeted therapy.


We now have an electrode that may be used for nasal tumors based on published material below:.


Radiol Oncol.2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430. doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec. Minimally InvasiveElectrochemotherapyProcedure for TreatingNasalDuct Tumors inDogs using a Single Needle Electrode. Maglietti F,Tellado M,Olaiz N,Michinski S,Marshall G


Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we useelectrochemotherapy(ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. MATERIALS AND METHODS:In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.RESULTS:In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treatednasalpassage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treatnasaltumors with encouraging results. Those clients not electing to participate with this therapy will be followed and data used for comparison. Rechecks may also be done with RDVM but advanced imaging post treatment would be necessary to follow response. While the study is for canine patients, there is no reason not to look at feline and wildlife with the same or similar diagnosis.


The procedure involves a short general anesthesia and is generally an outpatient procedure. Minimal side-effects have been noted and anti-inflammatory pain management may be necessary for a few days post procedure


For more information:

LINK TO TEXTBOOK:

https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-80668-2

https://www.vetspecialists.com/vet-blog-landing/animal-health-articles/2024/01/23/electrochemotherapy-cancer-treatment
current_roster.tagline: Nasal Cancer Treatment
current_roster.name: Nasal Cancer Treatment with Electrochemotherapy
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: The investigational drug (PLX4720) is a novel small molecule inhibitor of the BRAF, which is a gene involved in sending signals in cell growth, this gene is altered in many types of cancer. PLX 4720 is closely related to vemurafenib (Zelboraf, PLX4032), another BRAF inhibitor approved for the treatment of human melanoma carrying activating mutations in BRAF. It was recently determined that approximately 80% of canine bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinomas-TCC) carry activating mutations in BRAF identical to those found in human melanoma. Unfortunately, vemurafenib has unfavorable oral bioavailability in dogs, necessitating the use of another analog with better pharmacokinetic properties. Recently, healthy volunteer client owned dogs were enrolled into a clinical trial to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of PLX4720 given orally. This was well tolerated and provided critical data regarding expected pharmacokinetic variability and likely dosing necessary to reach biologically relevant blood levels of drug for the current clinical trial. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the biologic activity associated with oral administration of PLX4720 to dogs bladder cancer and with BRAF mutation, and to assess adverse events associated with chronic PLX4720 dosing. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? Eligible patients (any breed of dog) must meet all of the following criteria: Be greater than 1 year of age Weigh at least 5 kg Have a diagnosis of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder with measurable disease Be medically healthy with no clinically significant physical findings Prior chemotherapy or radiation must be completed 2 weeks prior to study entry Be able to receive oral medication on a daily basis Urine must be positive for the BRAF mutation What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? All dogs will receive PLX4270 once per day, dogs will receive PLX4270 for 28 days at which time an assessment of response to therapy will be performed. If biologic activity is evident, owners will be given the opportunity to continue on therapy in a compassionate use setting. Recheck exams will be performed at Days 7, 14 and 28 (the final visit). Analysis of dogs for tumor response will be performed by ultrasound examination of the bladder. Standard clinical chemistries (CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis) will be performed during the study. Additionally, plasma will be collected at each visit to assess trough blood levels of PLX4270. The initial dose of PLX4270 for dogs will be 30 mg/kg, with dose escalations in 30 mg/kg increments until a maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is identified or until biologic activity in 50% or more dogs is documented or until pharmacokinetic analysis determines that no benefit would be obtained by continuing to increase the dose. Client Compensation If your dog participates in this research, he/she will have the following benefits: complete blood work, urinalysis, and abdominal ultrasound at the initial visit and at conclusion of the study at no charge to you. In addition, the cost of the recheck exams for Day 0, 7, 14 and 28 will be covered. Owners are financially responsible for the initial exam fee, BRAF urine testing, thoracic radiographs, and sedation for the abdominal ultrasounds.
current_roster.name: Dogs with bladder cancer (Transitional Cell Carcinomas-TCC)

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: The purpose of this project is to characterize the most common type(s) of kidney disease in American Boxer dogs in order to identify a possible genetic cause of the disease. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? An American Boxer Dog diagnosed with kidney disease, along with its close relatives, is eligible for participation. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will participate in this study on one occasion at either your regular veterinary office or a specialty veterinary practice. This visit may take approximately one hour. Both blood and urine will be used for diagnostic testing, and DNA will also be isolated from the blood for genetic analysis in order to detect possible mutations that are causing the disease. Client Compensation The AKC-CHF grant will cover the cost of the renal biopsy / autopsy evaluation (if this is performed), urinalysis, serum chemistry, urine protein gel electrophoresis, and DNA isolation (approximately $850 value). The client will pay for the appointment for the clinical evaluation, CBC analysis prior to biopsy, and the biopsy procedure to obtain the tissues.
current_roster.name: Characterization of Renal Disease in American Boxer Dogs

current_roster.description: NC State University College of Veterinary Medicine is looking for dogs with Osteosarcoma for a clinical trial investigating the drug, Bortezomib, as a promising new treatment. Currently, the outcome for treating Osteosarcoma in dogs is poor, but scientists at Duke have recently shown Bortezomib to be a very safe and effective drug. Patients will receive surgical standard of care (affected limb amputation), followed by Bortezomib injections. Injections are twice weekly for 2 cycles followed by a 10-day rest period for a total of 3 cycles. Patients will receive routine bloodwork and radiographs throughout the study
current_roster.name: PILOT STUDY: PHASE 2 OF THE MDH PIPELINE-BORTEZOMIB AS FIRST LINE THERAPY FOR OSTEOSARCOMA

current_roster.description: While current treatments (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy) can be extremely useful for many forms of cancer, some dogs can experience relapse or may not be good candidates for these treatments. New therapies for cancer are needed, both in dogs and in humans. This study drug inhibits a novel cellular pathway that appears to be very important for allowing tumors to avoid being recognized and destroyed by the immune system. This drug has been studied in rodents and monkeys, and is non-toxic at doses that are more than 10 times higher than the doses to be used in this study. It has also been studied in more than 200 humans with cancer, both by itself and with other treatments. The drug has been very well tolerated, and tumor shrinkage has been observed in different forms of human cancer. The goal of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this drug given to dogs with certain types of cancer (lymphoma, soft-tissue sarcoma, osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs, or hepatocellular carcinoma) that have not yet been treated or have failed other types of treatment.
current_roster.name: Preclinical Evaluation of a Novel Adenosine A2A Inhibitor in Dogs with Spontaneous Neoplasia

current_roster.description: Canine soft tissue sarcomas are a group of tumors that are locally invasive and are often difficult to completely remove surgically. In up to 32% of patients, these tumors regrow within a year of surgical removal. For tumors that cannot be completely removed, local regrowth is expected. Adjunctive treatments, including radiation and chemotherapy, are recommended to reduce the rate of tumor regrowth, but these options only partially improve outcome. Recent advances in the field of oncolytic viral therapeutics have showcased the potential effectiveness and safety of this treatment modality. Our preliminary data indicate that intratumoral injection of a myxoma virus is safe with no evidence of viral shedding in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas. However, viral replication within sarcomas is limited in this spontaneous tumor model. Oclacitinib is a JAK inhibitor that is approved for use in dogs and has shown safety and efficacy in the treatment of allergic skin disease. This drug also inhibits a specific pathway of immune signaling, which could allow viral replication to occur in the tumor for a longer period of time, leading to a more effective immune response against both the cells infected with virus and bystander tumor cells. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the immune response to combination oclacitinib and post-operative myxoma virus injection in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas. We will also collect preliminary data to evaluate if the combination therapy might reduce tumor recurrence in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas.
current_roster.name: Combination use of a Janus Kinase Inhibitor and a Recombinant Myxoma Virus to Treat Soft Tissue Sarcomas in Dogs

current_roster.description: While conventional chemotherapy can induce remission in many dogs with lymphoma, relapse almost always occurs, and dogs with T cell lymphoma tend to have outcomes that are worse than average. Novel therapies for lymphoma, especially T cell lymphoma, are needed. This investigational drug inhibits a novel cellular pathway that has been shown to induce cell death in some T cell lymphoma cells. Inhibitors of this pathway hold great promise for treating T cell lymphoma. The investigational drug has shown good activity against lymphoma cell lines in culture. This drug has been tested in rats at doses 10 times higher than the doses we plan to use, and in normal healthy dogs at the approximate dose we plan to use, without evidence of any adverse effects. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this investigational drug given to dogs with T cell lymphoma that have not yet been treated or have failed chemotherapy. Duration of the study will be dependent upon duration of responses observed. Initially, 6 dogs will be enrolled at a twice daily starting dose based upon preclinical data. Dogs will be evaluated weekly for the first 4 weeks, then biweekly thereafter for toxicity and response to therapy. Dogs experiencing progressive disease at any time will be removed from study. After at least 6 dogs have completed treatment or have received treatment for 12 or more weeks, a reassessment of dosing and additional dogs may be added thereafter.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Dogs with T-cell Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Pilot study assessing safety and determining effects of GLP-1NLS therapy, delivered to the myocardium of dogs via ultrasound targeted microbubble destruction.
current_roster.name: Gene transfer study in Doberman Pinschers with congestive heart failure secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)

visible_sc_items.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

current_roster.description: This trial is designed to evaluate the safety and preliminary pain management and anti-cancer effectiveness of a novel therapy in dogs with bladder transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). The trial involves one-time treatment administered directly into the bladder using a urinary catheter. Dogs may receive a second treatment one month after enrollment if warranted. The treatment will be administered under sedation or general anesthesia. There is no placebo in this trial. An estimated 15 client-owned dogs with will be enrolled. Owners will be required to complete quality of life surveys, collect a daily urine sample for visual analysis, and record the urine collection results in a provided journal. The trial site will train the owners on collection and evaluation techniques. Trial visits include the dogs initial consultation, treatment day (Day 0), and then recheck visits on Days 7, 14, 28, 56, and 84. Anti-cancer therapies must be discontinued 21 days prior to enrollment. Medications targeted at the treatment of TCC-associated pain, except for CBD and other cannabinoids, are acceptable provided they have been administered for at least 2 weeks prior to enrolling in the study.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial Evaluating a Novel Therapy for the Treatment of Transitional Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: Canine Degenerative Myelopathy (DM) is a progressive and ultimately fatal neurodegenerative disease affecting older dogs. DM is paralleled both clinically and genetically by the equally devastating human disorder amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or Lou Gehrig's disease. DM and ALS are associated with a mutation in the superoxide dismutase 1 gene (SOD1), making this gene a target for both canine and human therapeutics.We have determined the appropriate dose of a gene-silencer, the anti-canine SOD1 U1 Adaptor, required to effectively silence SOD1 expression in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), refined the method of administration by injection into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and concluded that it is safe. The aim of this clinical trial is to determine whether the same single dose and method of SOD1 U1 Adaptor administration will cause the same SOD1 gene silencing in dogs affected with DM.
current_roster.name: SILENCING THE CANINE SOD1 GENE IN CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM FOR TREATMENT OF DEGENERATIVE MYELOPATHY- A PILOT STUDY

current_roster.description: Diabetes mellitus has reached epidemic proportions in people and is also a relatively common disease in cats (prevalence of about 0.5%). The frequent administration of injectable insulin poses a challenge and a tremendous emotional barrier to successful treatment in people and in treated cats. Therefore, novel treatments that enable decreased frequency of injection while maintaining safety is highly desirable. Currently, insulin products being used in the veterinary field must be dosed two times per day, posing a compliance issue for pet owners. In this study, a novel insulin formulation will be assessed. Based on preliminary data in non-diabetic research animals, this formulation is expected to have a long half-life, appropriate for clinical use as a single injection every 5-7 days. Such low frequency of administration would lead to significant improvement in owner compliance. Also, it will significantly improve the quality of life for pet and owner, therefore justifying a study to investigate the use of this insulin in dogs and cats.This is an unmasked, self-controlled, single arm pilot field effectiveness study using client-owned cats and dogs diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. Cats and dogs will be treated with a novel ultra-long acting insulin formulation (Akston insulin). The effect of the drug will be assessed by comparing glycemic control (based on clinical signs, fructosamine and interstitial glucose concentrations using a continuous glucose monitoring unit) while on a standard insulin therapy (for one week) vs. treatment with an escalating dose of the study insulin when the latter is administered once every 5-7 days over 6-8 weeks.
current_roster.name: Novel insulin formulations for minimizing pain and discomfort caused by injections

current_roster.description: We are investigating 2 new imaging agents, that can be injected intravenously, localize to the blood vessels of tumors and can then be detected using a noninvasive imaging test called ultrasound. Certain types of cancer therapies work by inhibiting the growth of tumor blood vessels and new, easy ways to measure changes in tumor blood vessels would help predict whether a patient will benefit from these types of cancer therapies. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the ability of these investigational imaging agents to predict clinical benefit (tumor shrinkage or stabilization) in dogs with soft-tissue sarcomas treated with anti-blood vessel therapy, and compare the results obtained with these investigational agents to those obtained with CT scans and tumor biopsy.
current_roster.name: Contrast Enhanced Ultrasound in Dogs with Soft Tissue Sarcomas

current_roster.description: The aim of this study is to understand the impact of irradiating the lymph nodes that are associated with sinonasal cancer in dogs with respect to the bodys immune response to the cancer. Lymph nodes are critical sites for immune responses. For certain cancers, like carcinoma of the head and neck, radiation is routinely targeted to these lymph nodes in order to kill any tumor cells which may be harbored within; however, radiation is also likely to kill immune cells which also reside within the lymph nodes. It is currently unknown, for human and veterinary cancer patients, how lymph node radiation affects the immune response mounted against cancer cells within the tumor and throughout the body. In order to understand more about this important question, we will perform a clinical trial in dogs with sinonasal cancer, treated with radiotherapy targeted to their tumor, with or without radiation therapy targeted to the tumor-associated lymph nodes within the head and neck. We will collect tumor, and lymph node tissues over time to gain information about the patients immune response. The results of this study will be impactful for improving cancer treatments for both dogs and people with carcinoma of the head and neck.
current_roster.name: Impact of regional lymph node irradiation on the anti-tumor immune response for canine patients with sinonasal cancer

current_roster.description: The primary objective of this study is to determine the efficacy and safety of TANOVEA-CA1 (rabacfosadine for injection) in the treatment of lymphoma in dogs.
current_roster.name: A randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled field study to determine the efficacy and safety of TANOVEA®-CA1  (rabacfosadine for inj

current_roster.description: The oxygen level in tumors carries a very high impact on efficacy of radiation therapy and chemotherapy. Low oxygen level in tumors can result in unexpectedly poor treatment outcome. In this project, a special camera will be tested to capture dynamic changes in tumor oxygen level in anon-invasive manner. A minimally invasive fiberoptic sensor-based measurement of oxygen level is performed simultaneously in order to correlate with the camera-based reading. This camera-based technology has been shown to work in rodent models. Once a clinical workflow for this novel technology is established in veterinary setting in this project, this technology will be tested in human clinical oncology setting. The cost of the CT scan for radiation planning and the cost of the radiation set up/planning fee are covered. Costs for the course of radiation are the responsibility of the pet owner andwill vary depending on the protocol.
current_roster.name: An Imaging Study of Cycling Hypoxia in Canine Tumors during Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to evaluate the clinical activity of Immunolight Therapy (IT) in dogs with spontaneously-occurring non-Hodgkins lymphoma. The effect of localized IT treatment of 2 lymphomatous lymph nodes on systemic disease burden will be measured through a combination of lymph node size reduction (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; RECIST), radiographic assessment of thoracic lesions, and cytologic assessment of previously affected nodes. Safety will also be assessed; all clinical and biochemical toxicities will be graded according to the Veterinary Comparative Oncology Group Common Terminology criteria for Adverse Events (VCOG-CTCAE) v1.1 (Veterinary Comparative Oncology, 2010).
current_roster.name: Phase II Study: Immunolight Therapy for Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Cancer is common in dogs and people. Tumor size is often used to decide if a treatment regimen is effective, but this assessment is limited since a tumor could be responding by forming necrotic (dead) portions that are not leading to a reduction in size. Contrast enhanced ultrasound can be used to image markers of tumor blood flow that will provide more information on how much of the tumor is affected by treatment, and will allow us to adjust treatment as needed. The purpose of this study is to establish and validate targeted contrast enhanced ultrasound to image biomarkers of tumor response to therapy in dogs with soft tissue tumors.
current_roster.name: Soft Tissue Sarcoma Clinical Trial

current_roster.description: Our long-term goal is to identify, develop and characterize the most efficacious treatment for individual patients with OSA (osteosarcoma). To achieve this goal, we have identified proteasome inhibitors as the most efficacious drug across all OS cell lines. We have validated the effectiveness of these drugs in vivo using both canine and human PDXs. Our next step is to complete the MDH pipeline (mouse-dog-human) by testing our lead drug candidate, proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib, in the clinic. We hypothesize that bortezomib will be safe and effective in treating dogs and humans with OS.
current_roster.name: Bortezomib as a Novel Therapy for Canine Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma (OSA) is the most common type of bone cancer in dogs, primarily occurring in the fore- and hindlimbs. It is an aggressive tumor with local bone destruction and severe pain where it originates and early metastasis (spread) to other sites within the body. The primary site of metastasis is to the lungs with >90% of dogs having at least microscopic metastasis at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, although surgical removal of the tumor via amputation of the affected limb provides palliation, these patients will eventually die from the development of multiple tumors within the lungs in only a few months. The addition of chemotherapy to address these secondary tumors increases survival over amputation alone and has been the accepted standard of care (SOC) for decades. However, the average survival still does not exceed a year and only a small percentage of dogs survive two years or longer. Thus, more effective treatment protocols are desperately needed. In human oncology, an approach that has been previously investigated is the delivery of low-dose radiation to the lungs (total lung irradiation; TLI) in the hopes of killing the microscopic cancer cells that are present. In these human studies, low-dose TLI, alone or combined with chemotherapy, was found to be safe but clinical benefit varied. Although safety data exists for TLI in healthy and tumor-bearing dogs, its effect on survival in dogs with OSA has been studied on a very limited and non-optimized basis and never in conjunction with SOC: amputation and chemotherapy. Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate TLI plus SOC for dogs with OSA in a prospective clinical trial. After undergoing amputation (either here at NC State or at another institution) dogs will be enrolled and starting within 3 days following surgery will begin a protocol of 10 daily fractions of TLI followed by 6 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy (as per our protocol for the adjuvant treatment of canine OSA; may be performed here at NC State "preferred" or with another veterinarian if the clients cannot pursue chemotherapy here). Following completion of the carboplatin protocol dogs will then be monitored with serial thoracic radiographs performed every 2 months (our standard practice) to assess for metastatic disease and any potential adverse effects of TLI. Our primary objective is to evaluate the effect of adding TLI to SOC on metastasis-free interval (MFI; the time from amputation to development of the aforementioned lung nodules or spread elsewhere, e.g. bone) and overall survival time (ST; the time from amputation to death or euthanasia). Our secondary objective is to obtain short- and long-term safety data by using serial bloodwork, chest x-rays, and respiratory (client-provided history, physical exam) assessments. We hypothesize that the addition of TLI will significantly improve patient outcome and will be well-tolerated with minimal to no hematologic or respiratory toxicity.
current_roster.name: Prophylactic Total Lung Irradiation Combined with Standard of Care for Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Cavalier King Charles spaniels (CKCS) suffer from two conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord. The first condition, Chiari-like malformation (CM), is a developmental abnormality of the skull that results in compression of the brainstem and cerebellum. This crowding can lead to abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the spinal cord forming CSF filled cavities called syrinxes or Syringomyelia (SM). Together, CMSM causes neuropathic pain and itch by disrupting normal sensory pathways. We have identified dogs from our preliminary studies that have severe signs of neuropathic pain and itch even when treated with routine medications including gabapentin and omeprazole. Recent studies have shown that electromagnetic fields can aid in neuroprotective pathways and can reduce pain and inflammation. This technology has been used in human clinical trials as well as canine trials for spinal cord injury. The aim of this study is to perform a randomized, blinded cross over clinical trial using placebo and active pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) technologies (established Assisi loop) in severely affected CKCS that are already being treated with gapabentin and omeprazole to determine if PEMF is able to alleviate neuropathic pain and itch in these dogs. The Assisi loop is used in veterinary medicine currently to treat dogs with arthritic pain and are well tolerated with no reported adverse events.
current_roster.name: Novel treatment of neuropathic pain and itch in CKCS with Chiari-like Malformation and Syringomyelia

current_roster.description: Tumor hypoxia is associated with resistance to radiotherapy as well as increased likelihood of regional recurrence and metastases, and often leads to poor treatment outcome and prognosis. Our proposed method is an innovative minimally invasive technology combining ultrasound and acoustically-active oxygen delivery vehicles which will allow a physician to locally deliver oxygen to tumor tissue during radiation treatment and enhance tumor radiation sensitivity. This novel approach has the potential to substantially improve therapeutic treatment for cancer by both increasing tumor response to radiation, and reducing the radiation dose required for a therapeutic effect. If successful, ultrasound-mediated tumor oxygenation will have a wide reaching impact in cancer therapy and prognosis. There may be no direct benefit to your animal from its participation in this study. However, such participation may provide additional information about the extent of your animals disease and, therefore, influence the course of treatment to help your animal or other animals in the future.
current_roster.name: Treating Hypoxia via Tumorally Directed Oxygen for Improving Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the difference in overall survival between dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma (HSA) treated with splenectomy, Immunocidin (a non-specific immunotherapeutic), and concurrent doxorubicin, compared to those historically treated with standard of care (splenectomy and doxorubicin).
current_roster.name: Evaluating Immunocidin, a non-specific immunotherapy, for the treatment of canine splenic hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description: The Veterinary Medical Center at the University of Minnesota is conducting a study in dogs with high-grade glioma including glioblastoma (GBM), common primary malignant brain tumors, to develop novel immunotherapy strategies that are more effective than current treatments. These tumors are uniformly deadly in both dogs and people with median survival times of two months in dogs and ~ 14 months in people after standard of care treatment. This work aims to evaluate novel combinations of immune therapies in dogs with previously untreated brain tumors to determine the combination that provides the longest remission times with minimal adverse effects. Our ultimate goal is to develop a safe and effective postoperative treatment that avoids the standard therapy with chemotherapy and radiation therapy that can be translated to human GBM patients. Dogs with clinical signs (symptoms) that suggest the presence of a brain mass or tumor will be eligible for participation. Each dog should have a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of the brain to determine the location, size, and imaging characteristics of the mass. A small sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) may be collected for analysis after the MRI. Dr. Pluhar, the Principal Investigator, will examine the MRI to determine whether the characteristics of the mass are consistent with a diagnosis of glioma that is amenable to surgical removal, which would make your dog eligible to participate in the treatment study. Thorough physical and neurological examinations, blood screening tests, and imaging of the chest and abdomen should be done to make sure that your dog is healthy enough to undergo general anesthesia. If your dog is in adequate physical condition based on these tests, he/she can be enrolled in the study. Inclusion criteria will be: (i) any dog with an intracranial mass and MRI consistent with diagnosis of GBM that is (ii) suitable for surgical resection; (iii) is healthy enough to undergo chemotherapy; and (iv) informed consent provided by the dogs owner. Note: Dogs that do not display a GBM diagnosis upon surgical biopsy will not continue in the trial, but will be treated by standard care. The Exclusion criteria for our trial will be (i) severe neurologic dysfunction, especially changes in level of consciousness that may indicate pending brain herniation; (ii) tumor not amenable to surgical resection; (iii) existence of concomitant disease that would affect the dogs long-term prognosis and preclude completion of chemotherapy or vaccine therapy, and (iv) French bulldogs, which we have found do not respond to vaccine-mediated immunotherapy. Study: All dogs that meet the requirements listed above will have a surgical biopsy to definitively identify the specific tumor type and grade at the time of surgical removal of as much of the tumor as possible. All dogs will be randomly assigned to receive one of the three additional immunotherapies as described above to enhance anti-tumor immunity. The vaccine used for immunotherapy will be created from the dog's own tumor cells grown under special conditions that will improve how they stimulate the dog's immune system. The vaccines should cause the dog's immune system to recognize and kill any tumor cells that were not removed during surgery. The gene therapy has been shown to be effective in killing primary brain tumors in rats and mice and safe in a previous study in dogs that was conducted by the PI. Each dog will be placed under general anesthesia supervised by a board-certified anesthesiologist during the surgical procedure that will be performed by Dr. Pluhar, with assistance from an MD neurosurgeon. After approaching the dog's brain with the appropriate craniotomy, as much of the tumor mass as possible will be removed. A portion of the tumor will be submitted for histopathology to get a definitive tumor type and grade and the remainder will be used to create the vaccines. Dogs in the gene therapy groups will have injections of the vector in the brain tissue around the site of tumor removal. A brain MRI will be performed immediately after surgery to assess how much of the tumor was removed. Each dog will recover from anesthesia and have postoperative care in the intensive care unit until discharged from the Veterinary Medical Center. Each dog will receive (1) several doses of a vaccine created from their own tumor cells with the CD200 inhibitor, or a drug used to activate the gene therapy with (2) or without (3) the CD200 inhibitor, according to a color-coded calendar that summarizes the treatment schedule. In general the vaccines and/or CD200 inhibitor will be given once a week for 3 weeks starting about 10 days after surgery, then once a month for 3 months, then once every 8 weeks until there is MRI evidence of tumor recurrence. Each dog will have regular follow up examinations during the 12-month period of the study or until euthanasia, when necessary. The follow up protocol including timing and exams is as follows: Complete physical and neurological examinations and quality of life assessment at each vaccination starting at suture removal about 10 days after surgery. At 4, 8, and 12 months after surgery, a brain MRI as well as complete physical and neurological examinations and quality of life assessment will be performed.
current_roster.name: Immunotherapy for canine primary brain tumors

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Cancer vaccines, directed against a variety of different tumor antigens, can generate T cell responses, yet alone typically fail to control or reverse tumor growth. Among the morest important reasons why cancer vaccines fail is their inability to overcome the immune suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Therefore, combining cancer vaccines with immunotherapy approaches that modify the TME is an attractive option for improving vaccine efficacy. The drugs losartan and propranolol have both been shown to modify the tumor microenvironment and reduce immune suppression caused by the tumor. The goal of this study is to evaluate an osteosarcoma tumor lysate vaccine in combination with losartan and propranolol in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma The tumor vaccine will be given every 2 weeks for six treatments and then monthly for up to one year. Dogs will also be sent home with oral losartan and propranolol to be given twice daily. Rechecks will be required every 2 weeks following the start of treatment until the vaccine therapy is completed, and every 4 weeks thereafter if tumors are stable or better. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments. The study covers all costs related to the trial for thefirst 6 months (including examinations, blood work, chest radiographs, the vaccine, and the losartan and propranolol). After the initial 6 months, the study will continue to pay for the vaccine for up to one year, and all other costs arethe responsibilityof the petowner.
current_roster.name: Cancer Vaccine and Pharmacological Tumor Microenvironment Modification Trial for Canine Metastatic Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: This study aims to compare the effectiveness of intra-articular Autologous Protein Solution (APS) versus corticosteroid plus hyaluronan for treating hip osteoarthritis in dogs. Dogs with bilateral hip osteoarthritis are eligible for inclusion in this study. Enrolled dogs will receive a complete orthopedic examination, radiographs of the hips, knees, shoulders, and elbows, objective gait analysis and treatment with APS in one hip and corticosteroid plus hyaluronan in the other hip. Dogs will be sedated and blood will be drawn for APS processing. All costs associated with the aforementioned diagnostics and treatments are covered by the study. Owners will complete questionnaires both before the injection and at each recheck visit. Enrolled dogs will return to Colorado Canine Orthopedics and Rehab for re-evaluation a total of three times over the following six month period for objective gait analysis. Clients will receive a financial cash incentive for each recheck that is completed on-time ($50 at one-month, $100 at three-months and $200 at six-months).

It is an important clinical problem in dogs that affects both the dog's quality of life and the bond with their owners. The goal of this project is to assess a novel treatment (PEMF) to improve the quality of life in dogs with separation anxiety.

current_roster.description: Xerostomia, or dry mouth, affects over 8 million people in the U.S and occurs as a result of salivary dysfunction due to autoimmune disease, medication usage, smoking, aging, and radiation therapy for head and neck cancer. Absence of saliva severely compromises the oral health and quality of life of patients: saliva protects the oral mucosa, facilitates food digestion and articulation, and aids in the re-mineralization of dental hard tissues. There are no viable long-term treatments for salivary dysfunction, driving a need for new, translatable solutions. We have devised a new promising therapy for improving salivary function and saliva flow that is based on stem cell-mediated regeneration via local delivery of a novel drug delivery system within a gel (alginate) that will enable uniform distribution within the tissue and controlled release of the drug (cevimeline). Testing in mice has shown that the drug is efficacious in promoting stem cell proliferation within the salivary glands in a fashion consistent with controlled release. Based on these exciting data, we seek to enroll dogs who will be undergoing radiation therapy to see if the same treatment that worked in mice will work in dogs. If we are successful, this therapy could help many people with dry mouth from radiation therapy and may be used to treat radiation side effects in dogs in the future. To understand if the therapy will work in dogs, we will give a dose of radiation to one salivary gland. Because dogs have multiple salivary glands, we do not anticipate that this dose will cause dry mouth in your pet. Once dogs are enrolled into the study, they will be assigned to one of four treatment groups: alginate (carrier) only, cevimeline only, alginate + cevimeline, or no injections (control). A single dose of radiation therapy will be administered to one salivary gland. The radiation protocol for treatment of your pets tumor will then be completed. Dogs that are assigned to one of the treatment arms will have injections of the assigned treatment into a salivary gland 14 days after radiation therapy. Saliva, a small amount of blood, and biopsies of the salivary gland will be collected prior to injection and at 7, 14, and 30 days post-treatment. Additional rechecks beyond Day 30 may be requested depending on the treatment arm.
current_roster.name: Promote salivary gland regeneration using therapeutic delivery of cevimeline

current_roster.description: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a prevalent condition in cats. Advanced CKD is associated with hyporexia, vomiting, and weight loss. Ulcerative or erosive gastropathy are not observed in advanced CKD cats. Additionally, our preliminary studies suggest that CKD cats do not have a more acidic gastric pH compared to healthy cats. Thus, the beneficial role of acid suppressants in the treatment of CKD cats is unknown and warrants investigation. Omeprazole has pH-independent effects including anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. Therefore, omeprazole therapy may be beneficial to ameliorate GI signs in cats with CKD. Indeed, clinically, we have observed that CKD-related gastrointestinal (GI) signs such as hyporexia and vomiting improve with acid suppressant therapy. Moreover, the International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) recommends omeprazole therapy for cats with IRIS stage III and IV CKD but states "further investigations are needed on the use of these drugs to determine whether they are useful for managing gastrointestinal disturbances in cats with CKD". Accordingly, the proposed study would be the first to evaluate the effect of omeprazole therapy in cats with CKD.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the Effect of Omeprazole on Clinical Signs in Cats with Chronic Kidney Disease

current_roster.description: NC State University College of Veterinary Medicine is investigating a new treatment for osteosarcoma. This study is pre-clinical and is currently only accepting amputated limbs from dogs with distal radial osteosarcoma. These samples are needed to evaluate the use of percutaneous cementoplasty in the multimodal management of canine osteosarcoma for a future clinical trial.
current_roster.name: Percutaneous Cementoplasty in the Management of Radial Osteosarcoma in Dogs

current_roster.description: An insulinoma is a type of cancer that occurs in the pancreas. This type of cancer can be difficult to diagnosis due to its small size and vague symptoms caused by the tumor. Insulinomas can also spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body and this spread can also be difficult to detect. Locating and removing the insulinoma along with any spread to other organs is very important to improve clinical signs and possibly cure patients. The purpose of this study is to compare the ability of multiple imaging procedures to detect insulinoma tumors in dogs. The goal of this study is to determine how well these imaging procedures can identify the tumor and if any of these procedures has an advantage over the other. These imaging procedures include CT, MRI, and PET-CT. CT uses x-rays and MRI uses a large magnet to produce detailed images of the body. PET is a form of nuclear imaging that uses injected radiopharmaceuticals to help detect subtle diseases/changes in the body at the cellular level. PET produces a much lower quality image than CT and MRI, but PET can be combined with CT to increase the detail of the image without losing the ability to detect subtle disease processes. Pre-enrollment visit (within 14 days of Day 1): This will include the first appointment with CSU Oncology Service to review your pets history and discuss the study. If all of the necessary pre-enrollment diagnostics (bloodwork and chest x-rays) have not been performed prior to/are not available by this first appointment, then this appointment will also include obtaining any remaining necessary diagnostics. *The following days may not be sequential, but likely will occur within a one-week time period. Day 1: Your dog will be dropped off in the morning to undergo general anesthesia for imaging procedures. Your pet will be under anesthesia for 2-3 hours on this day and will be given a dose of a radiopharmaceutical called F18-FDG for the purpose of imaging. This radiopharmaceutical emits a low dose of radiation. Following the imaging procedures, your dog will remain in-hospital until the radiation levels are low enough that they can go home without any risk to the people around them. This is almost always by the end of the day. If it is more convenient your pet can stay overnight in the hospital at no cost to you. Day 2: The patient will have a second general anesthesia to finish imaging procedures and for surgery with sample collection. Anesthesia time will vary from 1 hour (if imaging only) to several hours if surgery is performed the same day. The patient will remain hospitalized after surgery until allowed to go home. +/- Day 3: If surgery cannot be performed for any reason on Day 2, it will be performed on Day 3.
current_roster.name: Study to compare different imaging methods (MRI, CT, and PET/CT) for diagnosis and staging of canine insulinoma

current_roster.description: The primary objective of the study is to evaluate, under field conditions, the clinical effectiveness and safety of resiniferatoxin (RTX) compared to a sham treatment for the control of pain associated with osteoarthritis of the elbow in dogs. The hypothesis being tested is that, on study Day 30, the clinical effectiveness of RTX (the Investigational Veterinary Product or IVP) is superior to the effectiveness of a sham treatment (ST). The field safety of RTX will be evaluated over a period of 90 days. The results of this study will serve as substantial evidence of effectiveness to complete the requirements of the New Animal Drug Application (NADA) effectiveness technical section. A single intra-articular injection of RTX is expected to produce analgesia by targeting the same transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel to reversibly deactivate the end terminals of primary afferent pain fibers within the joint and capsule. This study will enroll dogs with chronic pain due to osteoarthritis of both elbows and will be treated bilaterally.
current_roster.name: ZOE-06

current_roster.description: This study is for dogs with bone cancer in their leg who are interested in amputation and have not yet received chemotherapy. The study aims to evaluate how effective Flash Proton Radiation Therapy can be as a treatment for osteosarcoma in future studies; however, this study does not offer flash proton radiation as a treatment. One dose of radiation is preformed for study purposes whereas typical radiation as a treatment for osteosarcoma consists of multiple radiation treatments. We hope to find out if flash proton radiation is more effective than standard radiation therapy for dogs with osteosarcoma by studying how the bone and tissue react to the radiation following amputation. The flash proton therapy may decrease normal tissue damage, increase a dog's ability to recognize and kill cancer cells, and decrease pain at the site of the tumor until amputation. An initial screening visit is required at the Veterinary Hospital at the University of Pennsylvania for a physical examination, bloodwork, chest x-rays, limb x-rays if not previously done, and an aspirate of the lesion. If you agree to have your dog participate in this study, your dog will have the radiation therapy study visit approximately 5 days before his/her scheduled amputation procedure. At this visit, your dog will be anesthetized and will be randomly assigned (like flipping a coin) to receive either standard or flash proton RT. An area of the tumor will be treated with one of these two methods of radiation. An adjacent area of healthy bone, still within the affected limb to be amputated, will also be treated with the opposite method of radiation. Approximately 5 days after radiation, your dog will have the scheduled amputation according to standard of care. At that time we will collect additional samples of bone and tumor tissue from the limb after removal.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Flash Proton Radiation Therapy in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Purpose To determine if histotripsy, a novel treatment that can destroy tissue without radiation or heat, can effectively treat canine osteosarcoma. Background Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Typically, OS is treated with a combination of surgical removal of the primary tumor and chemotherapy for metastatic disease. Surgical removal of the tumor usually involves limb amputation or limb salvage surgery. Limb salvage surgery can have high complication rates, and not all dogs are suitable for limb amputation. Even though chemotherapy delays metastatic disease development, most dogs with OS ultimately succumb to metastasis. Histotripsy is a novel treatment that mechanically breaks down tissues and can potentially induce the immune system to attack cancer cells. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of histotripsy to treat dogs with OS, to ultimately advance the development of histotripsy as a non-surgical limb salvage treatment option for OS and an immunotherapy treatment against metastatic disease for OS. Study Design Dogs will be evaluated for eligibility at either theAnimal Cancer Care and Research Center in Roanoke, VAor the mainVeterinary Teaching hospital in Blacksburg, VA. Qualifying dogs will undergo a non-invasive histotripsy treatment of the tumor 1-5 days prior to standard-of-care limb amputation surgery. Travel will be required to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital in Blacksburg for the histotripsy treatment. Tumor samples will be obtained after limb amputation and evaluated by a pathologist at Virginia Tech. Results from this routine evaluation will be provided to you. Enrolled patients will need to return for recheck visits at 2 weeks and one month after completion of chemotherapy, and at 6, 9, and 12 months after surgery. With advanced notice, these recheck visits may be performed by your local veterinarian. If the rechecks are done remotely, the visit costs are not covered by the study. Contact If you'd liketo proceed with a study screening appointment, please ask your veterinarian to initiate a referral using this link:https://cancercare.vetmed.vt.edu/appointments-and-referrals.html. Please note that the cost of the screening visit is typically not covered by the study. If you'd liketo be contacted with more information about this study and/or would like to discuss a case prior to referral, please complete our phone consultation request form:https://virginiatech.questionpro.com/t/AUEYyZu6hU. If your query is urgent, please call the Animal Cancer Care and Research Center on 540-526-2300.
current_roster.name: Histotripsy for treatment of canine appendicular osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether a new prescription diet can delay the progression of early mitral valve disease in dogs. Many dogs like yours have heart murmurs caused by a leaky heart valve (sometimes called degenerative valve insufficiency or mitral valve disease). Mitral valve disease is a progressive condition that causes enlargement of the heart and can eventually lead to heart failure. The progression of mitral valve disease may be slowed with medication in dogs that have enlarged hearts, but there is currently no proven method to slow the disease process in the early stages of the disease, prior to heart enlargement. Nestle-Purina has developed a new dog food that is specially formulated to slow the progression of early mitral valve disease in dogs. This study, sponsored by Nestle-Purina, is being conducted to evaluate whether this new diet can, in fact, slow the progression of mitral valve disease by delaying heart enlargement.
current_roster.name: Effect of a novel diet on the progression of early mitral valve disease in dogs

current_roster.description: While surgery, radiation therapy and conventional chemotherapy can be useful for the management of osteosarcoma in dogs, improvement is often short-lived and not all dogs may be candidates for treatments like surgery or radiation therapy. New forms of treatment are needed for both dogs and people with osteosarcoma for this reason. The new drug GEM-IB combines a bone-targeting drug (ibandronate) with a potent cancer drug (gemcitabine) to increase the concentration of cancer drug exactly at the site of the tumor. This drug has shown good activity against osteosarcoma in mice, and laboratory studies suggest that combining this drug with the conventional chemotherapy drug docetaxel (DTX) significantly improves effectiveness. Pilot studies in normal dogs with the starting doses of both drugs in this study have demonstrated excellent tolerability. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor/anti-pain effects of this combined treatment given to dogs with osteosarcoma that have not yet been treated with surgery, radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Dogs will receive both drugs intravenously once every 21 days. Recheck visits will be required 1, 3-4, 7, 14 and 21 days after the first treatment, then every three weeks thereafter. Dogs will be eligible to continue receiving treatment at no cost as long as the drug is tolerated and dogs are experiencing clinical benefit (pain control and lack of tumor worsening). Analysis for tumor change will be performed through the use of imaging (X-rays), and limb use will be measured through gait analysis. Standard bloodwork will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include blood/urine collection over the course of the study to determine how the investigational drug is affecting changes in bone turnover. Imaging will be performed using standard sedation/anesthesia protocols.
current_roster.name: Safety and Effectiveness of GEM-IB/Docetaxel in Dogs with Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Purpose: This clinical trial evaluates the safety and efficacy of papaverine (PPV) as a method to reduce tumor hypoxia (low oxygen) in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. Tumor hypoxia is a barrier to effective radiation therapy of solid tumors, so elimination of hypoxia will enhance effectiveness of radiation to treat cancerous tissue in dogs and humans.Radiation therapy involves the application of electromagnetic radiation to an area of interest using a linear accelerator (radiation-generating machine). This study will not involve radiation, but evaluate a drug that may make radiation therapy more effective. The drug papaverine has been given to humans for over 100 years with an excellent safety profile. Researchers at Ohio State have identified an unknown effect of papaverine that reduces oxygen consumption in tumor cells. Studies in rodent tumors have shown that the effect of papaverine on reducing oxygen consumption reduces hypoxia and increases the effectiveness of radiation therapy.We are now asking if papaverine can reduce hypoxia in canine sarcoma. The current study will be an addition to the regular treatment of your dog's tumor, and will not affect how that therapy is given. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To be included in the trial, dogs must fulfill the following criteria: 1.Body weight of at least 5 lbs or 2.27 kg 2.Adequate organ function as indicated by standard laboratory tests 3.Skin or subcutaneous soft tissue sarcoma as diagnosed by cytology or histopathology. Tumor can be new or recurrent. 4.Minimum tumor size of 2cm diameter. 5.Able to undergo general anesthesia and surgery for treatment of soft tissue sarcoma Exclusion Criteria Dogs with the following criteria or conditions will be excluded from the study: 1.Evidence of underling disease conditions such as clinically significant abnormalities in their labwork that would indicate renal, cardiac, or hepatic dysfunction. 2.Result of diagnostic testing (cytology and/or histopathology) are not clearly documented. 3.History of prior radiation therapy to tumor. What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? Prescreening (Day -3 to -7): Pre-Treatment Diagnostics and ScreeningAfter signature of Owner Informed Consent, the dog will have a medical history completed and undergo a physical examination. Blood and urine samples will be collected and submitted for complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis. Visit 1 (Day 0): General anesthesia and pre-treatment MRI, PPV Administration and post-treatment MRI.Each dog will undergo a physical examination. Prior to general anesthesia, the patient will have been fasted 10 hours before admission or overnight during hospitalization but can receive water ad libitum until the morning of the planned general anesthesia. The dog will be premedicated using a protocol developed by the board-certified anesthesiologist. The dog will have an MRI of the tumor. Following completion of MRI the dog will have papaverine administered IV and be monitored. General anesthesia will be maintained and sixty minutes following completion of papaverine administration the dog will be transported back and have a repeat MRI of the tumor. Visit 2 (Day 7): Pimonidazole treatment, general anesthesia, and surgical excision of soft tissue sarcoma.One week following general anesthesia and MRIs, the dog will be readmitted to the hospital and a physical examination performed. Following a catheter placement, 2-4 hours prior to surgery pimonidazole will be administered. Premedication will be given then shortly after general anesthesia will be induced and maintained. The soft tissue sarcoma will be surgically removed. A small sample will be taken from the tumor for testing and the rest of the tumor will be submitted for pathology. Following recovery from surgery the dog will receive pain medications as needed and be discharged from the hospital following recovery. Client Compensation The study is funded by a National Institutes of Health (NIH) research grant. The study costs will be covered by the research grant. Drugs (pimonidazole and papaverine), bloodwork (study blood draws), processing of tumor sample to measure hypoxic regions, MRIs for oxygenation measurements (including anesthesia for 2 hours) will all be covered by the research grant. The study will cover all the required appointment charges and contribute $1049 towards surgery and anesthesia for tumor removal. The study will not cover any other costs or cost of the treatment to your dog's tumor or hospitalization due to any other reason. The study will not cover cost of ICU due to any complication associated with standard treatment of the tumor.
current_roster.name: Use of papaverine to reduce low tumor oxygen in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma

current_roster.description: We want to evaluate the clinical efficacy of a new product (Intesto-Guard) in dogs with chronic diarrhea. IntestoGuard contains a combination of probiotics and prebiotics, which may reduce and control clinical signs of chronic diarrhea cases. The purpose of this studyis to compare the outcome of 2 groups of dogs with chronic enteropathy: -One group treated with hypoallergenic diet, together with IntestoGuard -One group treated with the hypoallergenic diet and a placebo The participation will last for 3 visits at the hospital, over a 6 week-period. -Visit 1: Day of enrollment. The dog will be randomly assigned to one of the 2 groups mentioned here above. This visit will occur as follows: o A physical examination will be performed and blood, feces and urine will be sampled. o A GI endoscopy will be performed for diagnostic purposes, during which intestinal samples will be taken. o An abdominal ultrasound will be performed. o An hypoallergenic diet will be provided for the entire study period. All of the above, including the diet, is part of routine management of a dog with chronic enteropathy, regardless of the study. - Visit 2: Day 14. On this visit, a physical examination will be performed, and blood, urine and feces will be collected again, as described above. - Visit 3: Day 42. This visit is similar to Visit 1. The same samples will be collected, and the GI endoscopy will be repeated.
current_roster.name: IntestoGuard: new drug tested for dogs with chronic diarrhea

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is an aggressive and highly metastatic cancer in both dogs and humans.Gefitinib, a small molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), approved as a first-line treatment for human metastatic non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) that contain specific EGFR mutations, has also been shown to improve survival in non-EGFR mutated NSCLC when intercalated with traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy. This potential EGFR-independent effect may occur in part through the effects of gefitinib on other molecular targets, includingthe serine/threonine kinase Receptor-Interacting Protein kinase 2 (RIPK2), which is expressed on many immune cells, including macrophages.In experimental models of osteosarcoma, perioperative gefitinib has been shown to reduce metastatic burden through RIPK2 and macrophage dependent mechanism.Based on these results, we predict that the addition of gefitinib to SOC will show clinical benefit in canine osteosarcoma, thereby setting a precedent for the evaluation of such combinations in clinical trials involving human patients.
current_roster.name: A multi-center Phase I/II evaluation of the addition of perioperative and intercalating gefitinib to standard of care treatment fo

current_roster.description: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to characterize the most common type(s) of renal disease in the Greyhound breed. Anecdotally, this breed appears to be predisposed to chronic kidney disease characterized by protein loss in the urine (proteinuria); however, there are multiple causes of proteinuria ranging from hypertension (pre-renal proteinuria), to renal parenchymal injury (true renal proteinuria) to lower urinary tract disease (post-renal proteinuria). To definitively identify the region of renal injury, evaluation of renal tissue (e.g. biopsy or autopsy sample) is often required. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must be a: Purebred greyhound with clinical evidence of renal disease or Purebred greyhound with normal renal function but related to a greyhound with clinical evidence of renal disease What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? There are multiple types of samples that can be submitted for this study. 1) Whole blood and serum 2) Urine (collected either free catch or cystocentesis) 3) Renal tissue collected via biopsy from dogs in which renal biopsy is recommended by the veterinarian to diagnose kidney disease and develop a treatment plan -OR- Renal tissue collected postmortem Client Compensation: The tests being offered are routine diagnostics in the evaluation of kidney disease, and the client will receive the results of the clinical data and /or tissue analysis depending on the type of sample submitted. Other Information: Samples can be shipped from clinic locations outside of the Ohio State University.
current_roster.name: Renal Disease in Greyhounds

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Recent studies indicate that certain immune cells such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes play an important role in tumor metastasis in diseases such as osteosarcoma. Certain anti-tumor drugs, such as toceranib, have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib (PalladiaTM) is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib as well. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as toceranib, together with losartan exerts significantly greater antitumor activity than either drug alone. The drugs losartan and propranolol have both been shown to modify the tumor microenvironment and reduce immune suppression caused by the tumor. The goal of this study is to evaluate the anti-tumor effects of a 3-drug combination of toceranib, losartan, and propranolol in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma. Initially your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests, which may include blood tests, urinalysis, blood pressure, and chest x-rays. The results of these initial tests will determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are part of the routine testing done in patients with osteosarcoma and may be performed even if you decide that your pet will not participate. Your dog will be sent home with oral losartan and propranolol to be given twice daily and oral toceranib to be given every other day. Rechecks will be required every 2 weeks following the start of treatment until the week 12 visit, and every 4 weeks thereafter until week 24 if tumors are stable or better. Chest x-rays will be performed every 8 weeks while on study. At the week 2 visit, your dog will need to stay in the hospital all day for serial blood collections following propranolol administration. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments.
current_roster.name: Pharmacological Tumor Microenvironment Modification with 3-Drug Combination in Canine Metastatic Osteosarcoma
