current_roster.description: Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of cancer in cats, and may be associated with injections or vaccines. They can invade tissues that are vital to normal function, and complete surgical removal can be impossible without amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be removable by surgery, but it could still recur at the surgical site or in a distant site like lymph node or lung.One attractive option for such cases is immunotherapy. We propose using mechanical high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to kill tumor cells and release antigens from tumors, stimulating the patients anti-tumor immune response. We hope to find out if HIFU application can both kill tumor cells and activate the immune system in cats. To determine if the treatment is effective, we are recruiting cats with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo HIFU treatment prior to surgical removal of the tumor.
current_roster.name: Focused ultrasound treatment of feline sarcomas

current_roster.description: To investigate whether intratumoral injections of NBD peptide can promote tumor cell death in canine high grade soft tissue sarcomas (STS) that have active NF-KB (signaling pathway) activity. Basic study design: Screening visit - staging (blood work, urinalysis, chest x-rays) + incisional biopsy of the mass (to confirm diagnosis of sarcoma and also to determine whether the NF-KB pathway is overactive in the mass). If the overactive pathway is identified, then within one week: Daily tumor injections for 4 days with the NBD peptide (outpatient procedure). On day 5, the tumor is removed via definitive surgical excision (or if it is non-resectable, a second incisional biopsy will be obtained).Following surgery - recheck visits every 2 months for a total of 3 visits (physical exam and chest x-rays). Coveredcosts: Physical examinations throughout the course of the study. General health blood and urine tests at screening and one day after the last NBD peptide administration. Chest x-rays at screening and every 2 months there-after for a total of 6 months. Two biopsies of the tumor performed under light sedation or general anesthetic. Immunohistochemical analysis of the tumor (to determineNF-kappaB expression). $500 towards definitive surgery (to be performed one day following the last NBD peptide administration. This would replace the second biopsy procedure) Treatment of any toxicity your dog develops secondary to NBD peptide administration. Please contact the VCIC at 215-573-0302 or study coordinator, June Chiango, at jchiango@upenn.edu for more information about this study.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Nemo Binding Domain (NBD) peptide for dogs with soft tissue sarcoma

current_roster.description: Purpose To investigate the safety and antitumor activities of a new ultrasonic technology, called histotripsy, that can noninvasively destroy (ablate) tumor tissue using acoustic energy, in dogs with brain tumors. Background Primary brain tumors (PBT) are a significant cause of illness and death in dogs. Surgery remains a common treatment for canine PBT, with the goal of removing as much of the tumor as possible. However, significant numbers of canine PBT are considered inoperable due to their location in the brain, and conventional, invasive surgical techniques can cause serious side effects. Even when surgery goes well, the tumor may regrow after surgery. New treatments, particularly for PBT that cant be removed by surgery or that have regrown after surgical removal, are needed to improve quality and quantity of life of affected dogs. This proof-of-concept of study will provide data necessary to refine histotripsy technology and explore new, non-invasive techniques. The techniques we are developing have the potential to allow precision image-guided, non-invasive treatment of PBT using ultrasonographic equipment and treatments that are currently in use in the majority of small animal veterinary practices, which may make treatment cheaper and more accessible.Please note that while our eventual goal is to be able to offer histotripsy as a non-invasive option, for this study we need to be able to surgically remove the patient's brain tumor and test it. This helps us ensure that the treatment works and is safe. This study is funded by the Focused Ultrasound Foundation and the American Kennel Club.
current_roster.tagline: Treating brain tumors with focused ultrasound
current_roster.name: Using a novel ultrasound device to treat canine brain tumors through an implanted polymer

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma (OSA) is an aggressive, devastating bone cancer that occurs in people and dogs. This cancer is locally invasive, typically destroying the bone where it originates, and it also readily moves to other parts of the body, particularly the lungs. Standard-of-care treatment (amputation and IV chemotherapy) confers a short survival time of typically 9-12 months. This pilot study will evaluate the combination of standard-of-care treatment and high-dose vitamin C to determine if immune activation will help prolong survival in dogs diagnosed with OSA. We hypothesize that this combination will be safe, and will confer a survival advantage in dogs with OSA.
current_roster.name: Combination High-Dose Vitamin C and Chemotherapy for Dogs with Bone Cancer (Osteosarcoma)

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether the B cell lymphocyte (a white blood cell) plays a role in the development of chronic pain in dogs with an injury to their cranial cruciate ligament. Dogs will be able to take part in the study if they have ruptured their cranial cruciate ligament, are a candidate for a surgical procedure named TPLO (tibial plateau leveling osteotomy), and plan to have the TPLO surgery performed at the UC Davis VMTH.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the immunologic signature of chronic pain in dogs with cranial cruciate ligament rupture

current_roster.description: To assess the effectiveness of cryoablation to minimize growth in both cancerous and benign tumors. Cryoablation is a freezing technique that may kill or shrink the tumor, alleviate pain, and assist the body in rejecting cancer. Cryoablation is performed by advancing a small needle through the skin into a tumor and freezing the tumor in place. The hypothesis of this study is that cryoablation can be used as a minimally invasive alternative to surgical removal of mammary masses. Cryoablation can generally be performed without significantly affecting the pets overall health while maintaining the pets appearance cosmetically. Pets can typically resume their usual activities within a few days with minimal side effects. The study will test a new device being developed for veterinary medicine. There is some data that support cryotherapy as a means to also kill tumor cells that have escaped the primary mass, e.g., metastasis. In the introductory phase, your pet will be treated with cryoablation of the mammary mass followed by surgical resection. Cryoablation will be performed at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy. Your pet will be randomized to a commercially available cryotherapy device or the Kubana Cryotherapy device for treatment. Surgical resection will be performed by your veterinarian or veterinary surgeon ~2 weeks after treatment. The pet owner is responsible for the cost of obtaining a diagnosis of the mass prior to treatment. The cryotherapy treatment cost and surgical resection are fully funded. Additional treatment related to mammary cancer, e.g., chemotherapy, if needed, is not covered in the clinical trial.
current_roster.name: Kubanda Cryotherapy of Mammary Tumors in Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major cause of morbidity in cats, especially as they age. The rate of progression in cats varies from months to years but can be managed through medical intervention and nutrition. Nutrition is arguably the most important aspect of CKD management. By manipulating the composition of a patient's diet, we can slow the progression of disease, minimize uremic symptoms, and improve quality of life. The goal of this clinical trial is to investigate the effects of differing protein concentrations on muscle mass, as well as differing phosphorus concentrations on progression of CKD. What qualifies my cat for enrollment in this in this trial? Cats diagnosed with IRIS stages 1, 2 or 3 are eligible to participate. Exclusion criteria include other uncontrolled systemic illnesses, complications of CKD such as kidney infection or ureteral obstruction, decompensation of CKD requiring hospitalization and intravenous fluid therapy. What does enrolling my pet in this clinical trial involve? After screening and enrollment, your cat will be randomized to receive a study diet, all of which would potentially be appropriate for this stage of your cat's disease. You will be asked to transition your cat completely to that new diet over a period up to 6 weeks. You will be asked to bring your cat back for evaluation 1 month after enrollment and then every 3 months thereafter for up to 1-2 years, or until your cat progresses to the next stage of CKD. You will be asked to bring a fresh fecal sample with you to each visit and labwork and imaging will be performed at each visit. Client Compensation: Your cat will receive free cat food (dry and/or canned), standard of care labwork monitoring of CKD, $25 incentive per visit, and assessment of their disease by a board certified internal medicine specialist for 1-2 years.
current_roster.name: Impact of Diet on Cats with CKD

current_roster.description: Elbow dysplasia is common in dogs, particularly large breed dogs. Elbow dysplasia leads to the development of elbow osteoarthritis. Elbow osteoarthritis creates pain and a lameness in the front leg of affected dogs. Nutritional supplements such as glucosamine, chondroitin, or omega 3 fatty acids have shown some benefit in relieving the signs of lameness in dogs with osteoarthritis. The purpose of this study is to determine whether dogs with elbow arthritis who receive a food supplement that contains undenaturated collagen II are using their affected legs better than when they receive a placebo.
current_roster.name: The elbow dysplasia UCII nutritional supplement study

current_roster.description: Naturally occurring cancers in dogs have been as used as models for human cancers for many reasons; however, the genomic profiles of many of these cancers are still incompletely understood. Further definition of these genomic landscapes will allow for improved development of novel diagnostics and therapeutics to diagnose and treat these cancers. The objective of this study is to develop cancer models of osteosarcoma and oral melanoma for use in future studies investigating the use of novel therapies.
current_roster.name: K9 tumor And Blood sampling for Osteosarcoma and Oral Melanoma (KABOOM)

current_roster.description: This study is evaluating a specialized CT scan to better understand the blood vessel patterns associated with limb soft tissue sarcomas. This information will be used to help identify future novel treatments for dogs having soft tissue sarcomas on their lower legs. Enrolled dogs will be anesthetized and have a CT scan of the lower limb with additional CT images following routine intravenous contrast injection. Study participation is complete after the CT has been performed.
current_roster.name: Investigating the blood vessel patterns of canine limb soft tissue sarcomas

current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To establish the feasibility, safety, and tolerability of High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) in the treatment of canine soft tissue sarcomas (STS), and to characterize the tumor response and time to progression after HIFU treatment. Background Soft Tissue Sarcomas are a common form of cancer in dogs that can invade tissues vital to normal function. As in humans, complete surgical removal remains the treatment of choice, with aggressive surgery recommended to ensure the best outcome. Surgical removal can sometimes be impossible without leg amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be surgically resectable, but it could still recur at the surgical site or spread in a distant site like lymph node or lung. Radiation therapy is often recommended when surgery cannot completely remove the tumor, to help reduce the risk of local recurrence. Unfortunately, these therapeutic approaches can be unsuccessful and associated with significant discomfort, disfigurement, and financial burden to the owner. Thus, there is a need for novel, less invasive, and more effective therapeutic options. High intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) is a non-invasive, outpatient ablative technique that has the potential to answer these unmet needs. Based on previous studies by our team, we hypothesize that a single HIFU treatment in dogs diagnosed with STS will result in complete tumor ablation, with minimal side effects.
current_roster.name: Treating soft tissue sarcomas in dogs using focused ultrasound as an alternative to surgery

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to compare post-operative pain management after orthopedic surgery in dogs receiving gabapentin alone, versus a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) medication alone, versus gabapentin and NSAID combined. Gabapentin is commonly prescribed, and while known to be safe, the efficacy of gabapentin for pain control acutely after orthopedic surgery in dogs is not known.


Dogs enrolled in this trial will have a complete physical and orthopedic examination in the normal course of the orthopedic appointment. Further screening will include radiographs of the affected limb and full blood work and urinalysis. Dogs will be randomized into one of 3 study groups (all groups receive pain medication(s)); dogs have a 1/3 chance of being in each of the groups. If on pain medications prior to surgery, a 5 to 30 day "wash-out" (depending on the exact medication) ("wash out" = no pain medications) will be required prior to surgery. Upon return to the hospital for surgery, we will perform a gait analysis (walking on a pressure-sensing mat), pain scoring, and a blood draw for drug levels. A tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO) surgery will be performed in standard fashion with standard anesthesia. Each enrolled dog will stay in-hospital for 2 days after surgery for pain assessment and treatment, gait analysis, and blood draw for drug levels. Study patients will be sent home with 12 days of pain medications, and we will need to see each dog back at 12 days after surgery for suture removal as well as pain assessment, gait analysis, and blood draw for drug levels. Following the 12-day post-operative appointment, the study will be finished but we will continue to work with each case during the normal 3–4-month recovery period from TPLO surgery.
current_roster.tagline: Pain management in dogs undergoing knee surgery
current_roster.name: Pain management in dogs undergoing knee surgery

current_roster.description: When a person or dog is diagnosed with cancer it is important to determine if the disease has spread throughout the body and to monitor them carefully to see if the chemotherapy they are getting is working. The vast majority of dogs that have been diagnosed with lymphoma and receive chemotherapy do great they feel better, their lymph nodes go back to a normal size and they honestly dont know they are sick. But is it not uncommon for some cancer cells to remain in the body in spite of the medications. The testing performed in this clinical trial is being looked at to see if we can figure out which dogs still have cancer. If we can do that our next step in a future clinical trial would be to try and figure out how to also get rid of those cells. On the first day of the study your pet will be placed under anesthesia for imaging. Initially we will do an F18-FDG PET/CT. This is a special form of imaging that involves giving your pet a small dose of a radioactive substance. The radiation dose is small enough that we expect no harm to be associated with it, and it is a substance that weve given to many dogs without problems. They will be under anesthesia for a few hours for the imaging then recovered in a special area of the hospital until the radioactive substance is almost completely gone. When your dog is discharged from this procedure, he or she will be safe for you to pet and touch. In almost every case that we have done this on (>350 dogs and counting) the dog will be able to go home the same night they had the imaging. While your pet is under anesthesia there will be some samples taken with a small needle from a few lymph nodes. As well we may decide to do a similar sample from other regions if there are areas we see on the F18 FDG PET/CT that make us concerned that the cancer has spread to them. These areas may include certain organs such as the liver or spleen. If we need to sample these organs we will use an ultrasound to guide us to limit risks as much as possible. We will also collect a blood sample for analysis prior to anesthesia and imaging. After the initial imaging your pet will be treated with any chemotherapy protocol you and your oncologist have agreed on. Your pet will need to have the same imaging and sampling performed after halfway through the chemotherapy protocol, then again 1-3 weeks after your pet has finished the chemotherapy. If your pets lymphoma is determined to have recurred during chemotherapy, additional imaging and sampling will be required at that time.
current_roster.name: F18 FDG PET/CT and cytology for canine lymphoma

current_roster.description: This study will evaluate a new method to identify gum disease in dogs undergoing a planned procedure under anesthesiaand when following a prescribed oral care routine for 6 months.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of new methods to identify gum disease in dogs

All patients will also continue to receive standard-of-care therapy (oral cyclosporine), which will be tapered according to patient response. Patients will be require to attend eight (8) visits within 7 months to the University of Pennsylvania Veterinary Hospital.

The study includes 7 assessments with a board-certified dermatologist over the course of 8-weeks.
current_roster.name: A Multi-Center, Pivotal, Clinical Effectiveness Study of a Canine-Specific Biologic (KIND-037) for the Treatment of Atopic Dermati

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the optimal dose of mustargen that can be administered when used as single agent and its side effects when given to dogs with cancer. Mustargen (also known as mechlorethamine) is a highly effective drug for the treatment of cancers, such as lymphoma in dogs. This chemotherapy often is used combined concurrently with other chemotherapy drugs. However, its administration as single agent in dogs diagnosed with cancer has not been documented. Mustargen administration along with vincristine is associated with some well-known side effects, including transient gastrointestinal upset and bone marrow suppression. We expect that, when mustargen is used on its own, its toxicity would be less, but this has yet to be investigated in dogs. The efficacy of mustargen against other cancers in dogs is unknown.
current_roster.name: Dose finding study of Mustargen in dogs diagnosed with cancer

current_roster.description: Standard therapy for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma has long been amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy to prevent or slow the growth and spread of cancer. With this form of treatment, survival times of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma is on average about 10 to 12 months with little improvement in survival occurring over the past two decades. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the addition of immunotherapy with an inhaled IL-15 (an immune stimulatory molecule called a cytokine) to the standard treatment in patients with osteosarcoma to see if it improves outcome. Our group, as well as others, have found that immunotherapy with inhaled cytokines can cause large osteosarcoma tumors in the lungs of dogs to shrink. Because the lungs are most often the first site for these tumors to spread, we believe that treating earlier when fewer cells are in the lungs could improve the outcomes seen with chemotherapy alone.
current_roster.name: Evaluating a new immunotherapy combined with standard of care treatment in dogs with osteosarcoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Robert Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description: This is a multi-site prospective 6-9 patient escalation study with 3 canine patients per group, each group having progressively more difficult to access tumors that measure >5cm in diameter. The first group will consist of canine patients with tumors that are superficial, just below the skin; the second group will consist of canine patients with tumors that are submuscularorlocated such that there is > 3.5 cm of intervening normal tissue between the tumor and the skin surface; and the third group will consist of canine patients with tumors that are intra-cavitary (i.e., intra-abdominal). The Deep CIVO injection system consists of (1) five custom-designed 25-gauge stainless steel hypodermic needles multiplexed into a single cylindrical 12-gauge outer cannula and triggered to extend up to 4 cm beyond the end of the cannula into the tumor by the action of a single lever; (2) a cartridge magazine with up to 5 loaded vials containing saline and fluorescent tracking microspheres; and (3) visualization lights and glasses which enable visualization of the fluorescent tracking microspheres during surgical excision of the injected mass. Ultrasound-guidence helps target the CIVO device to the optimal location and depth within the tumor. Following insertion of the needles into the tumor, microliter volumes of saline and/or drug, mixed with the fluorescent tracking microspheres, will be injected in a columnar fashion through each needle into a single solid tumor. Following the injection procedure, the tumor will be excised either immediately following the injection or within 1-3 days according to standard of care surgical oncological principles.Adverse events will be monitored on an ongoing basis throughout the study. When the first group of patients has been enrolled, an interim analysis may be conducted to evaluate safety and feasibility. After the second group of patients has been enrolled, a second interim analysis may be conducted. Patients will be on study for approximately 2 months.Screening: days -28 to 0; Treatment (injection procedure and tumor removal: days 1-7; Follow-up: one visit between day 11 and 21 and one visit on day 29 (2).
current_roster.name: A preclinical feasibility study evaluating the use of Deep CIVO, a novel intra-tumoral micro-injection device, in canine patients

current_roster.description: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the second most common acquired cardiac disease in dogs. The preclinical phase of DCM, often referred to as occult DCM (ODCM), can last for approximately two to three years. Current optimal management of dogs with ODCM includes pimobendan and/or antiarrhythmic medication. Once dogs with ODCM progress to the clinical phase of the disease, dogs often experience congestive heart failure and have limited (less than one year) life spans with diminished quality of life. This study aims to investigate if a new treatment, rapamycin, can reduce heart size and improve function during the occult/preclinical stage of dilated cardiomyopathy (ODCM) in dogs already receiving pimobendan. Dogs that pass the echocardiographic and full screening tests are eligible to enroll in this 6-month study. Dogs must be at least three years of age to be enrolled.
current_roster.name: RAPAMYCIN TREATMENT IN PRECLINICAL CANINE DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY (THE REPAIR STUDY)

We will be utilizing multiple technology platforms to investigate the disease from a range of biological sample types. Looking for Golden Retrievers, Labrador Retrievers, and West Highland White Terriers Atopic Cohort and Healthy Cohort dogs
current_roster.name: Atopic Dermatitis Clinical Study

current_roster.description: Although limb sparing for bone tumors has been performed for over 30 years in dogs, the complication rate for this surgery remains very high. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications, and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. 3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely tricalcium phosphate. Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the tricalcium phosphate, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing will be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat. Following entry into the study, dogs will have a CT scan of the affected limb prior to surgery. The images obtained with the CT scan will be used to make the 3D-printed implants that will be used in the limb-sparing surgical procedure. We hope that the limb-sparing surgery will be able to occur 5-7 days after the CT scan. In the event that this needs to be delayed due to technical difficulties with the implant production, we may recommend that your dog receive a dose of intra-arterial chemotherapy in the time between the CT scan and surgery. Two weeks after surgery, dogs will begin carboplatin chemotherapy, administered every three weeks for a total of 6 treatments. Follow-up bloodwork, orthopedic exams, gait analyses, and chest and limb x-rays will be performed at various points throughout the chemotherapy protocol and every 2 months thereafter until 18 months post-op, then every 4 months indefinitely.
current_roster.name: Personalized, bioreplaceable endoprosthesis to perform limb sparing in dogs

current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To determine if high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), a treatment that can destroy tissue using sound waves, will result in tumor cell death and immunologic activation in cats with sarcomas. Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of cancer in cats, and are sometimes associated with injections or vaccines. They can invade tissues that are vital to normal function, and complete surgical removal can be impossible without amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be removable by surgery, but it could still recur at the surgical site or in a distant site like lymph node or lung. One attractive option for such cases is immunotherapy. We propose using mechanical high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to kill tumor cells and release antigens from tumors, stimulating the patients anti-tumor immune response. We hope to find out if HIFU application can both kill tumor cells and activate the immune system in cats. To determine if the treatment is effective, we are recruiting cats with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo HIFU treatment prior to surgical removal of the tumor. Study Design Prior to enrolling in the study, your cat must undergo cancer staging, including a complete physical exam, lab work, tumor biopsy and a CT scan. These procedures are at owner expense. If your cat meets the eligibility criteria, s/he will be scheduled for the HIFU treatment within ten (10) days of enrollment. HIFU will be applied to the tumor under general anesthesia. Your cats fur/hair will be clipped over the tumor as is standard for any ultrasound in cats. The treatment will be delivered in a series of bursts of sound that will be focused on the tumor to kill the cancerous cells through unbroken skin surface. The HIFU treatment is expected to take 30-60 minutes, but may take longer for some patients. Your cat may be sent home the same day, or if due to timing of the treatment or for the safety of your pet, s/he may need to stay overnight while recovering from anesthesia. Your cat's surgery will take place at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital in Blacksburg, VA 4-6 days following treatment. Your cat will be discharged according to standard procedures, based on the surgeons discretion. Your cat will return for a recheck 2 weeks after the surgery. Compensation The screening (eligibility) tests, surgery, and post-surgery recheck visits are not fully covered by the study. Your total out of pocket costs are estimated to be between $2900 and $3400. Screening: Lab work and chest x-rays cost, approximately $900 if performed at ACCRC. If performed by your regular veterinarian, they can be sent to ACCRC to begin the screening process. Tests and images of insufficient quality will not be accepted. An exam and CT scan with the oncologists at ACCRC will be necessary to fully determine whether your cat is eligible to enroll. Baseline visit: If, at the baseline CT scan, the surgeons deem that the tumor cannot be safely removed or you do not agree to the recommended surgery, the cost of the CT scan and biopsy will be out-of-pocket at $2000.Surgery: If your cat is enrolled, it is expected that the surgery visit out-of-pocket fees will be $2000-2500. Once your cat is eligible and enrolled, the study will provide $5,000 worth of diagnostics, treatment, and medical care. Specifically: The entire cost of the baseline CT scan and radiologist interpretation, up to $350 for general anesthesia for the CT scan, $250 for the biopsy and histopathology, the exam fees and study-required lab work, up to $350 for the general anesthesia and HIFU/histotripsy treatment, and $2,000 of the cost of the surgery visit. You are responsible for any clinical fees exceeding the above costs, fees for surgery and post-operative care exceeding $2,000, any fees associated with medical complications of the HIFU therapy, and diagnostics or treatments performed not associated with the study or other medical problems that arise during the study. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED
current_roster.name: Treating feline sarcomas with high-intensity focused ultrasound

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate the role of the ADAMTS-13 enzyme in abnormal blood clotting in dogs with chronic liver disease Background The purpose of this study is to evaluate for abnormal clotting ability in dogs with chronic liver disease. Dogs with chronic liver disease may be at higher risk of blood clotting disorders, but the mechanism for this isnt well understood. This study hopes to determine the activity of an enzyme that plays a role in blood clotting, along with other known blood clotting parameters, in dogs with liver disease. Study Design Dogs undergoing routine liver biopsy will be evaluated in this study. If you agree to enroll you dog, we will obtain a small blood sample in order to assess your dogs blood clotting parameters. Your dog will not receive a liver biopsy for the purpose of this study, but only as part of a routine clinical work-up by our Internal Medicine service. For the study, we will collect an extra blood sample, beyond what is typically needed as part of routine clinical care. All other procedures undertaken are part of the routine clinical assessment and care of dogs with chronic liver disease. Compensation There are no costs to you for your pet to participate in the study. The study does not provide any compensation; however, the results of this study may benefit future animals who are at risk of developing blood clots.
current_roster.name: Blood clotting parameters in dogs with chronic liver disease

current_roster.description: The study population will be client owned cats with a history of seizures (more than one seizure) that present to UWVCfor euthanasia. Euthanasia may or may not be related to seizures or neurologic disease in general. The owners and managing clinicians will be counseled about the goals of the study and asked to consent to the study (see attached consent form). Clinical features of the cat's seizures will be extracted from the medical records. Cats will be euthanized asplanned by their owners.After euthanasia, the cats will be immediately perfused through the ascending aorta in order to preserve the sensitive hippocampi. The sections will then have an MRI performed at WIMR. After imaging, brains will be sectioned and processed using special stains (Nissl and Timm's stain) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) followed by microscopic evaluation and quantification using StereoInvestigator software, blinded to clinical presentation. Cats will be grouped based on clinical seizure phenotype: 1) TLE-like group: cats with hypersalivation, staring, mydriasis, and orofacial focal seizures, and 2) non-TLE group: cats with grand mal or other motor seizures lacking these features. Outcomes of hippocampal ratio and volume on MRI, and quantitative hippocampal staining for hilar neurons (Nissl) and mossy fiber sprouting (Timms), as well as IHC for parvalbumin, somatostatin, cholecystokinin, and neuronal GABA transporters will be compared between the two groups.
current_roster.name: Linking feline and human temporal lobe epilepsy

current_roster.description: Cryoablation is a freezing technique using a needle placed through the skin to kill or shrink masses or tumors and alleviate pain. The goal of this trial is to determine the effectiveness of cryoablation of tumors under the skin as an alternative to surgical resection. Cryoablation can generally be performed without significantly affecting the pet's overall health. For smaller masses that are not cancerous, we wish to determine whether cryoablation can be cosmetically better than surgical removal. Typically, dogs & cats may also resume their usual activities within a few days with minimal side effects. We will be testing a new device from Kubanda Cryotherapy that is being developed for veterinary medicine. This device has been used to treat subcutaneous, e.g., under the skin, benign and malignant masses in seven dogs. The masses in these dogs were later removed with surgery to determine the percentage of the masses that were killed by the device. All owners were pleased with the treatment in this first phase. In this second phase, we will monitor the disappearance of the mass in your pet over 1 year. Cryoablation will be performed under sedation or general anesthesia to minimize your pet's movement during the procedure. You will be responsible for obtaining blood work (and X-rays of the chest) as part of a pre-anesthetic work-up, and the determination of the mass type, typically by fine needle aspirate (FNA) and cytology. If accepted into the trial, you will pay a nominal fee (~$100) for the procedure. Participation in follow-up phone calls and visits will result in repayment of the initial fee.
current_roster.name: Cryoablation for lumps, bumps, and tumors in dogs and cats

current_roster.description: GSTs (glutathione-S-transferases)are enzymes which help the body eliminate (detoxify) environmental chemicals and certaindrugs. People that have low activity genetic variants in GSTs have a higher risk of certain cancers, such as lymphoma and bladder cancer, especially if they are exposed to certain chemicals in the environment.We want to determine whether the same is true for dogs. Human patients with low activity GST variants also havea higher risk of toxicities from certain drugsused to treat cancer and immune-mediated diseases. We also want todetermine if this is true in dogs. We are focusing on four canine GST genes, GSTT1, GSTT5 (unique to dogs), GSTM1 and GSTP1. We have found variants that are likely to affect enzyme function in each of these genes in dogs.Our overall goal is to see whether these variants are a risk factor for environmental cancers such as lymphoma, bladder cancer, and other tumorsin dogs, and whether risk for these tumors is a combination of GST variants andexposure to environmental chemicals (as measured in the urine or blood). We also wantsee whether GST variants are associated with adverse outcomes from certain drugs in dogs, including azathioprine, lomustine, and others.
current_roster.name: Genetic and Environment Risk for Lymphoma in Boxer Dogs

current_roster.description: Dogs that are recruited to the study will undergo a series of 24-hour ambulatory ECG (Holter) assessments. Holter monitors record the patient's heart rhythm continuously for 24 hours. Dogs identified to have AFwill be recruited to the study and they will undergo a baseline Holter assessment to determine the average 24-hour HR. Dogs enrolled in the studywill then be started on either amiodarone or diltiazem. The Holter assessment will be repeated 3 weeks after starting the anti-arrhythmic medication to determine if there has been an adequate response in HR. The goal HR is an average HR over 24 hours of 125 bpm or less. If the HR remains inadequately controlled, then the dog will be started on the second anti-arrhythmic drug (i.e. if the dog is on diltiazem and his HR is >125 bpm, then the veterinarian will start amiodarone). Two additional Holter assessments will be performed at specific time-points. These time-points are determined based on the dog's response to the medications. The dogs will also be monitored for adverse reactions to the medications. This will include performing bloodwork (complete blood cell count, liver biochemistry profile, thyroid profile), eye exam, blood pressure assessments and quality of life questionnaires for clients. This testing will be performed each time the dog is presented for a Holter assessment.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of efficacy of amiodarone or diltiazem to achieve optimal heart rate control in dogs with atrial fibrillation

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel anti-cancer therapy in dogs with measurable cutaneous cancer. The goals include (1) documenting toxicity associated with calcium electroporation and (2) to decrease the size/eliminate the cutaneous tumor. Tumors will be treated by injecting calcium followed by electroporation. Electroporation entails running electric pulses over the tumor while the patient is under anesthesia. Please review the following information related to participation in this study.
current_roster.name: Ca Electroporation in Dogs with Measurable Cutaneous Cancer

current_roster.description: To establish the safety, tolerability, and maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of oral TdCyd and Aza-TdC when administered daily for 5 days a week for 2 weeks, with one week off, q 21-day cycles, to canine patients with refractory or treatment-nave high-grade lymphoma or non-sarcomatous solid tumors. The effects of treatment on re-expression of select genes (e.g. p16) silenced by methylation in serial tumor biopsies will be evaluated along with alterations in the tumor methylome, in addition to DDR/apoptosis/autophagy markers assessed in a multiplex assay. Assessment of DNMT1 and DNMT3 status will also be evaluated. Query of these same PD markers may be assessed within circulating tumor cells collected within expansion cohorts after an efficacy signal is identified.
current_roster.name: COTC027

current_roster.description: Inactivation of tumor suppressor genes is one mechanism to induce cancer development. This can occur secondary to mutation to these genes or by a change to the DNA called hypermethylation. Drugs that prevent hypermethylation have been shown to be useful in the treatment of cancer. In this study, we will evaluate two hypomethylating nucleosides, TdCyd and Aza-TdC. The goal of this study is to identify a maximally tolerated dose (MTD) of TdCyd and Aza-TdC in tumor-bearing dogs. A secondary goal is to evaluate the metabolism of the drugs as well as the effects on the tumor. Dogs will be assigned to receive either TdCyd or Aza-TdC, and the dose will be based on the results of previous dogs enrolled into the study. Dogs with a variety of tumor types may be eligible, including lymphoma, melanoma, histiocytic sarcoma, and various carcinomas. Once your dog has been determined to be eligible, some initial procedures for the study will be performed, including blood sample collection, lymph node aspirates, tumor biopsies, and bone marrow aspirate (lymphoma dogs only). Your dog will then return for the first day of the study, at which time he/she will receive the first dose of the oral study drug, and then will have serial blood collections for 4 hours after administration 5 time points total). Your dog will return to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital on Days 8, 12, 15, and 22 for physical exam, tumor measurements, blood/urine collection, and lymph node aspirates. Tumor biopsies will also be performed on Days 8, 12, and possibly 22, depending on response to treatment. Repeat chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound +/- bone marrow aspirate will be performed on Day 22. You will be required to administer oral doses of the study drug at home on Days 2, 3, 4 and 5 and on Days 9, 10, 11. Your clinician will provide instructions on when and how to provide this medication to your dog. If your dog is responding to treatment at the Day 22 visit, he/she is eligible to stay on the study and continue to receive the study drug for an additional 22 days. Your dog will need to come to the hospital for appointments on days 8, 10, 15, and 22 of this second cycle. Physical exams and blood/urine collection will occur at each visit, and lymph node aspirates will occur on days 10, 15, & 22, and tumor biopsies on days 10 & 22. Repeat chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound +/- bone marrow aspirate will also be performed on Day 22, and all dogs will be off study after this visit. If at any time your dogs disease gets worse, he/she will be withdrawn from the study.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment for Dogs with Lymphoma and Solid Tumors
current_roster.name: COTC027: Preclinical Comparison of Two Hypomethylating Nucleosides in Tumor-Bearing Dogs

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the immune response, safety and efficacy of a novel anti-cancer therapy in dogs with measurable oral melanoma. The goals include (1) predicting tumor specific proteins through sequencing of an individuals tumor (2) documenting toxicity associated with vaccination with a personalized peptide vaccine and immune stimulatory medications (3) tracking the immune systems anti-tumor response (4) decreasing the size/eliminate the oral melanoma.
current_roster.name: Canine Melanoma Peptide Vaccine

current_roster.description: This randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled, GCP pivotal field study is evaluating the effectiveness and safety of verdinexor for the treatment of nave or first relapse lymphoma stages II, III, and IV in client owned dogs. Diagnosis of lymphoma must be confirmed by cytology or biopsy for the dog to be eligible for this study. Dogs will be randomized to receive the investigational veterinary product or a placebo treatment (tablets) to be administered with food twice weekly at least 72 hours apart for 8 weeks. After receiving treatment in-hospital on Day 0, the dog will be required to return to the study site on Days 7, 14, 28, 42, and 56 for follow up evaluation visits. Owners will be required to report and record abnormal daily observations and dosing using a phone app at home throughout the study.
current_roster.tagline: Dogs with Lymphoma
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Canine Lymphoma Evaluating a Novel Therapy in a Placebo-Controlled Study

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate the role of ADAMTS13, an enzyme related to blood clotting, in dogs with presumptive idiopathic immune thrombocytopenia Background Immune thrombocytopenia results in low platelet numbers, which often predisposes affected individuals to excessive bleeding. In humans, immune thrombocytopenia can be difficult to tell apart from immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, since both conditions result in low platelet numbers and may cause excessive bleeding. Reduced activity of ADAMTS13 is the underlying cause of immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. The primary aim of this study is to determine whether a portion of dogs with presumptive idiopathic immune thrombocytopenia have reduced ADAMTS13 activity, which may represent a disease process similar to immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura in people. Study Design Dogs undergoing routine evaluation for immune thrombocytopenia (abdominal ultrasound, chest x-rays, complete blood cell count, and urinalysis) will be evaluated in this study. Your dog will not receive these tests solely for the purpose of this study, but as part of a routine clinical work-up by the Veterinary Teaching Hospital. As part of the study, we will collect an extra blood sample, beyond what is typically needed as part of routine clinical care, and a bleeding score assessment will be performed. All other procedures undertaken are part of the routine clinical assessment and care of dogs with immune thrombocytopenia.
current_roster.tagline: Blood clotting in dogs with immune thromobocytopenia
current_roster.name: Evaluating blood clotting in dogs with idiopathic immune thrombocytopenia

current_roster.description:
Multiple companies are offering services that recommend "targeted therapy" for dogs with cancer, using drugs that are approved for the treatment of some types of cancer in humans. However, most of these drugs have not been studied for effectiveness in dogs, nor do we know how much or how often they should be given. The goal of this study is to measure levels over 24-96 hours of these drugs following a single oral or subcutaneous dose, in pet dogs with cancer. Dogs will receive a single oral or subcutaneous dose of a given agent at the dose recommended by the company, followed by blood collection 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 24 hours later. For one specific drug, samples will also be collected 0.25, 48, and 96 hours post-treatment. Following the 24- or 96-hour blood collection, dogs will be off study and eligible for any other treatment.

Your dog will receive a single oral or subcutaneous dose of one of these drugs at a dose that is predicted to cause no side effects. A small amount of blood (approximately 1 teaspoon) will be collected at the time points above. Collection of the blood samples will take all day. Your dog will need to return the following day for 1 additional blood draw, or alternatively, they can stay overnight at no cost to you. Some dogs will need to return for blood collection 48 and 96 hours after administration. After the 24- or 96-hour blood sample is drawn, the study is over and your dog is eligible to receive any additional treatment that is recommended.

Although the drugs we are studying have caused minimal side effects in laboratory dogs at the doses we are planning to use (even when given every day for several weeks), they have not been studied in pet dogs, which may be older and have other medical issues. Therefore, side effects (although extremely unlikely) could range from mild to severe, up to and including the death of your dog. Medications will be provided as needed to treat/prevent any side effects that might occur.

Costs covered by the clinical trial for eligible enrolled dogs include the cost of all examinations, drug dispensing, and blood collection. You will be responsible for the initial exam fee, and tests to confirm that your dog is eligible. Participating owners will receive a $500 credit to their dog’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital account, which can be applied to the initial testing or used to reduce costs of other cancer treatment when the study is complete.
current_roster.tagline: Blood Levels after Single Dose of Targeted Agent in Dogs with Cancer
current_roster.name: Single Dose Plasma Pharmacokinetic Analysis of Targeted Anticancer Agents in Tumor Bearing Dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if OKV-1001 is safe and more effective than prednisone alone for the treatment of IMHA. OKV-1001 is a new formulation of a drug called mycophenolic acid (MPA) that is used in the treatment of IMHA. This is a double-blinded, placebo-controlled study. Your dog must be diagnosed with IMHAthat is not believed to be caused by any medications or vaccines, be >12 months of age, be able to take oral medications, and have been treated with glucocorticoids (such as prednisone) for less than seven days prior to enrollment.Your dog must not be on any other immunosuppressive medication for other conditions (such as atopic dermatitis, etc) or have a previous diagnosis of IMHA.
current_roster.name: Investigating OKV-1001 for treating dogs with IMHA

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: If you agree to have your dog enrolled in the study, the usual treatment for septic peritonitis will be performed. Fluids and medications will be used to stabilize your dog prior to surgery. At the time of surgery, a multilumen catheter will be placed to facilitate blood sampling, reducing the potential need to place multiple IV (intravenous) catheters. Standard-of-care surgery and aftercare will be performed. These risks will be discussed with you by the attending veterinarian and you will sign a separate consent for surgery and anesthesia. The study treatment, injection of the novel drug (ODSH) or a placebo (saline), does not start until immediately after surgery. We will first perform a blood test to assess your dogs ability to clot his/her blood. As long as this is within an expected range, we will administer the first dose of the experimental drug or the placebo. Each dog will have a 50/50 chance of receiving either ODSH or a placebo. This will be done by computerized randomization which is like the chance of flipping a coin. You will not know what treatment your dog has received and neither will his or her clinician. We plan to give five doses total, at eight hour intervals for 32 hours. After the five doses, a blood sample will be collected 40 hours post-surgery for the study. Before each dose is given, we will re-test your dogs blood clotting ability. If the clotting test result is abnormally elevated, meaning your dogs blood is taking a longer time to clot, a lower dose or no dose of the drug will be given. If blood clotting ability remains within an expected range, meaning the time your dogs blood is taking to clot is within a normal or mildly prolonged range, the drug dose will remain the same. We will also be carefully tracking all clinical signs related to bleeding throughout your dogs time in the trial to ensure that he or she tolerates the treatment. If your dogs clinician feels that the treatment should be ended at any time, the study treatment will be discontinued. Your dog will require 7 blood tests in total. Several of these are already performed as part of the standard-of-care for this condition. At each test we will take less than 13 ml (one tablespoon) of blood. Most if not all of these blood samples will be taken from a catheter already in place and therefore, collection will not cause additional discomfort to your dog.
current_roster.name: A Double Blind, Placebo Controlled Dose Escalation Trial of a Novel Therapeutic Strategy for the Treatment of Canine Sepsis

current_roster.description: Postoperative regurgitation is a common side effect of general anesthesia in dogs and is of significant clinical concern due to the increased risk for aspiration pneumonia (lung infection due to inhaling stomach contents when regurgitation occurs). Dogs known to be at high risk for this include brachycephalic (dogs with short noses/flat faces) and dogs undergoing orthopedic or gastrointestinal surgery. A major contributing factor to postoperative regurgitation is the effect of the opioid pain medications that are administered as part of the patients analgesic plan. While opioids are the best method of pain control available, they can reduce peristalsis (the normal movement of the intestines), leading to undesired side effects such as regurgitation and constipation. The current gold standard to prevent postoperative vomiting is to administer an antinausea drug called maropitant citrate prior to surgery. Maropitant works within the portion of the brain that controls nausea in order to prevent vomiting; however, it does not target the underlying factors contributing to the postoperative regurgitation (reduced peristalsis) and will therefore not have an effect on reducing regurgitation or constipation.Methylnaltrexone (MNTX) is an opioid blocker (i.e. inhibits the effects of opioids). MNTX is able to specifically inhibit the effect of opioids within the intestines (i.e. preventing the loss of peristalsis) while preserving the opioids pain reducing properties. This means your pet will still receive the beneficial pain control normally achieved through opioids, but will not be at as high of a risk for postoperative complications brought on by regurgitation. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetic analysis of methylnaltrexone in healthy dogs

current_roster.description: Insulinoma is the most common pancreatic cancer in dogs. Tumor cells secrete excessive insulin which results in hypoglycemia (low blood sugar); this can be life threatening. The treatment of choice is surgical removal of the primary tumor and any sites of metastasis (tumor spread), when possible, in order to help reduce insulin levels and improve outcomes. Unfortunately, many dogs with insulinomas will eventually relapse due to the high rate of metastatic disease.Cancer can release small fragments of DNA into the blood stream. OncoK9 is a commercially available test that can detect these cancer fragments for some types of cancers. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the OncoK9 liquid biopsy blood test can be used (in conjunction to standard-of-care blood glucose and insulin levels) to detect insulinoma cancer cells in the blood both prior to surgery as well as up to 1 year after surgery.
current_roster.name: The Utility of OncoK9 Liquid Biopsy for the Detection of Canine Insulinoma

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is the most common malignant bone tumor in the dog. While surgery and chemotherapy are the main treatments for most osteosarcomas, most dogs will unfortunately eventually develop spread of their tumor. New treatments are needed to improve the outcome in both canine and human patients with osteosarcoma. Vismodegib is a drug that is approved for the treatment of basal cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, in humans. It appears that canine and human osteosarcoma, like human basal cell carcinoma, rely on a cell signaling pathway called the Hedgehog pathway (which is inhibited by vismodegib) for cell growth, survival and spread, and in mouse models of osteosarcoma, treatment with vismodegib results in delayed osteosarcoma spread, Vismodegib has been studied in laboratory dogs for safety, but has not been studied for the treatment of canine cancer. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and molecular effects of vismodegib treatment, combined with surgery and chemotherapy, in dogs with osteosarcoma. After amputation, your dog will receive vismodegib orally once daily, and will receive a total of 4 doses of carboplatin as an injection every 3 weeks for 4 treatments. They will be rechecked 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 11, 14 and 17 weeks after treatment is started and monthly thereafter, with every-other-month rechecks of chest X-rays. Visits will generally take about 4 hours. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (no evidence of tumor spread). Analysis for tumor spread will be performed by monthly physical examinations and every-other-month chest X-rays. Standard bloodwork and urinalysis will be performed at each visit. Small skin biopsies (around the size of a pencil eraser) will be performed at the time of amputation and 2 and 8 weeks after starting vismodegib. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the effect of vismodegib on cell function. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 5 teaspoons.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Drug with Amputation and Chemotherapy for Canine Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Phase-1 Evaluation of Vismodegib Plus Carboplatin in Dogs with Spontaneous Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description:
This study is currently on hold to enrollment due to a national shortage of carboplatin


We know from people and dogs with this type of bone cancer, that the pain associated with the tumor is severe. In people, after they receive their first round of chemotherapy, there is a significant reduction in the pain severity and of course an improvement in quality of life while undergoing treatment. A very important component of treatment in dogs, is ensuring effective pain control. What we dont know is the impact of adding chemotherapy to the pain control plan. This will help us inform current recommendations and the design of future clinical trials. The goal of this study is to determine the effect on lameness, activity and sleep quality in dogs with long bone osteosarcoma after a dose of intravenous carboplatin. Once enrolled, your dog will get a single dose of carboplatin chemotherapy, which is the standard of care drug we use in this disease. Around this treatment we will measure your dogs response to treatment by using an activity monitor placed on a collar, measure the forces going through each leg while walking and ask you to complete a brief survey. This will be repeated weekly for 3 weeks total at which time the study will be complete and your dog will be eligible to undergo any treatment that you would like based on the recommendations from your care team.
current_roster.tagline: The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma targeted to treat macroscopic OS metastases to the lungs. Recent studies show that certain immune cells, such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes, play an important role in tumor metastasis in osteosarcoma and other cancer types. Certain anti-tumor drugs, like toceranib (PalladiaTM), have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins (receptor tyrosine kinases) important for cancer growth. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib therapy. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of high-dose losartan and toceranib can significantly slow tumor growth and, in some cases, stimulate significant tumor shrinkage in dogs with macroscopic OS lung metastases. More recent studies indicate that the use of a drug called defactinib may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. The purpose of this trial is to determine whether the 3-drug combination of Palladia, losartan, and defactinib can give better cancer control in dogs with metastatic OS than the original 2-drug combination (Palladia/losartan). A secondary goal of this study is to assess gene expression in a type of immune cell called macrophages present in the lungs of dogs with metastatic OS. This will be accomplished through a procedure called bronchoalveolar lavage. Initially, your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests which may include blood tests, urinalyses, blood pressure, and x-rays of the chest. Test results will help determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are routinely performed in patients with osteosarcoma and may be done even if you decide that your pet will not participate in a clinical trial. Following enrollment into the trial, your dog will undergo pre-treatment bronchoalveolar lavage under general anesthesia. This must be done prior to Day 0, but cannot be scheduled on the same day. Day 0 will be scheduled one to two days following bronchoalveolar lavage and involves the first administration of study drugs, then serial blood sample collection over 8 hours. We will collect more study blood the following day, 24 hrs after the first doses of medications. You will be sent home with oral losartan (twice daily) and oral defactinib (once daily), and oral toceranib (once every other day) after the 24 hour blood sample is collected. Your dog will then return two weeks later (Week 2) for study blood collection. At Week 4, your dog will return for chest x-rays, blood pressure, blood and urine tests and study blood collection. One month later (Week 8), your dog will return for the second broncheoalveolar lavage performed under general anesthesia, chest x-rays, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Follow-up visits will be required 4 weeks thereafter until disease progression is identified. Blood will be collected for study purposes (~1.5 tablespoons) at every visit for the study. Chest x-rays will be performed prior to enrollment and monthly thereafter. Blood pressure will be performed on Day 0, Week 4, Week 12, and monthly thereafter. Dogs will remain on the study as long as their pulmonary nodules do not progress in size and no new nodules are identified on chest x-rays. If your dog dies while on the study, a post-mortem examination and tumor collection may be necessary to explain the cause of death. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments.
current_roster.tagline: 3-Drug Combination Treatment for Metastatic Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) Inhibition to Improve Losartan-Toceranib Immunotherapy in Canine Metastatic Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Osteoarthritis (OA) is estimated to affect as many as 60% of the nearly 90 million adult dogs in the United States. The quality of life in affected dogs is adversely affected by pain, stiffness, various degrees of lameness, and an overall decrease in normal activity.Osteoarthritis is initiated by articular cartilage damage resulting from a wide range of causes such as trauma, infection, and mechanical or developmental disorders. Management of affected dogs is generally multifaceted, and may include weight reduction, surgery, exercise and activity modification, physical rehabilitation, disease-modifying osteoarthritic agents, the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs), and injections of medications or biologic therapies.Management of OA with injectable agents is especially attractive because of the perceived efficacy and relative lack of adverse events. As patients with elbow OA age, susceptibility to adverse drug events (ADEs) in dogs treated with drugs such as NSAIDs seems to increase, and many dogs with pre-existing concurrent medical conditions are at higher risk for ADEs. Further, some owners are reluctant to use NSAIDs due to concerns raised about NSAID used in animals as well as in people. Therefore, there is a need to effectively improve the quality-of-life of patients with OA. While injectable agents such as corticosteroids may be effective, there are also a number of adverse events, some of which may result in more rapid deterioration of cartilage.Biologic therapies, while effective, are costly. A cost-effective, safe, and easy to administer intra-articular treatment for elbow osteoarthritis is attractive.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment for Dog with Osteoarthritis
current_roster.name: Treatment response of a novel intra-articular injection of in dogs with elbow osteoarthritis.

current_roster.description: Enrolling dogs in a fully funded clinical trial to evaluate a once-weekly insulin treatment. Owners must be willing to commit to the visit schedule over a 6-month duration. This study will cover the following (at no cost to the Owner): -Study Visits -Medications -Laboratory Testing -A stipend for the transition back to conventional insulin at the end of the trial
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Diabetic Dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to demonstrate that novel treatment with an existing oral tablet formulation increases lifespan, maintains Health Related Quality of Life HRQL and mitigates the development of frailty. We will also collect samples that will be used to advance the science of the field of canine aging and longevity.
current_roster.tagline: Canine Aging and Quality of Life
current_roster.name: The Effect of Novel Treatment with an Oral Medication on Canine Longevity.

current_roster.description: Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed. Both protocols involve treatments every 7-14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.
current_roster.tagline: CHOP LOPP chemotherapy for lymphoma
current_roster.name: CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy as a first line treatment for naïve peripheral T cell lymphoma in dogs

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in dogs. Injectable multi-drug chemotherapy remains the standard of care, and is associated with high response rates and meaningful prolongation of life. However, a minority of dogs with lymphoma are treated with injectable chemotherapy, in part due to an inability of non-specialty practices to safely handle these drugs. However, there are no established effective chemotherapy protocols for previously untreated canine lymphoma that do not involve drugs that require special handling. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of a combination of the drugs asparaginase, procarbazine, prednisone, and lomustine (APPL) given to dogs with previously untreated lymphoma. Your dog will receive up to 2 injections of asparaginase subcutaneously (under the skin), and will receive oral lomustine, procarbazine and prednisone at home. They will be rechecked weekly for the first 4 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter. Visits will generally take about 1 hour. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease stabilization or meaningful tumor shrinkage). Dogs experiencing a complete response (complete disappearance of all evidence of lymphoma) will receive a total of 5 every-4-week cycles of treatment, followed by monthly rechecks. Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement. Standard bloodwork will be performed at each visit. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 2 teaspoons.
current_roster.tagline: APPL for Lymphoma in Dogs
current_roster.name: APPL for Canine Multicentric Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Dogs with insulinoma diagnosed by cytology or histopathology (biopsy) will be considered for treatment. After initial consultation, dog will be enrolled in the trial if the dog is not a good candidate for surgery. If dog already had surgery but still experiencing hypoglycemia (low blood glucose), this dog can be also enrolled in the trial. Either abdominal ultrasound or CT scan is needed within 14 days of initiation of trial. A bloodwork will be performed before chemotherapy and if these values are adequate, vinorelbine will be administered intravenously. Continuous glucose monitoring device (FreeStyle Libre) will be placed on the skin on the first day of chemotherapy and glucose level will be monitored for initial 14 days. Chemotherapy is repeated once every 2 weeks at University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center. The response to the treatment will be assessed by glucose level and abdominal ultrasound in 1 and 2 months.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of vinorelbine for the treatment of canine insulinoma

current_roster.description: Irreversible Electroporation (IRE) uses electrical pulses to destroy the membranes of cells within a tumor mass. The therapy is rapid and involves the placement of electrodes followed by the delivery of electrical pulses. This results in the destruction of tumor cells within a well-defined space, leaving a margin of healthy, viable tissue. IRE has been used to treat human tumors for the last decade. Currently, a variant of IRE (electro-chemotherapy) is used to treat horses with squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma tumors. The pulses ablate some cancer cells while helping chemotherapy penetrate into surviving cells. However, the mono-polarity nature of the waveform causes intense muscle contractions in the horses which requires that they be anesthetized and laid on their side before the surgical procedure. The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate, high frequency IRE (H-FIRE), a technique that uses an alternating polarity waveform to eliminate these muscle contractions and enable treatment of patients without general anesthesia. Tumor cell death following H-FIRE treatments is necrotic and apoptotic in nature and occurs over a period of days after treatment. The only open wound caused during surgery is that from the needle entrance path making it an ideal modality for treatments in locations with a high risk of infection
current_roster.name: Treatment of Large Skin Melanoma OR Squamous Cell Carcinoma Tumors in Horses using H-FIRE

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate biological samples from cats with IBD and LGITL and perform comprehensive genetic studies assessing the differences between them. Background Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and low-grade intestinal T-cell lymphoma (LGITL) are two common diseases affecting cats. Both diseases can cause diarrhea, vomiting, pain, and malabsorption of food. However, recent data indicate that those two conditions may represent a continuum, and more studies are necessary to better understand the conditions. Since the diseases are similar and the symptoms overlap and are nonspecific, diagnosis can be challenging, and may require expensive and invasive procedures. In addition, although the general treatment for both conditions is similar, treatment may mask more aggressive and potentially costly diseases. Thus, developing better diagnostic approaches is essential to provide better care to feline patients. In this study, we will analyze blood and small fragments of the intestines ofcats with each disease and perform comprehensive genetic studies evaluating the differences. This broad approach has not been applied to studying IBD and LGITL before. We believe it can provide valuable data, indicating what differentiates and causes each disease. Our long-term goal is to identify and develop blood-based diagnostic tests to differentiate IBD from LGITL. We hope our study will improve the health care and well-being of cats who suffer from these conditions. Study Design We will screen cats who have clinical suspicion of having IBD or LGITL and who require endoscopic evaluation for final diagnosis. Once diagnosis of IBD or LGITL is confirmed, the cat will be enrolled. We will use the same samples collected for diagnostic purposes (small fragments of intestinal mucosa collected during endoscopy) to perform whole-genome sequencing, spatial transcriptomic analysis, and RNA sequencing. These laboratory techniques allow the evaluation of cellular function at the molecular level, helping to shed light on the mechanisms of diseases. Aiming to cause minimal distress to enrolled cats, we intend to minimize the collection of extra samples. Thus, we will use leftover samples collected for diagnostic purposes (i.e., mucosal biopsies during endoscopy, and whole blood submitted for complete blood count) during routine clinical workups, not material collected for this studys sole purpose. The exception is the collection of additional blood samples in cases where the remaining volume after clinically-indicated blood work is less than 2 mLPatients can be enrolled regardless of the decision to pursue treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Genetic diagnosis of cats with GI disease
current_roster.name: Developing blood-based diagnostic tests to differentiate inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and low-grade intestinal T-cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: An open-label, prospective, multi-institutional, fixed-schedule, prospective pre-clinical trial will be performed to evaluate 4VGS-001 (Anti-CTLA) in combination with radiation therapy in dogs with stage III or IV oral malignant melanoma. The treatment period is 10 weeks during which 3 doses of radiation therapy will be administered over a one-week period followed by 4 doses of VGS-001 given at 3-week intervals. The total observation period will be 29 weeks. During this time, dogs will be evaluated for objective response (CR, PR, or SD). Dogs will be evaluated on an intent-to-treat basis. Dogs with documented progressive disease (increase in size of either the primary tumor or metastatic lesions) will undergo re-evaluation 2 weeks later to confirm disease progression and not pseudoprogression. Overall tolerability and biological activity will be based on clinical and pharmacodynamic endpoints.
current_roster.tagline: Fully canine anti-CTLA4 mAb in combination with radiation therapy for dogs with stage III and IV oral malignant melanoma
current_roster.name: Pilot study to evaluate a fully canine anti-CTLA4 mAb (VGS-001) in combination with radiation therapy in dogs with stage III and I
current_roster.top_investigator: Nicola Mason BVetMed, PhD, DACVIM, FRCVS, Professor of Veterinary Medicine

current_roster.description: Urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common type of bladder cancer to affect dogs. Treatment often involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, with the aim being to reduce the size of the tumor, alleviate symptoms, and improve the dog's quality of life. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment approach for many types of cancer, including canine urothelial carcinoma. Immunotherapies aim to harness the body's immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. They can be particularly attractive for treating cancers that are difficult to access surgically or that have metastasized (spread to other parts of the body).This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy when used in dogs with urothelial carcinoma. The therapy specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells, which usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells. Immunotherapies that are able to inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively.Urothelial carcinoma in dogs shares many biological and molecular features with human urothelial carcinoma, including their ability to be shielded from the immune system. Human clinical trials in urothelial carcinoma investigating similar immunotherapies have shown these therapies to be more effective than traditional chemotherapies in some cases. Development of an immunotherapy that is safe and beneficial in canine urothelial carcinoma patients will advance veterinarians ability to treat this disease and will provide an important model to inform future canine and human clinical trials in this area. This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma.
current_roster.tagline: Immunotherapy for bladder cancer in dogs
current_roster.name: Fully Canine Anti-PD1 for Urothelial Carcinoma in Dogs: Safety and Tolerability

current_roster.description: The goal of oral cancer surgery is to remove all cancer cells to prevent local recurrence and distant spread to other organs. However, there is currently no pre-operative or intraoperative diagnostic test that is capable of accurately identifying all cancer cells, especially at the leading tumor edge where there is only microscopic disease. Thus, to ensure no cancer cells are left behind, a border of grossly normal appearing tissue (up to 2 cm) is also removed during surgery.
