Yet, in the oral cavity, removal of bordering healthy tissue is typically associated with severe structural, functional and cosmetic side effects. Most notably, the ability to eat may be compromised. There is an urgent need for intraoperative diagnostic tests that can delineate healthy from cancer tissue in real-time. The aim of this study is to evaluate the use of florescence lifetime imaging with Protophoryin IX (a natural intermediate in the iron pathway that fluoresces under blue light) to accurately diagnose cancer versus normal tissue during surgery. We will also characterize the tissue changes that drive differences in florescence emission between the tumor, peritumoral region (area of potential pre-malignant cells), and healthy tissue with spatial transcriptomics. This will allow us to also create biomarkers for early diagnosis of cancer and decide when florescence imaging is most likely to be helpful. If successful, the use of florescence lifetime imaging with PpIX during surgery would ensure the surgeon successfully removes all cancer cells while simultaneously sparing normal healthy tissue.
current_roster.name: Flourescence Lifetime Imaging for real time surgical guidance in oral tumors

current_roster.description: Sinonasal cancer is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed progress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to evaluate a new radiation treatment known as Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT). A current method of radiation therapy used to treat canine sinonasal carcinoma (SC), called stereotactic body radiotherapy therapy (SBRT), distributes a high dose of radiation uniformly across the tumor. Lattice radiation therapy (LRT) differs from SBRT in that instead of administering that uniform high dose of radiation throughout the tumor, several small spheres of high dose radiation are administered within the tumor and the rest of the tumor receives a lower dose of radiation. LRT has shown promise in early studies to provide tumor control with low normal tissue toxicity, suspected to be due to improved blood flow and immune responses compared to uniform, high dose radiation therapy. Our goal is to look at the differences in the tumors immune response during and after treatment as well as the clinical response with LRT compared to our standard SBRT. Dogs enrolled into this study will be treated with LRT. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush under anesthesia. The following procedures will be performed in all dogs enrolled in the study: CT scan for radiation therapy planning Lattice radiation therapy; 3 treatments given once daily over consecutive business days under general anesthesia Nasal flush, 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Blood collection (9-19 mL), 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Tumor biopsy at the 2 week post-LRT time point under general anesthesia Recheck CT scan 3, 6, 12 months, and 18-months post-LRT under general anesthesia.
current_roster.tagline: Lattice Radiation Therapy for Nasal Carcinoma
current_roster.name: Lattice radiation therapy’s effect on the immune response in canine sinonasal carcinoma

current_roster.description: Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a highly aggressive and malignant vascular tumor occurring most commonly in dogs. Dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma have a poor prognosis, with fewer than 20% of dogs surviving 9 months with surgery and adjuvant doxorubicin chemotherapy. Paclitaxel is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer today, with potent activity against a wide variety of tumors. Paclitaxel interferes with normal microtubule function during cell division and induces cell cycle arrest. In addition, several studies have shown that paclitaxel has antiangiogenic properties. Paclitaxel targets both the tumor stroma and the vasculature, and it has been shown to inducetumor control in human patients with soft tissue angiosarcomas. The conventional formulation of paclitaxel (Taxol) has been associated with acute adverse events in dogs, which has largely precluded the use of paclitaxel as a chemotherapeutic in veterinary oncology. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal Vet, uses a proprietary formulation based on retinol derivatives (XR-17), which encapsulate paclitaxel to form nanosized micelles. Previous studies with Paccal Vet have demonstrated a tolerability profile that is generally similar to other chemotherapy drugs used in veterinary oncology. Moreover, anti-tumor activity in selected cancers in dogs, including mast cell tumors, squamous cell carcinoma, and mammary cancer has also been reported for Paccal Vet. These findings suggest that Paccal Vet may be a promising treatment option for dogs with hemangiosarcoma. It is important to note that none of the chemotherapeutic agents commonly used in veterinary oncology clinics for the treatment of hemangiosarcoma have been approved for veterinary use.
current_roster.tagline: Post operative Paccal Vet for the treatment of canine splenic hemangiosarcoma
current_roster.name: An indication-seeking pilot study of Paccal Vet in dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma following splenectomy
current_roster.top_investigator: Sharon Shor, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), Veterinary Oncologist

current_roster.description: This study aims to identify the etiology of canine dysautonomia (CD) by investigating Clostridium botulinum-like bacterial isolates collected from soil and feces related to CD cases. The project utilizes an -omics approach to examine bacterial isolates and attempt to identify a putative neurotoxin and characterizes relevant plasma alterations from the cases. If fully successful, this study will identify an etiology for CD in dogs and build an understanding of disease biology.
current_roster.tagline: Combining Traditional and Multiomic Approaches to Elucidate the Cause and Mechanisms of Canine Dysautonomia
current_roster.name: Combining Traditional and Multi-omic Approaches to Elucidate the Cause and Mechanisms of Canine Dysautonomia

current_roster.description:
By 2030, approximately three-quarters of all cancer will occur in low- or middle-income countries (LMICs) where access to current treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy are often severely limited. The limitations are both the high-cost and complex infrastructures required for many of the interventions and the lack of resources to manage their toxic side effects.

Therefore, there is a large, unmet need to develop effective cancer therapies that are more applicable to these settings. Unfortunately, the trend in cancer therapy research is overwhelmingly toward more complex and personalized approaches that, while potentially valuable in high-income countries (HICs), will likely have little impact on cancer control in low-resource settings. It is striking that substantial attention is currently focused on U.S. cancer disparities that are almost always less than two-fold across populations, whereas global disparities in access to preventative and therapeutic interventions are often ten-fold or greater, yet they are largely ignored, despite the limited access to palliative care in many low resource settings. Fion in resource-limited settings also contribute.

Owner Responsibility

COTC033a: The owner is responsible to bring their pet to UW until the trial is completed which will 15 weeks after the first injection. This will include 3 weeks of the primer phase, then 10 days of break, then 9 weeks of the treatment phase or the time a dog develops a progressive disease.

COTC033b The owner is responsible of bringing their pet to UW until the end of the trial which will be 12 weeks after the first injection. This will include 1 week of the primer phase, then 14 days of break, then 9 weeks of the treatment phase or the time a dog develops a progressive disease.
current_roster.tagline: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers in Canine Patients
current_roster.name: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers in Canine Patients
current_roster.top_investigator: David Michael Vail, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description:
In collaboration with the UW Carbone Cancer Center, we are developing a new approach to the treatment of cancer that has spread beyond the primary tumor (metastatic cancer). This trial involves 3 ways to stimulate a patient’s own immune system to fight their cancer 1) “Immune checkpoint inhibition” (ICI), 2) “in situ vaccination” (ISV), and 3) low-dose radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT).

ICI involves injections of a monoclonal antibody that targets the “immune checkpoints” (the “brakes”) of the immune system that cancer cells use to escape detection by cancer-killing immune cells. ICI therapy results in a lifting of the brakes and in some patients allows the immune system to recognize and actively kill cancer cells throughout the patient’s body. The ICI therapy used in this study is an IV drug called Gilvetmab that is USDA conditionally approved for use in dogs.

ISV involves a combination of standard doses of external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) that targets your dog’s primary cancer along with an injection directly into your dog’s primary cancer of an immune stimulant called PIC. The combination of EBRT and PIC has been shown in mouse tumors to turn the mouse’s own tumor into an anticancer vaccine resulting in cures in significant percentage of mice.

RPT involves giving a low dose of a radioactive molecule that is designed to target cancer cells specifically. This low dose does not kill cancer cells specifically, rather it changes the way the cancer cells are recognized by the patient’s immune system. We have shown that low-dose radiation, if delivered to all sites of cancer in a mouse, results in enhanced immune killing of the cancer cell.

This trial is seperated into 3 arms (Arm# 1, Arm# 2a, Arm# 2b). We will initially enroll patients to Arm #1. After completion of Arm# 1, patients will be randomized between Arm# 2a and Arm# 2b).

Clinical Protocol for Arm #1 Dogs with advanced (metastasized, spread) cancer may be eligible for this study. If your dog does enter the clinical trial, ICI therapy will start on Day 1. When your dog is to receive RPT, your dog would first receive an intravenous injection of a radioactive tracer, 86Y-NM600, which is an imaging agent (it is not therapeutic). PET/CT scans will be performed at 1-, 24-, and 48-hours post 86Y-NM600 injection. Your dog will be under general anesthesia for the PET/CT scans. Results of the PET/CT scans will allow us to determine the dose of RPT that will deliver the planned amount of radiation to all tumor sites. Because this is a radioactive substance, your dog would need to be hospitalized until it is determined that your dog is no longer radioactive (up to 6 days).

Clinical Protocol for Arm #2a and Arm# 2b Dogs with advanced (metastasized, spread) cancer may be eligible for this study. If your dog does enter the clinical trial, ICI therapy will be started 2 weeks before receiving EBRT and intratumoral PIC. Only half of the dogs in this trial will receive RPT but all dogs will receive ICI, EBRT and intratumoral PIC- your dog will be randomized to either receive RPT or not in addition to the other treatments. If your dog is to receive RPT, your dog would first receive an intravenous injection of a radioactive tracer, 86Y-NM600, which is an imaging agent (it is not therapeutic). PET/CT scans will be performed at 1, 24, and 48 hours post 86Y-NM600 injection. Your dog will be under general anesthesia for the PET/CT scans. Results of the PET/CT scans will allow us to determine the dose of RPT that will deliver the planned amount of radiation to all tumor sites. Because this is a radioactive substance, your dog would need to be hospitalized until it is determined that your dog is no longer radioactive (up to 6 days).
current_roster.tagline: Combination Radiation and Immunotherapy for Advanced Cancer
current_roster.name: Combination Radiation and Immunotherapy for Advanced Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: David Michael Vail, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo removal of the spleen, followed by standard care therapy in addition to the vaccine. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate, your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.
current_roster.tagline: Canine Splenic Hemangiosarcoma Vaccine
current_roster.name: Vaccine Study for Dogs with Splenic Hemangiosarcoma

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Dogs with OA will be randomly divided into two groups: one group will receive the study treatment (Mitragyna speciosa), and the other group will receive a placebo (sugar pill). Neither the dog owner or the veterinarian will be aware of which treatment each dog is receiving. Each treatment will be initiated for 4 weeks. After receiving the first treatment, animals will be crossed over to the opposite treatment for 4 weeks with a 2-week washout period in between. At the start and end of each 4-week period, blood will be collected for a complete blood count, and biochemistry analysis; a biochemistry analysis will also be performed in the middle of each 4-week period (2 weeks). At the middle (2 weeks) and the end of each 4-week block, blood samples will be obtained for evaluation of plasma concentrations of mitragynine. Dogs will be assessed at the beginning and end of each 4 week period for pain by using a combination of a physical exam, a wear​able monitor that documents pain (PainTrace), gait analysis, an at home activity monitor (health monitoring collar; PetPace), and a pet owner survey.
current_roster.tagline: Mitragynine Osteoarthritis Placebo-Controlled Study
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the effect of mitragynine on naturally occurring osteoarthritic pain in a canine model

current_roster.description:
PORPHYSOMES are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). PORPHYSOMES can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). This equipment allows for image-guided surgery, tumour margin assessment and lymph node staging. PORPHYSOMES can also be used to in combination with photoablation – photodynamic therapy (PDT) to deliver treatment directly to the tumour and/or kill any cells remaining after surgery.  

 

For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Challenges can include tumours that are too large to safely remove or metastatic disease (spread) that cannot be removed. PORPHYSOMES -enabled therapies can have an immediate impact on cancer management providing better patient outcomes. This study is important for both human and animal health. PORPHYSOMES are ground-breaking research and the information gained will be used to treat future dogs, cats and humans with cancer. A human clinical trial is planned to be conducted in 2022. 

The purpose of this study is to evaluate the potential applications of PORPHYSOMES and PDT in veterinary clinical patients.
current_roster.tagline: Nanoparticle therapy for canine thyroid tumours
current_roster.name: Exploration of nanoparticle therapy in combination with surgery for canine thyroid tumours

current_roster.description: Three hospital visits will be required for each dog. Visit 1 will involve of patient screening and enrollment. For chronic kidney disease patients, this visit will coincide with a patient’s normal veterinary visit recheck schedule. During that visit a patient history, physical exam, and blood draw will occur to measure complete blood count, biochemistry panel, and SDMA. A free catch urine sample will also be collected for urinalysis. If a free catch urine sample cannot be obtained, then a cystocentesis may be performed. For healthy dogs, the same will occur, but their appointment will be scheduled based on client and pet availability. Dogs meeting the inclusion criteria will then return for two additional hospital visits 1 week apart. For both objectives, during visit 2 dogs will be randomly assigned to receive a single oral dose of 20 mg/kg gabapentin or placebo. After receiving either gabapentin or the placebo, the dogs will be kept in a quiet space within the hospital to minimize hospital-associated stress. Three hours later blood pressure will be measured on either the fore or hindlimbs using an oscillometric blood pressure device. The systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressures will be recorded. Five readings will be obtained during each visit, with the average of each blood pressure component recorded. For visit 3 the dogs will receive the opposite treatment to complete the crossover study. As before, blood pressure readings will be obtained three hours later using the same oscillometric blood pressure device on the same limb with the same technical assistants. During the study hospitalization dogs will be monitored hourly. At the conclusion of the data collection time (same day) the dogs will be discharged from the hospital to the care of their owners.
current_roster.tagline: Assessment of gabapentin's effect on blood pressure in dogs
current_roster.name: Assessment of gabapentin's effect on blood pressure in dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Michael W. Wood DVM, PhD, DACVIM (SAIM), Associate professor

current_roster.description:
Mast cell tumors are common tumors in dogs comprising approximately 16-21% of all canine skin tumors. For tumors that are not surgically excisable, finding additional therapies are invaluable. We know that hypofractionated radiation therapy alone results in acceptable outcomes; however we aim to determine if combining hypofractionated radiation therapy with immunotherapy could enhance tumor control and treatment outcomes.

The primary objective of this study is to determine the overall response rate (complete response and partial response) for dogs receiving hypofractionated radiation therapy in combination with gilvetmab for non-resectable cutaneous or subcutaneous mast cell tumors.

All dogs will be treated with radiation therapy which will be given on Days 0, 7, and 21 of the study. They will also receive gilvetmab (given as an IV infusion) every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments starting on Day 7. They will also have concurrent treatment with prednisone, certirizine, and omeprazole. Visits will be required on Days 0 and 7 and then every 2 weeks until the Day 133 visit. CBC and chemistry profile will be performed every 4 weeks during gilvetmab treatment. The study is complete after the Day 133 visit. If at any point your dog’s disease progresses or they experience unacceptable side effects from the study medications, they will be withdrawn from the clinical trial.
current_roster.tagline: Combined Radiation Therapy and Gilvetmab for Treatment of Mast Cell Tumors in Dogs
current_roster.name: Combination of Radiation Therapy and Gilvetmab for Mast Cell Tumors in Dogs

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to determine if oral KCl supplementation will increase serum chloride concentrations and thereby suppress the RAAS in dogs with CHF and hypochloremia (low blood chloride concentrations). Hypochloremia has been recently shown to be a negative prognostic indicator in both dogs and people with CHF, possibly because it causes RAAS activation, and so investigating methods to correct it are warranted. Oral KCl supplementation is one way to provide chloride to the body without giving extra sodium. Additionally, the potassium supplementation might prove helpful for dogs with CHF. Bloodwork will be frequently monitored to be sure that chloride and potassium concentrations do not become too high. We will also assess the effect of increasing blood chloride levels on the RAAS. Because RAAS activation contributes to heart disease progression, addressing chloride through supplementation could be a way to slow disease progression in dogs with CHF.
current_roster.tagline: Potassium Chloride Supplements for treatment of Congestive Heart Failure
current_roster.name: Potassium Chloride Supplements for treatment of Congestive Heart Failure

current_roster.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinomas are a common oral cancer in cats. These tumors are locally aggressive and associated with tissue and 
bone destruction. The average survival time of cats with this oral tumor type is reported to be 3 months or less, even after
aggressive treatment. Many owners elect to pursue palliative (pain relief) care options rather than cancer treatments. However, 
there can be challenges with palliative care as the selection of pain medication for cats is limited and most require oral
administration. There is an unmet need for pain medications that are safe and effective at maintaining a good quality of life for
cats with oral tumors. Therefore, the goal of this study is to evaluate a currently available injectable drug, which is marketed for the treatment of arthritis pain in cats, for its ability to also provide relief of pain associated with oral cancers.
current_roster.tagline: Assessment of Solensia and Meloxicam in Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
current_roster.name: Pilot study of Frunevetmab (Solensia) and Meloxicam for palliative therapy of feline bone-invasive oral squamous cell carcinomas

current_roster.description: This is a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of an oral therapy for the treatment of pruritus associated to allergic dermatitis.
current_roster.tagline: Dogs with Allergic Dermatitis
current_roster.name: Dogs with Allergic Dermatitis

current_roster.description: This is a clinical trial evaluating the use of a new chemotherapy drug, palbociclib, in tumor-bearing drugs with certain cancers. Palbociclib is currently used in humans with breast cancer and other tumors. It has been given to laboratory dogs to report some pharmacokinetic and toxicity data in preclinical trials. The intent of the clinical trial is to measure drug levels in dogs with cancer to determine a recommended prescription dose. We will also describe side effects and, while not a primary endpoint of the study, tumor response.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluation of palbociclib in tumor-bearing dogs
current_roster.name: Pilot study evaluating palbociclib in dogs with melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, mammary carcinoma, or anal sac adenocarcinoma

current_roster.description: The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs diagnosed with non-resectable cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs) for a clinical research study. The purpose of this trial is to investigate novel biological characteristics associated with toceranib phosphate (Palladia®) resistance in canine cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs).
current_roster.tagline: Palladia Resistance in Mast Cell Tumors
current_roster.name: Comparative Molecular Analysis for Acquired Toceranib Resistance in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors

current_roster.description: The purpose of this research is to investigate a new anti-cancer drug, trametinib, that specifically ‘targets’ growth signals found in cancer cells from companion (pet) dogs. This study will determine the anti-tumor efficacy of trametinib in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma. We will measure and document how much the cancer shrinks upon treatment, and how the drug helps improve the patients’ outcome and life expectancy. Additionally, the study will test whether markers in the genes within the tumor can predict the response from treatment, which in the future can help select those dogs that are more likely to respond positively to treatment. Finally, in a simple blood test we will determine whether effective drug levels are present in the patient.
current_roster.tagline: Phase II Open-label Non-randomized Multicenter Clinical Trial of Trametinib for Dogs With Histiocytic Sarcoma
current_roster.name: Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Marilia Takada, DVM, MSc, PhD, DACVR

current_roster.description: Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) is a disease that affects brachycephalic, or flat-faced dogs, such as French bulldogs and pugs. This syndrome is caused by changes in the structure of the skull and result in narrowing the passage of air flow from the nostrils to the windpipe (trachea). These anatomic abnormalities cause obstruction of airflow resulting in difficulty breathing, airway noises, and even collapse and death. Many of these dogs also suffer from gastrointestinal signs, such as regurgitation and vomiting, which are thought to be due to the changes in the upper airway. The aim of this study is to investigate the frequency of regurgitation or reflux into the nasopharynx (the top part of the throat and nasal cavity) in dogs affected by BOAS as compared to healthy, non-brachycephalic dogs. This will be accomplished using 48-hour at home pH monitoring. The results of this study will help to guide further research into issues affecting brachycephalic dogs and into medical and surgical treatments to help improve their quality of life.
current_roster.tagline: Nasopharyngeal Reflux in Dogs Affected by Brachycephalic Obstructive Airway Syndrome
current_roster.name: Nasopharyngeal Reflux in Brachycephalic Obstructive Airway Syndrome Dogs Compared to Healthy Controls

current_roster.description:
The study will investigate how vision loss, hearing loss, and dementia in dogs relate to each other, We anticipate that restoring vision will improve cognition (reduce dementia), but dogs with co-existing hearing loss will have less improvement. This work will help dog owners and veterinarians have better, evidence-based discussions about the predicted outcomes of cataract surgery and determine how cataract surgery in older dogs impacts quality of life.


Note: This is a survey-based study for dog owners of dogs that are planning to have cataract surgery performed in the near future. Owners must have established care with a veterinary ophthalmologist, and have a scheduled date for cataract surgery to be eligible. No funds to offset costs associated with cataract surgery will be provided. Owners will receive a small financial incentive ($10 gift card) for participation once eligibility is confirmed and study procedures are complete.
current_roster.tagline: Cataracts and cognition in dogs
current_roster.name: Cataracts and cognition in dogs

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the outcomes for dogs treated palliatively with standard amputation (no chemotherapy). Recent data indicates that at least 35% of dogs do not appear to benefit from standard chemotherapy for this disease. To better understand whether chemotherapy is truly beneficial, this trial aims to document the outcomes prospectively and accurately for dogs whose owners have elected to treat only with surgery (amputation). There will be about 120 dogs taking part in this study across North America.

Standard therapy for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma has long been amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy to prevent or slow the growth and spread of cancer. With this form of treatment, the median survival time of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma is between 10-14 months (43% alive at 1-year, 24% alive at 2-years). Importantly, recent large trials have found that 35% of dogs will develop metastatic disease within 15-weeks of surgery, despite chemotherapy. Prior studies from the 1970s and 1980s indicated that the median survival of dogs treated with palliative amputation alone (no chemotherapy) was 4-6 months (12% alive at 1-year, 2% alive at 2-years). However, dogs in the palliative study did not receive all the same screening tests or follow up as dogs receiving chemotherapy in more recent trials. The purpose of this study is to determine outcomes more accurately for dogs undergoing amputation alone for osteosarcoma that have undergone complete screening and follow up imaging.
current_roster.tagline: Characterization of naturally occurring osteosarcoma in dogs
current_roster.name: Characterization of naturally occurring osteosarcoma in dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Robert Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description:
The goal of this study is to characterize the hemostatic abnormalities in dogs with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer undergoing surgical removal and to determine when their hypercoagulability (increased tendency for blood to clot) resolves post-operatively. Additionally, we aim to determine the incidence of thromboembolism (blood clots) in hypercoagulable patients diagnosed with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer following tumor removal.


Dogs with suspected primary hepatocellular or adrenal neoplasia will undergo standard-of-care procedures, including blood work (CBC, chemistry, and PT/PTT) and CT of the abdomen. Upon enrollment, a TEG and fibrinogen level will be obtained before surgery for the study. Dogs will return in 10-14 days for re-check full-body CT and blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, PLT, fibrinogen). Dogs will return in 15-21 days for re-check blood work. Dogs will continue to return for recheck blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, fibrinogen, and PLT) until their hypercoagulability, based on an elevated TEG G-value, resolves.


If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 10-14 day post-surgery visit, they will be asked to come back for 3 and/or 4-week post-surgery visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 4-week post-surgery visit, it will present as needed for 6, 8,12, and/or 16-week post-operative visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 16-week post-operative visit, blood work re-checks will move to a monthly schedule until resolution is achieved. No future visits are required once a dog becomes normocoagulable. No future visits are required, and monthly blood work will discontinue if a dog remains hypercoagulable at 6 months post-operative (day 182).


The study will cover the cost of your dog's pre-operative chest and post-operative abdominal and chest computed tomography (CT) scan. Additionally, the study will cover the cost of each recheck examination fee and the cost of performing blood work (TEG, PCV/TS, platelet count, and fibrinogen) pre-and post-operatively.


Routine blood work (PT/PTT, CBC, chemistry panel, blood type prior to surgery) will not be covered by the study. The study does not cover the cost of your dog's other preoperative workup (primary tumor biopsy/FNA, pre-operative abdominal CT, thoracic radiographs, etc.), primary tumor removal, hospitalization, post-operative care, or additional oncologic care (radiation therapy or chemotherapy). Costs associated with adverse events (including but not limited to hematoma, and incisional complications) are not covered by the study.

current_roster.description:
Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma targeted to treat macroscopic OS metastases to the lungs.


The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the activity of a drug which targets a distinct cell signaling pathway for treatment of metastatic osteosarcoma (OS) in dogs. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that the use of a drug called defactinib may have direct anti-tumor effects as well as an ability to modulate the tumor promoting microenvironment. Therefore, this trial is designed to determine whether this defactinib drug can provide cancer control in dogs with metastatic OS.


Initially, your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests which may include blood tests, urinalyses, blood pressure, and x-rays of the chest. Test results will help determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial.These tests are routinely performed in patients with osteosarcoma and may be done even if you decide that your pet will not participate in a clinical trial. 


Following enrollment, dogs will begin treatment with defactinib, which is given orally twice daily. On the first day of treatment, dogs will receive the first dose of defactinib in hospital followed by serial blood sample collection over 8 hours. We will collect more study blood the following day, 24 hrs after the first doses of medication. You will be sent home with defactinib to be given twice daily after the 24-hour blood sample is collected. Your dog will then return two weeks later (Week 2) for an exam, blood work and urinalysis, and study blood collection. At Week 4, your dog will return for blood pressure, blood and urine tests and study blood collection. One month later (Week 8), your dog will return for chest x-rays, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Follow-up visits will be required 4 weeks thereafter until disease progression is identified. Blood will be collected for study purposes (~1.5 tablespoons) at every visit for the study. Chest x-rays will be performed prior to enrollment and every 8 weeks thereafter. Blood pressure will be performed on Day 0, Week 4, Week 12, and monthly thereafter. Dogs will remain on the study as long as their pulmonary nodules do not progress in size and no new nodules are identified on chest x-rays.


If your dog dies while on the study, a post-mortem examination and tumor collection may be necessary to explain the cause of death. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group – all dogs will receive all study treatments.

current_roster.name: Novel Therapy for Metastatic Bone Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that have macroscopic metastases to the lungs. CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells are a modified version of a T cell, a type of immune cell, that alters them so they can target and destroy cancer cells. Dogs have been previously treated with CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells at other institutions and the treatment has been well-tolerated, but the new CAR T cells being evaluated in this trial have not been evaluated in dogs with cancer, though safety studies were done in healthy dogs, without side effects. The goal of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of canine CAR T cells, which will be generated by gene modification of your dogs white blood cells, and then infused back into your dog by an intravenous catheter. In order to help the CAR T cells expand in the body more effectively, your dog will also have to be treated with bone marrow suppressing drugs (fludarabine and cyclophosphamide) for 2 days before the CAR T cells are given back. To help increase the effectiveness of the CAR T cells once they are recruited to the tumor tissues, dogs will be treated daily with oral losartan and propranolol before and after CAR T administration.
current_roster.tagline: CAR T cells for Metastatic Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the safety and anti-cancer activity of fibroblast activation protein (FAP) targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, alone or in combination with orally administered immunotherapy drugs, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. FAP is a protein that is expressed on the surface of tumor cell and can be recognized by a T cell. CAR T cells are when a patient’s own cancer fighting white blood cells are modified to express a receptor which binds a specific molecule expressed on the surface of a tumor cell. The two oral immunotherapy drugs being used in combination with FAP CAR T cells (losartan and toceranib [Palladia]) have already been extensively evaluated in a prior trial in dogs with bone cancer and have demonstrated considerable anti-cancer activity, with minimal toxicity. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that FAP CAR T cells can exert robust killing of canine OS cells and may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. Therefore, this trial is designed to determine whether FAP CAR T cells are safe alone and in combination with losartan and toceranib, and if losartan and toceranib can improve tumor infiltration of FAP CAR T cells.


At the start of the study, dogs will have blood drawn (~3 ½ tablespoons) to be used for generation of the CAR T cells. Dogs will also be sedated to have a small sample of their tumor taken for study purposes. They will return 10 days later for an exam, bloodwork, and for oral chemotherapy to reduce the number of normal lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) to maximize the effectiveness of the CAR T cells. A second dose of chemotherapy will be given at home by the owner the following day. Dogs will then return 14 days after the initial visit for an exam, blood and urine tests, blood collection for study purposes, and CAR T cell infusion. The infusion is given over 15 minutes, and then dogs will stay in the hospital until the end of the day for monitoring. Dogs will return 3 and 7 days later for an exam, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Fourteen days after the CAR T infusion, the tumor will be removed surgically. Visits will be required 2 and 6 weeks after surgery for an exam, blood/urine tests, and blood collection for the study. The study is complete after the visit 6 weeks post-surgery (total study duration of 10 weeks).


Some dogs enrolled in the study will receive two oral immune modulating drugs (toceranib and losartan) for the first ~4 weeks of the study. These will be given at home by the owners 1-2 times daily. Owners will know ahead of time whether or not dogs will be receiving these drugs.
current_roster.tagline: Novel CAR T cell treatment for Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Dogs
current_roster.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy

current_roster.description:
Purpose

To obtain information on the effects of H-FIRE, a therapy that can destroy tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma.


Background

Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. It primarily affects large and giant-breed dogs, but can affect dogs of any breed and age. The cancer frequently metastasizes to the lungs. New treatment options are needed for osteosarcoma, because patient survival times have improved little over the past several decades.


High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) is a novel non-thermal technique that can precisely destroy tumors while sparing critical structures. H-FIRE also potentially induces an anti-tumor immune response, which may help to guard against further metastatic disease development.


This study proposes to evaluate the feasibility and safety of treating canine metastatic osteosarcoma lung tumors with H-FIRE, and to learn more about the effects of H-FIRE on patients with metastatic osteosarcoma. Because canine osteosarcoma is similar to human osteosarcoma, this work may inform future studies to evaluate the use of H-FIRE in people.

North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine is currently enrolling canine patients that have 1-2 liver tumors into a clinical trial that is using a new therapy called INSPIRE, which uses electrical pulses to safely destroy the cells within a tumor.


This study has two treatment group:


One group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and their tumors are eligible for surgical resection, the patients in this group will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment followed by liver lobectomy a week later to remove the tumors.


The second group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary Hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and the tumors are not eligible for surgical resection, patients will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment. Patients will then be monitored over a 9-month period which includes five recheck appointments, during which patients will receive a CT scan and bloodwork to monitor the tumors.

current_roster.description: Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency (EPI) is a condition resulting from the animal’s inability to produce sufficient pancreatic enzymes. As a consequence, while eating normally, affected dogs might not be able to sufficiently digest and absorb nutrients, especially fat. There is no cure for this disease. The current standard of care therapy for dogs with EPI is pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) administered with each meal. PERT can be associated with challenges including significant cost to the owners, and side effects such as gingival bleeding and intolerance to the protein. A special diet, called cEMO, contains kibble coated with hydrolyzed (broken down) fat. Feeding EPI dogs with the cEMO diet might be an alternative solution to the use of PERT by allowing fat absorption even in the absence of pancreatic enzymes.

current_roster.description:
Clinical signs of nausea, vomiting, and dysrexia (abnormal appetite behaviors) are common in feline patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Weight loss and loss of lean body mass in these patients is likely attributable to changes in appetite as well as processes such as cachexia (weight loss due to an underlying illness) and sarcopenia (loss of muscle mass and function associated with aging). Poor appetite is perceived as an important aspect of quality of life and can cause significant emotional distress to caregivers. A better understanding of the effect of management of inappetence in CKD on quality of life will improve our ability to help feline patients with CKD. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to assess the effect of appetite stimulation on quality of life in cats with CKD.


What does enrolling my pet in this clinical trial involve? 

At the time of screening, your cat will receive a physical examination and comprehensive laboratory screening to confirm stage of CKD and exclude other newly diagnosed conditions. They will then be randomized to receive either mirtazapine transdermal ointment or placebo. Both are an ointment that will be administered transdermally to the inner surface of the ear flap once daily. Cats will be randomized into one of two groups (mirtazapine or placebo) and then switch to the other group after two weeks. We will follow up via phone one-week following enrollment to address any questions or concerns. You will bring your cat back for two recheck visits (Week 2 and Week 4) for a physical exam, blood and urine collection, and blood pressure measurement. From the time of initial screening to the completion of the study, you will be asked to complete the online Vetmetrica Quality of Life survey* - a validated instrument to assess quality of life in cats - on a weekly basis, as well as a daily log of appetite.


Client Compensation:

There is no cost to you for enrolling your cat in this study. The exams and diagnostics performed at enrollment, Weeks 2 and 4, and the cost of the mirtazapine transdermal ointment medication used, are covered by the study alone. In the unlikely situation that an adverse event that requires treatment occurs as a result of taking part in this study, the cost of treatment will be covered by the study.
current_roster.tagline: QOL in cats with CKD
current_roster.name: The Effect of Transdermal Mirtazapine on Quality of Life in Cats with Chronic Kidney Disease

current_roster.description:
Immune cells infiltrating soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are a potential target for novel treatment strategies. Macrophages are the predominant infiltrative immune cell within the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) in human soft tissue sarcomas (STS). There is limited information about the STS TIME in dogs; however, macrophages, an immune cell, have been identified previously. Our study aims to better chacterize macrophages within canine STS. After routine surgical removal, masses will undergo routine microscopic evaluation. In addition, specific cell staining (immunofluorescence) will be performed on tumor sections to further characterize infiltrative macrophages.


The study provides only $700 toward the cost of surgery and biopsy results. All remaining costs are the responsibility of the owner. The total cost of diagnostics and surgical intervention is dependent on the individual dog and its tumor; however, costs are typically between $2500-5000.

Metastatic disease prevents a unique clinical setting especially when the patients is still stable. Options are limited for treatment but may include oral and IV chemotherapy options. With the advent of PD-1 inhibitors, we are now looking to combine the inhibitor with either Telomerase or HER2 immunotherapy in combination as the combined therapies should improve response while minimizing adverse effects and battling the cancer through specific mechanisms.


Trends Cancer 2023 Jul;9(7):543-553.

 doi: 10.1016/j.trecan.2023.04.002. Epub 2023 Apr 27.

Immune mechanisms of toxicity from checkpoint inhibitors

S Jennifer Wang 1, Stephanie K Dougan 2, Michael Dougan 3


Abstract

Immunotherapy has changed the treatment landscape for cancer over the past decade. Inhibitors of the immune checkpoint proteins cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen (CTLA)-4, programmed death (PD)-1, and PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) can induce durable remissions in a subset of patients with metastatic disease. However, these treatments can be limited by inflammatory toxicities that can affect any organ system in the body and in some cases can be life threatening. Considerable progress has been made in understanding the drivers of these toxicities as well as effective management strategies. Further research into understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that drive toxicity will enable better prediction of toxicity and development of optimized therapies for these toxicities that avoid interfering with antitumor immunity. In this review, we discuss our current understanding of the inflammatory toxicities from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and propose optimal treatment strategies for these toxicities.


Clinical protocol: Patients will be treated with standard of care anti-PD1 SOP: Administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion over at least 30 minutes either manually or with a constant rate syringe pump. Repeat administration every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments. Antihistamine administered intramuscularly (IM) 15-30 minutes before treatment to prevent or reduce the severity of infusion-related reactions, 20-30 minutes following administration, patients will be sedated with propofol, dexdomitor and O2 via intubation for GET (see below).


GET: DNA Plasmid: The N-10-4B electrode to be inserted into the cranialis tibialis after immediate injection of dTERT or dHER2 DNA/plasmid. Minimal bleeding to be controlled with direct pressure.


Antisedan to be administered IM.


*Regarding the use of this technology (gene-electrotransfer or GET) as the method for vaccine delivery, numerous studies, including the one below, support the improved immune response compared to injections under the skin or in muscle.

Published online 2023 Jul 19. doi: 10.3390/pharmaceutics15071981

PMCID: PMC10385748

current_roster.description:
This study investigates the effects of Sascupreel, which is a plant-based homeopathic medication, in addition to standard medical treatment (diet alone), for dogs with food-responsive chronic enteropathies. Commonly used analgesic medications addressing abdominal pain in dogs with chronic enteropathies have significant disadvantages, such as decreasing blood flow to abdominal organs and causing GI effects (such as with NSAIDs) or inducing GI stasis (such as with opioids). There is, therefore, an urgent need to establish better treatment modalities for abdominal pain in dogs with chronic enteropathies. Spascupreel has shown promise in reducing abdominal pain and cramping in rats and humans and has the potential to address abdominal pain without causing any side effects when used to treat canine chronic enteropathy. We hypothesize that dogs receiving Spascupreel will show an improvement of their clinical signs and quality of life scores compared to those receiving placebo.

The study is a blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled study lasting 6 weeks in duration.

current_roster.description:
Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a common type of cancer in dogs. While HSA can occur in different parts of the body, it is most often found in the spleen. These tumors are aggressive and can spread to other organs quickly. Dogs that undergo surgery alone for splenic HSA typically have very short survival times, ranging from 1 to 3 months. Adding doxorubicin (DOX) chemotherapy to surgery has shown slight improvements, but around 90% of dogs still develop spread within a year. Therefore, new treatment methods are urgently needed.


This study aims to assess the safety and effectiveness of a specially designed vaccine for HSA when given with standard surgery and DOX chemotherapy. Dogs diagnosed with stage 1 or 2 splenic HSA, that have received spleen removal surgery within the past 3 weeks, may qualify for this study.


Three weeks or earlier after surgery, dogs can be evaluated for the study. Your dog will go through various diagnostic tests, including blood tests and urinalysis. The results will determine if your dog can participate in this clinical trial. If eligible, chest X-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be performed to gather important information before starting treatment. All dogs will then receive standard DOX treatment, which is given intravenously every 2 weeks for a total of 5 treatments.


This research is a placebo-controlled trial. All dogs will receive standard DOX chemotherapy, but half will also get the HSA vaccine, while the other half will get a placebo vaccine. No one involved in your dog’s care will know which vaccine is given. The vaccine will start at the time of the first DOX treatment and continue every 4 weeks for up to 48 weeks.


Your dog will return to Colorado State University every two weeks for the first 8 weeks, then once a month until week 48. Blood samples (approximately 5 teaspoons) will be taken at each visit, and chest X-rays and ultrasounds will be repeated every two months.

current_roster.description:
In this clinical trial, dogs with naturally occurring glioma brain cancer will take part in this clinical trial to test how well a new protein-blocking treatment fights their brain tumor. This treatment works by attaching to and removing a protein that is only found on the surface of tumor cells. By doing this, it also removes other proteins that help tumors resist current therapies, grow, and avoid the immune system. These proteins are also linked to the formation of cancer stem cells.


The goal of this study is to see if the treatment works in dogs before moving on to more detailed research. If the results are promising, researchers will apply for funding to expand the study and eventually explore how this treatment could help humans with brain tumors.


Study Plan:

  1. Days -14 to -1: Dogs will go through testing, including MRI scans, neurological exams, tumor biopsy, and bloodwork, to confirm they have glioma.
  2. Day 0: The first injection will be given under the skin.
  3. Days 14 to 180: Additional injections will be given every two weeks under the skin.
  4. Day 84: Blood tests will be done to check organ health.
  5. Every 3 months: Blood tests will be repeated throughout the study.
  6. Every 6 months: MRI scans will be repeated until the dog passes away.
  7. After death: Tissue samples will be collected. Owners will decide when to euthanize their dog if necessary, but euthanasia is not required for this study.


Owners will need to travel with their dog to Colorado State University Veterinary Teaching Hospital for all appointments.

current_roster.description:
Study Title: Evaluation of a Multi-Species Medicinal Mushroom Complex in the Management of Canine Oral Malignant Melanoma


Background & Rationale:

Oral malignant melanoma (OMM) is one of the most aggressive cancers in dogs, accounting for a high percentage of oral tumors and known for its rapid progression and poor prognosis (Bergman, 2007). It accounts for 30–40% of all oral tumors in dogs, and median survival times are typically 3 to 6 months in advanced cases, even with aggressive therapy. Current treatments such as surgery, radiation, and immunotherapy have limited success, and recurrence is common. This study seeks to evaluate the safety and potential therapeutic benefits of a multi-species medicinal mushroom complex in managing OMM progression and enhancing quality of life.


Medicinal mushrooms have demonstrated immunomodulatory, antioxidant, and anti-tumor properties in preclinical and clinical settings (Lindequist et al., 2005; Wasser, 2014). This study will use a blend of nine mushroom species, selected for their complementary bioactive compounds and documented mechanisms relevant to cancer suppression:


  1. Chaga (Inonotus obliquus): Contains betulinic acid, inotodiol, and polyphenols with demonstrated antioxidant and anti-proliferative effects. Shown to suppress NF-κB activity and reduce angiogenesis (Park et al., 2014).


  1. Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi): Rich in triterpenoids and beta-glucans that enhance natural killer (NK) cell activity and promote apoptosis in tumor cells. Demonstrated ability to modulate cytokine profiles and inhibit tumor proliferation (Boh et al., 2007).


  1. Hericium erinaceus (Lion's Mane): Inhibits cell proliferation via inflammatory pathway modulation. Exhibits cytotoxicity in gastric and colon cancer cell lines (Lee et al., 2014).


  1. Trametes versicolor (Turkey Tail): Source of polysaccharide-K (PSK) and polysaccharide-peptide (PSP), which enhance macrophage and T-cell activity. Used in human cancer immunotherapy in Asia (Eliza et al., 2002; Torkelson et al., 2012).


  1. Phellinus linteus: Exhibits anti-angiogenic and pro-apoptotic activity by suppressing PI3K/AKT and MAPK signaling pathways (Song et al., 2003).


  1. Wolfiporia extensa (Poria): Known for anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects. Shown to reduce tumor cell adhesion and migration (Zhang et al., 2013).


  1. Lentinula edodes (Shiitake): Contains lentinan, a beta-glucan used in cancer therapy for its ability to enhance immune function and inhibit tumor cell proliferation (Ng and Chan, 1997).


  1. Cordyceps militaris: Contains cordycepin and polysaccharides with proven immunostimulatory, antioxidant, and antitumor properties. Studies have shown cytotoxicity against various cancer cell lines, including melanoma, and stimulation of macrophage activity and cytokine production (Zhao et al., 2014; Paterson, 2008; Zhou et al., 2009).


  1. Cordyceps sinensis: A highly valued entomopathogenic fungus in traditional Chinese medicine. Exhibits antitumor, immunomodulatory, and anti-inflammatory effects. Polysaccharides and nucleoside analogs such as cordycepin are credited with its bioactivity. It has demonstrated the ability to inhibit proliferation and metastasis in melanoma and other tumor cell lines while enhancing macrophage and NK cell activity (Koh et al., 2003; Yue et al., 2013).


Hypothesis for Canine Oral Malignant Melanoma Study:

Dogs diagnosed with oral malignant melanoma that receive daily medicinal mushroom supplementation will experience slower tumor progression, potential tumor regression, and an improved quality of life over an 18-month period.


Study Design:

This is a prospective, single-arm observational cohort study enrolling 20 client-owned dogs with histologically confirmed oral malignant melanoma. The sample size is based on feasibility and aligns with prior pilot studies evaluating mushroom therapies in canine oncology (Brown and Reetz, 2012).


Inclusion Criteria:

  1. Histologically confirmed oral malignant melanoma


  1. No chemotherapy or radiation within the past 6 months


  1. Owner consent for participation and adherence to study protocol


Intervention:

Daily oral administration of a mushroom complex containing equal parts of the nine listed species.

Dose: 100 mg/kg body weight per day, based on the established dosing from the Penn Vet hemangiosarcoma study (Brown and Reetz, 2012)


Study Duration:

12 months


Outcome Measures:

  1. Tumor size, measured monthly by calipers and/or imaging


  1. Time to tumor progression, stabilization, or resolution


  1. Recurrence rate in dogs with prior surgical resection


  1. Owner-reported quality of life metrics (appetite, energy, comfort) via monthly questionnaires


Data Analysis:

Descriptive statistics will summarize tumor metrics. Linear regression will assess progression trends. Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests will evaluate tumor size changes over time. Kaplan-Meier analysis will be used to estimate time to progression or resolution.


Ethical Considerations:

This is a non-invasive, adjunctive therapy study. All dogs will remain under routine veterinary care, and no standard treatments will be withheld. Owners will provide informed consent, and adverse events will be closely monitored and documented throughout the study.


Significance and Potential Impact:

This study will be the first to systematically evaluate a comprehensive, multi-mushroom supplement for oral malignant melanoma in dogs. By generating preliminary data on tumor response, quality of life, and safety, this project has the potential to advance integrative oncology and support development of evidence-based, natural adjunct therapies that improve clinical outcomes in veterinary cancer care.


References:

current_roster.description:
Oral melanoma is a highly aggressive disease with poor outcomes and no effective treatments. Our recent research has shown that a weakened form of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is safe, and can trigger strong anti-tumor effects.


By injecting a small amount of this weakened virus directly into the tumor, we aim to activate the dog's immune system to fight the cancer. Additionally, we will collect and expand immune cells from the tumor, as these cells are more likely to recognize and attack cancer cells. These enhanced immune cells will then be reinfused into the patient to target existing or potential metastatic disease.


To evaluate our therapy, we will first perform a tumor biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and analyze the immune cells already present (Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes). We will then inject the tumor with the weakened virus. One week later, the tumor will be surgically removed, and immune cells from the cancer will be expanded for future use if metastases are present or develop later. After treatment, we will closely monitor the patients through periodic blood tests and imaging (CT scans) every three months.


A small group of dogs (randomly selected) will be the control, and while not receiving the virus injection, they will have their immune cells extracted from the tumor and expanded to be reinfused in case of progressive disease.


Cost of tumor biopsy, two CT imaging sessions, trial-related blood work, the viral reagent and injections, the collection priming and reinjection of the immune cells. Additionally, participating dogs are eligible to receive a $800 post-trial incentive.
current_roster.tagline: Novel immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
current_roster.name: Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Shay Bracha, DVM, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description: Corneal ulceration is a common complication in mechanically ventilated patients that will require treatment with eye drops for several days to weeks after diagnosis. Patients on the mechanical ventilator are not able to blink due to severe neurologic disease or the level of sedation required to facilitate endotracheal intubation. There is currently no published research on the incidence of corneal ulceration in mechanically ventilated animals. The goal of our study is to determine if the temporary tarsorrhaphy will aid in preventing corneal ulceration.
current_roster.tagline: Temporary Tarsorrhaphy to Prevent Corneal Ulceration in Mechanically Ventilated Dogs
current_roster.name: Temporary Tarsorrhaphy to Prevent Corneal Ulceration in Mechanically Ventilated Dogs

current_roster.description: The Ethos Stratification of Outcomes for Lymphoma In Dogs (Ethos-SOLID) study is a clinical trial focused on better understanding the genetics behind canine lymphoma. By studying changes in the DNA of these cancers, researchers hope to identify patterns that could lead to more personalized treatment options. The goal is to find markers in the tumor and blood that can help predict how the cancer will behave and guide more effective treatment decisions.
current_roster.tagline: SOLID (Stratification of Outcomes for Lymphoma In Dogs)
current_roster.name: SOLID study for lymphoma in dogs

current_roster.description:
Myc (a family of transcription factors encompassing c-, N-, and L-Myc) is a pleiotropic, evolutionarily conserved transcription factor. Myc is one of the most frequently amplified oncogenes in most (perhaps all) human cancers (Dang 2012, Whitfield 2017) and often correlates with aggressiveness of the disease (Wolfer 2010; Lee 2015). In breast cancer, Myc is overexpressed in 30–50% of high-grade tumors, is markedly elevated in triple-negative breast cancer and even further elevated in tumors that display a drug-resistant phenotype (Fallah 2017). In non-small cell lung cancer, Myc amplification is found in up to 30% of malignancies (Ahmadzada 2018; Kalkat 2017).


A new novel peptide that inactivates Myc has been developed and is currently in human trials. The goal of this study is to determine the tolerability and feasibility of administering this novel peptide to dogs with cancer to inform future efficacy studies.
current_roster.tagline: COSMyc-IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial
current_roster.name: COSMyc- IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial

current_roster.description: Chronic ulcerative stomatitis (CCUS) leads to painful inflammation in dogs' mouths, negatively impacting their quality of life. While treatments such as tooth extraction and medication help some dogs, the underlying cause remains unknown. This work aims to investigate if viruses are involved in causing CCUS and if a combination of specific medications (pentoxifylline, niacinamide, and metronidazole) typically used for this disease is truly an effective treatment method. Patients will undergo periodontal treatment and extraction of teeth with moderate to severe periodontal disease, supragingival resorption, or teeth with endodontal disease. Tissue and swab samples will be obtained from affected mucosa under anesthesia during the first (day 0) and last visit (day 120). Periodontal disease parameters and a Canine Chronic Ulcerative Stomatitis Disease Activity Index will also be monitored on days 0, 14, 30, 60, 90, and 120. Blood work will be performed at days 30 and 120.
current_roster.tagline: Helping improve the overall well-being of dogs
current_roster.name: Canine Chronic Ulcerative Stomatitis (CCUS)
current_roster.top_investigator: Maria Soltero-Rivera, DMV,Dipl. AVDC &EVDC, Assistant Professor

current_roster.description: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in dogs is a complex disorder characterized by a significant reduction in platelet count due to complex immune dysregulation. ITP can cause life-threatening bleeding and is a veterinary emergency. This disease is treated with steroids, vincristine, and other immunosuppressive medication and dogs. Recent advances have revealed that plasma-derived exosomes, small membrane-bound vesicles released by cells, play a pivotal role in intercellular communication and may contain disease-specific biomarkers. One such potential biomarker group is RNAs, which help regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally in recipient cells. Recent research in human immune thrombocytopenia has shown differences in RNA profiles between humans with ITP and healthy controls. This study seeks to delineate the expression profiling of RNAs contained within plasma-derived exosomes to discern their potential as markers of immune dysregulation in canine ITP. These results may be useful in performing future studies to further investigate the differences in response to treatment for dogs with immune-mediated disease.
current_roster.tagline: This is a study to determine if biomarkers in the blood can predict how well treatment is working for these patients.
current_roster.name: TIDBITS: Biomarkers associated with response to immunosuppression in Immune Mediated Thrombocytopenia

current_roster.description:
Feline Idiopathic Cystitis (FIC) is a multifaceted psycho-neuro-endocrine disorder affecting an estimated 1.5% of pet cats in the US (Lund, Armstrong et al. 1999). This condition often progresses to urethral obstructions (UO), posing severe complications, including acute kidney injury, azotemia, hyperkalemia, and potentially fatal outcomes if left untreated. Even in milder cases without obstruction, cats experience intermittent stranguria, hematuria, and pollakiuria. Current treatments for FIC and UO focus on symptomatic relief, including restoring urethral patency, diuresis, pain management, dietary adjustments, and stress reduction. Despite efforts, there is no definitive cure, leading to frequent recurrence in some cats, with perineal urethrostomy being the most definitive option available to mitigate obstruction risk (albeit not addressing recurrent cystitis itself). 

Management of these cases can require extensive hospitalization, lifelong dietary and husbandry adjustments, and potentially surgical interventions, placing significant financial and emotional burdens on caregivers and in some cases, resulting in euthanasia or abandonment of the affected cat.

Despite considerable research efforts into treatment and etiology, akin to human interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, the underlying pathophysiology remains elusive. Various biomarkers have been proposed for diagnosis and prognostication(He, Fan et al. 2022). However, a comprehensive understanding is hampered by the complexity and variability of the disease.

In response to these challenges, we propose an ambitious biobanking initiative to systematically collect and annotate samples from affected cats. This endeavor aims to establish a robust repository of data that can support multiple studies, accelerate research into pathophysiology, and advance novel diagnostic and treatment options for both felines and humans with this condition. By facilitating a deeper exploration of biomarkers and disease mechanisms, this initiative seeks to catalyze a transformative impact on our understanding and management of FIC.
current_roster.tagline: FICUSS- Feline Idiopathic Cystitis Urine, Serum and Stool repository
current_roster.name: FICUSS Repository: Feline Idiopathic Cystitis Urine, Serum and Stool Repository

current_roster.tagline: Pulse Therapy with Clorazepate or Levetiracetam for Cluster Seizures
current_roster.name: Comparison of clorazepate and levetiracetam as pulse therapy for the in-home management of cluster seizures in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy: a pilot study

current_roster.description:
This study investigates the effects of Spascupreel, which is a plant-based homeopathic medication, in addition to standard medical treatment (diet alone), for dogs with chronic enteropathies. Commonly used analgesic medications addressing abdominal pain in dogs with chronic enteropathies have significant disadvantages, such as decreasing blood blow to abdominal organs and causing GI effects (such as with NSAIDs) or induce GI stasis (such as with opioids). There is therefore an urgent need to establish better treatment modalities for abdominal pain in dogs with chronic enteropathies. Spascupreel is a plant-based homeopathic medication that has shown promise in reducing abdominal pain and cramping in rats and humans, and therefore has the potential to address abdominal pain without causing any side effects in canine IBD. We hypothesize that dogs receiving Spascupreel will show an improvement of their clinical signs and quality of life scores compared to those receiving placebo.


The study is a blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled study lasting 6 weeks in duration. Dogs will be screened for study inclusion based on history, physical examination, and baseline labwork (chemistry, CBC, urinalysis, GI Panel, cortisol, serum serotonin, fecal float). In addition, all dogs will have a full abdominal ultrasound performed. Dogs meeting inclusion criteria will be transitioned to a hypoallergenic diet for two weeks (if not done previously). If improvement in clinical signs is noted, enrolled dogs will be randomly assigned to receive either Spascupreel (according to label specifications) or placebo orally daily for the 6-week study duration. The hypoallergenic diet will be continued for the duration of the study. All dogs will be monitored at home by the owners who will be asked to record a daily activity score and daily fecal score. Owners will be asked to fill out a quality-of-life questionnaire on a weekly basis. All dogs will return for recheck visits to the hospital at Week 2 and Week 6, during which physical examination will be repeated, and blood and feces will be collected for analysis. All of the above-mentioned procedures and office visits will be paid for by study funds.
current_roster.tagline: Effects of Spascupreel on chronic enteropathies in dogs
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the Effect of Spascupreel on Chronic Enteropathies in Dogs

current_roster.description:
Purpose of the study: 

This study seeks to determine whether a new treatment can be safe and effective to stop osteosarcoma or bone cancer that has spread or metastasized beyond the tumor in the limb.  Your pet will receive a small amount of a radiotherapy, which consists of a radioactive compound linked to a monoclonal antibody, called “225-Actinium 3F8 (225Ac-3F8) in a vein. We will then do a specialized type of imaging called Single Photo Emission Computed Tomography(SPECT) combined with a computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan to determine whether your pet’s tumor takes up this agent. We will also take samples of blood, urine, and feces to try and determine the maximum dose that your dog can tolerate. We may then give an additional dose of 225Ac-3F8 in a vein several days later to treat your dog. We will follow-up with sampling of the blood and another specialized imaging called Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) at approximately 40 days after treatment to determine your dog's response.
current_roster.tagline: Radiotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Bone Cancer in Dogs
current_roster.name: Radiotherapy Trial for Metastatic Bone Cancer in Dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Dara Kraitchman, VMD, PhD, Professor and Director

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of genetically engineered CAR-T cells as a treatment for your dog's cancer. The CAR-T cells are made from your dog's own immune cells. Patients will be screened at the University of Pennsylvania's veterinary hospital to determine their eligibility for the study. This study will involve a screening visit for medical history and blood tests, a pre-conditioning visit, the treatment visit where the drug is administered, and monthly follow-up visits to assess the safety and effectiveness of the drug to treat your dog's cancer.
