current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to determine if freezing fatty tumors (lipomas) will cause them to shrink and die. Cryoablation is a common freezing technique to kill cells and tumors. We are seeking to determine whether this minimally invasive method of freezing tumors would be a good alternative to surgical removal. The procedure will involve an enhanced device that has been previously tested in dogs with tumors under the skin and in the mammary gland.


Dogs of any breed or sex, and aged 6 years or younger, are eligible to participate. Dog owners must have a relationship with a veterinary hospital in the Baltimore-DC region and are currently vaccinated for rabies. Inclusion criteria include:

  1. at least one fatty tumor (lipoma) no larger than a golf ball on the trunk of the body
  2. patients in good health with no underlying heart, liver, or kidney disease
  3. patients without chronic skin conditions or diabetes
  4. no prior treatments such as chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or immunotherapy for other cancers
  5. the owner has the ability to understand and to sign a written informed consent document and is willing to comply with the study protocol, and has the ability to transport their pet to CIGAT at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD for up to 3 visits
  6.  the owner is willing to provide follow-up information for a minimum of one year following treatment


If accepted into the study, the pet owner will also be financially responsible for pre-anesthesia bloodwork at their own veterinarian. It is also recommended that pets over three years of age obtain chest X-rays prior to anesthesia. The cost for cryotherapy and a follow-up exam are funded by the study.


Your dog's veterinary medical records with your regular veterinarian will be reviewed to determine eligibility for inclusion. We may also speak with you and ask for pictures of your dog's mass. Your dog will then be examined at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy (CIGAT) at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD. A fine needle aspirate may be taken of the mass to determine the type of mass. If the mass appears to be a lipoma, you will then be asked to perform bloodwork (with X-rays of the chest highly suggested) as part of the pre-anesthetic examination at your regular veterinarian. The bloodwork and X-rays are not covered in the clinical trial. Within 2 weeks, your dog's fatty mass will be treated by freezing (called cryoablation) at CIGAT. There is no charge for this treatment. Your dog's response to treatment will be followed by telephone and email interviews for up to one year.
current_roster.tagline: Freezing Lipomas in Dogs
current_roster.name: Cryoablation of Fatty Tumors in Dogs

current_roster.description:
This study collects information about the physical status, blood pressure and selected laboratory parameters of cats that belong to one of two groups: a) they are healthy; b) they have been confirmed to have chronic kidney disease (CKD). The purpose of the study is to assess whether administration of a probiotic changes the natural gut microbial flora (microbiome) of these cats, and influences markers of renal (kidney) health and phosphate homeostasis through this microflora change. This project wishes to recruit cats that have CKD, IRIS Stage 2-4. We will be assessing the microbiome, and effect of a probiotic on CKD status, in particular calcium/phosphate metabolism. The study is a blinded (owner) cross-over prospective trial.


The gastrointestinal microbiome, a complex community of bacteria, eukaryotes, viruses, and archaea, potentially influences gastrointestinal phosphate availability and calcium:phosphate (Ca:P) homeostasis in the host through modulation of gastrointestinal pH and production of metabolites.  Limited cross-sectional evidence comparing healthy and chronic kidney disease (CKD) cats suggests that CKD cats have an altered, dysbiotic, gastrointestinal microbiome, with altered fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles, and correlated increases in serum uremic toxins. These changes may affect gastrointestinal integrity and lead to progression of CKD. However, there is scarce information how the feline gastrointestinal microbiome behaves over time in health and CKD, of its association with phosphate loading, the correlation between uremic toxins and Ca:P parameters, and whether Ca:P homeostasis can be positively modulated by giving a probiotic. This study aims to address these knowledge gaps. We will utilize shallow shotgun metagenomics to examine the composition and functional potential of the gastrointestinal microbiome of healthy and CKD cats over 24 weeks, and correlate findings with concurrent dietary diaries, clinical records, serum uremic toxin concentrations (urea, creatinine, indoxyl sulfate, p-cresol sulfate) and parameters of Ca:P homeostasis (including serum phosphate, ionized calcium, vitamin D, FGF-23 and PTH). Furthermore, the impact of an oral probiotic on the gastrointestinal microbiome and Ca:P homeostasis will be assessed in a cross-over trial. The potential feline health benefits of this study are immediate: 1) scrutinization for prognostic gastrointestinal and renal markers will help to optimize CKD monitoring, and 2) probiotic administration may reduce detrimental renal secondary hyperparathyroidism and progression of CKD.
current_roster.tagline: Probiotics for CKD in cats
current_roster.name: CKD and probiotic trial in cats

current_roster.description:
The goal of the study is to assess for infiltration of immune cells into tumor samples collected, as well as to monitor for disease progression after surgery. The enrollment will be limited to dogs cytologically diagnosed with soft tissue sarcomas that are at least two centimeters in diameter, undergoing a marginal resection.


Marginal excision of the mass will be performed in all dogs as clinically indicated, following the standards of care. Additional testing, specifically immunohistochemistry, of the tumor sample once removed, will be performed to identify immune cells within the sample. Routine staging post-operatively, as outlined below, will be performed until local recurrence and metastatic disease develop, 24 months of follow-up is reached, or death occurs. Dogs will undergo chest radiographs with sedation given as needed at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months. If a lymph node is suspected to have metastatic disease or if local recurrence is suspected, a fine needle aspirate of the lymph node or recurrent mass, respectively, will be performed.


The study covers the costs associated with the histopathology of the tumor once removed. Additionally, the study covers the costs of recheck examinations, chest radiographs with associated sedation if needed, and fine needle aspiration of suspected metastatic lymph nodes and local recurrence at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months post-operatively. The study does not cover the cost of preoperative evaluation, preoperative diagnostics, surgery, and general anesthesia for tumor removal beyond the histopathology charge, hospitalization, post-operative care, diagnostics beyond those outlined above, and additional treatment (such as additional surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy).
current_roster.tagline: Characterization and Prognostic Evaluation of Infiltrative Immune Cells in Canine Soft Tissue Sarcomas
current_roster.name: Characterization and Prognostic Evaluation of Infiltrative Immune Cells in Canine Soft Tissue Sarcomas
current_roster.top_investigator: Hunter Piegols, DVM, DACS-SA, ACVS Fellow-Surgical Oncology

current_roster.description:
Canine cognitive dysfunction (CCD) is a well-recognized disease in older dogs that mimics the cognitive changes from which humans with dementia suffer. This study aims to conduct a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled veterinary clinical trial of a novel genetically engineered L-DOPA bacterial live-therapeutic (LDBL) in conjunction with Benserazide (BZ) and Entacapone (ENT) in an established CCD model of human Alzheimer's disease (AD)-like dementia. The study will assess pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), safety, and efficacy. Study activities include blood draws for complete blood count (CBC), chemistry panel, and drug levels, owner-completed environmental and behavioral (cognitive evaluations - Canine Dementia Scale (CADES), Canine Cognitive Dysfunction Rating (CCDR)) surveys, chest radiographs, brain MRIs + cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) taps, stool collection for gut microbiome analysis, neurologic + physical examinations, and cognitive battery testing over the period of 18 months. The study drug (or placebo) will be given for the first 12 months, followed by a 6-month period of post-treatment monitoring. General anesthesia is required twice for MRIs and CSF collections.


Study Outline:

Enrollment (Month 0): Owner-completed surveys (environmental/lifestyle, CADES, CCDR), physical + neurological examinations, thoracic radiographs, blood sampling (~20mL) collected for CBC, chemistry panel, biomarker analysis, drug levels, and biorepository banking, stool sampling collected for gastrointestinal microbiome analysis, cognitive battery testing, brain MRI, CSF sampling collected for fluid analysis and biorepository banking, begin twice daily dosing of LDBL + BZ/ENT OR placebo + BZ/ENT vehicle suspension.


Month 3: Owner-completed surveys (CADES, CCDR), physical + neurological examinations, blood sampling collected for CBC, chemistry panel, biomarker analysis, drug levels, and biorepository banking, stool sampling collected for gastrointestinal microbiome analysis.


Month 6: Owner-completed surveys (CADES, CCDR), physical + neurological examinations, blood sampling collected for CBC, chemistry panel, biomarker analysis, drug levels, and biorepository banking, stool sampling collected for gastrointestinal microbiome analysis, cognitive battery testing.


Month 9: Owner-completed surveys (CADES, CCDR), physical + neurological examinations, blood sampling collected for CBC, chemistry panel, biomarker analysis, drug levels, and biorepository banking, stool sampling collected for gastrointestinal microbiome analysis.


Month 12: Owner-completed surveys (CADES, CCDR, exit survey), physical + neurological examinations, blood sampling collected for CBC, chemistry panel, biomarker analysis, drug levels, and biorepository banking, stool sampling collected for gastrointestinal microbiome analysis, cognitive battery testing, brain MRI, CSF sampling collected for fluid analysis and biorepository banking, stop twice daily dosing (every 12 hours) of treatment OR placebo.


Months 15 and 18: Owner-completed surveys (CADES, CCDR), physical + neurological examinations, blood sampling collected for CBC, chemistry panel, biomarker analysis, drug levels, and biorepository banking, stool sampling collected for gastrointestinal microbiome analysis, and cognitive battery testing.


Weekly Monitoring Surveys: Owners will be sent weekly surveys (drug diary, symptom tracker) to complete detailing the events for that patient's study medication administration and any symptoms (related or unrelated to the study medications) their pet is having for the week prior to completion. These surveys are separate from the CADES and CCDR surveys, which are completed at each visit.
current_roster.tagline: Treating Dog Dementia with Twice-daily Liquid Medications
current_roster.name: Treating Canine Dementia with Twice Daily Liquid Medications

current_roster.description:
Purpose

To evaluate the effects of histotripsy, an ultrasound-based treatment that can non-invasively destroy tumor tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with liver tumors. 

Background

In this study, we are evaluating the effects of histotripsy, an emerging technology that used focused ultrasound waves to mechanically destroy tumor tissue, on dogs with liver tumors. Histotripsy has the ability to precisely destroy tumors non-invasively and without using heat or radiation. Histotripsy also has the potential to stimulate the immune system into fighting off remaining or microscopic tumor. Our team’s previous research has evaluated the safety and efficacy of histotripsy for bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumors in dogs. We are now interested in how histotripsy affects liver tumors in dogs.


Histotripsy was FDA-approved for the treatment of liver tumors in humans in 2023, with promising clinical results. We now want to investigate how histotripsy treatment affects liver tumors in dogs, followed by surgical resection (removal) of the tumor 1 week after histotripsy. This allows us to evaluate the effects of the histotripsy treatment in the tumor tissue while providing the patient with standard-of-care. This study also includes blood sample collection before and after histotripsy (at the screening, treatment, and surgery visits) to let us explore how the immune cell populations change after histotripsy treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating an ultrasound technology for the non-invasive treatment of liver tumors in dogs
current_roster.name: Noninvasive Treatment of Liver Tumors in Dogs

current_roster.description:
Lymphoma is a common disease in dogs, and new treatments are needed. Multiple “nonspecific immunomodulator” drugs, which can stimulate the immune system to better attack cancer, are showing promise in human and canine cancer. The goal of this study is to measure the safety and immune effects of injecting one of these drugs into a lymph node in dogs with B-cell lymphoma. Dogs will receive a single injection of the drug into a lymph node affected by lymphoma, followed by careful observation for the day. 24 hours after injection, the study will be complete and dogs will be eligible for any other treatment.


Your dog will receive a single injection of this drug at a dose that is predicted to cause no side effects. A small amount of blood (approximately 1-2 teaspoons) will be collected before and 24 hours after injection. Fine needle aspirates of the lymph node will be obtained before and 24 hours after injection to look for changes in the lymphoma cells. After the 24-hour samples are collected, the study is over and your dog is eligible to receive any additional treatment that is recommended.


Although the drug we are studying has caused no side effects in laboratory dogs at higher doses than the dose we are planning to use, it has not been studied in pet dogs, which may be older and have other medical issues. Therefore, side effects (although extremely unlikely) could range from mild to severe, up to and including the death of your dog. Medications will be provided as needed to treat/prevent any side effects that might occur.


Costs covered by the clinical trial for eligible enrolled dogs include the cost of all examinations, drug injection, blood collection, and overnight hospitalization if elected. You will be responsible for the initial exam fee, and tests to confirm that your dog is eligible. Participating owners will receive a $500 credit to their dog’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital account, which can be applied to the initial testing or used to reduce costs of other cancer treatment when the study is complete.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Immune Therapy for Dogs with B Cell Lymphoma
current_roster.name: Injection of a Novel Immunotherapy Agent into a Lymph Node in Dogs with B Cell Lymphoma

current_roster.description:
Epistaxis (nose bleeds) is a relatively common clinical presentation in dogs often resulting from a variety of causes, including trauma, foreign bodies, infections, coagulopathies, and neoplasia. While mild cases may resolve spontaneously, severe or recurrent epistaxis can be life-threatening and often requires immediate intervention. Current treatment options for managing epistaxis in dogs are limited, and while systemic therapies and nasal packing are often employed, they can be cumbersome and may not always provide timely or effective hemostasis. Cases such as these highlight the unmet need for a reliable, easy to use topical hemostatic agent that can be rapidly and effectively applied during active bleeding episodes.


A novel plant-based hemostatic gel that has been designed for rapid and effective hemostasis will be studied. Unlike traditional methods, it works almost instantly upon application, allowing for formation of a stable clot that can help control bleeding without the need for external pressure or packing. Its ease of use and fast-acting properties make it a promising solution for the management of epistaxis in dogs, offering a potential alternative to existing treatments that are often cumbersome and less reliable in providing immediate hemostasis.
current_roster.tagline: SOLACE- for canine nose bleeds
current_roster.name: SOLACE - for Dogs with Nose Bleeds

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description:
The aim of this study is to determine if cats with chronic rhinitis (FCR) will respond to intranasal steroid treatment. There is no current standard of care treatment for this disease, and it can be associated with significant morbidity, greatly impacting the cat’s quality of life.


Cat owners will be asked to fill out a survey (SNIFLD-C questionnaire) to determine how severe their cat’s disease is at enrollment, during treatment, and after treatment for 4 weeks. Based on their SNIFLD-C scores, we hope to determine if treatment with an intranasal steroid drop (fluticasone or prednisolone) is better than treatment with a placebo (saline).


Cats diagnosed with biopsy-confirmed lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis (LPR), which is a form of FCR, will be eligible for enrollment. They will be randomly assigned to receive placebo (saline) or fluticasone drops. If a cat does not respond to treatment (either placebo or fluticasone) after 2 weeks, they can be automatically enrolled in a second-tier treatment option (fluticasone for saline cats, and prednisolone for fluticasone cats). We are hopeful that this study can provide evidence-based treatment options for cats with this condition.

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

current_roster.description:
Embolization is a minimally invasive cancer treatment in which particles are used to block the blood supply to a tumor. For liver tumors, the particles are delivered to the tumor using a catheter (long, thin tube) placed into an artery in the neck or thigh and threaded through the blood vessel until it reaches the specific blood vessel providing blood to the tumor. This is called Trans-Arterial Embolization (TAE). In some cases, chemotherapy is delivered directly to the tumor through this catheter immediately prior to delivering the particles that block the blood vessel. This is called Trans-Arterial Chemoembolization (TACE). Both TAE and TACE are used to treat liver tumors in dogs, but it is unknown if adding chemotherapy to embolization (TACE) has any benefit over embolization alone (TAE). The first purpose of this study is to compare the outcomes of dogs receiving TAE to dogs receiving TACE. 

Both computed tomography (CT) angiograms and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) are used to evaluate tumors in dogs. In people, CEUS has been shown to be more accurate than CT for assessing how effective the embolization procedure was in cutting off blood supply to the tumor. In dogs, a CT scan is the current standard for post-embolization evaluation. The second purpose of this study is to compare the accuracy of CEUS and CT scan following embolization.
current_roster.tagline: TAE/TACE for Canine HCC
current_roster.name: Embolization and Chemoembolization in dogs with non-resectable liver tumors
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. Dana L. Clarke, VMD, DACVECC, Associate Professor of Interventional Radiology

current_roster.description: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a condition that causes progressive deterioration of the heart’s function that commonly leads to death within 6 months of the diagnosis of congestive heart failure. Gene therapy is a novel approach to treat diseases like DCM. For the current study, genes will be introduced into muscle cells using a delivery agent called a “vector”. This vector is a highly modified virus that can usually enter cells without causing disease and is one that has been shown to be safe in human gene therapy. When the vector carries genes into cells, the cells can make normal proteins which in turn may improve muscle function. Our study will determine if gene therapy can slow down progression of DCM in affected dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Gene Therapy for Dobermans with Dilated Cardiomyopathy
current_roster.name: Gene Therapy for Dobermans with Dilated Cardiomyopathy

These conditions may lead to persistent discomfort, secondary infections, and reduced quality of life if not properly managed. Preventive measures should be taken to minimize flare-ups and recurrence. This study will investigate the efficacy of two antibody treatments to treat dogs with allergic skin conditions. These treatments are called immune Ig and anti-idiotypic Ig. They have been tested in people and in lab studies, and safety studies have also been done in dogs. These treatments are not yet approved for dogs, and this study will help us learn if they are helpful for dogs with skin allergies.

current_roster.description:
Background and purpose


For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decrease in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.


What happens in this study


  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical examination, full blood work, urinalysis
  2. A pre-operative biopsy performed at enrollment, to confirm squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma
  3. Intravenous administration of the anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 theranostic probe twice before surgery
  4. Near infrared fluorescence Imaging performed at 8 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours after probe delivery
  5. Repeat biopsy or curative intent surgery after the second anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 probe administration
  6. Follow-up visits at 7 days and 4 weeks


IACUC: 24708

Study number: VCCT-26-008
current_roster.tagline: New theragnostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer!
current_roster.name: Combinatorial Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer

current_roster.description:
In Florida and the Southeastern United States, dogs are frequently diagnosed with pythiosis, an oomycete or fungus-like disease that often has a poor prognosis. Mefenoxam is an agricultural fungicide, frequently prescribed as first line medical therapy along with other antifungals, antibiotics, and steroids. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the action of oral mefenoxam in dogs diagnosed with pythiosis. It is hypothesized that mefenoxam will significantly improve the clinical signs in dogs with pythiosis in a short period of time. Information gained from this study will help validate use of mefenoxam as part of our treatment protocol for pythiosis.


This study is a small-scale trial lasting a total of 28 days and involves 24 hours of hospitalization and 3 additional veterinary visits. In order to be enrolled, your dog will have a prior diagnosis of pythiosis based on culture with PCR, ELISA, and/or histopathology with PCR. They will also have a previous abdominal ultrasound or body mapping to document lesions if they are diagnosed with gastrointestinal or cutaneous pythiosis, respectively. A baseline workup including complete blood count, chemistry panel, and urinalysis will have been performed prior to enrollment. Enrolled pets will have the first standard dose of mefenoxam administered in hospital. Continued treatment with mefenoxam will be performed by owners at home every 24 hours as part of the ongoing medical management for pythiosis. Pets will be fasted for a period of 8 hours (overnight) prior to each visit. During hospitalization an IV catheter will be placed to facilitate blood sampling. One blood sampleof 5 ml (~1/3 tablespoon) will be drawn prior to administration of the first dose of mefenoxam, then additional samples will be drawn at 15 minutes, 30 minutes, 60 minutes, 90 minutes, 2 hours, 4 hours, 6 hours, 10 hours, and 24 hours after the first dose. Samples will be acquired from the IV catheter up to the 10-hour time point. If at the 24-hour timepoint there is difficulty obtaining a sample from the IV catheter, blood will be drawn by routine venipuncture from another vessel. After the first 24 hours your pet will be discharged on standard medications for the treatment of pythiosis including mefenoxam, terbinafine, minocycline, and prednisone. Additional visits will occur 7, 14, and 28 days later for single blood samples to monitor mefenoxam levels. These additional blood samples will need to be drawn 1-2 hours after your pet’s daily dose of mefenoxam.
current_roster.tagline: Mefenoxam Pharmacokinetics after Initial Oral Administration in Dogs with Pythiosis
current_roster.name: Mefenoxam Pharmacokinetics After Initial Oral Administration in Dogs with Pythiosis

current_roster.description:
Gliomas are among the most common and most aggressive primary brain tumors in pet dogs. Established definitive treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, or a combination of these treatments. Surgical resection alone does not improve survival times achieved with supportive care alone, and is therefore not recommended. Radiation therapy provides an average of 14 months of survival time. The purpose of this study is to investigate a novel treatment option with the goal being to improve outcomes for dogs with high grade gliomas. Treatment in this study consists of removal of the brain tumor, followed by injections of a Zika virus vaccine along with anti-tumor vaccines. The combination is meant to trigger an immune response against any tumor cells that remain in the brain after surgery. These injections are done under the skin.


This is a single site, prospective, single arm clinical trial with no control (placebo) group. Treatment will consist of surgical removal of the tumor, then three weekly injections of the virus along with anti-tumor vaccines. Dogs will undergo recheck MRIs every four months for a year or until there is evidence of tumor regrowth, whichever comes first.
current_roster.tagline: Stimulating the immune system in the treatment of high-grade glioma
current_roster.name: Combining Zika virus vaccines and autologous tumor lysates in pet dogs with high-grade gliomas
current_roster.top_investigator: Susan Arnold, Susan A. Arnold, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Neurology)

current_roster.description:
Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.


The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment. Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.

The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.

Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.


Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Please note: All treatments and relevant follow up must be performed at Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine. Investigational treatment will not be sent to outside clinics.
current_roster.tagline: Quasiorganelle therapy for histiocytic sarcoma
current_roster.name: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma

current_roster.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.


IACUC: 24677

Study number: VCCT-26-017
current_roster.tagline: New treatment with autologous FAP CAR-T cells for sarcomas
current_roster.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)

Copper associated liver disease is one of the most common liver diseases in dogs and Labrador retrievers are at risk. Copper associated liver disease is caused by too much copper build up in the liver. If this disease is not diagnosed or treated, it can cause a lot of liver damage and ultimately, liver failure.


The goal of this study is to use new technologies to better understand how to diagnose these diseases with blood tests and see how they differ from healthy Labrador retrievers.


We are enrolling Labrador retrievers with increased liver values on bloodwork and healthy Labradors. If your Labrador is healthy and already undergoing a surgery such as a spay, neuter, or gastropexy, the liver sampling will be in addition to that and a portion or all costs of the surgery will be covered.

Pet owner responsibilities

current_roster.description:
Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) treatment consists of delivering a low dose of chemotherapy, followed by short electric pulses to the cancer. With the delivery of the electric pulses, cell membranes are transiently opened allowing chemotherapy directly into the cell. Treatment may be repeated over the course of weeks or months to achieve regression of large lesions. Targeted Electrochemotherapy employs lower dosages of chemotherapeutic drugs than standard chemotherapy protocols. In the clinical use of electrochemotherapy, side effects are uncommon and patients maintain or improve quality of life. Currently, Electrochemotherapy in animals is under a short anesthesia and with a variety of electrodes available to us, many tumor types and locations (including internal cancers) are candidates for this therapy.


Targeted Electrochemotherapy, in veterinary oncology (dogs, cats, exotics and horses), has been dominated by centers in Europe and South America. Here at Veterinary Oncology Services, there is not a location where cancer may not be treated. It may be used for a wide variety of tumors including:


Sarcomas in the mouth, eyelid, foot pad, skin or distal limb and their scars, Feline vaccine-associated fibrosarcoma before and after surgery, Melanoma in the mouth, eyelid or foot pad, Squamous cell carcinoma in mouth, eyelid, ear, nasal planum or foot pad, Incompletely resected soft tissue sarcomas where aggressive surgical treatment would necessitate amputation, Localized cutaneous lymphoma in dogs or cats, Local control of mast cell tumors including scars, Perianal & rectal tumors, prostate, pancreas, Hepatocellular carcinomas/adenomas, Perianal tumors, Sarcoids, sarcoma and squamous cell carcinomas in horses, Superficial tumors on exotics (small mammals, birds & zoo animals) If you have a patient that may benefit from this therapy, please do not hesitate to contact us at 845 205 2768 or info@petcancerinformation.com. Please visit our website at www.petcancerinformation.com


For more information:

https://www.vetspecialists.com/vet-blog-landing/animal-health-articles/2024/01/23/electrochemotherapy-cancer-treatment

current_roster.name: Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) Cancer Treatment

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the outcome of treating veterinary patients with minimally invasive tumor ablation technologies including cryoablation and microwave ablation. These methods are growing in the treatment of a variety of cancers in the human medical field, but information in veterinary patients is currently very limited. To date we have completed a study on cryoablation in nasal tumor patients, and this technique has been very successful in reducing tumor volume in nasal tumor patients - although there are no more spots in the formal nasal tumor study, because of this success, we continue to offer this technique as a clinical service to nasal cancer patients, and are expanding the types of cancer that we are evaluating. Contact: Call 530-752-1393 and ask to speak to the Soft Tissue Surgery scheduling coordinators (Conni, or Caleb) to schedule an appointment with Dr. Michele Steffey. The coordinators will likely advise you to send your pet's medical records and imaging results for Dr. Steffey's review. If, based on this information, your pet is deemed an appropriate candidate, an appointment will be scheduled. Participation Requirements: In order to participate in this study, your pet must have solitary malignant soft tissue or bony mass that is deemed amenable to ablation. Tumor types that MAY be amenable to this treatment include lung tumors, kidney tumors, adrenal tumors, and bone tumors in certain locations. however determination of eligibility is complex and relates to the size of the lesion as well as proximity to/involvement of other important nearby structures. Tumors that are superficial (involving or near to the skin) or that involve the gastrointestinal tract are not amenable to this treatment. Initial Evaluation for Participation: Evaluation by the V.M.T.H. Small Animal Surgery, Internal Medicine, or Oncology services. Procedures: If you agree to participate, under general anesthesia, ablation probes will be placed into your pet's mass under ultrasound guidance and the tumor will be ablated. Benefits: This treatment method may only be palliative, but it is our hope that in appropriately selected patients, we may improve quality of life as well as longevity. Owner Responsibilities: The study will cover the cost of the ablation probes and generator. Costs of pre-operative workup, general anesthesia, recommended imaging, hospitalization, and general management of the disease process or any complications that occur during treatment are your responsibility.

current_roster.description: Purpose To determine a safe and effective dose of the chemotherapy drug oxaliplatin in the treatment of cancers in dogs Background This study is designed to determine whether the human chemotherapy drug oxaliplatin can be administered to dogs with cancer. This drug shows promise of being less toxic and more effective than current canine cancer therapies, but additional studies are needed to establish a dose for veterinary use. We therefore seek to undertake a Phase-1 study to determine the safety of oxaliplatin in treating dogs with cancer Eligibility Dogs must weigh > 10 kg Diagnosis of solid tumor Dogs must not have received conventional chemotherapy or kinase therapy for the past 3 weeks or radiation therapy for the past 4 weeks before beginning treatment Exclusion Criteria Other life-limiting disease or an expected survival of < 6 weeks without treatment Study Design A complete physical exam, including relevant diagnostic imaging, will be undertaken to determine eligibility. Owners will be asked to keep a brief, daily record of any side effects or changes in the dog's behavior during this 3-week period. The estimated value of these services is $1200. In addition, clients will receive a $50 hospital credit for each recheck visit completed on time. Contact Mindy Quigley, Clinical Trials Coordinator Office Phone: (540) 231-1363 | Email: vettrials@vt.edu Website: http://www.vetmed.vt.edu/clinical-trials If your query is urgent, please call the Small Animal Hospital on (540) 231-4621 and ask for the oncologist on duty.
