current_roster.description: This study aims to investigate the efficacy of a novel anti-clotting drug (rivaroxaban) compared to clopidogrel in preventing the recurrence of arterial thromboembolism (saddle thrombus) in cats with heart disease. Information gained from this study will help researchers improve treatments and clinical management strategies to delay or prevent these often-fatal clotting complications in cats with heart disease. Qualified participants include cats with heart disease that have survived an arterial thromboembolism. Once enrolled, a cat will be randomized to receive one of the two drugs to be studied, and will receive the assigned drug free of charge for 2 years. Regular rechecks with a cardiologist will be partially funded by the study over a 2 year period, and echocardiographic data and activity surveys will be entered using a dedicated study website. There is a 24 hour hotline for owners once a cat has been enrolled in the study to answer any questions about the medication.
current_roster.tagline: Anticoagulation in cats with heart disease
current_roster.name: SUPER-CAT: a Study of the Utility of Rivaroxaban or Clopidogrel for prevention of recurrent Arterial Thromboembolism in cats

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: This is a National Cancer Institute (NCI) trial sponsored by the Morris Animal Foundation for dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma. Standard of care therapy is defined as surgical amputation of the affected limb, followed by four doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy (one dose given every 21 days). Carboplatin has been used to treat appendicular OSA in dogs for over 20 years, but thereremains potential for life-threatening side effects from surgery, chemotherapy, and/or cancer progression. All dogs enrolled into this study will receive standard of care (SOC) therapy and will be randomized to receive rapamycin therapy or not following the SOC protocol.Rapamycin is a drug currently approved to induce immunosuppression in human patients receiving organ and bone marrow transplants. Previous work suggests that rapamycin might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting mTOR, an important cancer pathway. Previous studies in mice, in addition to work with rapamycin analog drugs in human patients, suggest that mTOR inhibition might be effective in the treatment of several types of cancers. Objective: To evaluate if orally administered rapamycin, following standard of care therapy, improves long-term disease control in dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma. Client Compensation: Following determination of your dogs eligibility and limb amputation, costs associated with this study will be provided, including a $1000 hospital credit towards your dogs limb amputation surgery. This study covers the cost of carboplatin chemotherapy, which is standard of care therapy. Should your dog be randomized to receiverapamycin, the cost of the drug and required monitoring will also be covered by the study. In the event any complications arise during the study period while rapamycin is being administered (4 months), your dogs management will be covered by study funds up to $2000.00. This would include any unanticipated hospitalizations.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Orally Administered mTOR inhibitor Rapamycin in Dogs in the Adjuvant Setting with Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Akkermansia muciniphila is a bacterium that inhabits the mucosa of the intestines and is crucial in maintaining its health. Decreased numbers of these bacteria have been observed in cases of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). Administration of Akkermansia muciniphila as a probiotic improved intestinal and systemic health in mice by decreasing intestinal permeability, decreasing inflammation and increasing secretion of the hormone GLP-2. In the study proposed here we will evaluate the effect of oral administration of Akkermansia muciniphila on intestinal permeability and GLP-2 secretion in dogs with naturally occurring IBD that failed conventional treatments (other than immunosuppressive drugs). Objective of the trial: This study aims to measure the effect of a probiotic (Akkermansia muciniphila) on intestinal permeability, inflammation, and GLP-2 secretion in with naturally occurring IBD that failed conventional treatments (other than immunosuppressive drugs). What qualifies my dog for enrollment in thetrial? Prior to entry in this study, your dog must have a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease confirmed by: A food trial An antibiotic trial Intestinal biopsies Your dog cannot be treated with steroids at the time of the trial or at least for 1 month before What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? During the 4 weeks of the study, you will be administering 2 capsules to your dog once a day. You will need to return to the OSU Veterinary Medical Center once a week to obtain treatment supplies. Dogs taking part in this study are required to return to the OSU Veterinary Medical Center on days 3, 16, and 30 for examinations. In each of these exams, one fecal sample and 2 blood samples will be obtained (one before and one after feeding). Client Compensation: No direct compensation is provided and the owner is responsible for testing related to initial diagnosis (prior to entry into the study).The study will cover the cost of pre- and post- treatment GLP-2 and LPS assays, follow-up recheck examination fee, and treatment supplies.
current_roster.name: Dogs with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)

current_roster.description: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) or dry eye is a devastating disease that causes ocular pain and potentially blindness. It is seen more frequently in West Highland White Terriers in comparison to many other breeds. We are interested identifying the genetic components of this disease as well as characterizing this disease better with examination and testing of the tear film and ocular surface and in select patients using advanced imaging techniques. Procedures: Routine ophthalmic examination and tear film tests Blood collection for DNA analysis
current_roster.name: Understanding the Genetics of Dry Eye Syndrome in West Highland White Terriers

current_roster.description: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to determine how various nutritional and hormonal factors are affected in dogs with chronic kidney disease (CKD). We will evaluate concentrations of vitamin D metabolites and other hormones (e.g., parathyroid hormone) that can affect the development of renal secondary hyperparathyroidism (RHPT) in order to then develop novel medical and dietary therapeutic strategies. Inclusion Criteria: Dog must be diagnosed with CKD and staged by the International Renal Interest Society guidelines Dog must be at least one year of age Dog must not be diagnosed with any other disease known to affect vitamin D or PTH concentrations First your dog will have a physical examination and blood pressure measurement. Then your dog will have blood and urine collected to evaluate a complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry profile, ionized calcium, urinalysis, urine protein: creatinine (UPC) ratio and urine culture. A small amount of blood will be stored for later evaluation of your dogs vitamin D status and other hormones that are known to play a role in the development of RHPT. Your dog will only need to have blood and urine collected at one time and the total amount of blood collected is considered very safe for dogs. In some animals, venipuncture may result in bruising or hematoma formation at the site of blood collection. In rare cases, cystocentesis may result in hematuria or infrequently bladder rupture. Client Compensation: The study will cover the costs of a CBC, biochemistry profile, ionized calcium, urinalysis, UPC, urine culture and blood pressure, vitamin D metabolite and hormone concentrations.Client Cost:Owners are responsible for all other costs.
current_roster.name: Dogs with chronic kidney disease

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant tumor arising from the secretory epithelium of the walls of the anal sacs. AGASACA displays aggressive biologic behavior and is both locally invasive and highly metastatic, frequently spreading to the lymph nodes early in the course of the disease. Multiple treatment methods have been utilized in the management of AGASACA, including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, electrochemotherapy, and various combinations thereof. However, there is currently no widely-accepted standard of care therapy for canine AGASACA, other than surgical resection of the primary tumor followed by an adjuvant therapy, such as chemo. One chemotherapeutic agent, cisplatin, is postulated to have potential benefit, but in its nave form it has some significant side-effects. Reformulation of cisplatin as a conguated nanoparticle should improve targeting to the primary tumor site and lymph nodes. This then allows for the use of smaller doses of the cisplatin, thereby reducing side-effects while enhancing efficacy. Objective: The primary purpose of this study is to demonstrate the feasibility of localized subcutaneous administration of a nanoparticle formulation of cisplatin, and to demonstrate that this modified formulation accumulates in tumor tissue and local lymph nodes. Client Compensation: The study covers the cost of nanoparticle cisplatin, blood work, urinalysis and recheck exam for dogs enrolled. In addition, any adverse events arising as a result of the HA-PT administration up to $750.00, as well as surgery up to $2000.00 will be covered by the study. Owner is responsible for the costs associated with initial pre-enrollment diagnostic work-up and staging.
current_roster.name: Localized nanoparticle delivery of cisplatin in dogs with naturally-occurring metastatic apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma.

current_roster.description: Purpose of the Study: Pulmonary metastasis continues to be the major cause of mortality among human and canine patients with osteosarcoma. A series of investigational agents will be evaluated in dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma with the hopes of identifying new drugs that help dogs live longer after being diagnosed with osteosarcoma. Rapamycin is a drug that may help slow down the progression of cancer cells, by blocking a pathway that helps cancer cells grow and opening up a pathway that promotes cell death. In doing so we hope that rapamycin would slow the spread of osteosarcoma to different parts of the body, most commonly the lungs. It is hoped that slowing the progression of osteosarcoma will result in longer survival of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma. Should you decide to enroll your pet into this clinical trial, your dog will receive standard of care therapy, which includes amputation and four doses of carboplatin given once every three weeks. After your pet completes the carboplatin therapy they will begin receiving rapamycin, which will be given once daily at home MondayThursday for up to four months. Inclusion Criteria: Dogs with histologically or cytologically confirmed appendicular osteosarcoma Dogs must be at least 25 kilograms in weight Dogs cannot have been treated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or bisphosphonates Dogs cannot have any evidence of metastatic disease Dogs cannot have any significant co-morbid illness affecting the kidney, liver, or bone marrow Eligibility Diagnostics: Prior to study entry, pet owners will be financially responsible and required to have the following diagnostics performed on their pet: 1) Screening blood work and urinalysis; 2) thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound; 3) cytologic or histologic confirmation of appendicular osteosarcoma. Treatment: All dogs enrolled will receive standard of care, which includes limb amputation and systemic chemotherapy. Some dogs will go on to receive oral rapamycin at home for four months. Compensation: The study will pay for $1,800 for amputation and $200 per chemotherapy treatment. All additional costs associated with the investigation will be paid for by study funds, which include all costs directly associated with scheduled recheck visits (drug administration, hospitalization, and blood work) during the entirety of the study period. Pet owners will be responsible for initial diagnostics performed to confirm study
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Orally Administered mTOR Inhibitor Rapamycin in Dogs in the Adjuvant Setting with Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Surgery is performed by a team including a veterinary neurosurgeon and an MD neurosurgeon. The surgery to remove the brain tumor may be combined with medical therapy such as new chemotherapy regimes or immunotherapy.
current_roster.name: Canine glioma surgery

current_roster.description: Dr. Jody Lulich at the Minnesota Urolith Center (MUC) is investigating the connection between kidney stones and chronic kidney disease in cats.If cats with radiographically or ultrasonographically diagnosed kidney stones have a kidney removed during therapy, succumb to their illness, or are humanely euthanized, we can learn a lot by evaluating the structure of the kidney. Place whole, intact kidneys (without cutting them open) in formalin.If the kidney capsule can be removed, formalin can fix the tissue more effectively, but this is not necessary.Ship them to Dr. Jody Lulich at the Minnesota Urolith Center.To receive shipping instructions so that we cover mailing cost, please email Dr. Lulich atlulic001@umn.edu.One of the most compassionate acts we can perform as veterinarians and as cat owners is to contribute samples to scientists working to cure this disease.
current_roster.name: Feline Kidney Stone Study

current_roster.description: Mirtazapine is a medication that has been used in human medicine as an antidepressant. The drug widely used in veterinary medicine due to the presence of several desirable effects, namely its significant anti-nausea, anti-vomiting and appetite stimulating properties. It has been shown to be effective in increasing weight and appetite and decreasing vomiting in cats with chronic kidney disease. However, many owners have difficulty administering pills to their cat. We believe that mirtazapine, like many other medications, could be effective when formulated as a transdermal gel that can be applied to the skin of the ear. The purpose of this study is to perform a study to document the appetite stimulation properties of the transdermal form of the drug in cats with kidney disease. Cats with stable chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2-5 mg/dL) are potentially eligible for entry into the study. Diagnostic tests required before enrollment include a serum biochemistry profile, complete blood count, urinalysis, urine culture, blood pressure, and thyroid level. Exclusion criteria include other systemic illnesses, complications of CKD such as pyelonephritis or ureteral obstruction, or decompensation of CKD requiring hospitalization and intravenous fluid therapy. Other concurrent therapies such as dietary management, famotidine, potassium supplementation, anti-hypertensive medications and subcutaneous fluids are acceptable if they are given consistently throughout the study period. The study involves bringing the cat into the hospital for three visits and administering a gel to the ear for a total of 6 weeks. There are two treatment periods (placebo transdermal gel, mirtazapine transdermal gel) and the cat will receive both in a randomly determined order. During the two transdermal treatment periods (placebo or mirtazapine) the owner will administer the gel daily for 3 days then every other day for three weeks, fill out a daily log sheet, and then bring the cat in for the hospital visit on the last day of gel administration. During this day, the cat will get a physical exam and weight, and have a blood sample drawn to check kidney values and to measure serum mirtazapine.
current_roster.name: Assessment of transdermal mirtazapine as an appetite stimulant in cats with chronic kidney disease

current_roster.description: This is a randomized trial for dogs with confirmed B-cell lymphoma (LSA). All patients receive standard of care chemotherapy (25-week CHOP). If patients are deemed in complete remission following completion of the first chemotherapy cycle, then the patient (if eligible based on inclusion/exclusion criteria) will be randomized to receive either continued chemotherapy alone or chemotherapy in combination with the Merial B-cell LSA vaccine. The study is blinded, thus, the clinician and owner are unaware ofthe treatment group into which the patient is entered. Patients receive 4 doses (vaccine or saline placebo) at 2-week intervals followed by single dose boosters at 3-month intervals until the conclusion of the study. Patients in the chemotherapy-only treatment group are eligible to receive the vaccine at no cost upon relapse.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs with naive B-cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: Lomustine (CCNU) is an oral chemotherapy agent commonly used in veterinary medicine with efficacy against a wide variety of cancers. Chronic administration can adversely affect the liver resulting in elevated liver enzymes and in rare cases severe liver dysfunction. This is generally a cumulative effect and the use of liver-sparing medications may ameliorate this. The goal of this study is determine if the use of Hepato TruBenefitsas a novel liver supplement for dogs lessens or prevents the CCNU-induced elevation of ALT in dogs.Qualifying patients will be randomly assigned in to two groups - a treatment or non-treatment group. One group will receive Veterinarian Recommended Solutions Hepato TruBenefitswhile the nontreatment group will receive no treatment.Once enrolled, all patients will receive examinations at no cost for the duration of the trial. Patients randomized to the treatment group will receive the product at no cost. Partial funding for chemistry panels performed (up to 12-15) is provided to all dogs entered in the trial. If a patient in the non-treatment group experiences significant increases in liver enzymes, that patient is able to cross the subject over into the treatment group. Post completion of the trial, enrolled patients can receive the product lifelong at no cost.
current_roster.name: Hepato TruBenefits™ Clinical Trial

current_roster.description: Purpose of the study: To compare efficacy and safety of masatinib to placebo in dogs with grade 2-3 non-resectable mast cell tumors. Mastinib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Primary Eligibility Criteria: Dogs diagnosed with grade 2-3, aggressive, non-resectable mast cell tumors. Will need to have biopsy of tumor to determine eligibility. No prior chemotherapy or radiation treatment for mast cell tumor. 3-week washout from steroids. Overall healthy otherwise, with no evidence of bone marrow involvement of mast cell tumor. Study Protocol: Dogs will either receive oral masatinib (2/3 of those enrolled) or placebe (1/3 of those enrolled) given daily at home. Recheck visits every 2 weeks for physical exam and bloodwork; abdominal ultrasound, chest x-rays and lymph node aspirates done every 4 weeks. Dogs are eligible to continue on study until progression of the disease is detected. Owner Responsibilities:Follow appointment schedule required by study protocol. Be comfortable administering oral medications. Fill out daily treatment and activity log. Bring in all medications and owner diary to each appointment. Financial Incentives: Once informed consent is signed, all costs associated with the study are covered by the study. Includes costs of screening tests to determine study eligibility.
current_roster.name: Phase 3 clinical trial of masitinib in dogs with aggressive mast cell tumors

current_roster.description: The primary purpose of this study is to test two investigational medications to determine if either one, or both, work to potentially decrease signs of pain of osteoarthritis in dogs. Procedures: Physical and lameness examinations (each visit), X-rays (Visit 1 only), blood and urine collections, treatment with one of two investigational drugs, Carprofen (Rimadyl) or placebo, and completion of daily questionnaires regarding your dogs health. Owner Responsibilities: Attend four separate clinic visits times over approximately 6 weeks, give the provided investigational drug, Carprofen (Rimadyl) or placebo capsules to your dog by mouth twice daily for approximately 14 days, and complete the required daily diary accurately and fully each day. Benefits: The study will cover the costs of all study procedures.Upon completion of the study, you will be eligible to receive a $150 Visa gift card.If your dog experiences any adverse events (uncomfortable, severe or life-threatening), the sponsor will cover the reasonable and necessary veterinary fees and expenses related to the event; however you will be responsible for any veterinary care and costs for your dog thereafter. Results from this study may include direct relief of pain due to arthritis in your dog.

current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To establish whether testing urinary calcium at different times of day can determine if a dog has calcium oxalate urinary stones or is at risk for developing them. Background Miniature schnauzers have a strong breed predisposition to a type of bladder stones known as calcium oxalate uroliths. The stones can be asymptomaticin one study up to 24% of apparently healthy schnauzers had uroliths. Uroliths can cause damage and pain, even in dogs who display no obvious symptoms. Therefore, improving our ability to diagnose these stones is important. This study aims to determine whether testing urinary calcium at different times of day can better differentiate between dogs have that have formed calcium oxalate urinary stones and healthy dogs. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Contact Dr. Susan Carr, Internal MedicineOffice Phone: 540-231-4621 | Mindy Quigley, Clinical Trials CoordinatorOffice Phone: 540-231-1363 If your query is urgent, please call the Small Animal Hospital at 540-231-4621 and ask for theinternal medicine doctor on duty.

current_roster.description: Congenital heart defects occur in a variety of dog breeds, with the most common being the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Although this is a correctable disorder in most puppies, it requires thoracic surgery or a catheter-based procedure which can be expensive and is not without risk. Therefore, determining the genetic cause of PDA in dogs would be highly desirable so that dogs could be screened and the genetic mutation could be eventually bred out of the canine population. Although some breeds are more predisposed to developing PDAs (including the Pembroke Welsh Corgi), most PDAs occur sporadically so genetic testing could be difficult. However, we have had the opportunity to study several lines of Corgis with a very high incidence of PDA. We are working with geneticists at the Broad Institute to perform DNA testing on these families of Corgis and other unrelated Corgis with PDAs in order to identify the gene mutation association with this common genetic defect in the breed. Using these related and other affected dogs, our goal is to identify the DNA mutation which can then be tested in larger populations of Corgis in future studies. Testing does not have to be conducted at the Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine but PDAs must be confirmed by echocardiography. Blood (5 ml) can be collected by the primary care veterinarian or cardiologist and submitted directly to the Broad Institute. Please contact clinicaltrials@tufts.edu for sampling and shipping instructions (and consent forms).
current_roster.name: Heart disease in Pembroke Welsh Corgis

current_roster.description: Background Urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence (USMI) or "spay incontinence", is the most common cause of urinary incontinence in spayed female dogs,and is commonlycaused by the loss of urethral tone and insufficient urethral pressures. Urinary incontinence affects more than 20% of spayed female dogs, with medium and large breeds more commonly affected. In the majority of the cases urinary incontinence is caused by dysfunction of the muscles controlling the urethral sphincter. This condition results in urinary leakage during recumbency and other activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure. Left untreated, urinary incontinence can result in urine scalding, recurrent urinary tract infections, and pet relinquishment. Current treatment can include hormone therapy and other drugs to strengthen the muscle tone of the urethral sphincter, collagen injections, or surgery. Recently, we have reported that injection of muscle progenitor cells into damaged urethral sphincters can restore normal function in dogs. Study Objective The purpose of this study is to examine the effectiveness of cultured muscle cells for the restoration of urethral sphincter function in dogs with naturally-occurring urinary incontinence. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? - Female dogs diagnosed with Urethral Sphincter Mechanism Incompetence (USMI) or "spay incontinence" and have failed standard therapy. Dogs recently diagnosed with USMI can also be enrolled in this study. - Dogs should be in generally good health and have no illnesses that may interfere with the study evaluation. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign an informed consent allowing a small muscle biopsy (approximately 0.5 cubic inches)to be obtained from your dog'sleg,under sedation and local anesthesia. The incision will be sutured and your dog will be discharged from the hospital. After the muscle cells have expanded to the required number (generally about 2 weeks), your dog will return to the hospital for injection of these cells via a surgical procedure. This will require an overnight stay so that your dog will have adequate time to recuperate while being observed. The urethral tone will be assessed through urodynamic testing at baseline and then again at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months after cell injection. This testing involves placement of a urinary catheter and measurement of the urethral pressure over the length of the urethra. The test is performed with your dog under general anesthesia. These procedures do not require an overnight stay. Client Compensation Costs associated with this study will be provided, to include study visits, anesthesia, biopsy, and stem cell injection, an estimatedworth of $2,500. Client Contact Dogs with USMI and owners who are interested in this study should be referred to the Internal Medicine Service for evaluation. For more information, please contact: Lyndy Harden at lbharden@ncsu.eduor Dr. Shelly Vaden at 919-513-6670.

current_roster.description: Feline chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS) is a poorly defined disease which causes severe and painful inflammation affecting the gums and the back of the mouth. Currently, no treatments that are available are ideal, predictable and without possible complications. In prior studies in over 20 cats, IV administration of a cats own stem cells were shown to not only be safe, but, in most cases (about 70%), substantially improved or completely resolved the stomatitis. Therefore, the purpose of this double-blinded study is to treat cats for which all current treatment modalities have failed and have a poor quality of life. Once enrolled in the study patients will return to the hospital for bloodwork at one, three, and six months. Following the bloodwork, patients will then go under anesthesia to collect tissue to process the stem cells. Approximately two weeks later patients return for stem cell administration twice, one month apart. Final recheck visits will be at three and six months after the last stem cell administration. Total enrollment time is 12 months. ELIGIBILITY:Cats diagnosed with gingivostomatitis that have had full-mouth dental extractions performed and have not responded to treatment for at least six months. Cats cannot be receiving or have received in the 14 days prior any local or systemic antibiotics or immunosuppressive medications (i.e. steroids, cyclosporine.) COMPENSATION:Owners pay for the examination fee and any necessary diagnostics needed to determine candidacy in the study. Owners are also responsible for the cost of any take home medications and complications/adverse events during the study. All other procedures are covered by the study. OWNER RESPONSIBILITIES:The initial appointment will include the examination and diagnostics to determine eligibility. If eligible, your cat will go under anesthesia and have an oral biopsy and collection of fat for the production of stem cells. After the stem cells are processed (about two weeks) your cat will return to Cornell for two treatments while under anesthesia one month apart. Additional recheck visits are also required at 3 and 6 months after the initial treatment for examinations and a sedated oral biopsy at the final visit. Veterinarians and owners will be blinded as to whether each patient receives his/her own stem cells or a placebo. If your cat receives the placebo you will have the opportunity at the end of treatment to have the stem cell injections. current_roster.description: Purpose of study: Pain from osteoarthritis (OA) can restrict dogs from daily activities such as walking and climbing stairs. Common medications for OA pain are short-acting, may give incomplete relief, and may have potential side effects. The new treatment in this study is being evaluated for efficacy and safety to provide long-lasting pain relief following a single treatment. This is a 28-day, placebo-controlled study. Dogs will either receive the study medication injected into the stifle or elbow joint most affected by OA, or a sham injection involving a needle being inserted but nothing injected. Dogs will be anesthetized for the procedure. The study team will be closely monitoring the dogs during and after treatment. Description of study: - Two randomly assigned groups, 1 in 2 chance of receiving study drug - Visits: four visits (screening, injection day (Day 0), rechecks at 2 weeks and 4 weeks) - Procedures include physical and lameness exams, owner assessments, X-rays at screening, anesthesia and injection of a single joint, blood and urine sample collection at screening visit - Owners will answer three questionnaires at each visit and maintain an owner observation record at home Telephone interviews: two interviews (7 days prior and after treatment), answering two questionnaires during each interview. The study covers costs of the study medication, study related visits and tests. Owners who complete the study are eligible for a payment of $350. For questions and to schedule an appointment, please contact Sara Pracht (see above).

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effect of music as an add-on therapy for dogs with medically refractory epilepsy. Epilepsy is the most common neurological condition encountered in veterinary practice. The term primary (idiopathic) epilepsy is used to describe recurrent seizures with a presumed genetic or inherited basis, for which no underlying structural or inflammatory brain disease has been identified. Most dogs with primary epilepsy are managed with antiepileptic drugs, including Phenobarbital, potassium bromide, levetiracetam and zonisamide. However, it has been estimated that up to 30% of dogs with epilepsy do not attain acceptable seizure control despite appropriatedrug therapy, and are considered refractory to treatment. The incidence of refractory epilepsy is similar in humans, with approximately 30% of patients classified as having drug resistant seizures. Furthermore, despite the recent introduction of numerous new antiepileptic medications, the overall incidence of refractory epilepsy has remained fairly consistent in humans. This appears to be the case in dogs as well. Non-medical treatment options are often explored as a means to more effectively treat patients with refractory epilepsy. Listening to Mozarts Sonata for two pianos in D major, K.448 (Mozart K.448) has been shown to have a beneficial effect on several neurological disorders in humans, including epilepsy. The hypothesis set forth in this study is that Mozart K.448 is an effective add-on therapy for dogs with primary epilepsy that are refractory to traditional AED treatments. Study Objective The primary objective of the study is to determine whether or not the playing of Mozart K.448 results in a decrease in seizure frequency in dogs with refractory epilepsy. A secondary objective is to document any adverse effects and owner-perceived changes in quality of life associated with classical music therapy. The findings from this pilot study will provide information on the potential role of music therapy in the treatment of epilepsy in dogs. Results of this study will be utilized to support the design of a larger scale, randomized controlled trial evaluating the effect of music in the treatment of refractory epilepsy in dogs. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? To be eligible for this study your dog must have: - A diagnosis of primary epilepsy based on characteristic signalment and clinical features of the disease (onset of seizures between 1 and 7 years of age, a minimum 1 year history of seizures, normal neurologic exam and normal blood work and urinalysis) - A history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures with currentfrequency of >2 seizures per month - Currently being treated and at a therapeutic level with at least 2 antiepileptic medications What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To be enrolled in this study, you must provide an informed consent for participation. Day 0: Your dog will be evaluated with a full physical and neurologic examination. Blood and urine samples will be collected. If your dog fits the above criteria, they will be formally enrolled. Day 1-90: You will be asked to complete a seizure diary for at least 3 months to calculate monthly seizure frequency. If you dog has an average of >2 seizures per month during this period, your dog will remain enrolled in the study. Day 90-180: You will then be provided a copy of Mozart's Sonata K.488 (compact disc or downloaded version) with instructions on how to conduct music therapy sessions and documentation at home. For 3 months you will be required to administer a music therapy session (21 minutes)twice a day. You will be required to keep a complete daily record. Post completion of the 3 month treatment, you will be asked to return to the veterinary hospital without your dog, to return completed daily record, seizure history and complete a questionnaire on your pet's quality of life.Ashort time after the completion of your dog's treatment period (~30-40 days) you will be contacted to complete a post-study survey. Client Compensation All diagnostics (blood work and urinalysis) will be compensated for enrollment in this study. Client Contact For any questions relating to this study, please contact Julie Nettifee-Osborne (919-513-6812 or Julie_Osborne@ncsu.edu).
current_roster.name: Music as an add-on therapy for refractory canine epilepsy: A pilot study.

current_roster.description: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by the bodys response to a serious infection. It is associated with severe illness, long stays in the hospital and a high risk of death. Although sepsis in cats is less common than in dogs, cats have a higher risk of dying from their infection.Cats with sepsis tend to have low heart rates, low body temperature and stomach pain. It is not known why they develop these clinical signs or why they have lower survival rates compared to people or other companion animals. It is these unique aspects of sepsis in cats that are the basis for our study.We will enroll cats with naturally occurring sepsis and examine multiple facets of the syndrome to provide insights into why they behave differently compared to other species. Our investigators will therefore assess the diagnostic results of these cats to help determine what makes them different to other species and to develop new diagnostic tests and treatments.
current_roster.name: Analyzing Feline Sepsis: Why are Cats Not Small Dogs?

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation Sudden acquired retinal degeneration syndrome (SARDS) is a common cause of sudden, irreversible blindness, affecting predominantly middle-aged female dogs. Affected dogs often have additional signs such as increased appetite, weight gain, increased thirst and urination, similar to dogs with hyperadrenocorticism (Cushings disease). The underlying cause of this condition is not understood. The purpose of this study is to better understand the causes of this disease by examining the presence of self-antibodies in animals with SARDS, and pineal gland function, an important regulator of day/night rhythm. In order to understand SARDS in the context of endocrinopathy, we wish to compare SARDS with confirmed untreated Cushings cases. Our hope is to develop better diagnostic tests to help confirm SARDS at an earlier stage. We are currently enrolling for a pilot treatment trial for SARDS patients as well- more information on request What qualifies my dog for enrollment? Cases with untreated Cushings disease, or cases with a high suspicion of Cushings disease are eligible. We seek pituitary-dependent Cushing's cases, so further testing may be indicated to confirm the diagnosis at the time of enrollment. Any dog receiving systemic immunosuppressive medications will not be eligible. A clear view of the retina myst be possible in both eyes as determined during your visit to NCSU, this may exclude cases with severe corneal disease or advanced cataracts. Dogs must not be receiving treatment for hyperadrenocorticocism. Certain tests must be performed either during the study or prior to enrollment: CBC, serum biochemistry, ACTH stimulation testing, urinalysis, blood pressure measurement. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To be enrolled in this study, you must sign an informed consent. You dog will bescheduled for anappointment at NCSU College of Veterinary Medicine, during that appointment an ophthalmic examination, blood and urine sampling will be performed, and your dog will undergo retinal imaging and electroretinography (a test of retinal function). Client Compensation Cases confirmed at NCSU as having pituitary-dependent hyperadrenocorticism will receive a credit for up to $300 worth of diagnostics and/or medication. Results of all standard tests will be provided. Client Contact For more information on this study, please contact: Dr. Katherine Lunn (kflunn@ncsu.edu), Dr. Freya Mowat (fmmowat@ncsu.edu), Melanie Foster (melanie_foster@ncsu.edu).
current_roster.name: Defining the underlying causes of SARDS in dogs

current_roster.description: Purebred Pug dogs with symptoms of hind limb weakness and ataxia will be evaluated by board-certified neurologists for potential enrollment in the study. The dogs will receive a physical and neurologic examination, and are eligible for enrollment if a neurologic deficit is localized to the T3-L3 spinal cord. Enrolled dogs will receive pre-anesthesia bloodwork screening, and advanced diagnostic imaging (CT and MRI) under anesthesia. Buccal swabs will be collected and tested by the University of Missouri Animal Molecular Genetics Laboratory for genetic predisposition to Degenerative Myelopathy. Owners will provide periodic updates on their dogs condition through telephone consultation and/or re-examination, and postmortem examination (necropsy) will be performed by a board-certified pathologist at the end of the dogs natural life or after euthanasia. In January 2013, a condition termed constrictive myelopathy was reported in 11 adult Pug dogs (J Am Vet Med Assoc 2013; 242:223-229). This degenerative spinal cord disease caused progressive hind limb ataxia (incoordination) and paresis (weakness) in affected dogs, often with urinary and/or fecal incontinence. Imaging studies and surgery revealed fibrous thickening of the dura mater at the thoracolumbar junction, causing spinal cord constriction. The fibrous thickening was thought to be secondary to instability of the vertebrae in the area, which was believed to be associated with hypoplasia or aplasia of caudal articular processes. Another condition reportedly common in Pugs is spinal arachnoid diverticulum (SAD), in which a fluid-filled dilation of the subarachnoid space causes spinal cord compression. The pathology of SAD may also include fibrous thickening of the dura, and since both CM and SAD appear to be common in Pugs, questions arise as to the relationship of the 2 conditions, as well as their relationships to vertebral malformations in the breed. The overall goals of this study are: 1) to determine the underlying pathogenesis (mechanisms) behind CM and SAD; 2) to assess the potential relationship of these 2 diseases; and 3) to assess the potential relationships of these conditions to previously described vertebral malformations (hypoplasia and aplasia of caudal articular processes). Dr. Patterson, a veterinary pathologist, may be contacted regarding postmortem examination of affected Pugs not officially enrolled in the study. A CD containing a MRI, along with medical records and radiology reports, must be available for such dogs. Scheduling and shipping arrangements of refrigerated (not frozen) animals must be discussed in advance, if possible. Dr. Jon Patterson DVM, PhD, Dipl ACVP, Professor 163 Diagnostic Center for Population and Animal Health 4125 Beaumont Road Lansing MI 48910-8107 Phone: (517) 353-9471 E-mail: patter12@msu.edu
current_roster.name: Pug Myelopathy (Constrictive Myelopathy, Spinal Arachnoid Diverticula, and/or  Vertebral Articular Malformations)

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: This trial evaluates the administration and clinical response to a new conjugate of cisplatin chemotherapy, administered in combination with palliative radiation therapy, in dogs with any naturally-occurring, externally-measurable, malignant tumor,which is not amenable to surgical resection for whatever reason. Cisplatin is considered one of the most potent and broad spectrum chemotherapeutic agents; however, is associated with significant side effects. This reformulation of cisplatin into a nanoparticle conjugate has shown promise as a safer, less toxic and efficacious alternative. What does enrollment into this trial involve? Enrolled dogs will be assigned to one of two study arms according to the owners' preference. One arm will receive only the cisplatin conjugate, and the second arm will receive the cisplatin conjugate in combination with radiation therapy. All enrolled dogs will receive the cisplatin conjugate administered directly into the primary tumor on study days 0, 7, 14, and 21, at incrementally increasing doses. The dogs enrolled in the second arm will also concurrently receive four fractions (doses) of radiation therapy to the tumor site once a week, for four weeks. Blood samples will be collected immediately prior to each dose of the cisplatin conjugate and also weekly for three weeks following the final dose. After study day 42 (or sooner if a dog is removed from the study), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional treatment options and/or ongoing monitoring with the owner. Client Compensation: The study covers the cost of the conjugated cisplatin, blood work, urinalysis and recheck exam for dogs enrolled. Owner is responsible for the costs associated with initial pre-enrollment diagnostic work-up and staging.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs with externally accessible malignant tumor

current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED. Malignant gliomas are aggressive cancers of the brain that affect dogs and humans. Temozolomide (TMZ) chemotherapy and radiation are the current standard-of-care therapies for gliomas. Although TMZ has been demonstrated to slow tumor progression, gliomas tend to become resistant to it over time. One way glioma cells develop TMZ resistance is by producing a protein called connexin-43. To combat resistance, we have developed a chemotherapy drug that inhibits connexin-43 and makes glioma cells more responsive to TMZ treatment. While TMZ is a systemic drug which is taken orally, the anti-connexin-43 infusion is a sustained release formulation delivered directly to the tumor site. Anti-connexin-43 has undergone extensive safety testing and is currently being used in Phase III human clinical trials for wound healing indications. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED. Please contact Mindy Quigley at vettrials@vt.edu if you have any questions.
current_roster.name: Combating chemo resistance in dogs with glioma brain tumors

current_roster.description: This study is designed to demonstrate the safety of Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine, Live Listeria Vector, an immunotherapeutic under evaluation as an aid in the treatment of dogs diagnosed with osteosarcoma. This product is not yet licensed. Dogs that have undergone amputation and received 4-6 doses of carboplatin may be screened and, if enrolled, will receive three doses of the immunotherapeutic.
current_roster.name: Field Safety Testing of Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine, Live Listeria Vector

current_roster.description: Background: Lameness is a condition associated with important economic losses in beef cattle operations. According to recent studies, approximately 85% of lameness in beef cattle originate in the foot. Delayed treatment of foot lameness can lead to septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint (DIJ) and associated anatomical structures. Digital infection in cattle causes severe chronic pain and is an animal welfare concern. Diagnosis of septic arthritis of the DIJ in cattle is uncommonly performed in the field and most cases are diagnosed by radiographic imaging or arthrocentesis at referral veterinary teaching hospitals or specialized practices. Objective: To evaluate if the duration of lameness, the number of antibiotic treatments received before veterinary evaluation, the degree of lameness, and the presence or not of asymmetric swelling in the affected foot are risk factors for infection of the distal interphalangeal joint and/or associated anatomic structures in single-foot lame beef cattle. What does enrollment into this trial involve? To be enrolled in this study, all cattle must be seen by the Livestock Service at KSU VHC for evaluation. Evaluation cannot be done by Field Services. Owners will be expected to sign a client consent form before their cattle can enter the study. All cattle will undergo a complete lameness examination including lameness scoring. During the lameness examination, the presence of swelling at the coronary band of the affected foot will be evaluated and the symmetry (even distribution) of the swelling will be determined in both digits. Arthrocentesis of the DIJ for cytologic analysis of synovial fluid will be performed in addition to radiographs of the affected foot. All study related-activities will be completed during one visit to the VHC. Client Compensation: The study covers the cost associated with radiographs, arthrocentesis and cytology. The owner is responsible for the cost of the initial lameness examination and all treatments.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for beef cattle with one-foot lameness

current_roster.description: Melanoma (cancer of pigment producing cells in the body) is malignant cancer of both humans and animals. The main treatment for the cancer in the dog is surgery. Unfortunately, a large number of these melanomas undergo metastasis (spread) following surgery, shortening survival. This occurs even when surgery is done early and the tumor is removed in its entirety. In an effort to improve survival, radiation and chemotherapy have been tried as adjunct (together with surgery) treatment. Some marginal improvements in survival have been achieved but results are still poor. Because melanomas have been known to induce an immune reaction in people and animals, developing a melanoma cancer vaccine holds promise as an adjunct treatment to surgery. In a previously completed study in normal dogs, we showed that a vaccine containing a melanoma antigen could induce an antibody response in dogs. We also showed that the vaccine could stimulate peripheral blood natural killer cells to kill melanoma target cells in a laboratory test. The current research is totest the vaccine in dogs withmalignant melanoma.
current_roster.name: Vaccine Study for Dogs with Malignant Melanoma

current_roster.description: Idiopathic chylothorax remains a challenging condition in dogs despite recent advances in minimally invasive surgery for treatment of the condition. Combinations of interventions including thoracic duct ligation, pericardectomy, omentalization and cisterna chyli ablation have been used for some years but are associated with prolonged anesthesia and surgical time and little information is available on the physiological responses to the interventions being performed. Thoracic duct ligation has been traditionally combined with pericardectomy by many surgeons including the authors even in dogs without any evidence of pericardial disease or constrictive pericardial physiology. Medicine and veterinary medicine is entering an era of personalized medicine and such a "one solution fits all" approach may be subjecting many dogs that lack significant pericardial disease to an unnecessary procedure that has potential for morbidity as well as cost to the owner. In this study dogs will undergo thorough pre-operative investigation of any potential pericardial disease using measurement of right atrial pressure profiles and echocardiography. Dogs with substantive evidence of pericardial disease or constrictive physiology will be excluded from the study. Those without evidence of pericardial disease or constrictive physiology will be entered into the study and will undergo a computed tomography lymphangiogram (CTLA) the day before surgery. This study will allow pre-operative evaluation of the thoracic duct anatomy in the caudal thorax. The following day the dogs will undergo a thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation using intraoperative near-infrared fluorescence or methylene blue to assist in intraoperative identification of all branches of the thoracic duct system. Immediately after termination of the surgery the dogs will be returned to the CT unit for a follow-up CTLA to confirm complete cessation of contrast flow through the thoracic duct system. Dogs will be followed clinically to evaluate whether resolution of chylothorax occurs using post-operative radiographs at 2 and 4 weeks post-operatively. At 3-6 months dogs will be placed under anesthesia again for CTLA to evaluate the physiological reponse to thoracic duct ligation. The aims of the study are to 1) assess the effect of complete confirmed cessation of thoracic ductal flow within the caudal thorax on chyle production in client-owned dogs diagnosed with idiopathic chylothorax and 2) to assess the development of lymphatic collateral circulation and to document the direction of chyle flow post thoracic duct ligation in dogs with idiopathic chylothorax.The central hypotheses for the study are that complete cessation of chyle flow through the thoracic duct system will result in resolution of chylothrax in client-owned dogs with naturally occurring idiopathic chylothorax and that chylous redistribution will occur through the development of lymphaticovenous anastomoses formed primarily within the peritoneal cavity.
current_roster.name: Effect of complete occlusion of thoracic duct chyle flow on outcomes in dogs with idiopathic chylothorax

current_roster.description: This study will investigate response and outcome data in canine patients treated with either single-agent mitoxantrone or mitoxantrone with 5-fluorouracil for first-line therapy for transitional cell carcinoma.
current_roster.name: Mitoxantrone versus combining mitoxantrone with 5-fluorouracil for the first-line treatment of canine transitional cell carcinoma:

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a naturally derived supplement made of both plant and green-lipped mussel extracts; these extracts contain omega-3 fatty acids and other anti-inflammatory compounds which are thought to decrease inflammation and joint pain when given orally. This study will involve three clinic visits over the course of six weeks. Dogs will be randomly assigned to receive the supplement or a placebo. Eligibility: Dogs at least 3 years of age weighing at least 10kg (22lbs) Additional eligibility criteria determined based on questionnaires Ability to attend all study visits Ability to administer oral medications
current_roster.name: A Study Evaluating an All-Natural Supplement in Dogs with Arthritis

current_roster.description: Canine degenerative myelopathy (DM) is an inherited, progressive spinal cord disease. Clinical signs are initially very mild and refer to a thoracolumbar spinal cord disease. Over time the clinical signs progress to lower motor neuron signs in the pelvic limbs, paraplegia, and later loss of motor function including in front legs with brainstem signs in the end stage. The mean duration of clinical course ranges from 7.7 to 20 months. Breed and also owner decision are important factors for survival since many dogs are euthanized when they reach a non-ambulatory condition. The goal of this study is to explore the therapeutic benefit of specific gene silencing of the superoxide dismutase (SOD1) in dogs diagnosed with DM. We would likely study disease progression of dogs with naturally occurring degenerative myelopathy treated with adeno associated virus AAV-Rh10-miR anti-SOD1 injected into the subarachnoid space in comparison to untreated control dogs. Our hypothesis is that silencing of the SOD1 gene will increase time of ambulatory function of treated compared to control dogs.
current_roster.name: Gene Silencing Therapy for Canine Degenerative Myelopathy

We need spayed female dogs that have been diagnosed with urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence and have failed standard therapy (i.e., Proin, DES). Eligible participants will have autologous progenitor muscle cells injected surgically in an attempt to restore the urethral sphincter function. Dogs with anatomical abnormalities that cause incontinence are not eligible. Enrolled participants will be monitored for 2 years and receive all study procedures free of charge.

This will be a single-arm, open-label, clinical trial (no placebo) All dogs enrolled will receive rabacfosadine every 21 days for up to 5 cycles. Asparaginase will be given concurrently with rabacfosadine for the first 2 treatments only.Rabacfosadine will be provided at no cost to owners. current_roster.description: Canine lymphoma is the most common type of canine neoplastic disease, and the most common cancer derived from blood cells in dogs. Very little research has been conducted to substantiate the potential beneficial roles of nutrition in the management of cancer in dogs thus far. Therefore, additional research to find nutritional modifications and functional ingredients that provide benefit for canine cancer patients is required. The new diet formulations being evaluated in this study have been shown to be well digested and to support normal health and function in healthy adult dogs. Similar formulations have been shown to provide health benefits such as enhanced intestinal health and chronic disease prevention in many species; however, the positive effects in canine cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy have yet to be determined. The goal of this study is to determine the tolerability and digestibility of this diet in dogs with lymphoma undergoing treatment with the CHOP chemotherapy protocol. We will also investigate metabolic changes that occur in dogs being treated with chemotherapy. We are currently enrolling patients into the control group, so no diet change will occur.
current_roster.name: Feasibility and tolerability of a complete and novel canine diet in canine patients treated for lymphoma
