current_roster.description: The aim of this study is to assess the effects of cannabinoids on seizure frequency in poorly controlled epileptic dogs. Epilepsy is reported to effect 0.5 to 5.7% of the canine population, making it the most common neurologic condition in dogs. Currently, a limited number of antiepileptic drugs (AED) are available for treating epilepsy in dogs. Cannabis-based treatments of epilepsy have received substantial attention in the media lately, including anecdotal reports of major improvements in pediatric epilepsy. Cannabidiol (CBD), a prominent non-psychotropic cannabinoid, has been shown to have anti-convulsant properties, offering a safe alternative to the psychoactive constituent, THC, in the treatment of canine epilepsy. The American Kennel Club is sponsoring a study at Colorado State Universitys College Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences to assess the effects of CBD on canine epilepsy.
current_roster.name: The Effect of Cannabidiol on Seizure Activity in Epileptic Dogs

current_roster.description: Small cell GI lymphoma is commonly diagnosed in older cats and recommended treatment of this cancer is an oral chemotherapy drug called chlorambucil in combination with prednisolone or prednisone. Despite the wide use of chlorambucil in cats, the pharmacokinetic parameters, i.e. how the body absorbs, metabolizes and eliminates the drug, have not been previously studied in cats. Knowledge of the pharmacokinetic parameters of chlorambucil in this population of older, cancer-bearing cats is critical to understand why some cats experience side effects with chlorambucil therapy and determine if variability in the metabolism of chlorambucil contributes to treatment failure. This proposal seeks to gain information regarding the PK parameters and metabolite profile of chlorambucil in cats with small cell lymphoid malignancies.
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetics of Oral Chlorambucil in Cancer-Bearing Cats

current_roster.description: Historically, no type of imaging has been capable of accurately diagnosing the spread of metastatic hemangiosarcoma or prostate cancer to bone and soft tissues in the dog. For humans suffering from prostate cancer at Johns Hopkins University, 18F DCFPYL, a small molecule inhibitor of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) has been shown to have high uptake at sites of metastases in patients with prostate cancer. This radiotracer is currently undergoing rigorous phase III clinical trials in people in order to gain FDA-approval. In dogs, staging tests and therapies have been inconsistently applied to canine patients with hemangiosarcoma and prostate cancer because these cancers can be difficult to diagnose. Canine hemangiosarcoma and prostate cancer express PSMA. The current study goal is to confirm that 18F DCFPYL PET-CT offers an improved sensitivity for the early detection of metastatic hemangiosarcoma and prostate cancer. This study involves a diagnostic test only. However, earlier diagnosis of hemangiosarcoma or prostate cancer will allow us to work on improved therapies for this disease; which will be the goal of a follow up study.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of 18F DCFPYL PET-CT for the Assessment of Hemangiosarcoma or Prostate Cancer

current_roster.description: Hyperparathyroidism is a disease whereby overactive parathyroid glands produce unchecked amounts of parathyroid hormone that leads to excessive levels of circulating calcium which can have serious consequences. Primary hyperparathyroidism in dogs can be successfully treated by removal or ablation of the affected glands. These procedures are relatively simple, associated with low morbidity and require only minimal aftercare; howevr, the most common complication following treatment is post-procedural low calcium levels (hypocalcemia). This occurs due to secondary physiologic suppression of PTH release from the remaining normal parathyroid glands. Although this suppression is typically transient, hypocalcemia can be a serious complication that if left untreated, can result in excitation of the nervous system (i.e. tetany and seizures) and life threatening cardiac abnormalities. Currently, there are no reliable markers or indicators to determine which dogs undergoing treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism will develop hypocalcemia. Current standard of care is to hospitalize all dogs post-procedurally to monitor serum calcium levels. This study aims to provide veterinarians with an ability to predict the likelihood of the development of this complication and consequently intervene pre or post-procedurally to reduce or eliminate its incidence.
current_roster.name: Uncovering mechanisms of post-procedural hypocalcemia in dogs with hyperparathyroidism

current_roster.description: **THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED *** Purpose To determine if the application of high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) can stimulate an anti-tumor immune response in dogs diagnosed with solid tumors. Background Solid tumors (soft tissue sarcomas, carcinomas, and mast cell tumors) are some of the most common tumors in dogs. Surgery has traditionally been the most effective therapy, although complete tumor removal isnt always possible. In some cases, a tumor may be surgically removed, but it could still recur at the surgical site or in a distant site like lymph node or lung. Successful treatment can sometimes include radiation therapy and/or chemotherapy. All of these treatments carry potential side effects.Because of the limitations of current treatment, immunotherapy is an active area of research. We are investigating the use of high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), which uses precisely-targeted heating as a non-invasive means to destroy cancer cells. The use of HIFU has been shown in humans to activate the immune system, leading to more effective destruction of cancer cells. We are testing whether focused ultrasound will also activate the immune system in dogs with solid tumors, enhancing the current approach to treatment. Eligibility Cytologically confirmed diagnosis of carcinoma, soft tissue sarcoma, or mast cell tumor Lesion size and location targetable using focused ultrasound Expected survival over 4 weeks without treatment Exclusion Criteria Solid tumors inside the chest or abdominal cavity Solid tumors that have invaded the surrounding bone (e.g. jaw or sinus tumors) Prior radiation therapy or surgery within the past three weeks Corticosteroids or other immune modulating therapies within the past three weeks Study Design To determine whether your dog is eligible for the study, a complete physical exam, lab work, and a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis are required. Depending on the location of the tumor, we will recommend appropriate diagnostic imaging. The cost of these procedures is typically $700-1,200 and is not covered by the study.Once enrolled, your dog will undergo a CT scan, a surgical biopsy, the HIFU treatment, and a surgery to remove the tumor. HIFU treatment will be performed on Day 0 (usually a Monday). HIFU will be applied to the tumor under general anesthesia. Your dog will be hospitalized under 24 hour monitoring until Friday of the same week. Blood samples will be collected daily to assess your pets immune response and definitive surgery to remove the tumor will take place on Friday. Your dog will then recover in the ICU and will be discharged as is standard for patients.Your pet will need to return to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital 2 weeks after the definitive surgery for recheck and suture removal. At the recheck visit, your pet will have a physical exam, and additional diagnostics if indicated. Compensation The cost of the required screening procedures is typically $700-1,200 and is not covered by the study. Once the pretreatment evaluation is performed at your cost, the study will cover the expenses for the subsequent lab-work, CTs, tumor biopsy and histopathology, the HIFU treatment, the cost of the hospital stay and associated costs, the cost of surgery and the cost of the scheduled recheck visit. The typical average cost of surgical resection of a tumor in our hospital is $3,000 to $5,000. You are responsible for any other clinical fees associated with medical complications of the HIFU therapy or other medical problems.
current_roster.name: Focused ultrasound to treat soft tissue sarcoma, mast cell tumors, and carcinomas

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a new combination therapy for the treatment of dogs with meningioma. This combination consists of oral hydroxyurea, a conventional chemotherapy drug used to treat brain tumors, and PAC-1, a new chemotherapy drug which has been shown to selectively kill cancer cells in recent clinical trials. This combination has not been evaluated in dogs with meningioma before. Dogs will be randomly assigned to receive either hydroxyurea or PAC-1 for seven days, after which all dogs will receive both medications orally. Dogs enrolled in this clinical trial will have six visits to Penn Vet as well as three overnight visits to the National Institute of Health in Bethesda, MD. All of these visits are required for study participation. At the final study visit dogs will have surgery at Penn Vet to remove the brain tumor.
current_roster.name: CBTC001: Study of two oral medications in treatment of canine brain tumors

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to identify the clinical feasibility, safety spectrum and both local and systemic benefits of non-thermal Nano-Pulse Stimulation in the treatment of stage I and II oral melanoma in dogs. Data from this study may be used to develop additional companion animal trials and to obtain FDA device approval for use in veterinary medicine.
current_roster.name: The Use of Nanosecond Pulses to Treat Canine Oral Melanoma

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is the most commonly diagnosed hematopoietic neoplasm in cats and is often treated with chemotherapy. Hope Veterinary Specialists is participating in a clinical study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of rabacfosadine in cats with lymphoma. Rabacfosadine is a novel, anti-proliferative chemotherapeutic designed to target and kill lymphoma cells and has been conditionally approved by the FDA to treat lymphoma in dogs (TANOVEA-CA1). The objective of this clinical study is to determine the dose-limiting toxicity and maximum tolerated dose of rabacfosadine in cats with lymphoma. A secondary objective is to evaluate the efficacy as determined by overall response rate and progression-free survival in treated cats.
current_roster.name: Tanovea (rabacfosadine) for feline lymphoma

current_roster.description: The absence of oxygen within a tumor is associated with resistance to radiation therapy as well as increased likelihood of regional recurrence and distant spread, and often leads to poor treatment outcome and prognosis. This study is evaluating a method that combines ultrasound and oxygen delivery vehicles which will allow us to locally deliver oxygen to tumor tissue during radiation treatment and enhance tumor radiation sensitivity. This novel approach has the potential to substantially improve treatment for soft tissue sarcoma by both increasing tumor response to radiation, and reducing the radiation dose required for the treatment to be effective. The purpose of this study is to evaluate tumor control in dogs treated with 5 fractions of stereotactic radiation therapy with or without the addition of oxygenated microbubbles.
current_roster.name: Treating tumoral hypoxia via ultrasound-guided oxygen release for improving radiation therapy

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: The purpose of this project is to characterize the most common type(s) of kidney disease in Dalmatian dogs in order to identify a possible genetic cause of the disease. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? A Dalmatian diagnosed with kidney disease, along with its close relatives, is eligible for participation. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will participate in this study on one occasion at either your regular veterinary office or a specialty veterinary practice. This visit may take approximately one hour. Urine and blood will be collected by a veterinarian or veterinary technician using minimal restraint. Both blood and urine will be used for diagnostic testing, and DNA will also be isolated from the blood for genetic analysis in order to detect possible mutations that are causing the disease. Client Compensation The owner of any participating animal will be financially responsible for costs associated with the treatment of complications or accidental injuries associated with this study.
current_roster.name: Characterization of Renal Disease in Dalmatians

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Neuropathic pain is a complex, chronic pain state that can develop secondary to osteoarthritis in people, leading to significant loss of function with substantial healthcare costs. Spontaneous torn knee ligament (Cranial cruciate ligament rupture-CCL) is the most common cause of pelvic limb lameness in the dog, and causes secondary osteoarthritis in the stifle. It is commonly corrected with tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO) surgery. Neuroanalgesic procedures including epidurals and direct nerve blocks are common prior to surgical correction of cruciate disease. This investigation will evaluate the efficacy of three common neuroanalgesic procedures on short term perioperative pain management and evaluate chronic sensory threshold as a measure of neuropathic pain in the dog. If dogs are shown to have chronic neuropathic pain with osteoarthritis, spontaneous CCL rupture in the dog may serve as a naturally occurring animal model for studying neuropathic pain in both dogs and humans. Which patients are eligible to participate in this study? Healthy dogs with a lameness due totorn knee ligament (cranial cruciate rupture) undergoing TPLO surgery as recommended by a board certified surgeon with no other orthopedic or neurologic disease. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? Your pet will be evaluated by a surgeon and deemed an appropriate candidate for a TPLO. Once enrolled, gait analysis will be obtained by having your pet walk over a pressure mat prior to and after surgery. Additionally, von Frey anesthesiometry data will be collected using an electronic system placed on the top of the paw before and after surgery. Your pet will receive one of three pain management protocols (epidural, nerve block, intravenous pain medications), which are all currently standard of care and all used routinely for dogs undergoing TPLO. Pain scores will be evaluated while in hospital. When your pet returns for 2 week suture removal, and recheck with radiographs 8 weeks after surgery, the walkway test and von Frey assessment will be repeated as part of their recheck examination. Your dog will participate in the trial for 8 weeks. This includes the first 24 hours after surgery, while your pet would normally be in hospital for a TPLO, the second is at their routine 2 week recheck for suture removal, and a final visit is the recheck examination at 8 weeks post-operatively. Client Compensation Clients participating in this study will be given approximately $200 of services. This includes the cost of the 8 week recheck examination fee and the standard recheck radiographs.
current_roster.name: Pain management in dogs undergoing torn knee ligament surgery

current_roster.description: Diabetes mellitus is an important health problem in both dogs and people. Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is caused by destruction of cells in the pancreas. This leads to a lack of a hormone produced in the pancreas called insulin that is responsible for decreasing blood sugar levels. T1D in people is caused by an attack by the bodys own immune system on cells in the pancreas (aka autoimmunity). Despite years of research, the exact reason for this immune attack is not known. Canine diabetes is similar to T1D in people and may also be due to autoimmunity, however research so far has not given a clear answer. Also, detailed studies of pancreatic function and metabolism over time have not been performed in diabetic dogs. In order to determine the cause of diabetes in dogs and to determine whether these dogs can be used as a model for the disease in people, more research is needed. The purpose of this study is to learn more about metabolism and immune function in diabetic dogsat diagnosis andover time. Both diabetic and healthy control dogs will be recruited. The study will consist of 3 visits over a one year time period (0, 6, and 12 months). At each visit, a physical exam will be performed and blood will be collected for baseline blood work (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis). Blood samples will also be frozen for future analysis of blood markers. Dogs will also undergo a mixed meal tolerance test. This test involves consuming a liquid meal (Ensure Plus) and then collection of periodic blood samples for 90 minutes following the meal to evaluate the function of the pancreas.
current_roster.name: Studying canine diabetes over time

current_roster.description: Diabetes mellitus is an important health problem in both dogs and people. Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is caused by destruction of cells in the pancreas. This leads to a lack of a hormone produced in the pancreas called insulin that is responsible for decreasing blood sugar levels. T1D in people is caused by an attack by the bodys own immune system on cells in the pancreas (aka autoimmunity). Despite years of research, the exact reason for this immune attack is not known. Canine diabetes is similar to T1D in people and may also be due to autoimmunity, however research so far has not given a clear answer. We believe that detecting dogs that are at risk of diabetes, or dogs that are in the early stages of disease, may be key to discovering why dogs get diabetes and whether early treatment may beneficial. The purpose of this study is to identify dogs of breeds at high risk for diabetes and follow them over time to look for blood markers that may help predict future diabetes or identify dogs with very early diabetes. Adult dogs of dogs breeds at high risk for diabetes will be included. Your dog will need to visit the UF Small Animal Hospital every 6 months for up to 4 years. The following procedures will be performed at each visit: a brief medical history, medication history, and physical exam (including body weight and body condition score). Blood sample (up to 10 mL (2 teaspoons)) from the vein of your dog. Blood collected at the visits will be used to test blood sugar and markers of blood glucose over time (eg. fructosamine or other tests). You will receive the results of the blood sugar immediately; the fructosamine and other blood glucose marker results will not be available immediately, but will be provided in the future. Blood will also be frozen and banked for use in future testing of diabetes biomarkers. If at any time point during the study your dogs fructosamine is above the normal range, your dog will enter the "high risk group" and we will ask that you bring your dog back for a mixed meal tolerance test to evaluate the ability of your dogs pancreas to produce insulin after a meal. This involves feeding a liquid meal (Ensure plus) and collecting periodic blood samples for 90 minutes following the meal. Dogs in the "high risk" group will be asked to return for study visits every 3 months instead of every 6 months.
current_roster.name: Identification of pre-diabetes in dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the activity of new immunotherapy agents for the treatment of osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. The ultimate goal is to find drug combinations that either stop the growth of tumor spread or that actually shrink the spread by stimulating the immune system to control the cancer Your dog will undergo several blood tests/diagnostics prior to and during the course of treatment to monitor blood counts and collect plasma/blood for additional genetic analyses. These blood draws amount to approximately 2 tbsp. of blood at each visit. Your dogs treatment for osteosarcoma will involve the administration of two drugs orally at home to help control the cancer: toceranib (Palladia) and losartan. Palladia received FDA approval to treat mast cell tumors in dogs in 2009. Since then it has been used to treat several types of cancer in dogs. Losartan is a generic version of a drug called Cozaar which is used to treat high blood pressure in people. Both drugs have been tested extensively in dogs with cancer either alone or in combination to ensure that the dose being given is safe.
current_roster.name: Optimizing Novel Immunotherapy Combinations Targeting the Tumor Microenvironment in Canine Spontaneous Osteosarcoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Cheryl London, D.V.M., Ph.D., DACVIM (Oncology), Professor in Comparative Oncology

current_roster.description: While surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy can be very effective for many dogs with cancer, new treatments are needed to deal with patients for whom these approaches do not work. Cancer treatment strategies designed to use the patients immune system to control the cancer hold great promise. One form of immunotherapy that is being investigated extensively in humans is called activated T cell therapy, where immune cells from the patient are removed, activated in the laboratory, with or without genetic modification, and then returned to the patient. The product in this study is called TBX-3440 and is a similar cell therapy approach (using a patients own immune cells); these cells are treated in the laboratory for a short time with a protein that allows them to react better once they are given back to the patient. The primary objective of this pilot study is to evaluate the early safety profile, immune system effects and antitumor activity of this investigational therapy given to dogs with cancer.
current_roster.name: Preclinical Evaluation of TBX-3440 in Dogs with Neoplasia

current_roster.description: Radiotherapy (RT)-induced dermatitis (radiodermatitis) is a painful inflammatory skin lesion that occurs in 95% of cancer patients treated with radiotherapy. Severe radiodermatitis causes painful skin erosion and ulceration, pain that can become resistant to standard pain medications, and can be a dose-limiting factor of cancer therapy. The involvement of multiple pathological processes prohibits treating radiodermatitis as burn wounds or atopic dermatitis. Currently, there is no effective treatment for radiodermatitis. We are working with a colleague at CU Denver who has developed a novel drug that has been shown to be effective in the treatment of radiation-induced oral inflammation in mice. The goal of this study is to determine if radiation dermatitis is diminished when treated with the novel drug compared to a placebo and to determine appropriate dosing required to observe an effect. Additionally, we will monitor for any unexpected toxicity associated with the treatment.
current_roster.name: Therapeutic Intervention of Radiation-Induced Dermatitis for Canine Cancers Treated with Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Gastrointestinal toxicity (GI) is a common side effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy administration primarily due to apoptosis of rapidly dividing enterocytes. Consequences include, treatment delays, dose reductions, impaired quality of life, increased expense, discontinuation and poorer patient outcomes. Severity of GI toxicity varies greatly, ranging from mild to severe. Measurement of Cytokeratin 18 (CK18), an intracellular structural protein released during epithelial apoptosis, and Alpha1-Proteinase Inhibitor (1-PI) in feces provides a non-invasive mechanism for evaluation of compromise to intestinal mucosa integrity. Evaluation in these biomarkers as predictors for chemotherapy-induced GI toxicity have been described in human cancer patients, but little is known about their utility in tumor-bearing dogs. The purpose of the trial is to identify non-invasive biomarkers that may help us predict patients at increased risk for chemotherapy-induced gastrointestinal mucositis, and offer them more aggressive prophylactic treatment and supportive care to limit the impact on quality of life and treatment outcome. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? Eligible patients (any breed of dog) must meet all of the following criteria: Dogs must have a diagnosis of a bone tumor (osteosarcoma) involving a limb. The owner must be willing to pursue amputation followed by chemotherapy (carboplatin x 4 doses). Dogs must be greater than 1 year of age and weigh at least 5 kg. No vomiting or diarrhea 2 weeks prior to enrollment. No evidence of pulmonary metastatic disease. Dogs must have adequate organ function as indicated by standard laboratory tests (complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis). Dogs must be medically healthy with no clinically significant physical findings upon examination, medical history, and clinical laboratory profile. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? This is a prospective clinical trial for dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma that have undergone an amputation and will be receiving carboplatin. Whole blood will be collected from your dog at the designated study visits for plasma CK18 levels. You will be required to collect a fecal sample from your dog and bring it with you at the designated study visits. Study visits will occur on day -14, 0, 7 and 21 of the study. Owners will be responsible for maintaining an owner diary throughout the study to document clinical signs associated with gastrointestinal mucositis. Client Compensation: You are responsible for all standard of care procedures performed prior to and including amputation. Following this, there are no additional costs to you associated with enrolling in the clinical trial. The costs of the first and second carboplatin chemotherapy, maropitant, chemotherapy administration, and PCCBC will be covered. Following the conclusion of the study (at day 21), any additional treatment that you elect to pursue will be your financial responsibility. This means that you will be responsible for all costs associated with carboplatin treatment # 3, carboplatin treatment # 4, and re-staging costs. If your dog develops toxicity associated with the administration of carboplatin at any treatment visit (carboplatin # 1 - 4) you are responsible for the cost associated with supportive care. You are responsible for the cost of supportive medications that will be discharged following each chemotherapy treatment to be used if needed.
current_roster.name: Gastrointestinal permeability in dogs with bone tumors receiving Carboplatin

current_roster.description: Primary angle closure glaucoma is a common disease in dogs, affecting approximately 1% of the population. Currently, even though there are multiple medical and surgical tools to treat glaucoma in dogs, the disease still results in permanent blindness in all dogs. This is due, in part, to the unpredictability and severity of the pressure spikes associated with this disease. Due to defects in the drainage apparatus of the eye, these spikes are often so severe that once they occur, they result in permanent, irreversible damage to vision in a matter of hours. And at this point, all the medical and surgical options are useless in recovering vision. If the timing of the spikes in intraocular pressure could be predicted, then the medical and surgical tools available could be implemented before these spikes occur, dramatically increasing the time dogs remain with vision.We believe there are measureable changes in the structure of drainage apparatus of the eye preceding an intraocular pressure spike and retinal damage. And these changes progress in a predictable and sequential manner, allowing for the approximate time until an intraocular pressure spike occurs to be determined. We will perform serial, detailed measurements of the drainage apparatus of the eye and correlate changes in these measurements to the time until a pressure spike occurs or retinal damage is detected. We will also evaluate the pupillary reflex to show it can be used as a sensitive indicator of the retinal damage caused by glaucoma.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Dogs with Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of a new diet specially formulated to dissolve struvite stones in the bladders of cats. Struvite stones are among the most common types of bladder stones that can form in cats. They can cause irritation and pain and can lead to blood in the urine and possible obstruction of the urethra (the urine outflow tract). Standard treatment is to either remove them surgically or dissolve them by altering the pH and other characteristics of the cats urine. This is done through medications or by exclusively feeding a diet that is specially formulated to promote stone dissolution. Most struvite stones can be dissolved in 1 3 months with strict dietary compliance.In this study, cats with suspected struvite stones will be provided with a nutritionally balanced and complete test diet. They will be monitored every 2 weeks for radiographic evidence of stone dissolution. In addition, acceptance of the diet and weight will also be monitored. For cats that fail to have stone dissolution occur after 56 days on the test diet, a cystotomy will be performed and the stones sent out for analysis.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Cats with Struvite Cystoliths

current_roster.description: Feline oral squamous cell carcinoma represents approximately 10% of all feline tumors. This is a locally aggressive tumor in the mouth that causes ulceration and bone destruction which can significantly impact the quality of life of affected cats. Treatment of this disease with surgery, chemotherapy or conventional radiation therapy has not been successful. Technological advances in radiation therapy over the past ten years have greatly improved the treatment outcome for many tumor types. Stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT) uses computerized treatment planning and computer guidance to sculpt the radiation dose to tumors. This allows the dose to normal tissues to be reduced so that treatment can be delivered more safely and rapidly. A recent evaluation of cats treated with SRT at CSU resulted in rapid improvement in clinical signs with minimal short term side effects, however some patients experienced long term effects including fracture of the bone, fibrosis of the tongue, oronasal fistula (communication between nose and mouth). Palladia (toceranib phosphate) is a newer drug that is approved for the treatment in canine mast cell tumors. Palladia has been studied in cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma and shown a positive impact on survival time with minimal toxicity. There is anecdotal information about the combined use of radiation and Palladia for treatment of oral squamous cell carcinoma in cats suggesting it would be well tolerated; however, dose and type of radiation are not consistent and outcome data are not reported. We hope to advance our knowledge of these difficult tumors and improve quality of life for your cat and other cats. The goal of this study is to assess the outcome of cats treated with Palladia and an SRT protocol. A secondary goal is to assess blood levels of Palladia in tumor bearing cats and determine if levels reached have anti-tumor activity.
current_roster.name: Combination Palladia and Stereotactic Radiation Therapy for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: Nationwide study! The Purpose of this study is to evaluate bacterial populations in the gastrointestinal tract of dogs with epilepsy and compare those to normal dogs.
current_roster.name: Is Gut dysbiosis associated with canine idiopathic epilepsy?

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate a minimally invasive surgical approach to the spinal cord to address intervertebral disc herniation. Background Traditionally, the standard approach to surgically accessing the spinal cord in dogs with intervertebral disc herniations involves a significant amount of soft tissue dissection and retraction. Many studies in people have shown that patients that have minimally invasive spinal surgery are more comfortable after surgery in comparison to patients undergoing open approaches. Studies also show that there are shorter hospital stays, fewer complications like blood loss and infection, and faster recovery times associated with minimally invasive spinal surgery. Our goal is to test whether a minimally invasive technique can result in less pain, quicker recovery, fewer complications, smaller skin incisions and less time in the hospital for dogs undergoing spinal surgery. This study is funded by theVeterinary Memorial Fund. Compensation The estimated cost for a traditional hemilaminectomy at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital is typically $4,500-$5,500. Owners of enrolled dogs will have a $500 credit applied to their bill, bringing their out-of-pocket estimate to $4,000-5,000. Enrolled dogs will also receive a postoperative MRI, a conversion to a traditional, open approach (if necessary), and 2-week recheck at no cost.Clients will be responsible for the cost for the surgery and recovery in the ICU, any after-hours emergency fees, and preoperative blood work. Owners are also responsible for the cost of an initial MRI to confirm diagnosis. MRI can be performed at our hospital or a referring facility. Any additional exam or therapy required for the treatment of the enrolled dog is not covered. Contact Melanie Dobbins, Neurology Case Coordinator Phone: 540-231-4137 | Email:mrc@vt.edu Mindy Quigley, Clinical Trials Coordinator Office Phone: 540-231-1363 | Email:mindyq@vt.edu
current_roster.name: Minimally invasive spinal surgery for dogs with disc herniation

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Degenerative lumbosacral stenosis (DLSS), also known as cauda equina syndrome, is a common disease affecting the lower spine of dogs, primarily large breed dogs. DLSS frequently affects Labrador retrievers causing compression of nerves in caudal lumbar region (cauda equina), nerve roots and vessels leading to pain and neurologic deficits. DLSS is typically diagnosed using advanced imaging, such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), however the correlation between clinical and imaging findings is complex, and newer methods may lead to advances and refinement in the diagnosis of the disease. We propose to characterize DLSS in Labradors using a combination of a novel kinematic MRI technique in combination with electrodiagnostic tests. In order to fully comprehend the disease, we need to perform thorough advanced imaging and functional tests of the lumbar spine of healthy and affected Labrador retrievers. This study will be the foundation for future therapeutic and genetic studies of DLSS in dogs. What qualifies my pet for enrollment in this in this trial? This clinical trial will evaluate clinically affected dogs and dogs with no signs of degenerative lumbosacral stenosis. To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: Clinical signs compatible with DLSS (lower back pain, reluctance to rise, not willing to jump) Minimal concurrent orthopedic abnormalities Radiographs of the lumbar spine with no evidence of orthopedic disease or neoplasia. Inclusion criteria for unaffected Labrador Retrievers will be the absence of clinical signs compatible with DLSS, orthopedic disease and x-rays of the lumbar spine with no apparent abnormalities. What does enrolling my pet in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will undergo the following procedures: Blood work (CBC and chemistry) Lumbosacral radiographs Electrodiagnostics MRI CT Client Compensation Dogs in the "normal" group will have all costs covered by the study. Dogs in the "affected" group will have the cost of the MRI, electrodiagnostics, CT and anesthesia covered by the study.
current_roster.name: Characterization of lumbosacral disease in Labrador retrievers

current_roster.description: Cats will wear a collar with a silicone tag at home for 7 days. We will collect the silicone tags to evaluate exposure and body burden of certain chemicals in house cats with hyperthyroidism. We will be collecting a one-time a blood sample from the hyperthyroid cats.
current_roster.name: Validation of silicone tags as measure of OPFR & PBDE exposure/body burden in house cats

current_roster.description: This is a clinical trial of an experimental therapy to treat skin tumors in horses. Horses commonly develop skintumors and these tumors frequently are infiltrative and large, making them difficult to remove with surgery or othertypes of therapy. In some cases, tumors of these types recur after surgery, requiring repeated treatments tocontrol their size. The proposed new therapy, high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE) kills tumor cellsby applying high voltage, high frequency electrical energy directly to tumors. The energy causes gaps to form intumor cell membranes, and these cell leak and die. This therapy has been used on several clinical patients andhas shown to be effective in controlling tumors. A current variant of electroporation is used to deliver chemotherapy to tumors, however the mono-polarity of the waveform causes intense muscle contractions in the horses which require that they be anesthetized and laid on their side.H-FIREuses an alternating polarity waveform to eliminate these muscle contractions and enable treatment of patients without general anesthesia.
current_roster.name: Treatment of Large Skin Tumors in Horses using High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation

current_roster.description: Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) is a common disease that affects all breeds of dogs and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Intravascular hemolysis of erythrocytes in IMHA is caused by complement activation and is often fatal. No current treatments target complement activation in canine IMHA. Our preliminary data show that human C1 esterase (C1-INH) reduces canine complement-mediated hemolysis by more than 80% in vitro. We recently completed an MAF sponsored pharmacokinetic analysis of an FDA licensed formulation of C1-INH,Ruconest in dogs. This confirmed that C1-INH is safe to administer to dogs, and effectively inhibits canine complement mediated hemolysis ex-vivo. We expect that intravenous (IV)administration of C1-INH will ablate complement activation in dogs with intravascular IMHA and propose to evaluate the efficacy of this drug in a randomized controlled trial (RCT).We hypothesize that intravenous C1-INH reduces intravascular hemolysis in dogs with IMHA.
current_roster.name: C1 Inhibitor in Canine Intravascular Hemolysis (C1INCH) Trial

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in humans worldwide, but primary lung tumors are relatively uncommon in veterinary patients. While smoking has been strongly associated with the development of lung cancer in people, no definitive risk factors have been identified for dogs. Approximately 85% of lung tumors in dogs are bronchoalveolar carcinomas, whereas the most common types of lung tumor in humans are non-small cell cancers, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. The most common clinical sign reported in dogs with primary lung tumors is coughing; however, up to 30% of these tumors are found incidentally, with no apparent clinical signs. These tumors are generally visualized using chest X-rays and/or CT scan. The gold standard to obtain a definitive diagnosis is surgery to remove the lung lobe followed by histopathology. Cytological diagnosis may be attempted prior to surgery via fine needle aspirate of the lung mass, usually with ultrasound or CT guidance. Reported success rates of diagnosis using this technique range from 38% to 90% in dogs. A company we are working with has developed a novel device that aims to provide bronchoscopic access to peripheral lung tumors while providing real-time visualization of the tumor. This device could provide a novel, minimally invasive way to aspirate lung tumors in dogs, with a potentially higher possibility of obtaining a pre-surgical diagnosis. This technology could also be used in humans with peripheral lung tumors in the future. The goal of this study is to assess the ability to accurately visualize and obtain aspirates of lung tumors using a novel access/visualization and needle aspiration device in dogs with suspected primary lung tumors. At the first study visit, a blood sample will be submitted to determine your dogs blood type. Your dog will then be put under anesthesia for a CT scan of the skull and thorax. Immediately following the CT, an ultrasound-guided aspirate of the tumor will be performed to obtain a diagnosis. Once the CT images have been reviewed, we will be able to determine definitively if your dog is eligible to continue on the study. If so, your dog will return for the second visit within 3 weeks of visit 1 (length of time depends on scheduling conflicts with the study team). At this visit, a sample of your dogs breath will be collected using a special mask, and then your dog will be anesthetized for the bronchoscopy procedure. Aspirates of the tumor will be obtained with the novel device and the results will be compared to those from the ultrasound-guided aspirates. The 1st 3 dogs enrolled into the study will be kept in the hospital overnight for monitoring. If those dogs all do well, then your dog will be able to go home the same day assuming it is deemed safe for him/her to do so.
current_roster.name: Use of a novel navigation system to obtain transbronchial aspirates of peripheral lung tumors in canine model

current_roster.description: Gallbladder disease is common in cats and dogs and can lead to significant illness and even death. The routine surgical approach to remove the gallbladder usually requires surgeons to open the intestine (duodenotomy) to ensure the common bile duct draining the liver is open before removing the gallbladder. This adds risk as this intestinal incision can leak after surgery requiring an emergency surgery. This procedure also add time to the surgical procedure and to the anesthetic event which can be deleterious to unstable or ill patients.
current_roster.tagline: Dye to assist with gallbladder removal
current_roster.name: Evaluating a new dye to help with gallbladder removal
current_roster.top_investigator: Nicole Buote, DVM, DACVS-SA, Associate Professor

current_roster.description: Radiation therapy is a fundamental treatment option for patients with cancer. Not only does radiation therapy kill the cancer cells which are directly targeted by the radiation; radiation exposure also serves as an immune stimulus that promotes anti-tumor responses within the tumor and throughout the body, leading to enhanced local and metastatic cancer control. This anti-tumor immune response has been shown to be boosted when radiotherapy is combined with immunotherapy. Combining radiation therapy and immunotherapy is an exciting new approach which has generated optimism for improved outcomes for patients diagnosed with aggressive cancers. The goal of this study is to determine the effects of treating canine cancer patients with a combination of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) with either an injectable immunotherapy or vehicle control. Once enrolled, dogs will have blood samples collected for study purposes and then will be anesthetized for a CT scan for radiation planning. While under anesthesia, a small piece of tumor will be collected for the study. Dogs will then return to start SBRT, which will be given in 3-5 treatments every day or every other day (depending on tumor type and location). At the time of the last radiation treatment, the tumor will be injected with either the immunotherapy drugs or a placebo. Dogs will then return two weeks after completing radiation for blood work (complete blood count and chemistry profile), study blood collection, and sedation for tumor biopsy. The study is complete after this visit.
current_roster.name: Integrating immunotherapy with radiotherapy to improve tumor control for canine cancer patients

current_roster.description: Temozolomide (TMZ) is an oral prodrug of dacarbazine, an injectable chemotherapy agent given over several hours. An oral formulation is generally more convenient, and TMZ appears to have fewer blood-related side effects compared to dacarbazine, although it does cause vomiting if not given with a meal 20-30 minutes post-administration. Temozolomide use has been published in dogs with melanoma, refractory lymphoma and glioma. However, the optimal dose has not been established, and TMZ has not been used in other tumor types that have responsiveness to dacarbazine, such as hemangiosarcoma and histiocytic sarcoma. This trial aims to better define the optimal dose of this drug, defined as the maximally tolerated dose (MTD), which is the dose that is expected to have the most effectiveness against the tumor without unmanageable side effects. A secondary goal is to determine the response in various tumor types.
current_roster.name: Dosing and effectiveness of oral temozolamide in melanoma, lymphoma, histiocytic sarcoma, and hemangiosarcoma in dogs

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: This research study aims to assess the feasibility and safety of the intraoperative 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA)-mediated photodynamic therapy (PDT) procedure immediately after surgical resection, in canine patients with a newly-diagnosed probable high-grade glioma (HGG) based on clinical and radiological criteria and in whom surgical resection is achievable.
current_roster.name: Treating Brain Cancer in Dogs with Surgey and Photodynamic Therapy

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Purpose: Natural killer cells (NK cells) are a type of white blood cell, and a component of the natural defense system (immune system) that control several types of tumors and infections by limiting their spread.In recent years, the use of treatments that boosts the bodys natural defense system (immunotherapy), have made significant advances in people, and there is evidence to suggest that bone tumors can be susceptible to this type of treatments.The purpose of this study is to establish evidence of effectiveness of natural killer (NK) cells from healthy dogs given in combination with chemotherapy to dogs with bone tumors (osteosarcoma). What qualifies my pet for this trial? Eligible patients (any breed of dog) must meet all of the following criteria: Confirmed osteosarcoma Weight at least 25kg Measurable disease that is amenable to surgical removal via amputation (No evidence of cancer spread based upon physical exam and thoracic CT). ONLY newly diagnosed dogs are eligible with no prior therapy for osteosarcoma (conventional or metronomic chemotherapy, ionizing radiation, bisphosphonates). Dogs receiving analgesics including NSAIDs, gabapentin, tramadol, or other will be eligible for study inclusion Dogs must undergo full post-mortem examination (necropsy) if they die while on study What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? Dogs enrolled in this study will undergo standard of care treatment for osteosarcoma. This includes amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on an every 21 day schedule. A dose of NK cells will be given (Intravenously) to your dog 24 hours prior to limb amputation. Blood samples will be obtained immediately prior to the NK cell infusion, 8 hour post infusion, immediately prior to surgery and 24 hours after NK cell infusion. NK cells will be infused post-operatively at 2-4 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours post-amputation (total of 3 doses) and additional blood samples obtained. On weeks dogs are not receiving carboplatin they will receive a dose of NK cells intravenously. After completion of all 4 cycles of adjuvant carboplatin/ NK cell therapy, dogs will be restaged and confirmed as having no evidence of disease based on thorough physical examination and 3-view thoracic radiographs. Follow-up visits every 8 weeks are required after completion of chemo-immunotherapy for physical examination, CBC, correlative sample collections, and thoracic radiographic examination. Client Compensation Owners are responsible for all costs associated with determining trial eligibility (e.g. initial office visit, bone aspirate or biopsy, cytology/histopathology, screening bloodwork) amputation and supportive care medications.For eligible, enrolled dogs, the clinical trial will cover all scheduled study costs (carboplatin chemotherapy, NK cell infusions, CBC, chemistry profile, and recheck thoracic radiographs). In the event of side effects/toxicity, up to $500/patient will be provided to manage these events.
current_roster.name: Natural killer (NK) cell therapy for canine bone cancer

current_roster.description: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a prevalent condition in dogs. Advanced CKD is associated with hyporexia, nausea, and vomiting. These gastrointestinal (GI) signs are typically attributed to direct injury to the gastric mucosa as a result of uremic toxins and gastric hyperacidity. However, gastric mineralization, gastric gland atrophy, and hypergastrinemia, rather than gastric ulceration, are more often observed in dogs with CKD. Gastric pH studies have not been performed in dogs with CKD and the contribution of hypergastrinemia and gastric hyperacidity, if present, to clinical signs of GI upset in dogs with CKD are unknown. Yet it is common for dogs with advanced CKD to receive gastric acid suppressant drugs in spite of the fact that they often receive >3 additional daily medications. This daily "pill burden" likely leads to reduced medication compliance, a reduction in quality of life, and disruption of the human-animal bond. Moreover, the administration of the acid suppressants to dogs with CKD may not be benign. Studies have not been performed to determine if gastric acid suppressants are warranted in dogs with CKD. Accordingly, the proposed study would be the first to evaluate gastric pH and serum gastrin in dogs with CKD to determine if gastric hyperacidity is associated with CKD in dogs. 48-hour continuous intragastric pH monitoring will be performed, via radiographic guided placement of a non-invasive pH monitoring capsule, in 19 aged-matched, healthy dogs and 19 dogs with IRIS late stage III or IV CKD. Mean intragastric pH and serum gastrin will be compared between dogs. We anticipate that this study will help to determine if gastric hyperacidity exists in dogs with CKD. Accordingly, the specific objectives of this proposal are to: (1) Evaluate mean intragastric pH, mean percent pH distribution, and serums gastrin in dogs with IRIS late stage III or IV CKD compared to age-matched healthy control dogs. And, (2) to determine if serum gastrin is increased in dogs with naturally occurring CKD. Our study results will help to support a recommendation for or against acid suppressant therapy in dogs with CKD.
current_roster.name: THE BURNING TRUTH: Gastric Hyperacidity in Canine CKD? A pilot study.

current_roster.description: Rapamycin is an immunosuppressive that has significant anticancer activity. It has been approved for use in several human cancer indications. Anecdotal reports of Rapamycin activity in canine hemangiosarcoma and other cancer types have been made over several years, however its activity has been unpredictable. Recent genomic analysis of these cancers provides a scientific basis for this sporadic activity based on the existence of several genotypes that may each be uniquely responsive to Rapamycin. Based on its reported tolerability in dogs (alone and in combination with chemotherapy) it is reasonable to now ask if Rapamycin may improve treatment outcomes for dogs with cancer. This study will be evaluating the tolerability of a novel formulation of Rapamycin. The latest version of this study seeks to do so with a novel, oil-based formulation of the drug. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.tagline: Pharmacokinetics of a Novel Oil-Blend Rapamycin Formulation in Dogs with Cancer
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetics of a Novel Oil-Blend Rapamycin Formulation in Dogs with Cancer

current_roster.description: Sorafenib is a cancer treatment that has been approved for use in human renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. It has a distinctive inhibitory activity that may be especially valuable at preventing the harmful resistance mechanism known as evasive resistance (the promotion of metastasis despite drug activity against the primary tumor) in numerous cancer types. We have previously reported on the tolerability and hints of clinical activity of Sorafenib in dogs with cancer. This background provides a rationale for the further study of Sorafenib in dogs with cancer. In this study we seek to define an optimal dosing schedule for Sorafenib and will also assess its tolerability in dogs with cancer.
current_roster.name: Sorafenib for the Treatment of Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description: Evaluating the safety and efficacy of rabacfosadine (Tanovea-CA1) when combined with doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide and prednisone (T-CHOP) in dogs with previously untreated spontaneous multicentric lymphoma.
current_roster.name: Efficacy of Rabafosadine, Vincristine, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin and Prednisone (T-CHOP) in Dogs with Untreated Lymphoma.

current_roster.description: The Dog Aging Project (DAP) is a large-scale longitudinal study (minimum of 5 years) of aging in companion dogs that will directly advance canine health, support the human-animal bond, and change the paradigm of geroscience research for all species. The goal of the Dog Aging Project is to identify the genetic and environmental factors that influence healthy aging, and to understand how these factors shape aging, through a nationwide canine study. The DAP will include the study of 10,000 companion dogs, living at home with their owners. The dogs will represent a diversity of breeds and ages, both males and females, sterilized and intact, and having a full range of health status. They will come from geographically diverse homes, and from owners of diverse ethnic backgrounds and socioeconomic status. The Longitudinal Study Population will be divided into three subcohorts, including a Foundation Cohort of 8900 dogs, a Precision Cohort of 925 dogs, and an Intervention Cohort of 350 dogs, which will partially overlap with the Precision Cohort dogs. This expansive and complex project is designed as four supportive cores and four interactive projects, each of whose functions are critical to overall success. Administration, data management, cohort recruitment and retention, and environmental data gathering will all be accomplished by the cores. Project 1, the clinical project, will analyze new measures of the phenotype of canine aging that have never before been attempted on a large scale, and will assess these novel metrics as predictors of mortality and health span. Project 2 will collect and analyze genomic data, Project 3 will collect and analyze systems biology data (metabolome, microbiome, and epigenome) to understand the mechanisms by which genome and environment exert their effects; and Project 4 is a randomized controlled clinical trial of rapamycin. The Specific Aims of Project 1 include:1) Develop and evaluate a Canine Comorbidity Index (CCI) that can be used as a predictor of mortality and clinical outcomes, and a marker of aging in the companion dog. Successful completion of this Aim will provide a practical tool that is useful for standardizing descriptions of canine comorbidity, and that elucidates the relationship between acquisition of comorbidities and risk of mortality; 2) Develop and evaluate a Canine Frailty Score (CFS) with components that are prognostic for health outcomes in the companion dog and can be used as markers of aging. Frailty in aging humans is associated with negative health outcomes. The ability to describe aging companion dogs against a standardized CFS will improve accuracy in comparisons of clinical status among dogs of varying genetic background and environment and shed light on the concept of health span versus lifespan;3) Determine whether or not age-related chronic activation of the inflammatory response (inflammaging)mediates the progression of aging in the companion dog, by developing and evaluating a Canine Inflammaging Panel (CIP). Inflammaging is an emerging field, and while widely thought to be critical in aging, its downstream effects may take decades to appear in humans. The ability to explore relationships between inflammatory measures and health outcomes. The Specific Aims of Project 2 include:1) Generate high-resolution genetic data and enabling resources for canine genomics. Although whole genome sequence (WGS) data are rapidly accumulating for phenotypically diverse dogs, to date these data have not been analyzed with a single unified bioinformatics pipeline, which limits their overall utility, as variant calls are sensitive to many analysis parameters. Thus, this Specific Aim will analyze over 700existing WGS and call variants with a unified analysis pipeline to more comprehensively identify canine genomic variation and characterize patterns of linkage disequilibrium, which will enable more powerful genetic association studies. The sequencing data will also enable customization of SNP genotyping panels to maximize power.2) Comprehensively investigate the genetic architecture of lifespan and age-related disease phenotypes. These studies will provide an unparalleled opportunity to systematically study the genetic basis of aging and age-related traits in dogs, including common comorbid disease phenotypes, cellular and immune related traits, and measures of frailty developed in Project 1, and systems biology phenotypes developed in Project3.3) Investigate the genetic architecture of centenarian dogs. Studies of exceptional longevity provide unique insights into the determinants of healthy aging. This Specific Aim will leverage the participating veterinary community to identify canine centenarians, dogs who are within the top 0.1% of lifespan for their size class, and test the hypotheses that rare and common variation contribute to exceptional longevity. The Specific Aims of Project 3 include:1) Identify and genetically map metabolomic predictors of lifespan in companion dogs. The metabolome represents a complex ensemble of small molecules that provides a biochemically defined mechanistic link between genotype and downstream phenotype. We will test the hypothesis that genetic and environmental influences on aging within and among dog breeds are a result of variation in the baseline levels and/or longitudinal trajectories of the metabolome, and that observed effects of age on metabolites in lab models are conserved in companion dogs.2) Determine the effect of aging on the gut microbiome, and identify aspects of the microbiome that predict variation in aging within and among breeds. The canine microbiome shares much similarity with the human microbiome, but little is known about the relationship between the microbiome and genotype-specific aging. Using novel tools that we have developed, we will test our hypotheses that the microbiome is predictive of breed-specific aging, and that compositional shifts in the microbiome are indicative of specific aging-related phenotypes, laying the groundwork for microbiome-based diagnostic tools for canine age-related disease.3) Develop and implement an epigenetic clock for aging in companion dogs. Recent work in humans suggests that epigenetic modifications of chromatin accessibility are associated with age, and diagnostic of health status. This Specific Aim will develop and test an epigenetic biological clock for the companion dog. If we find an epigenetic biological clock, we will test the novel hypothesis that the clock ticks faster in shorter lived breeds, and through collaborations with Core D and Projects 1, 3 and 4, will seek to identify the mechanisms by which epigenetic variation acts as a biological clock.4) Develop a multi-omic systems biology model of aging in dogs. The three -omic domains studied in Aims 1-3 for this Project, combined with the genetic domain studied in Project 2, form a complex web of interactions. This Specific Aim will develop and evaluate several multi-omic comprehensive models of aging. The Specific Aims of Project 4 are: 1) Determine the effects of rapamycin treatment on lifespan, disease incidence, and co-morbidity in middle aged, large breed companion dogs. There are abundant data that rapamycin can extend lifespan and improve health span in laboratory mice. Using the Intervention Cohort, this aim will create the Test of Rapamycin In Aging Dogs (TRIAD) trial, a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial in which healthy, middle-aged dogs are treated with either placebo or rapamycin (sirolimus) for a three-year period. A sufficient number of dogs will be enrolled to ensure that at least 350 complete the study (i.e., are evaluatedat the final follow-up at three years, or die while enrolled). This Aim will measure the effects of a rapamycin on survival to three years, the primary endpoint of the TRIAD RCT.2) Assess the ability of rapamycin to enhance cardiac function in middle-aged companion dogs. Studies in mice show that rapamycin improves cardiac function in middle-age animals in as few as ten weeks. Ourpublished preliminary data suggest that ten weeks of rapamycin treatment similarly improves cardiac function in middle-aged dogs. Specific Aim 2 will test the effect of rapamycin treatment on left ventricular cardiac function through regular electrocardiogram and echocardiography. Independent of the outcome of Specific Aim 1, documentation of long-term improvements in cardiac function following rapamycin treatment in dogs will bring us closer to similar human applications in the future, while immediately providing a clinical approach to alleviating these specific age-associated functional declines in dogs.3) Define the effects of rapamycin on the serum metabolome, gut microbiome, and epigenome in middle-aged companion dogs. Aim 3 will determine the effects of rapamycin treatment in dogs on the serum metabolome, the gut microbiome and the peripheral blood mononuclear cell epigenome. Through our close collaboration with Project 3, we will gain insights into the effects of rapamycin on whole animal physiology, greatly expanding the impact of Aims 1 and 2 by generating
current_roster.name: The Dog Aging Project

current_roster.description: This study aims to compare fecal microbiota transplantation and probiotics as treatments for acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS) in dogs. Prior to entry in this study, your dog must have a diagnosis of acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome, based on initial screening blood work and short duration (<48 hours) of clinical signs and negative screening for infectious disease. If your dog takes part in the study, he/she will have blood drawn for measurement of red and white blood cell counts (CBC), serum biochemistry panel (electrolytes and organ function) for inclusion, and intestinal permeability (LPS) at the time of admission to the hospital, after 72 hours of hospitalization (CBC, LPS), and at a 14-day recheck (LPS). Urine concentration will be measured in some dogs to estimate dehydration. We will also collect fecal samples on the day of admission to the hospital, after 72 hours of hospitalization, and after 14 days to look at bacterial population changes (dysbiosis index). For this clinical trial, your dog will be enrolled into one of three treatment groups: 1) probiotics with standard-of-care therapy, 2) fecal transplant with standard-of-care therapy, or 3) standard-of-care therapy without probiotics or fecal transplant. Your dog will receive either a daily probiotic medication or placebo in powder form for the 14 days of the study and either a single fecal microbiota transplant or saline enema on the day of admission. Your dog will also receive standard-of-care therapy, including IV fluids and anti-emetics, as indicated. As a participant in this study, blood will be drawn using either a needle and syringe or butterfly catheter from a jugular or peripheral vein as deemed appropriate, and the samples submitted for testing. The procedures will be performed using standard protocol. Naturally-voided fecal samples will be collected in the hospital for infectious disease testing. For fecal transplant (FMT), prepared stool from healthy donor dogs will be administered once as an enema using a red rubber catheter.
current_roster.name: Pilot Study Comparison of Fecal Microbiota Transplant versus Probiotics as Treatment for Acute Hemorrhagic Diarrhea Syndrome in Do

current_roster.description: Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant tumor arising from the secretory epithelium of the walls of the bilateral anal sacs. AGASACA accounts for 17% of perianal tumors and 2% of all canine skin tumors in this species. AGASACA displays aggressive biologic behavior. It is both locally invasive and highly metastatic, with a reported metastatic rate of between 26 and 96%. Metastasis to the regional lymph nodes is frequently reported early in the course of the disease, whilst metastasis to distant sites, such as the lungs, liver, spleen and bone (and other heart, mediastinum, pancreas), is typically observed months to years later. Multiple treatment modalities have been utilized in the management of AGASACA, including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, electrochemotherapy, and various combinations thereof. Currently, there is no widely accepted 'standard of care' for canine AGASACA, other than to recommend surgical resection of the primary tumor, and to consider adjuvant therapies. Surgery alone is often inadequate in controlling either local and/or metastatic disease, although a more recent paper suggests that surgical outcomes may differ depending upon the stage of the patient, 11 and the extent of surgery performed. However, with surgery alone, local recurrence has been documented in 20 to 45% of dogs with AGASACA , and metastasis in 26 to 96% of cases. The primary purpose of this study is to evaluate the clinical impact of temozolomide in dogs diagnosed with apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA). Temozolomide is a chemotherapy drug used in human oncology to treat brain tumors, malignant melanoma, and more recently several different neuroendocrine tumors. Whilst AGASACA in dogs is not embryologically of neuroendocrine origin, it does share many characteristics with those tumor types, and can also respond to similar medications. The use of temozolomide in dogs has been previously reported for brain tumors, lymphoma, and malignant melanoma. Given that there is not a standard-of-care chemotherapy protocol for AGASACA, the investigators hope that temozolomide will demonstrate significant biologic activity for this tumor type, and become part of this diseases clinical management. All enrolled dogs will ideally receive 4 cycles (1 cycle = 5 days) of temozolomide, administered by mouth, at home, on study days 0/1 through 5, days 28 through 32, days 56 through 60, and days 84 through 88 (i.e. 1 cycle every month). Hospital visits will be scheduled immediately prior to each 5 day cycle of temozolomide, on study days 0/1, 28, 56, and 84. Appropriate chemotherapy recheck visits will also be scheduled for monitoring purposes 1 week after each 5 day cycle of temozolomide, on study days 12, 39, 67, and 95. A final study recheck will be scheduled on study day 112. Blood samples,+/- urine samples, will be collected at most of these recheck visits. Re-staging imaging, including thoracic radiographs (chest x-rays) and abdominal ultrasound, will be undertaken on study days 56 and 112. Participation in this study will cease at day 112.
current_roster.name: Biologic activity and safety of temozolomide in dogs with naturally-occurring apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma: a pilot stud

current_roster.description: Background Insulinoma, the most common pancreatic tumor in dogs, can cause potentially life-threatening hypoglycemia (low glucose). Insulinoma also aggressively metastasizes (spreads to other parts of the body), frequently to the liver and lymph nodes. Treatment of both primary and metastatic disease is essential for improving prognosis. Current treatment options for canine insulinoma are limited and may not provide long-term disease control. Novel treatment approaches are needed to improve long-term outcomes for dogs with this disease. High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) is a novel non-thermal technique that precisely destroys tumor cells while sparing normal organs. H-FIRE also potentially induces an immune response against the tumor, which may help to guard against metastatic disease development. This study proposes to evaluate the feasibility and safety of treating canine insulinoma with H-FIRE, and to evaluate the tumor immune response to H-FIRE.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE) for treatment of canine insulinoma

current_roster.description: Equine herpesvirus-1 (EHV-1) is very widespread in horse populations. Therefore, effective management is key to limiting the impact of EHV-1 on horse health and the horse industry. Test results for current detection methods, such as PCR and virus isolation, can take multiple days before they become available, meaning that the virus could spread before being identified. A novel DNA sequencing technology, the MinION nanopore sequencer, offers a new tool to rapidly detect and differentiate EHV-1 as a stall-side diagnostic and in field applications, with naturally occurring disease and outbreaks. For this study, we are seeking nasal swab samples from horses that are showing clinical signs consistent with EHV-1 and from horses that are from the same location as suspect EHV-1 shedding horses. Clinical signs consistent with EHV-1 may include nasal discharge, fever, ataxia, urine dribbling, decreased perineal tone, late-term abortions, or recumbency. This study involves confirming the presence of EHV-1 in the sample, as well as DNA sequencing the virus and assessing the molecular profile. If the horse is suspected to be shedding EHV-1, PCR testing can be performed and diagnostic results can be reported to the submitting veterinarian at no charge if an email is provided in the submission form. To submit samples, please contact Nadia Saklou (nsaklou@vt.edu) with EHV-1 Study in subject line. Sample submission forms, shipping labels and permits will be sent to you via email.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a rapid DNA sequencing technology for the detection of Equine Herpesvirus-1 in equine nasal secretions

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the pain relief effects of novel pain medication, tapentadol, in dogs with bone tumors of the limb. Currently there are limited effective pain medications for treatment of dogs with this disease. What qualifies my pet for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: Have a suspected or confirmed bone tumor (osteosarcoma) of a limb. Be on another oral pain medication (NSAID such as Rimadyl, Previcox or Deramaxx) for at least 3 days prior to starting the study. Dogs with a fracture of their bone tumor or dogs not on another oral pain medication (NSAID) cannot be enrolled in the study. What does enrolling my pet in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will undergo the following procedures: Prior to treatment with the study drug, you will be asked to fill out a baseline pain survey. A veterinarian will also perform a pain assessment and your dog will walk on a pressure sensitive walkway to more objectively assess his or her lameness. Your dog will be sent home with 5 days of the pain medication, after which time your dog will return to the hospital for a repeat of the surveys and procedures described above. Client Compensation Following completion of the study on Day 5, you will receive a $500 credit to be used towards further procedures (diagnostics and/or treatments for your dog's cancer) at OSU VMC.
current_roster.name: Novel anti-cancer drug for dogs with bone tumors (osteosarcoma) that has spread to their lungs

current_roster.description: Septic peritonitis is a common diagnosis in dogs and usually develops secondary to the rupture of a segment of intestine. This condition necessitates immediate presentation to the emergency room for surgical treatment. Surgery is then followed by antibiotic therapy. There are variable recommendations around the most appropriate duration to continues antibiotics following surgery. Previous studies have shown the prolonged use of antibiotics, especially multiple antibiotics, significantly increases the potential for the development of antibiotic resistant strains of bacteria. Human studies have shown that procalcitonin (PCT) concentrations are increased in patients with sepsis and it also strongly correlates with mortality in these patients. Additionally, investigators have evaluated a PCT-guided algorithm in human medicine for the de-escalation of antibiotic use, which led to decreases in length of hospital stay and the overall duration of antibiotic therapy. The results of this work highlights PCT as a promising biomarker for monitoring the response of sepsis to antibiotic treatment. This study seeks to evaluate the PCT levels in dogs with septic peritonitis as well as in dogs undergoing abdominal surgery for non-septic reasons (intestinal obstruction) to develop a PCT-guided antibiotic treatment algorithm for dogs similar to what has been developed in humans. Another significant challenge with sepsis is its initial diagnosis. Numerous studies have shown the the rapid diagnosis and implementation of antibiotics is paramount for the treatment of sepsis. There are currently no available diagnostics with the potential to provide a confirmed diagnosis of sepsis with a short enough turn-around time to be clinically useful. The current gold standard is to submit blood samples to a laboratory for culture analysis, which typically takes 3-5 days to obtain the results. This study will be collecting blood samples from dogs with sepsis at the time of diagnosis and will then perform Next Generation Sequencing to determine the most common bacterial pathogens in the blood of dogs with sepsis. These pathogens can then be used to develop a rapid point-of-care diagnostic that could be performed within the hospital to provide a diagnosis of sepsis in a time frame that would be clinically useful. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.name: Use of Procalcitonin for Monitor Sepsis Treatment Response and Genetic Sequencing to Develop Novel Sepsis Diagnostics

current_roster.description: Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is a frequently diagnosed condition in cats and is commonly treated with insulin therapy. The management of uncomplicated DM in cats requires significant medicalization, including frequent office visits, hospitalization, and frequent subcutaneous injections of insulin. All of this medical intervention is contrary to the instincts of cats, who would prefer to be at home. Since many cats have some component of type II diabetes, it is reasonable to ask if a dietary innovation that provides fat loss and other metabolic normalization could reverse the diabetic state in cats and induce an insulin remission. A new dry food diet has been shown to reduce body fat while maintaining lean muscle mass in cats. Furthermore, it may decrease insulin needs. Accordingly, the following clinical study now seeks to determine if feeding this new diet without concurrent insulin therapy can induce insulin remission in cats with uncomplicated DM.
current_roster.name: Diet to replace Insulin Administration as a Better and Effective Treatment In Clinical (DIABETIC) Cats

current_roster.description: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate responses to a standardized protocol using Immunocidin as a palliative therapy and to assess quality of life (QOL) outcomes in dogs diagnosed with solid tumors that are surgically removed before start of the therapy. The information from this trial will be used to develop a palliative care option for dogs whose owners can not afford chemotherapy or elect not to pursue other treatment modalities after the tumors are surgically removed. The main goal of this palliative therapy is to minimize the pets discomfort and improve his/her overall quality of life.
current_roster.name: Use of Immunocidin for palliative therapy in dogs diagnosed with solid tumors

current_roster.description:
Purpose: 
To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and immune effects of using a novel non-thermal ablation technique, high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE), for treating canine lung tumors. Background Canine lung tumors can occur as primary or metastatic tumors. New treatment options are needed for these types of tumors, as patient outcomes are often poor, and survival times have improved little over several decades.

High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) is a novel non-thermal technique that precisely ablates tumors while sparing critical structures.
