If an early clinical sign/phenotype can be identified, an opportunity may exist to design future studies to initiate early therapeutic intervention with immunomodulatory therapy as a means to more effectively treat PDE. Our objective is to identify neurological exam abnormalities in Pugs with high genomic risk for developing PDE, before the onset of the advanced clinical signs normally associated with the disease. We hypothesize that such an early clinical finding will not be present in a control population of dogs without a genetic risk for PDE. For at risk pugs that have exam findings consistent with PDE, a brain MRI and CSF analysis will be performed. If abnormalities consistent with PDE are found, then immunomodulatory therapy using an allogenic stem cell preparation will be administered and the pugs will be followed over a three-year period.
current_roster.tagline: STEEP
current_roster.name: Stem cells for Early Encephalitis in Pugs (STEEP)

current_roster.description: The goals of this study are to evaluate a newly developed questionnaire to assess pain and clinical signs associated with CM/SM in dogs and to evaluate how well a novel veterinary pain management product might treat the condition.
current_roster.tagline: CHASE Questionnaire*
current_roster.name: CHASE Questionnaire* to Assess the Safety and Efficacy of a Novel Pain Management Product in Dogs

current_roster.description: The cranial cruciate ligament is located in the stifle (knee) and provides stability to the joint. Injuries to the cranial cruciate ligament occur commonly in dogs and can lead to instability of the stifle joint. Surgery is often needed to correct this instability, however there are limited treatment options for owners who would like to try and pursue non-surgical treatment options.A new gel-like compound for veterinary use in dogs has been developed for injection into the joints of dogs suffering from various joint diseases. The compound mimics the properties of normal cartilage in the joint, thereby providing a cushioning effect and reducing cartilage grinding. Previous anecdotal use of the product in the stifle joints of dogs with suspected cranial cruciate injuries has suggested that it may provide some clinical benefit without the need for surgery. This study now seeks to investigate whether this potential clinical benefit is able to be demonstrated in a larger group of dogs.
current_roster.name: Intra-articular Injection of Cushioning Particles into the Stifle Joint of Dogs with Suspected Cruciate Ligament Injury

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917(EcN)) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine/piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer - also known as urothelial carcinoma.

To determine eligibility for this study, a basic screening visit including a physical exam, blood work, chest X-rays, a fecal exam for parasites, urinalysis, and potentially a genetic test for breeds (shepherds, sheepdogs, collies, old English sheepdogs) at high risk for carrying a mutation that increases the risk of side effects with some chemotherapy drugs will be conducted. All dogs enrolled will receive standard treatment for bladder cancer including vinblastine (a chemotherapeutic delivered intravenously) and piroxicam (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug given daily by mouth). Half the dogs enrolled in this study will be assigned to receive a probiotic (given daily by mouth) in addition to the standard-of-care therapy.

The other half of the dogs will be assigned to receive a placebo (given daily by mouth). Dogs will then undergo a standard treatment regime that includes bloodwork weekly to monitor for low white blood cell counts and IV infusions of vinblastine every 2 weeks unless contraindicated. On the first and last day of the trial, dogs will also undergo sedation/anesthesia for ultrasound and tumor measurement, cystoscopy (visualization of the inside of the bladder), biopsy (tissue collection) from the tumor, and urine collection from the bladder. Owners will be asked to provide free-catch urine and stool samples from their dog every 2 weeks and asked to complete regular questionnaires and logs of the dog's clinical signs and behavior. Owners will also be asked to provide follow-up urine and fecal samples 8 weeks after the trial conclusion.


Client Compensation:

For dogs that meet enrollment criteria and enroll in this study, screening, and subsequent medical management of your dog's bladder cancer for 8 weeks or up to 4 rounds of chemotherapy will be covered at no cost to the owner/agent. The probiotic/placebo will also be provided free of charge for the duration of the study(approximately 8 weeks or for up to 4 rounds of chemotherapy). Limited funding is also available to cover adverse events secondary to the treatment protocol and in accordance with your veterinary team's recommendations. Treatment for following the conditions will be covered as part of this clinical trial during the clinical trial period: Neutropenia, urinary tract infections (UTI) and UTI workups, vomiting/diarrhea. The owner/agent is financially responsible for all veterinary costs unrelated to bladder cancer management (e.g. food, heartworm medication, medications for other conditions). Owners are also financially responsible for all costs associated with bladder cancer management beyond the trial (e.g. after 8 weeks of treatment or 4 rounds of chemotherapy) and for diagnostics and treatments associated with presumed tumor progression. Owners are also financially responsible for adverse events or injuries unrelated to bladder cancer treatment/management.
current_roster.tagline: Probiome Canine Bladder Cancer Clinical Trial
current_roster.name: Probiome for Canine Bladder Cancer

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine / piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer - also known as urothelial carcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). We will evaluate tumor response, clinical side effects, and quality of life as part of this study. Additionally, we will evaluate immune response and characterize the stool and urine microbiome and metabolome to understand the potential effects of the probiotic. Our broader goal is to improve cancer care and outcomes in dogs with bladder cancer.
current_roster.tagline: Probiome Trial for dogs with Bladder Cancer
current_roster.name: Probiome Trial: Can probiotics improve outcomes in canine bladder cancer?

current_roster.description: Diarrhea is a common problem in dogs and is frequently treated with diet change, anti-diarrheal medications, or probiotics. Intestinal dysbiosis is a disruption in the normal healthy bacterial population in the intestinal tract and may contribute to the development of diarrhea. One approach to improve and treat diarrhea is to correct the altered balance of bacteria, using specific live bacteria, referred to as a probiotic (non-specific live bacteria are found in yogurt). A San Diego-based probiotic manufacturer has expressed interest in evaluating their 3-bacterial strain probiotic as a therapeutic product that can be used to treat clinical conditions in companion animals. This pilot clinical trial will assess if the 3-strain probiotic will improve diarrhea of any underlying cause and/or improve our measurement of altered bacterial populations (i.e., the fecal dysbiosis index). This pilot study will determine whether further development of this 3-strain probiotic is reasonable.
current_roster.name: Pilot study of a novel therapeutic probiotic in dogs with diarrhea and intestinal dysbiosis.

The study design and treatment are presented below.A total of 50 or more cats will be enrolled from approximately 8 sites in order to have at least 45evaluable cats completing the study. Cats will be randomly assigned to treatment group with a 2:1 ratio (2 I: 1 C).
current_roster.tagline: Feline CKD
current_roster.name: Pilot Safety and Effectiveness Study of an Allogeneic Uterine-Derived Cellular Therapy Preparation in Client-Owned Cats with Chron

current_roster.description: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) is an important protein necessary for the repair of DNA in cells. Cancer cells express a unique type of PCNA (termed caPCNA) which is only found at small quantities in non-cancer cells. Targeting caPCNA with drugs holds promise as a novel therapeutic option with potential for widespread use across multiple cancer types and the possibility of a low risk for side effects. The compound being studied here is a caPCNA inhibitor and has been tested at various doses in healthy dogs with the only side effect noted being diarrhea at higher doses. We now propose a study to investigate the tolerability of this compound in dogs with cancer with the goal of then advancing this drug into future clinical trials that evaluate its use for specific cancer types. The study duration is 35 days and consists of a total of 7 hospital visits. The trial is fully funded with no costs to the owner.
current_roster.name: Tolerability of a novel PCNA inhibitor in tumor-bearing dogs

current_roster.description: The primary purpose of this study will be to assess the safety of administration of EARLI-201 in dogs with known cancer as well as in normal healthy dogs. The secondary objective of this study is to measure how EARLI-201 distributes in the body and determine if it identify known cancer when used in combination with the 18F-FHBG radionuclide labeled tracer.
current_roster.name: EARLI

current_roster.description: This clinical trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of an investigational, orally administered veterinary drug for itching associated with atopic dermatitis, or skin inflammation, in dogs.
current_roster.name: Canine Atopic Dermatitis

current_roster.description: The main role of the thyroid glands is to produce thyroid hormones. Iodine is needed to produce these hormones and the sodium iodide symporter is an essential part of how thyroid cells take up iodine. Thyroid cells can sometimes become cancerous. Many of these thyroid tumors are controlled with surgery alone, but some may either come back within the neck or at distant sites, such as the lungs. A combination of surgery and radioactive iodine is commonly used in people with high risk, differentiated thyroid cancer to decrease the risk of thyroid cancer coming back. This combination has also been associated with good outcomes in dogs with thyroid cancer. Unfortunately, not all thyroid tumors in dogs take up iodine and identifying this currently requires expensive imaging before surgery that is not widely available. The primary purpose of this study will be to assess whether using special stains for the sodium iodide symporter can allow us to identify tumors that are taking up iodine after a thyroid tumor has been removed. This would limit the need for expensive thyroid scans before surgery and increase the number of dogs that could be considered for additional treatment if their thyroid cancer is aggressive
current_roster.name: Sodium Iodine Symporter

current_roster.description: A multicenter, randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled clinical trial to evaluate a novel investigational product in dogs with stage 3 and stage 4 intranasal adenocarcinoma.
current_roster.tagline: Intranasal adenocarcinoma
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Canine Intranasal Adenocarcinoma

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is the most common malignancy in cats and small cell gastrointestinal T cell lymphoma represents a large proportion of lymphoma diagnoses in middle age to older cats. The chemotherapy drug chlorambucil is routinely prescribed to manage small cell gastrointestinal lymphoma, however, the pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) or PK of this drug in cats has not been extensively studied. Compounded formulations of chlorambucil are frequently prescribed to veterinary patients in the United States as this allows for more accurate dosing of the medication to our smaller patients. However, we have previously demonstrated that the potency of compounded formulations of oral chemotherapy medications may differ by more than 10% of the labelled strength. This discrepancy in dosing could lead to under- or over-dosing of patients. To understand the potential clinical impact that use of compounded formulations may have in cats with lymphoma, a foundational understanding of the PK properties and relative bioavailability (how much active drug is absorbed by the body) of compounded chlorambucil is essential.In this study, we seek to better understand the PK, relative bioavailability, and potency of compounded formulations of chlorambucil in cats with small cell GI lymphoma. The night before their visit, cats will need to be fasted starting at midnight but can have access to water. The day of their visit, cats will get a physical exam and an intravenous catheter will be placed to facilitate blood collection through the day. They will be given their first dose of oral compounded chlorambucil and then have blood drawn at four set time periods throughout the day. Once the final blood sample is collected, cats will be released back to their owners to go home. Study participation will be complete after this visit.
current_roster.tagline: Pharmacokinetics of Compounded Chlorambucil in Cats with Lymphoma
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetics of Compounded Chlorambucil in Cats with Lymphoma

current_roster.description:
For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Surgery may not always be the best option for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) as it is challenging to obtain adequate clear surgical margins and often, the disease reoccurs. Adjuvant therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy and palliative options are ineffective or poorly tolerated and do not improve the overall survival rate of cats with OCSCC. We need to make improvements to staging and treatment.

PORPHYSOMES (pPs) are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). pPs can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). This equipment allows for image-guided surgery, tumour margin assessment and lymph node staging. pPs can also be used to in combination with photoablation – photodynamic therapy (PDT) to deliver treatment directly to the tumour. 

 

pPs-enabled therapies can have an immediate impact on cancer management providing better patient outcomes. This study offers a novel approach to the treatment of OCSCC in cats. The use of pPs is ground-breaking translational research and the information gained will be used to treat future dogs, cats and humans with cancer. A human clinical trial is planned to be conducted in 2024.
current_roster.tagline: Exploring a Nanoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
current_roster.name: Exploring a Nonoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats

current_roster.description:
This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of ch45H1, a novel anticancer agent, when given to dogs with cancer. This medication is designed to help your dog’s immune system fight their cancer. The data from this study will be used to assist in the development of additional novel cancer agents in humans.

ch45H1 will be given by intravenous (IV, injection into the vein) infusion to your dog on Days 1, 22, 43, and 64 (once every 3 weeks) for a total of 4 doses. This drug is given over 90 minutes following pre-treatment with an anti-nausea medication (ondansetron), a histamine blocker (diphenhydramine), and intravenous fluids.

Within this study, we ask that you permit serial biopsies of your dog’s tumor. A biopsy will be collected prior to the first dose of drug (pre-treatment), on Day 29 and possibly on Day 85, depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general. Your dog will return to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital on Days 21 and 22, 29, 42 and 43, 63 and 64, and 85. Serial blood collections will occur on Days 1, 21-22, 42-43, and 63-64 of the study. Single time point collections will occur on Day 29. Chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be performed for staging purposes prior to treatment and at Days 42 and 85.

If your dog’s cancer responds well to the treatment they receive, you will be asked to participate in an additional follow-up period of up to one (1) years’ time. During that time, you will need to continue to regularly (every 8 weeks) visit the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for examination, tumor evaluation (chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, and blood collection. At the conclusion of the study, your dog will undergo a final tumor biopsy.
current_roster.tagline: COTC031a: Novel Immune Therapy for Dogs with Lymphoma or Solid Tumors
current_roster.name: COTC031: Novel Immune Therapy for Dogs with Lymphoma or Solid Tumors

current_roster.description:
Cancer cells have a unique metabolism that is highly dependent on the abundance of glucose. Recent studies in mice have shown that calorie restriction slows cancer progression and improves response to chemotherapy. Other studies in dogs and people have also shown that short-term fasting can reduce chemotherapy side effects. It is not clear yet why this happens, but it is suspected that fasting positively impacts a patient's immune system and how it responds to their cancer. The purpose of this study is to learn more about how the tissue environment and immune responses that surround a tumor might be changed by short-term (48-hour) fasting.


Dogs will be screened at the screening visit (day -14 to day -1) and eligible dogs will be randomized and enrolled on Day 0 at which point a continuous glucose monitor and baseline clinical data will be collected; fasting, if applicable, will begin. All dogs will remain in the hospital starting on day 0 through Day 2 during which blood, urine, feces, and rectal and oral swabs will be collected. Day 2 (48 hours post fasting) will mark the completion of study participation and then care will be transferred to the surgical team for surgical excision per standard of care and discharge to owners. 

 

The duration of the study is 48 hours.

For dogs that meet all the criteria to participate, the cost of the initial biopsy, the hospitalization for the fasting period and all the related lab work and sample collection for the two-day study will be paid for by the study. These dogs and their owners will also receive $500 to use toward their dog's cancer treatment at the OSU Veterinary Medical Center.
current_roster.tagline: Fasting OSA/OM
current_roster.name: Can short-term fasting produce a favorable tissue immune response to help fight cancer?
current_roster.top_investigator: Shay Bracha, DVM, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo amputation or radiation of the affected limb followed immediately by vaccination every 3 weeks. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months after completing the initial series. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.
current_roster.tagline: Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine
current_roster.name: Vaccine study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description:
Mast cell tumor (MCT) is the most common malignant cutaneous tumor in dogs. While surgery remains the mainstay of treatment for most MCT, a subset has a high potential for eventual recurrence and metastasis and require systemic medical therapy following surgery in an attempt to delay or prevent eventual metastasis. Furthermore, some dogs may present with disease that is not amenable to resection owing to size, location, or multifocal or disseminated disease. Medical therapy for these patients remains suboptimal. Gilvetmab is a drug that works by targeting key regulators of the immune system and is conditionally approved for use in dogs. Toceranib phosphate (TOC, PalladiaTM) is a targeted therapy that is approved for use in dogs with MCT. Both gilvetmab and TOC have some reported activity against MCT in the gross disease setting; however, the combination has not been evaluated for safety or efficacy in any tumor type.

The primary objective of this study is to characterize the antitumor effects and adverse effect profile of combined treatment with gilvetmab and toceranib in dogs with measurable MCT.

All dogs will be treated with TOC (oral medication given every other day) and gilvetmab (given as an IV infusion every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments. They will also have concurrent treatment with certirizine and omeprazole. Visits will be required every 2 weeks until the week 20 visit. CBC only will be performed for the first 2 visits, and CBC, chemistry profile, UA/UPC, BP +/- imaging will be done every 6 weeks. If dogs have a complete response at the week 20 visit (i.e. tumor is no longer present), they will stop all treatment and come for monitoring visits every 6 weeks. Dogs whose tumors are still present will continue on TOC and recheck every 6 weeks for diagnostics. If at any point your dog’s disease progresses or they experience unacceptable side effects from the study medications, they will be withdrawn from the clinical trial.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment Combination for Dogs with Mast Cell Tumor
current_roster.name: Combination Therapy with Gilvetmab and Toceranib in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors

current_roster.description:
Osteoarthritis is said to affect 1/4 of the canine population. Nutritional intervention of steadfast Canine has shown to help with optimal soft tissue and joint support. Steadfast Canine is a powerful, daily chewable tablet that reduces injury recovery times and helps keep aging dogs active and comfortable.

Steadfast Canine is the only one available that contains the patented Natural Eggshell Membrane (NEM) and TelaFIRM combo. This provides soft tissue support for optimal joint health and accelerates healing for soft tissue injuries like cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) tears and more. 

We have controlled data from university studies, we now want your clinical observations for real world, in-the-field data on the product.


Submitting a minimum of 3 cases (with all samples supplied by us) and completing the 5 minute survey at the end of the study will get your clinic entered in our prize give-away

Click the hyperlink  "I want more information" under resources to be emailed the university studies.
current_roster.tagline: Arthritis Intervention
current_roster.name: Nutraceutical use in dogs with Osteoarthritis

current_roster.description: Dogs will be eligible for inclusion if they have a current diagnosis of blastomycosis and initial BUA concentration. Recruited dogs will be assessed with a review of the dogs' medical records. Included dogs’ owners will be given sterile urine collection cups and instructions to catch the first urinary void of the day, a mid-day sample, and last urinary void of the day to obtain samples for urine specific gravity and BUA concentration. Throughout the day, owners will be instructed to offer dogs additional oral fluid sources (chicken-flavored broth) in an attempt to exacerbate variation in daily USG. There is no risk to dogs from either encouraging drinking or voided urine collection.

current_roster.name: Does urine concentration affect blastomycosis urine antigen in dogs

current_roster.name: Dogs Scheduled to Receive Doxorubicin Chemotherapy

current_roster.description: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is a minimally invasive surgery to remove the gallbladder. This is commonly performed in people with gallbladder disease such as inflammation, infection, or mucocele formation. Gallbladder mucoceles also occur in dogs, and if progressive can form life-threatening bile obstructions or rupture, requiring emergency surgery. In people, using a fluorescent imaging agent during laparoscopic cholecystectomy has been associated with improvements in surgical outcomes. This study aims to evaluate whether ICG can improve visualization of the biliary tree in dogs and report on the peri-operative and short-term outcomes of dogs who undergo this procedure.
current_roster.tagline: ICG in laparoscopic cholecystectomy in dogs
current_roster.name: Indocyanine Green for dogs undergoing Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy

current_roster.description: Treatment: Dogs will be randomly divided into two groups: one group will receive the study treatment (kratom), and the other group will receive a placebo (sugar pill). Neither the dog owner or the veterinarian will be aware of which treatment each dog is receiving. Each treatment will be initiated for 4 weeks. After receiving the first treatment, animals will be crossed over to the opposite treatment for 4 weeks with a 2-week washout period in between. At the start and end of each 4-week period, blood will be collected for a complete blood count, and biochemistry analysis; a biochemistry analysis will also be performed in the middle of each 4-week period (2 weeks). At the middle (2 weeks) and the end of each 4-week block, blood samples will be obtained for evaluation of plasma concentrations of mitragynine. Dogs will be assessed at the beginning and end of each 4 week period for pain by using a combination of a physical exam, a wear​able monitor that documents pain (PainTrace), gait analysis, an at-home activity monitor (health monitoring collar; PetPace), and a pet owner survey.
current_roster.tagline: Effect of kratom on managing arthritis in dogs
current_roster.name: Effect of kratom on managing pain in dogs with osteoarthritis

current_roster.description:
Total hip replacement is performed in dogs affected by severe hip joint disease. Extradural anesthesia is the administration of a drug (i.e. bupivacaine) in the proximity of the spinal cord that causes a temporary loss of sensation of the dog’s back limbs. The use of extradural anesthesia in dogs undergoing total hip replacement can reduce pain and the amount of general anesthetic needed during surgery.

Major complications requiring a second surgery have been reported in about 10% of dogs after total hip replacement. It has been speculated that complications might be more likely if extradural anesthesia with bupivacaine is used. However, a recent study performed in the United Kingdom found that only 5.8% of dogs needed revision surgery after total hip replacement, despite extradural anesthesia being performed. Furthermore, none of these complications occurred during the first 24 hours post-surgery, reducing the likelihood that extradural anesthesia played a role in their development. To confirm those results, we would like to perform this study to prove that extradural anesthesia will not affect the post-surgical complication rate and the need for revision surgery, but will decrease the overall pain and analgesic consumption, improve the postoperative food intake, facilitating the recovery process of your dog.
current_roster.tagline: Effect of Extradural Anesthesia on Postoperative Complication Rate in Dogs Undergoing Total Hip Replacement.
current_roster.name: Effect of extradural anesthesia on postoperative complication rate in dogs undergoing total hip replacement
current_roster.top_investigator: Enzo Vettorato, DVM, PhD, DECVAA, FRCVS

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of bendamustine at different doses in dogs with lymphoma.

Bendamustine is a chemotherapy drug that is used to treat various types of cancer in people, including lymphoma. This drug has not been evaluated in dogs with cancer. This drug has been evaluated in healthy dogs at doses similar to the lower doses used in this study and was well-tolerated.

Different doses of bendamustine will be given to dogs in this study. The first group of dogs will get the lowest dose. If the study drug does not cause serious side effects, the next group of dogs will get a higher dose. The study doctor will watch each group carefully as they increase the dose. The doses will continue to increase for each group of dogs until there are side effects that require the dose to be lowered. Once this dose is found, the study is stopped.
current_roster.tagline: Bendamustine for Dogs with Relapsed Lymphoma
current_roster.name: Bendamustine for Dogs with Relapsed Lymphoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. Matthew Atherton, BVSc, PhD, DECVIM (Oncology)

current_roster.description:
Urethral obstruction (UO) is a common presentation for cats to the ER. Approximately 12% of those cats may have severe hyperkalemia. [Lee] Not only is this a life-threatening electrolyte derangement but it can add considerable cost to care due to prolonged hospitalization, monitoring, injectable medications and repeated blood work. Injectable calcium will stabilize the cardiac rhythm temporarily but does not alter the blood level of potassium ([K]). Ultimately, restoration of urine flow and IV fluid therapy will allow [K] loss, but may be unpredictable and for some cats with acute kidney injury (AKI), it may not be enough in the short term to guard against arrhythmias. In a recent study, UO cats with severe hyperkalemia had a lower survival rate to discharge (80%) than that reported for feline UO overall (89-95%). [Jones]

Relief of obstruction and administration of a balanced isotonic fluid therapy is the current gold-standard treatment for feline UO. [Cosford, Drobatz] There are a number of ancillary treatment options for hyperkalemia in the ER, including co-administration of insulin and dextrose (I/D), dextrose alone, bicarbonate, and albuterol. [Jones, Kline, Lindner] The efficacy of any of these treatments vs. simply restoring urine flow has not been adequately studied, but there is evidence that these ancillary treatments can increase complications. [Jones, Lindner] All ancillary treatments will increase the transport of [K] into the intracellular compartment but may not directly cause [K] loss. [Kline, Lindner] Given the rising cost of care for these patients and an increased risk of complications with insulin and bicarbonate [Jones], it is important to establish treatment efficacy when possible. While there are some comparative studies in feline UO regarding treatment protocols [Canei, Cunha, Finco, Freitas, Drobatz], there are no studies directly comparing the use of ancillary treatments vs. IV fluids alone in the treatment of severe hyperkalemia.

Our study, TSK-UO, is both a practical and academic endeavor in the ECC field. The practical goal of this study is to provide reliable treatment guidelines for ER veterinarians and move away from unnecessary treatments that have become “dogma by extrapolation.” By reducing the cost of lab work and hospitalization, we could decrease unnecessary complications and euthanasia. Secondarily, we would monitor potassium handling by the kidney post relief of the obstruction in order to investigate the mechanism and kinetics of potassium loss between treatment groups to complete a pathophysiologic map.
current_roster.tagline: Treatment of Severe Hyperkalemia in Feline Urethral Obstruction (TSK-UO)
current_roster.name: Treatment of Severe Hyperkalemia in Cats with Urethral Obstruction (TSK-UO)

current_roster.description:
Chronic enteropathy (chronic gastrointestinal disease) is common in dogs with chronic diarrhea being the most common symptom. Treatment for this condition is often aimed at controlling the symptoms rather than treating the underlying disease. In most case this includes a diet change or oral antibiotics. Recently, researchers have discovered that altering the gut microbiome (the bacteria that live in your intestines) in patients with chronic diarrhea can treat the underlying cause and improve symptoms. This study will enroll dogs with chronic diarrhea into one of two groups. Dogs will either receive traditional therapy with a hydrolyzed diet or the study product (a novel probiotic) along with a hydrolyzed diet. Dogs will be enrolled for 60 days and must exclusively eat the hydrolyzed diet.


During the screening period dogs will receive a thorough work up including blood work, UA, baseline cortisol levels, TLI, AUS and fecal float with a Giardia ELISA. Dogs will also have endoscopic biopsies and undergo Endoscopic, fecal and chronic enteropathy scoring. They will be sent home with instructions for transitioning to a HA diet and return once the biopsy results are in. The screening as well as follow up study visits will be covered by the study.
current_roster.tagline: Comparison of diet alone vs. diet and probiotic to control clinical signs of chronic enteropathy in dogs
current_roster.name: Comparison of diet alone vs. diet and probiotic to control clinical signs of chronic diarrhea in dogs

current_roster.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.
current_roster.tagline: Changes in Bone Density Following Radiation Treatment in Dogs with Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description:
Uremic toxins are substances that build up in the body due to decreased removal by the kidney. They are increased in patients with CKD and correlated to severity of disease. Indoxyl sulfate is one of the most studied uremic toxins and comes from byproducts of protein metabolism in the gut. It is thought to contribute to progression of CKD including increasing fibrosis and inflammation in the kidney as well as affecting other body systems such as the heart, bones, and muscle. Porus One (Renaltec) is a new patented pure carbon product that acts as an absorbent of the protein byproduct so that it cannot be absorbed and converted into indoxyl sulfate. Instead, it is excreted in the feces. Porus One has been shown to decrease indoxyl sulfate in normal geriatric cats. The purpose of this study is to assess its effect in cats with CKD.


At the time of screening, a complete history of diet and medications will be discussed. Your cat will receive a physical examination and comprehensive laboratory screening to confirm stage of CKD and exclude other newly diagnosed conditions (e.g. hyperthyroidism, hypertension). This will also be the first time you fill out a quality-of-life survey and provide a fecal sample you have collected from your cat. Your cat will need to be in the same fed state for every visit (either fasted or fed).

After confirmation of enrollment, your cat will be randomized to start in one of the groups. This is a 16-week crossover study, meaning each cat will be in either the Porus One + standard of care group, or standard of care only group for 8 weeks and then cross over to the opposite group. Porus One will be administered sprinkled into wet food or cat snacks (e.g. Churu) once a day for a total of 8 weeks. Administration should be greater than two hours from the time other medications are given.

The study team will check in with you every two weeks by email or phone to address any questions or concerns. No changes in medication or diet should be made during the study without discussing first with the study team.


There is no cost to you for enrolling your cat in this study. Your cat will receive complimentary assessment and management of disease overseen by a board-certified specialist in feline CKD as well as standard of care laboratory monitoring regardless of study group. Cats may benefit from this therapy and can continue it after the study at the caretaker's expense.
current_roster.tagline: Effect of Porus One on Reducing Uremic Toxins in Cats with CKD
current_roster.name: Effect of Porus One on Reducing Uremic Toxins in Cats with CKD
current_roster.top_investigator: Jessica Quimby, Professor; Vice Chair of Research

current_roster.description:
Background and purpose

The Dog Aging Project is an innovative research initiative that brings together a community of dogs, their caretakers, veterinarians, researchers, and volunteers to carry out the most ambitious canine health study in the world. The Dog Aging Project team will follow tens of thousands of companion dogs for ten years or more in order to identify the biological, lifestyle, and environmental factors that maximize healthy longevity. We expect to gain insights that will increase our ability to prevent, diagnose, and treat age-related diseases, thereby helping our dogs, and by extension, ourselves, live longer, healthier lives. The goal of the Dog Aging Project is to understand how genes, lifestyle, and environment influence aging. We want to use that information to help companion dogs and people increase healthspan, the period of life spent free from disease.

Dogs truly are science’s best friends. Though they age more rapidly than humans, they get the same diseases of aging, have a rich genetic make-up, and share our environment. Like humans, they have a sophisticated healthcare system. By studying aging in dogs, we can more quickly expand our knowledge of the aging process not just in dogs but also in humans.


The Dog Aging Project includes expert scientists and research veterinarians from over 20 research institutions and veterinary teaching hospitals. Our core leadership is based at Tufts University and Texas A&M School of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences.


By enrolling in the Dog Aging Project, you are performing community science. Community science springs from the premise that anyone and everyone can think like a scientist. After all, at its most basic, scientific discovery is the result of a fundamental curiosity about the world and how it works. Scientists ask questions, make observations, design experiments, and collect data to answer our questions. You don’t need a PhD or a lab coat to make important contributions to the world’s body of knowledge. At the Dog Aging Project, we view the caretakers of enrolled dogs as key research partners. Our participants are the key to building an incredibly powerful dataset that will allow us to meet our scientific goals.


What happens in this study

If you’re interested in having your dog participate in the Dog Aging Project, please first visit the study website at https://dogagingproject.org/ to nominate your dog for enrollment. After nominating your dog, you will receive a link to create a personal research portal. You will be led through a comprehensive health and life experience survey about your dog's lifestyle, environment, health and daily activities.


In the health and life experience survey, you will have an opportunity to indicate whether or not you are willing to request and upload your dog's veterinary electronic medical records. This step is completely optional. If you chose to upload records, the Dog Aging Project team will review them and there may be opportunities to be offered participation in clinical trials associated with the Dog Aging Project.


​Some smaller studies within the Dog Aging Project look at enrolled companions' genetic backgrounds or annual biological sample lab results. At the same time, the clinical trial associated with the Dog Aging Project explores the potential of rapamycin to improve healthspan. Eligibility and invitation into the smaller studies or the clinical trial are determined by a set of scientific and statistical standards so that the Dog Aging Project can remain as unbiased as possible. Please remember that the main part of the Dog Aging Project is a longitudinal, observational study, meaning they will be monitoring the dogs from a distance without any intervention.


Please note, the only way to be offered enrollment in one of the associated clinical trials is to start at the Dog Aging Project website with nomination and completion of the health and life experience survey.


Pet owner responsibilities

If you're interesting in having your dog be a part of the Dog Aging Project, you will simply need to visit the Dog Aging Project website at https://dogagingproject.org/ and follow the steps to enroll your dog and complete the health and life experience survey.


Participation requirements

Dogs of any age, sex, breed, and health status, living within the United States are invited to participate in the Dog Aging Project


Benefits and risks of participating

This is an observational, data-collection study only, and is not designed or intended to diagnose or treat any disease or condition. There are no direct benefits to your dog for participation in this study. However, participation greatly helps us learn more about the aging process in dogs and can potentially help benefit future companions.


Compensation

Enrollment in this study is on a volunteer basis. There is no compensation for those who enroll their dogs in the Dog Aging Project. There is no cost to participate.

Background and purpose

Rapamycin is an mTOR inhibitor which, at low doses, has been shown to increase lifespan and delay or reverse many age-related disorders in mice. The goal of TRIAD is to assess the effects of the medication rapamycin on health and aging in dogs. This study is designed to test if rapamycin treatment leads to any of the following benefits:

  1. Better heart health
  2. Improved mobility
  3. Prolonged cognitive function
  4. Increased lifespan

  4. Electrocardiogram


Neurology part of the project

  1. Physical exam including blood pressure measurement
  2. Sample collection (CBC/Chem/Urinalysis) [Chagas disease testing for dogs in Texas]
  3. Neurological Exam

Trial Overview

ELIAS Animal Health is currently conducting a study to assess safety and efficacy of ELIAS’s vaccine-enhanced adoptive T cell therapy combined with a novel adjuvant as a limb-sparing treatment for large-breed dogs newly diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma. The study, which will be funded by a grant from Morris Animal Foundation, will be conducted in collaboration with Dr. Jeffrey Bryan and Dr. Megan Mickelson at the University of Missouri-Columbia.


Trial Summary

  1. Treatment includes limb-sparing surgery to remove primary tumor, followed by vaccine-enhanced adoptive T cell therapy combined with a novel adjuvant.
  2. Patients must complete the 7-11 week protocol, conducted at the University of Missouri Veterinary School of Medicine, and return for periodic follow-up visits.
  3. Each patient will be monitored for 12 months post-diagnosis.

current_roster.description:
Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade. This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.

The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.


There will be two study groups:


The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.


The second group of dogs (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 with PD-1 blockade. Their tumor will measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return one week later for tumor measurements, blood sampling, and anti-PD-1 infusion. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second CMP-002 infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.
current_roster.tagline: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
current_roster.name: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs

current_roster.description: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is predicted to be the second leading cause of death within the next decade in the United States. Older dogs suffer from a similar disease, canine cognitive dysfunction (CCD). Currently, there is no easy way to diagnose doggie dementia nor an effective treatment. Therefore, the goal of this study is to learn about how dogs age and what types of changes happen in the brain of older dogs, compared to healthy younger dogs, by examining the blood, spinal fluid, and imaging (MRI) of the brain. The ultimate goal will be to find a simple diagnostic test and, more importantly, a cure for doggie dementia and maybe even for Alzheimer’s Disease.

current_roster.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.
current_roster.tagline: Polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography for surgical margin assessment for mammary tumors
current_roster.name: Mammary tumors in cats

current_roster.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.
current_roster.tagline: Electrochemotherapy for Bone cancers
current_roster.name: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO

current_roster.description:
Background and Purpose of the Trial

Epilepsy is reported to affect around 5% of the canine population, making it the most common neurologic condition in dogs. There are currently a very limited number of antiepileptic drugs (AEDS) available to treat epilepsy in dogs. The primary choice of AED is currently phenobarbital which, while typically effective, can come with side effects that can be hard for both the pet and the pet owner. Studies have shown that CBD can be effective in decreasing seizures when added to a primary AED and we are now exploring if CBD can be an effective primary therapy on its own. Dogs in this study will be randomly assigned to either phenobarbital or CBD at the beginning of the study. Over the course of the first 8 weeks, the dose may be titrated up; starting at week 8, the dose can no longer be adjusted, and no other medications can be added in without needing to withdraw the pet. At the end of the study, owners and the clinician will be unblinded to ensure the pet can continue the appropriate medication or make adjustments as needed.


Who Qualifies

  1. Dogs must be between the ages of 1 – 6 years when the first seizure occurs
  2. Dogs cannot currently be on any anti-seizure medications
  3. Dogs must have had at least 2 seizures in 6 weeks, with at least 24 hours separating the seizures
  4. Dogs must be otherwise healthy
  5. Owners must be willing to keep a detailed seizure log throughout the study

Study Design


Visit 1 | Day 0

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Verify eligibility criteria
  3. Blood draw for baseline blood levels
  4. Oral cotton swab for DNA analysis
  5. Start CBD or phenobarbital (owner will receive an oil and a pill, each to be dosed twice daily)
  6. Titrate dosing up if needed

Visit 2 | Day 14

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels

Visit 3 | Day 56

  1. End of titration period
  2. Neurologic exam
  3. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels

Visit 4 | Day 98

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels

Visit 5 | Day 140

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels
  3. One month of study drug to owner, along with instructions for continued use or discontinuation as needed

Financial Incentives

All exams, along with the study medication, will be covered by the study. Additionally, at the end of the study, the owner will receive a one-month supply of the drug the pet was on in order to continue dosing or transition to a different medication if needed.
current_roster.tagline: CBD/ Pheno comparison study for canine epilepsy
current_roster.name: A comparison of phenobarbital and CBD in the management of seizures in dogs

Evidence exists to suggest that aging of the kidney may contribute to the onset and progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Rapamycin is a drug that is a potential modulator of the aging process and additionally may decrease the formation of fibrosis (scarring) in the kidney. A feline formulation of the drug is available and the purpose of this study is to assess the potential benefit of the drug in cats with CKD.


Your cat will receive complimentary assessment and management of disease by a board-certified specialist in feline CKD as well as standard of care laboratory monitoring regardless of study group. Cats randomized to the study drug group will possibility benefit from this therapy. There is no cost to you for enrolling your cat in this study. You will receive complimentary physical examination for your cat and diagnostic testing. You will also receive $25 per visit incentive.

Thiamine deficiency has the potential to worsen heart function, so we are investigating whether thiamine levels are below normal in dogs that are receiving diuretic treatment (specifically with furosemide) for CHF. This will possibly help us identify dogs that are at risk for thiamine deficiency, which might lead to changes in treatment for these dogs.

current_roster.description:
B cell lymphoma impacts >250,000 dogs every year. The current standard of care is CHOP chemotherapy, a multi-agent protocol that takes 3-4 months of trips to the vet and costs $7,000-12,000 while only extending the life of a pet 10-12 months.


This clinical trial is evaluating the safety and efficacy of Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in dogs with B cell lymphoma. CAR-T cells are a type of engineered T cell (an immune cell found in mammals) that have had a series of genes added to them that make them professional killers of cancer cells expressing certain shapes, called antigens. In this trial for B cell lymphoma, the antigen the CAR-T cells will target is called CD20. CAR-T cell therapy is FDA approved for multiple blood cancers in humans and is a revolution in how cancer is treated, bringing cures to patients who have no other treatment options.


This clinical trial seeks to better understand the effects of the CAR-T cells on lymph node tumors and internal disease, as well as how CAR-T cells influence the dog’s immune system to re-activate and fight cancer on its own. The trial will also test different pre-treatments, determined based on the additive measurements of four target lymph nodes (called the "sum of longest diameters").


This trial is sponsored by LEAH Labs, a biotechnology company building living therapies for pets with cancer. The trial is 100% funded from enrollment, provides a generous adverse event stipend, and offers a stipend for future care.
current_roster.tagline: CAR-T cell therapy for canine B cell lymphoma
current_roster.name: Direct lymph node injection of CAR-T cell therapy in dogs with CD20+ diffuse large B cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: Ear infections can be harmful to both dogs and their owners. Infections can have severe consequences. Untreated chronic otitis can lead to deafness and neurological problems. Preventive measures should be taken to minimize the development and recurrence of otitis. The purpose of this study is to evaluate a possible new treatment option for dogs with recurrent bacterial ear infections; as antibiotic resistance in this type of infections is becoming increasingly common. This study will investigate the efficacy of bacteriophages to treat Pseudomonas otitis. Phages are benign viruses that feed on bacteria and effectively kill the bacteria. Our team has developed a cocktail of phages that was selected to address Pseudomonas using isolates from canine patients with active ear infections. Dogs will receive an otoscopic examination and cytological assessment every two weeks for six weeks.
current_roster.tagline: Investigation of Bacteriophage Therapy for Treatment of Ear Infections in Dogs
current_roster.name: Investigation of Bacteriophage Therapy for Treatment of Pseudomonas Otitis (Recurrent Ear infections) in Dogs

current_roster.description:
The goal of this study is to investigate two physical therapy protocols to establish if it could lead

to improve neurologic function in dogs with wobbler syndrome and a better quality of life. Dogs with signs of wobbler syndrome will schedule an initial appointment with the neurology service to assess their overall health and clinical signs. If indicated, they will have general anesthesia and an MRI of the neck performed to confirm a diagnosis of wobbler syndrome. After the diagnosis is confirmed, they will be assigned to one of two groups: A. He/she will have to come in for physical rehabilitation exercises at OSU for 5-6 months (twice a week in the first month, once a week for 2 months and every other week for the next month 2 months) and have exercises that you will do at home 5-6 times per week for 6 months OR B. He/she will have physical rehabilitation exercises you will have to do at home 5-6 times per week for 6 months. Some of the exercises include just walking your dog. We will provide you with the specific list of exercises and videos demonstrating the exercises. At follow-up appointments (30, 90, and 180 days after entering the study), he/she will have a neurologic exam, walk over a gait analysis plate, and have a sensor measure limb rigidity. You will also be asked to assess the quality of life of your dog at the end of the study period (6 months).


Client Compensation:

For dogs that meet the criteria as a study dog, the full cost of the MRI (if done for the project), anesthesia, and physical rehabilitation (22 sessions) will be taken care of by the study. The cost for the MRI and anesthesia will be refunded after the end of the study period. Owners are responsible for the initial diagnostics, including exam fees, blood work, and radiographs of the cervical spine. Any tests, procedures, or treatments beyond those specifically listed here are the owner's responsibility.

current_roster.description: Itch is the uncomfortable sensation underlying the desire to scratch. A neuropathic itch is a localized chronic itch caused by damage to the central nervous system or nerve fibers. In people, the chronic neuropathic itch is very difficult to treat, and it can significantly lower the quality of life. Unfortunately, with a few breed-specific exceptions, the neuropathic itch runs mostly undetected in dogs. Our goal is to identify peripheral skin and serum biomarkers specific to chronic neuropathic itch in dogs with the long-term goal of finding a targeted therapy for these cases. Moreover, we want to quantify how much the chronic itch affects the quality of life of these canine patients.

current_roster.name: Evaluation of peripheral and serum biomarkers of neuropathic pruritus in dogs

current_roster.description: This is an open-label, pilot study evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of Cowpea Mosaic Virus (CPMV) administered as an intratumoral injection in dogs with mast cell tumor, soft tissue sarcoma, melanoma, and thyroid tumors. CPMV will be administered as an injection into the tumor once weekly for 4 weeks. If there is >/= 25% reduction in tumor size, an additional 4 doses may be administered for a total of 8 doses. Dogs may have their tumors removed at the end of the initial 4 treatments or after 8 treatments. Hepatic and renal function tests will be monitored on the first day, at day 7 and 2,4, 6, and 8 weeks post starting treatment. Dogs will also undergo weekly physical examinations for any physical changes while on study. The tumor will undergo a biopsy before treatment, at day 14, and surgical resection will be considered at the end of study.

current_roster.description: This is an open-label, pilot study evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of radiation therapy combined with histotripsy in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. Radiation therapy will be delivered at once a week for 3 weeks and will be combined with histotripsy delivered twice a week performed 24-72 hours after radiation therapy, applied to the primary tumor using a clinical-grade histotripsy system and image guided targeting (ultrasound). Dogs may have their tumors removed at the end the study. Hepatic and renal function tests will be monitored on the first day and every other week along with physical examinations and owner interviews. current_roster.description:
Some cats are at risk of developing a condition called chylothorax. Chylothorax can occur because of a “leaky vessel” (known as the thoracic duct), which can cause accumulation of fluid (chyle) in the chest cavity. This excess of fluid within the chest cavity can impair the lungs during breathing and result in potentially life-threatening situations. Treatment of chylothorax in cats typically requires surgery to close the thoracic duct, preventing fluid from leaking into the chest cavity. Traditionally, surgical intervention of chylothorax requires opening the abdominal and chest cavities, causing a considerable amount of discomfort and even pain after surgery. Minimally invasive approaches have been developed, like thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation where closure is performed through small incisions with the use of a camera and specialized instruments. The addition of another technique, known as pericardiectomy (removal of the pericardium, which is a sac-like organ surrounding the heart) along with thoracic duct repair is often performed to reduce the chance of recurrence. Even with these techniques in combination, recurrence rates of up to 30-50% have been reported. Additionally, more recent studies suggest that pericardiectomy may not be necessary in all patients, but rather proper identification of the location of the thoracic duct before surgery by way of a CT scan and in surgery by way of contrast can improve outcomes for cats.


     Currently, there are no prospective studies for cats with idiopathic chylothorax using standardized preoperative diagnostics and surgical techniques for each patient. This includes the use of contrast material before and during surgery to better identify the thoracic duct and stop its flow at the proper location, which is highly dependent on each cat. The aim of this project is to assess the outcome of cats with idiopathic chylothorax undergoing thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation who have a standardized diagnostic workup preoperatively and successful preoperative and intraoperative thoracic duct visualization.


Cats are invited to participate in this study if they are at least 6.6 lbs (3 kg) or greater, greater than 2 years of age, and have been diagnosed with idiopathic chylothorax. Prior to inclusion into this study cats will undergo physical examination and be diagnosed with chylothorax using pleural effusion fluid analysis (abnormal buildup of fluid in the pleural space, which is a thin cavity between the lungs and the chest wall). If not already completed within two weeks of their planned surgery date, cats will undergo a complete physical examination, and blood will be collected for complete blood count and serum biochemistry prior to admittance in this study. Additionally, cats will receive a complete work-up for chylothorax including an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound), heartworm testing, chest x-rays, and pleural effusion fluid analysis. If cats have undergone surgery previously for chylothorax or if they have an identified underlying cause of chylothorax (e.g. cancer, heart disease, lung lobe torsion, etc.), they will be excluded from participation in this study.


Cats will be placed under general anesthesia for their first procedure. A CT scan will be conducted first, where a contrast solution (iohexol) will be injected underneath the skin around the anus and/or into the metatarsal paw pads, to highlight the thoracic duct. Under the same anesthetic event, your cat will also have a small incision made into its neck and a catheter will be placed in the jugular vein to measure pressures at the level of the heart.

At a later date, cats will be placed under anesthesia again for surgery. Three very small (5-10mm) incisions will be made near the ribs for insertion of special surgical instruments (thoracoscopic camera and instruments) to allow the surgeon to see inside the chest cavity and close the thoracic duct branches. The thoracic duct will be visualized using a dye injected around the anus prior to surgery. If the thoracic duct is unable to be visualized with this minimally invasive technique, an incision will be made into the chest cavity between two of the ribs and the surgery will proceed as an “open” thoracic duct ligation. A chest tube will be placed to monitor post-operative fluid production in all patients, as is standard of care for chylothorax patients.


All enrolled cats will be hospitalized post-operatively in the intensive care unit for a minimum of 48 hours for monitoring. Cats will be sent home once they are voluntarily eating and drinking, and their pain is deemed appropriately controlled with oral medications. All cats must be re-evaluated at the UF Small Animal Hospital at 1-, 3-, and 6 months after surgery for physical exam and chest x-rays to confirm occlusion of the thoracic duct and resolution of chylothorax. A repeat CT scan under anesthesia will be performed at 3 months post-surgery, or sooner if clinical signs reoccur before then.
current_roster.tagline: Thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation for cats with Idiopathic Chylothorax: A prospective clinical trial
current_roster.name: Thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation for cats with Idiopathic Chylothorax: A prospective clinical trial

current_roster.description: We are currently offering enrollment in a clinical trial on vagus nerve stimulation as a novel treatment option of canine epilepsy. Vagus nerve stimulation is a novel therapy that has shown promise in reducing seizure frequency and improving quality of life in people with epilepsy. Participation in the study may offer access to an innovative approach that goes beyond standard medical management, without causing the traditional side effect caused by antiepileptic drugs, and patients may benefit from close monitoring and advanced care throughout the trial.
current_roster.tagline: Testing a new device to help dogs with epilepsy have fewer seizures
current_roster.name: Evaluating Vagus Nerve Stimulation for Epilepsy in a Controlled Clinical Study

current_roster.description:
Hindlimb proximal suspensory desmopathy (HPSD) is a common cause of lameness in horses. Non-surgical conventional treatments of HPSD include local infiltration with corticosteroids and/or hyaluronan, extracorporeal shock wave therapy, and systemic application of NSAIDs in combination with corrective shoeing.  However, each of these have shown poor long-term results. Treatment of ligament injury utilizing orthobiologics such as platelet rich plasma (PRP) or a bone marrow aspirate (BMA) have been advocated to improve healing of these injuries. We hypothesize that intralesional treatment with CenTrate® BMA will improve the architecture of the injured suspensory ligament, as examined via ultrasound and MRI, returning horses to the expected level of athleticism more rapidly and with a lower rate of recurrence than horses treated with standard of care.


Horses presenting with hindlimb suspensory injury will be screened for study inclusion based on history, physical and lameness examination, labwork, radiographs and ultrasound examination to confirm location of injury. Horses meeting inclusion criteria will be admitted to the hospital to have a baseline MRI under anesthesia, and afterward will be randomized to receive standard of care therapy (consisting of a carefully structured rest and rehabilitation program including systemic NSAIDs, topical treatment, etc. according to individual needs), or receive CenTrate® BMA in addition to standard of care therapy.


Horses randomized to receive CenTrate® BMA will be sedated and receive a local anesthetic for bone marrow aspiration the day following recovery from MRI. The BMA will be injected into the affected suspensory ligament using guided ultrasound. Horses randomized to the standard of care group will not be injected or treated with any specific product; however the affected limb will be bandaged. The limbs of all horses will be bandaged in identical fashion, and owners will remain blinded to treatment.


The study is 8 months in duration. All horses will return for recheck visits to the hospital at months 1, 2, 3, 5, and 8 post enrollment, during which physical examination, lameness exam and ultrasound will be repeated. A follow-up MRI under anesthesia will be repeated at month 3 to assess imaging changes that may not be discernible with ultrasound. Horses assigned to the standard of care group initially will have the opportunity to receive treatment with CenTrate® BMA if improvement is not seen after 90 days of therapy.


Study funds are available to cover a substantial amount of the costs of each visit and associated diagnostics (ultrasound and MRI). In addition study funds will cover costs of the CenTrate® BMA treatment. Owners are financially responsible for pre-enrollment diagnostic costs. Stem cells will be developed from each horse’s bone marrow at no additional cost to owners, and will be available for future treatments or available for any additional injury the horse might sustain and stored at the University of Georgia for up to two years.

current_roster.name: Use of Equine CenTrate® Bone Marrow Aspirate (BMA) in Horses with Hindlimb Proximal Suspensory Desmopathy (HPSD)
