current_roster.description:
This is a six-month long randomized, double blinded, placebo-controlled study. This means that enrolled dogs will be randomly assigned to either a study treatment group (receiving one of the testing diets) or the control group. Specific food and treats will be provided exclusively for this clinical trial. Participants must exclusively feed their dogs with the provided food and treats, and refrain from giving any other edible treats, including table scraps, toppers, and/or supplements for skin or immune health. Enrolled dogs may be fed the trial treats up to a maximum of 10% of their daily caloric requirement. If needed, medication will be prescribed along with the study diet.


Enrolled dogs will be seen on day -7 (enrollment), 21, 27, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 180 (end of the study). At each visit, dogs will undergo a clinical evaluation and skin barrier function evaluations, which include tests of skin hydration and pH. Information on the quality of life of you and your dog will also be collected. At select visits, blood will be collected to run bloodwork consisting of a complete blood count and chemistry, to run markers of inflammation, and to save 2 extra serum cryovials and 1ml of blood to be stored for future analysis. In addition, a sterile swab will be used to collect bacteria from the skin in two locations (axillae and abdomen).


Owners will be required to complete daily medication logs (if prescribed medication), a weekly pruritus visual analog scale (PVAS) evaluation, and quality of life (QoL) surveys at each visit. Enrolled dogs will be equipped with an activity monitor to track the overall activity of the dogs. Owners will also be expected to collect fecal samples at home a total of three times for microbiome analysis.
current_roster.tagline: Double-blinded diet trial looking at the effects of an enriched diet on atopic dermatitis
current_roster.name: Assessing the Benefits of Main Meal Diets in Dogs with Canine Atopic Dermatitis

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to determine if a nerve test, performed on paralyzed dogs before surgery for a slipped disc, can predict whether they will regain the ability to walk.


All dogs in this study will undergo standardized, gold-standard diagnostics and surgical procedures. F-wave nerve conduction testing will be conducted preoperatively. At six months post-surgery, dogs will be categorized into one of two clinical outcome groups:

  1. Successful: Dogs that achieve independent ambulation.
  2. Unsuccessful: Dogs that remain non-ambulatory or experience IVDE-related mortality within the observation period. This includes cases of progressive myelomalacia or euthanasia due to prolonged non-ambulatory status (>3 months)
current_roster.tagline: A Nerve Conduction study on Dogs with Intervertebral Disc Extrusion
current_roster.name: Nerve Conduction in Dogs with Intervertebral Disc Extrusion
current_roster.top_investigator: Go Togawa, Assistant Professor of Neurology/Neurosurgery

current_roster.description:
Plasma cell pododermatitis (PCP) is a condition in which the paw pads become swollen, discolored, cracked, and occasionally ulcerated, due to infiltration by plasma cells. As the paw pad lesions are commonly considered characteristic of PCP, and often considered localized skin disease, diagnostics for systemic health are uncommonly performed. A subset of young feline patients presenting clinically for evaluation of kidney disease have either historical or current evidence of PCP, several of which were confirmed to be immune complex mediated glomerulonephritis (ICGN) when comprehensive renal pathologic assessment was performed. ICGN is a serious and potentially life-threatening disease that requires immunosuppressive therapy. The purpose of this study is to further investigate the link between these two diseases, determine over a two-year period how frequently cats with pododermatitis develop kidney disease, and monitor response to therapy.


Your cat will participate in this study for a duration of 2 years, during which time they will be evaluated by a veterinarian and have blood and urine samples collected every 6 months (if they do not have evidence of kidney disease) or every 3 months (if they have evidence of kidney disease). If at any point during the 6 month rechecks your cat has new evidence of kidney disease, re-check appointments will move to every 3 months. These appointments may occur either at your regular veterinary office or a specialty veterinary practice. Your cat will receive complimentary lab work for two years as described and if applicable, the availability of medical consultation about management of kidney disease from a board-certified specialist in feline chronic kidney disease.
current_roster.tagline: Pododermatitis and CKD
current_roster.name: Investigating the Association Between Feline Plasma Cell Pododermatitis and Glomerular Disease
current_roster.top_investigator: Jessica Quimby, Professor; Vice Chair of Research

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new, cat-specific medication for weight loss in overweight cats. Human weight loss has been revolutionized in the past few years with the introduction of GLP-1 agonist drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy; we are testing a similar medication in pet cats.

The study is designed as a prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial.

Cats that might qualify for the study will receive a screening physical examination with a veterinarian. If the examination indicates that the cat is a good candidate, screening lab work (blood and urine) will be run to ensure that the cat is otherwise healthy (week 0).

Cats that pass the screening examination and bloodwork will be eligible to enroll in the study, which involves 11 weekly visits after the initial screening visit. Enrolled cats will be randomly assigned to receive either the new drug or a placebo (saline).

On weeks 1 through 11, the cat will be examined by a veterinarian and weighed.

On weeks 1 through 10, the drug or placebo will be administered as an injection under the skin.

On weeks 2 through 11, we will ask some standard history questions to see if there were any side effects noted from the most recent injection.

On weeks 2, 5, and 11, we will obtain blood and urine to make sure the drug is not causing unwanted changes in body and organ function.

After the 11th week, cats that received placebo (saline) will then be eligible to receive weekly injections of the drug for free.
current_roster.tagline: GLP-1 agonist for overweight cats
current_roster.name: Clinical evaluation of a novel GLP1 agonist for weight loss in overweight and obese client-owned domestic cats

current_roster.description:
This study requires a single appointment at CSU located in Fort Collins, Colorado. During this appointment, owners of cats over the age of 12 years will complete a series of surveys detailing cognitive and lifestyle habits observed from the enrolled patient. Cats will have vitals (weight, heart rate, respiration rate, body fat index scoring, body temperature) recorded, physical and neurologic examinations performed, and have blood drawn to analyze gene expression profiles alongside plasma-based quantification of neurodegeneration biomarkers. By correlating gene expression changes with circulating levels of Amyloid-β, hyperphosphorylation of tau, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and neurofilament light chain, this approach may provide a minimally invasive platform to monitor disease processes at the molecular level.


Cats may be lightly sedated for the blood draw if deemed appropriate by the study PI to manage patient comfort and safety.
current_roster.tagline: Single Blood Collection to Study Aging in Cats over 12
current_roster.name: Researching Aging and Immune Function in Cats over 12

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether three times weekly dosing with oral rapamycin can reverse the heart muscle changes associated with subvalvular aortic stenosis (SAS) in dogs.

Dogs will undergo an initial screening for eligibility. If your dog enrolls, they will be randomized to receive either low dose rapamycin, high dose rapamycin, or placebo in a double blinded fashion and return for 3 and 6 month recheck visits.
current_roster.tagline: Oral rapamycin for Severe Subvalvular Aortic Stenosis (SAS) in Dogs
current_roster.name: Currently Enrolling Dogs wit Severe Subvalvular Aortic Stenosis (SAS)

current_roster.description: Dogs with bone cancer or osteosarcoma of the limbs will be first assessed with a specialized imaging called 18F-FDG PET-CT to determine that the tumor is limited to the leg. Once enrolled, the dog will be treated with an immunotherapy directly in the tumor followed by chemotherapy the next 1-2 days prior to amputation. The goal of this therapy is to increase the immune response to the tumor. After amputation, treatment with standard chemotherapy will be augmented with an immune checkpoint inhibitor. At three, six, and twelve months after amputation, non-invasive imaging will be performed to look for spread of osteosarcoma. All treatments performed at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD are free-of-charge. The immune checkpoint inhibitor will be provided free-of-charge. The owner will need to make arrangements for amputation and chemotherapy with a surgeon and medical oncologist, respectively.
current_roster.tagline: Immunotherapy for Osteosarcom
current_roster.name: Immune treatment of Canine Bone Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: Dara L Kraitchman, VMD, PhD, Professor of Radiology and Director CIGAT

current_roster.description:
Dogs and humans are the only species in which primary brain tumors are common. In dogs, a type of malignant tumor called a glioma accounts for approximately 35% of all spontaneous primary brain tumors. Even with treatment, the prognosis for both dogs and humans with gliomas is poor, and there is no cure. Current therapies such as radiation aim at extending quantity and improving quality of life. In this clinical trial, we are testing the safety and effectiveness of molecularly targeted cytotoxins, which are chemotherapeutic drugs, delivered directly to the patient's brain tumor. Developed by researchers at the Thomas K. Hearn Brain Tumor Research Centerat the Wake Forest School of Medicine, the unique chemotherapeutic drugs used in this trial are designed to affect only cancerous cells, and not normal brain tissue. Earlier generations of these molecularly targeted cyotoxins have been used safely and effectively in dogs with gliomas. Using specialized catheters the cytotoxins are infused directly into the tumor over a several hour period. The drug treatment is monitored continuously with MRI to allow the neurosurgeon to precisely track the drug delivery.

**As a dog owner, how can I participate in this trial? ** If you suspect that your dog may have a brain tumor, you should arrange for an appointment with your local veterinarian. They will perform a complete neurological examination, which is the first and fundamental step in establishing a diagnosis in animals with brain disease. It is also a prerequisite for them to determine which additional diagnostic tests to recommend. However, advanced imaging studies of the brain, such as MRI, interpreted in conjunction with the neurological examination and other supporting tests, are usually necessary to best characterize diseases of the brain. If your local veterinarian cannot perform an MRI, they will often refer you to a veterinary neurologist who offers this service. Our Neurology and Neurosurgery Service works on a referral only basis, which means that your local veterinarian must first evaluate your pet and arrange for an appointment to see one of our specialists. In order to be eligible for this specific clinical trial, your dog must have an MRI of the brain that demonstrates an abnormality consistent with a glioma.

Clinical Trial Inclusion Criteria: - Dogs of any age, breed, or sex between 3-45 kg in body weight - Clinical signs of mild to moderate neurologic dysfunction referable to the brain - MRI evidence of a single telencephalic intra-axial mass lesion consistent with a glioma - No clinical or other diagnostic evidence of other significant systemic disease. - Dogs must have gross, measurable disease (> 1cm in diameter) on a current MRI

We are happy to evaluate clinical and imaging findings to determine patient eligibility for this clinical trial.

To expedite this process, please complete and return our Neurology Clinical Trial Consultation Form: https://virginiatech.qualtrics.com/SE/?SID=SV_2ct6Cm6EegrTga1.
current_roster.tagline: New therapy for canine glioma brain tumors
current_roster.name: Clinical trial of a targeted chemotherapy drug delivered by a catheter to treat dogs with glioma brain tumors

current_roster.description:
In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of immune cells known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, made from the blood of a healthy donor dog, in dogs with bone cancer. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that have been shown to kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. 


This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. Covered procedures include:

  1. Bloodwork for general health screening
  2. Chest radiographs to be sure the osteosarcoma has not spread to the lungs prior to treatment
  3. Bone biopsy to confirm osteosarcoma and the presence of the B7H3 target protein
  4. Cellular therapy with iNKT cells
  5. Amputation of the affected limb (~10 days after cell therapy) and all post-op care/hospitalization
  6. Standard of care chemotherapy
  7. Follow up monitoring of bloodwork and chest radiographs


All clinical trial visits are in person at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
current_roster.tagline: CLINCIAL TRIAL FOR DOGS WITH NEWLY DIAGNOSED OSTEOSARCOMA
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Nicola Mason BVetMed, PhD, DACVIM, FRCVS, Professor of Veterinary Medicine

current_roster.description:
Acute diarrhea is one of the most common gastrointestinal complaints in companion dogs, affecting an estimated 10–14% of the domestic dog population annually. Episodes are frequently self-limiting but cause significant discomfort, owner concern, and veterinary utilization. In dogs with recurrent diarrhea (defined as episodes occurring every one to two months or more frequently), each acute episode represents both a welfare concern and an opportunity for targeted intervention.


Current management strategies range from dietary modification and fasting to over-the-counter stool firmers and, in more severe cases, antibiotic or prescription drug therapy. Few rigorously controlled studies have evaluated the efficacy of probiotic supplementation specifically timed to the onset of an acute diarrhea episode in dogs with a history of recurrent episodes.


A 7-day probiotic supplement containing live Peptacetobacter hiranonis, Enterococcus faecium, and Megamonas funiformis. These strains were selected based on a large, de novo sequencing survey of the gut microbiomes of healthy dogs compared to dogs with gastrointestinal disease. The product is a companion animal supplement composed of Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) ingredients. The product is commercially available and is not an FDA-regulated animal drug. The placebo is formulated to be organoleptically identical to the active product and contains no active probiotic strains.


Acute diarrhea episodes in pet dogs occur unpredictably and at home. A traditional clinic-based trial design would require owners to travel to a veterinary facility during an active episode — a logistical barrier that would systematically delay treatment initiation and select against enrollment. A fully decentralized, owner-administered virtual design allows treatment to begin within 24 hours of episode onset, mirrors real-world use conditions, and enables rigorous randomized controlled trial methodology without requiring any in-person investigator contact with animals.


All study procedures are conducted remotely. No investigator or study personnel will physically interact with enrolled animals. All products are administered by owners at home. This study is eligible for review by an IACUC under its virtual study framework.


The Purina Fecal Score (PFS)™ is a validated 7-point ordinal scale used to assess stool quality in dogs. It serves as the primary daily outcome measure in this study. The PFS™ visual reference chart must be displayed alongside every stool quality question across all survey modules.
current_roster.tagline: Radicle Canine Probiotic Study
current_roster.name: Radicle Canine Probiotic Study

current_roster.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.
current_roster.tagline: Intra-tumoral T-cell Engager Therapy for Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma
current_roster.name: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
current_roster.top_investigator: Kristen Couto, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), Veterinary Oncologist

current_roster.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.


Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Radiation for Transmissible Venereal Tumor in Dogs
current_roster.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
current_roster.top_investigator: Kathryn Wolfert, DVM, Medical Oncology resident

current_roster.description:
Canine chronic enteropathy (CE) is a long-term disorder of the intestinal tract in dogs, causing symptoms such as decreased appetite, vomiting, and diarrhea that significantly impact both affected dogs and their caregivers. CE is not fully understood, but may result from a complex interaction of genetics, environmental factors, changes in the gut microbiome, and an abnormal immune response.

Current treatment strategies aim to restore intestinal balance by targeting these contributing factors. This includes altering the gut microbiota through dietary interventions, prebiotics and probiotics, and regulating the immune system via immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive therapies.

N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) is a naturally occurring amino sugar that has shown promise in reducing intestinal inflammation in both human and rat models of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Its mechanism of action is thought to involve enhancement of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, which plays a critical role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity and regulating immune responses.

This study aims to investigate the potential therapeutic effects of NAG in dogs diagnosed with CE. By evaluating clinical symptoms, inflammatory markers, and microbiome composition, we aim to determine whether NAG can serve as a beneficial additional treatment for managing canine CE.


Participation in this study will last 4-8 weeks.

  1. Before starting the study, your dog will receive a physical examination, blood work, and fecal examination.
  2. If eligible, your dog will then be assigned to either the treatment group or the placebo group. The assignment is random and will be performed by one of our study administrators without knowledge about any of your dog's medical details.
  3. Your dog will have two to three study related visits.
  4. During the study trial period we ask that you follow the study protocol & only feed your dog the prescription diet and test substances. Feeding treats or diets other than the prescribed diet may cause clinical signs to continue.
  5. During the study, you will need to complete daily questionnaires to monitor the treatment effects.
  6. Please note: You cannot provide your dog with any food other than the prescription diet, and you cannot provide medications or supplements except for flea, tick and heartworm preventatives during the study.
current_roster.tagline: Investigating the effects of N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) in dogs with chronic enteropathy (CE)
current_roster.name: Investigating the effects of N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) in dogs with chronic enteropathy

current_roster.description: Ear infections can be harmful to both dogs and their owners. Infections can have severe consequences. Untreated chronic otitis can lead to deafness and neurological problems. Preventive measures should be taken to minimize the development and recurrence of otitis. The purpose of this study is to address the prevention of otitis. This study will investigate the efficacy of proactive use of topical steroids to prevent flare ups of otitis externa in allergic dogs with a prior history of recurrent otitis externa and not currently on other treatments for allergies. Owners and the investigator assessing the dogs will be unaware of group allocation. Dogs will receive an otoscopic examination and cytological assessment once a month for six months.
current_roster.tagline: Topical Prevention for dogs with Recurrent Otitis Externa
current_roster.name: Preventative Treatments for Recurrent Ear Infections in Dogs

current_roster.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.
current_roster.tagline: New Treatment for Cats with Oral Tumors
current_roster.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: This prospective randomized, blinded clinical trial will evaluate whether adding potassium chloride to the standard intravenous fluid treatment protocol administered to endurance horses improves recovery following endurance exercise. Horses requiring intravenous fluid therapy after elimination or completion of the Western States Endurance Ride will be randomly assigned to receive either the standard treatment protocol or the standard treatment protocol with additional potassium chloride. Blood samples will be collected immediately before and after the initial treatment to evaluate treatment response.
current_roster.tagline: Potassium supplementation for resuscitation fluids in endurance horses.
current_roster.name: Potassium Supplementation During Standard Intravenous Fluid Therapy in Endurance Horses

current_roster.description: This study investigates the role of low-dose radiation therapy (LD-RT) in treating Feline Interstitial Cystitis. FIC is a life-threatening disease that causes difficulty to urinate, or in some cases, urinary obstruction. Current treatments can help for a short time. Our main goal is to evaluate if LD-RT can improve the symptoms related to FIC, and delay or prevent recurrence of symptoms.
current_roster.tagline: Use of Low-Dose Radiation Therapy to Treat Feline Interstitial Cystitis
current_roster.name: Use of Low-dose Radiation Therapy to Treat Feline Interstitial Cystitis

current_roster.top_investigator: Marilia Takada, DVM, MSc, PhD, DACVR

current_roster.description:
Gliomas are among the most common and most aggressive primary brain tumors in pet dogs. Established definitive treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, or a combination of these treatments. Surgical resection alone does not improve survival times achieved with supportive care alone, and is therefore not recommended. Radiation therapy provides an average of 14 months of survival time. The purpose of this study is to investigate a novel treatment option with the goal being to improve outcomes for dogs with high grade gliomas. Treatment in this study consists of injections of nanoparticles (NPs) that target brain tumor cells and result in their death.


This is a single site, prospective, three arm clinical trial with no control (placebo) group. Each patient will be randomly assigned into one of these three groups. The treatment arms are:


1) surgical resection + nanoparticle administration

2) surgical resection + stereotactic radiation therapy

3) surgical resection + stereotactic radiation therapy + nanoparticle administration
current_roster.tagline: Utilizing microRNA encapsulated in nanoparticles in the treatment of high-grade glioma
current_roster.name: Using nanoparticles to deliver anti-tumor genes to pet dogs with high-grade gliomas
current_roster.top_investigator: Susan Arnold, Susan A. Arnold, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Neurology)

current_roster.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.


IACUC: 24619

Study number: VCCT-26-014


The study will provide $3000 toward initial diagnotic tests or radiation therapy for your pet.
current_roster.tagline: A clinical trial to characterize the clinical disease progression in dogs with glioma
current_roster.name: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description:
Traumatic wounds are among the most common reasons dogs are brought to veterinary hospitals, resulting from causes such as animal bites, road traffic accidents, and other injuries. These wounds can be a significant source of illness and may also carry a substantial financial burden due to the need for prolonged and labour-intensive treatment. Wound care in veterinary medicine often requires repeated veterinary visits, frequent bandage changes, and multiple episodes of sedation.


To address these challenges, we are investigating a novel wound product that may accelerate healing and improve outcomes. Placental-derived materials have shown promise in humans and in some reports for canine patients, but have not been directly evaluated for their use in wound healing in dogs. This study aims to fill that gap by investigating whether placental matrix can improve wound healing outcomes and time to complete healing


Study Procedures: All dogs will receive standard wound care at each visit. Dogs assigned to the treatment group will also have a single application of the placental matrix applied to their wound, covered with a bandage. This is a painless, non-invasive procedure performed during the sedation already needed for wound care, so no additional handling or restraint is required.


Follow-up visits will be scheduled depending on the wound's condition and will continue until the wound is fully healed. At each visit, wounds will be evaluated using a standardized wound assessment tool and photographs.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluation of Placental Matrix for Open Wound Management in Dogs
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Placental Matrix for Open Wound Management in Dogs
